item.title: [SCMP] As Singapore weighs joining China-led AI body, does it risk US retaliation?
item.description:
As Singapore considers joining a China-led body on artificial intelligence, analysts say membership would give the city state a bigger say in global governance matters related to the technology but may invite an unfriendly response from Washington.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo revealed in parliament earlier this week that Singapore had received an invitation to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Singapore would consider the proposal alongside its broader engagements with China and other international AI cooperation initiatives, she added.

Launched in July, the Shanghai-based bloc aims to build cooperation in areas such as AI governance, technical standards and development strategies.
item.content:encoded:
As Singapore considers joining a China-led body on artificial intelligence, analysts say membership would give the city state a bigger say in global governance matters related to the technology but may invite an unfriendly response from Washington.

Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo revealed in parliament earlier this week that Singapore had received an invitation to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Singapore would consider the proposal alongside its broader engagements with China and other international AI cooperation initiatives, she added.

Launched in July, the Shanghai-based bloc aims to build cooperation in areas such as AI governance, technical standards and development strategies.

Responding to a parliamentary question on Singapore’s strategic positioning between Waico and the US-led Pax Silica initiative, Teo said on Wednesday: “Whether we participate in any particular initiative depends on its objectives, the substantive areas of common interest, how it complements our existing engagements, and Singapore’s overall interests.

“It is therefore less meaningful to make one-to-one comparisons between individual initiatives.”

The Pax Silica initiative aims to help partners strengthen supply chains for minerals essential to AI. Singapore was among seven signatories that agreed to collaborate during its launch last December.

The government said the initiative aligned with its approach of pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation with international partners and reflected a “shared commitment to advance prosperity, technological progress and economic security”.

Teo added: “What matters most is the overall relationships we have with each of our partners, and how we can continue to work with them in ways that advance Singapore’s interests and contribute constructively to international cooperation on AI.”

‘Less about China’

Joining the China-led bloc would, in principle, be in Singapore’s interests by providing a platform to shape AI governance. But an intensifying superpower rivalry over the fast-evolving technology might complicate decision-making, analysts said.

Beijing has positioned Waico as a way to advance “AI for good and for all”.

William Heidlage, senior director of technology at strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia, said Singapore was likely to evaluate Waico membership based on whether it would have a say in AI issues.

“For Singapore, joining Waico is less about China and more about whether it can shape emerging AI governance from inside the room,” he said.

Teo said on Wednesday that it was in Singapore’s interest to ensure AI interoperability, noting that diverging international standards would pose difficulties for companies based in the city state.

Heidlage said the objectives of Waico and Pax Silica were complementary rather than contradictory for Singapore. “One seeks to prevent fragmentation in governance and the other seeks to prevent concentration in capability,” he said.

Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said accepting Beijing’s invitation could give Singapore a larger say in shaping governance standards. “This could be useful for Singapore if the organisation ends up being substantive and independent.”

Miguel Alberto Gomez, a senior research fellow at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, noted that joining Waico would give Singapore greater access to AI technology that could not be developed domestically, while reducing the risk of over-dependence on the United States and its partners.

But analysts cautioned that the decision could not be viewed independently of broader geopolitical friction.

Growing competition between Washington and Beijing made the invitation “less straightforward than before”, said Chong, suggesting that dual membership could prompt the US to impose restrictions that Waico’s benefits might not offset.

The invitation comes as countries face escalating pressure to choose between both superpowers in the AI race. While Pax Silica does not explicitly target China, its objective to reduce “coercive dependencies” is widely interpreted to reference China’s dominance and rare earths.

Reuters reported last month that Washington was preparing to tell a dozen countries to pick sides, warning they would be excluded from Pax Silica if they were to sign up for the Chinese framework. Kazakhstan is the only nation so far with membership in both initiatives.

Beijing, however, has said it firmly opposes forcing countries to take sides or creating bloc confrontation in AI.

Joining Waico might also limit Singapore’s ability to engage with parties leaning strongly towards either AI bloc, Gomez said. “This is not a novel situation for Singapore, and ultimately it must prioritise its own strategic interests.”

The city state, which has long maintained a stance of non-alignment, had to prioritise its own strategic interests while maintaining cordial relations with both powers, Gomez said.

“I do not think this reality is lost on both the US and China. Moreover, I would think both are aware of the value of having Singapore on side in the long run, especially in this region.”

Unified Asean position?

While a collective Asean position on Waico and Pax Silica would give the 11-nation bloc greater bargaining power, analysts said a consensus among its members would be unlikely due to diverging national interests.

Teo confirmed on Wednesday that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations had no position on either organisation.

Chong said Asean members could wield greater influence in shaping regulations and norms for AI initiatives if they used their collective weight. “It could also have the option of setting its own standards, given the accumulated economic, population and geographic size of Asean,” he said.

However, reaching an agreement would be challenging for a bloc operating on the principle of consensus. Tensions arising from competing AI frameworks could further strain internal cohesiveness, Chong added.

Singapore and the Philippines are the only two Asean members in Pax Silica, which is widely perceived as an effort to isolate China from key technology supply chains. Five other Asean members – Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia and Myanmar – were among the 29 original signatories at Waico’s launch.

A consolidated Asean position would require members to navigate competing interests and priorities, said Elina Noor, a non-resident scholar in the Asia programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

“In theory, it’s possible for Asean to form a common or consolidated position, but in reality, its members compete with each other on both the supply chain and governance fronts,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] No pit stops: Chinese coal mine makes big upgrade with autonomous electric trucks
item.description:
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.

Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel.
item.content:encoded:
In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash.

Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel.

This is the scene in Yimin – one of the five largest open-cast coal mines in China – which launched the world’s first large-scale fleet of cabless, electric autonomous mining trucks in May last year.

More than a year on, the performance of the 100-vehicle fleet offers a chance to assess how the technology has fared beyond the pilot stage – and whether it can be scaled up further to help upgrade China’s traditional energy sector.

“The autonomous electric trucks have helped us cut operating costs, improve safety and increase efficiency,” said Zhao Yaozhong, deputy manager for technology at the mine.

Beyond easing recruitment difficulties caused by harsh working conditions, the deployment has – more importantly – improved safety by reducing the scope for human error, analysts and industry insiders said. This consideration takes on particular importance amid renewed scrutiny of mine safety following a spate of recent accidents.

The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment

Zhao Yaozhong, deputy mine manager for technology at Yimin

Custom-built by heavy machinery maker Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group to withstand extreme cold, the self-driving trucks operate over a 5G network and Huawei Technologies’ cloud-based AI dispatching system, allowing them to navigate the mine and optimise routes in real time, according to the companies.

Automated swapping stations replace depleted batteries in about six minutes, while a dedicated solar microgrid supplies electricity, allowing the fleet to achieve zero-carbon status and run constantly.

“The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment,” Zhao said.

He noted that many mining accidents over the years had been linked to human factors, such as emotions or failures to follow operating procedures. Zhao contrasted this with the autonomous trucks, which he said executed commands precisely once given instructions to haul coal or overburden – the layer of rock and dirt covering a mineral deposit.

Coal mine safety has fallen back under the regulatory microscope in China following a gas explosion in May at the Liushenyu Coal Mine in Shanxi province. The blast killed 82 people, making it the deadliest coal mine disaster in more than a decade.

Aside from safety, the autonomous solution also offered cost savings, Zhao said, remaining cheaper to operate than conventionally driven trucks even after factoring upfront investments in the vehicles, battery-swapping stations and 5G cloud platform, as well as maintenance costs.

The savings have come mainly from lower labour and fuel costs, with the deployment replacing a crew of nearly 270 truck drivers with a smaller maintenance and support team – equivalent to about 220 fewer positions – and saving an estimated 13,300 tonnes of diesel.

Zhao said operating costs for the autonomous trucks were about 6.5 yuan (US$0.97) per cubic metre for hauling coal and overburden, compared with roughly 12 to 14 yuan per cubic metre for conventional haul trucks – almost half the cost.

Since the fleet was deployed in May last year, it has hauled about 28 million cubic metres (988.8 million cubic feet), saving nearly 200 million yuan (US$29.8 million) in operating costs, he added.

Coal has long been the backbone of China’s energy system, powering the country’s rapid industrialisation and still accounting for more than half of its energy consumption. Its dominant role has also helped cushion China from this year’s global energy shock, which saw a rapid increase in oil prices triggered by the US-Israel war with Iran.

Wang Hongzhi, head of the National Energy Administration (NEA), said at a press conference in June that “coal is our biggest source of confidence in maintaining a stable energy supply”, saying China should build up its major coal production bases in line with its national circumstances.

Meanwhile, upgrading and transforming the traditional energy sector has also become part of Beijing’s broader energy strategy.

A blueprint released by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA for China’s “new energy system” during the period covered by the country’s 15th five-year plan called for a “modern coal supply chain”, with wider adoption of green mining practices and the development of smart mines tailored to local conditions.

In another blueprint intended specifically for the coal industry over the period, the two agencies set a target to further advance smart mining across the sector and raise the share of production capacity at smart mines to 75 per cent by 2030.

Analysts from Citic Securities said regulators’ focus on ensuring a safe and stable coal supply amid energy security concerns was driving smart mining, which could also help address labour shortages and cut costs for coal companies.

“The industry’s development is therefore driven not only by central policy coordination and local development plans, but also by coal companies’ own willingness to upgrade,” the analysts said in a report on smart mining last year.

They estimated that smart upgrades could reduce mine staffing by 20 to 30 per cent, with the investment potentially paying for itself in about seven to eight years on labour savings alone.

Since its deployment in May 2025, the Yimin fleet has moved beyond the pilot phase, taking on more demanding operations as the mine prepares to add 200 more trucks by the end of this year.

Initially used to haul topsoil and rock on the surface, the trucks began hauling coal in November, Zhao said. The mine also relocated its battery-swapping stations into the pit to test whether the trucks could navigate more challenging terrain, such as the confined spaces of the coal-preparation plant.

“We need to verify the system’s stability, because we plan to deploy 200 more trucks by the end of this year,” he said.

For Yimin, the experience suggested that technology was no longer the main barrier to wider adoption. But replicating the model across China’s coal mines was another question, with differences in geology, infrastructure and power supply likely to determine how quickly it can scale.

“The technology behind autonomous electric mining trucks is ready for nationwide deployment, but the biggest challenge is whether individual mines have enough power infrastructure to support them,” Zhao said.

Yimin, China’s first coal-and-power integrated project, has an advantage in electricity supply, with the mine able to draw power directly from the affiliated Yimin power plant.

“For other mines, such as those in [the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region], the biggest issue is whether they have enough power supply,” he noted, adding that government efforts to encourage mines to develop microgrids combining solar and wind power with energy storage could offer a potential solution.

Developing smart microgrids in mining areas that coordinate power generation, grids, electricity demand and energy storage is also listed in the coal industry’s five-year plan, which calls for the integrated development and operation of solar and wind power, coal-mine gas generation, energy storage and smart control systems.

According to the Citic Securities analysts, autonomous trucks at open-pit mines and mining robots for underground operations were among the two most mature applications combining artificial intelligence with mining hardware in China, while home-grown large language models for mining provided the technological foundation for such integration.

“We expect … mining-specific large models to incorporate generative AI, further enhancing data analysis and decision-making capabilities while improving safety and energy efficiency in mining operations,” the analysts said.

item.title: [SCMP] Tiananmen vigil leaders jailed for up to 7 years, group fined HK$1.5 million
item.description:
Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close.

The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989.
item.content:encoded:
Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close.

The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989.

Lee, 69, and Chow, 41, were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months behind bars, respectively.

Former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty ahead of the trial.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the rule of law could only be upheld by imposing severe penalties on the accused.

“The law never allows anyone to blatantly harm their country and compatriots under the guise of promoting human rights, democracy and freedom,” he said.

Central government authorities in Hong Kong hailed the tough sentences as a manifestation of the city’s rule of law, while warning “external forces” against smearing the court’s decisions.

A spokesman for the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office said the alliance and the defendants “had long incited public hostility, hatred and disaffection towards the state regime”, adding that their offences had seriously challenged the constitutional order of Hong Kong and gravely violated the city’s national security law.

“They must be severely punished in accordance with the law,” the spokesman said.

The foreign ministry’s arm in Hong Kong said the alliance had undermined the central government’s authority “at both ideological and practical levels”.

Beijing’s liaison office said the defendants deserved severe penalties for attacking the party’s leadership, while the country’s Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong described the ruling as “widely supported” by society.

Ho is expected to complete his sentence in April 2028, assuming he is not granted a one-third reduction by prison authorities on the basis of good conduct during his incarceration.

Lee Cheuk-yan may be released in September or October 2029, whereas Chow may have to serve her sentence until early 2030. The pair intend to lodge an appeal.

Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, said the sentences did not only punish the alliance and its former leaders, but also those who subscribed to the group’s beliefs or previously attended its annual vigil at Victoria Park in Causeway Bay.

“I think free speech is already a thing of the past,” she said. “They were given such heavy sentences even though they had never resorted to any unlawful means.”

Chow’s mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun, said her daughter had only intended to “speak the truth”.

The elder Chow added that she was not free to speak her mind because of a police investigation against her.

Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee said the case was serious and warranted five to 10 years’ imprisonment under a two-tier sentencing regime of the national security law.

They noted the offence lasted for 14 months after the law took effect on June 30, 2020, during which the defendants persisted with their offensive conduct on social media and during public events at a time when Hong Kong remained “turbulent and unsettled”.

“Despite the defendants’ belief that their agenda of ‘ending one-party dictatorship’ might be in breach of the [Chinese] constitution and the national security law, they recalcitrantly pursued their course of conduct and strenuously promoted their agenda. This was a premeditated act,” the judges said in a 19-page written ruling.

The European Union said about the sentencing: “This ruling undermines confidence in the rule of law and harms Hong Kong’s reputation.”

Meanwhile, the court adjourned handling the prosecution’s request to confiscate the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture, created by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, pending further arguments.

Galschiot has repeatedly demanded that the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) artwork be returned to him since it was seized by police’s national security department in 2023.

Steve Li Kwai-wah, the department’s chief superintendent, argued the sculpture belonged to the alliance and was used to incite others to undermine the party.

“I think the rationale is very simple. You created something and gave it to someone else. Can you ask to take it back any time you want?” Li said.

Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung said that any item relevant to the commission of an offence should be confiscated.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Galschiot said he intended to request his government to take diplomatic action so that the sculpture could be returned to “its rightful owner”.

Former trade union leader Carol Ng Man-yee, who was released from prison last year after serving 45 months for a subversion offence, and former alliance standing committee member Tang Ngok-kwan were among those who attended the brief hearing on Friday.

Ng said she felt relieved the three defendants finally got to know when they might be released, but said she was still saddened by the outcome.

Tang Ngok-kwan urged the public to continue to honour those who died in the 1989 crackdown in a “reasonable and lawful” manner.

The alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to commemorate the event and called for democratic reforms across the border and the end of one-party rule.

Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.

item.title: [SCMP] How Asian shipyards in Japan, Korea and Philippines keep US warships battle ready
item.description:
After being stranded in the South China Sea following a power failure in July, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Benfold was towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines for emergency repairs.

The facility is among the repair and maintenance hubs the US Navy has been developing in the region, strategically pushing for allies to perform major maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work on US naval vessels given the decline of its shipbuilding base at home.

The repair work on the Benfold in the Philippine port took about 10 days before it resumed operations.
item.content:encoded:
After being stranded in the South China Sea following a power failure in July, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Benfold was towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines for emergency repairs.

The facility is among the repair and maintenance hubs the US Navy has been developing in the region, strategically pushing for allies to perform major maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work on US naval vessels given the decline of its shipbuilding base at home.

The repair work on the Benfold in the Philippine port took about 10 days before it resumed operations.

While US law mandates that major warships be built domestically, outsourcing MRO to foreign yards offers more flexibility, especially for forward-deployed vessels.

Naval vessels homeported outside the United States are not strictly prohibited from receiving foreign MRO services and deployed US-homeported ships may also be serviced by foreign workers under specific conditions.

The capacity of regional allies in the western Pacific, including Japan and South Korea, is particularly vital, given their distance from the continental US as well as Washington’s intensifying strategic competition with Beijing.

“By establishing the ability to repair and sustain larger numbers of ships closer to potential conflict areas in the Indo-Pacific, the United States could potentially support extended deployments – including during wartime – by reducing the need to recall ships to the US mainland for repairs,” the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies said in a recent report.

South Korea and Japan’s advanced shipbuilding industries rank second and third in the world, respectively, in terms of capacity. The Philippines and Singapore, meanwhile, occupy strategically important positions in the region and have long served as key partners for the US military.

Meanwhile, China at No 1 accounts for more than half the world’s shipbuilding capacity, providing a solid industrial base for its rapidly expanding navy.

Shipyards in the region

The US Navy runs the US Naval Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Centre (SRF-JRMC) at its bases in the region. It is headquartered at the Yokosuka Naval Base in Kanagawa prefecture, with detachment sites in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, and Singapore’s Changi Naval Base.

The organisation employs local workers and occasionally outsources certain tasks to local contractors.

In addition to the directly operated SRF-JRMC, the US Navy has been expanding a network of private companies in the region through its Master Ship Repair Agreement (MSRA). The certification qualifies a shipyard to bid on and perform MRO work on military and support vessels.

For instance, the US Navy issued solicitation notices last month, inviting bids from MSRA and Agreements for Boat Repair (ABR) holders to carry out minor repair and maintenance of the America-class amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli and San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS New Orleans, both homeported in Sasebo.

Japan

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI)’s Yokohama Dockyard & Machinery Works is the largest ship repair yard in Japan, with abundant experience in repairing civilian and naval vessels. It has two dry docks, seven piers and seven jib cranes. The dock can accommodate huge ships of up to 270,000 tonnes, according to the company.

The yard serviced the Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Milius in 2019 as part of a pilot trial – the first time the US Navy had outsourced such work to local Japanese firms.

Last year, MHI became the first Japanese yard to secure a regular overhaul contract for the USS Miguel Keith, a Puller-class expeditionary mobile base.

Sumitomo Heavy Industries Marine & Engineering is another prominent MSRA holder. The company website says it has focused on repair work mainly for the US Navy in Yokosuka in recent years. They provide repair services to ships belonging to the Seventh Fleet, including nuclear-powered aircraft carriers, and “are engaged in repairing” US Army vessels including landing craft.

Sasebo Heavy Industries sits next to the Sasebo Naval Base and shares a dry dock with the US Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force. Having suspended new shipbuilding in 2022, the company now focuses exclusively on ship maintenance and repair.

Japan Marine United Corporation operates five ship-repair yards across the country, at Isogo and Tsurumi in Yokohama, as well as Kure, Maizuru and Innoshima. The Maizuru facility took part in the repair of the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Fitzgerald last December.

South Korea

Unlike in Japan, the US Navy does not have a direct ship-repair facility in South Korea. Instead, it collaborates with major local shipbuilders, primarily for logistical vessels. Notably, MSRA certifications for South Korean contractors have been mainly awarded in the past few years, reflecting the US Navy’s strategic shift towards MRO outsourcing.

In July 2024, Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) made history as the first South Korean shipyards to obtain MSRA from the US Navy, shortly after the former acquired the Philly Shipyard in Pennsylvania.

Hanwha Ocean conducts its repair works at the Geoje shipyard on an island off the southeastern coast near Busan.

It completed South Korea’s first MRO project – maintenance of the USNS Wally Schirra dry cargo and ammunition ship – in 2025 and also worked on the USNS Yukon, a replenishment oiler assigned to the US Navy’s 7th Fleet.

HHI secured the overhaul project for the Lewis and Clark-class dry cargo and ammunition vessel USNS Alan Shepard in August 2025 after efforts to tap into the US by forming an alliance with the US-based military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls. The work was carried out at a berth near HD Hyundai Mipo Dockyard in the southeastern city of Ulsan from last September.

HJ Heavy Industries, a mid-sized shipbuilder, became the third South Korean firm to pass US Navy evaluations to get an MSRA in January this year, after signing a contract in December to carry out a midlife maintenance contract for the 40,000-tonne Lewis and Clark-class dry cargo ship USNS Amelia Earhart at its Yeongdo shipyard in Busan.

SK Oceanplant, another major defence contractor that has built more than 30 South Korean naval and coastguard vessels including the latest Ulsan-class Batch-III frigates, officially signed the MSRA in February. The company operates a 430-metre (1,410 foot) ultra-large floating dock in its shipyard in Goseong on the southern coast and conducts maintenance for more than 30 commercial vessels annually.

Samsung Heavy Industries, one of South Korea’s “Big Three” shipbuilders alongside Hanwha Ocean and HHI, has reportedly begun the MSRA application process and aims to complete certification this year.

Singapore

Strategically located at the entrance of the Strait of Malacca, the crossroads connecting the West Pacific and Middle East, Singapore has long been a hub for US naval operations. Along with the SRF-JRMC’s Singapore detachment, the US Navy primarily works with two local MSRA-holding partners.

State-owned defence contractor ST Engineering Marine operates facilities such as its Benoi and Gul yards. Its recent MRO contracts came not only from the Pacific Fleet, but also the Military Sealift Command and Naval Supply Systems Command. It was awarded a contract in February for the regular overhaul of Safeguard-class rescue and salvage ship USNS Salvor.

Government-linked Sembcorp Marine held an MSRA before its merger with Keppel Offshore & Marine in 2023 to form Seatrium Limited. Its Tuas Yard has a repair dock that is 400 metres (1,310 feet) long and 14 metres deep, one of the deepest in Asia for mega vessels, while the Admiralty Yard is equipped with multiple dry docks and quays, including one that is 13 metres deep.

India

The US Navy has also expanded cooperation with India against the backdrop of deepening defence ties under the framework of its Indo-Pacific strategy. It has certified Indian shipbuilders Mazagon Dock and Larsen & Toubro with MSRAs in 2023. Mazagon’s facilities are in Mumbai and Larsen & Toubro runs the Kattupalli Shipyard in Chennai.

In 2024, the third Indian MSRA was awarded to state-run Cochin Shipyard. Under these agreements, the Indian contractors will primarily support ships under the US Navy’s Military Sealift Command.

The Philippines

Although the Philippines lacks an advanced domestic shipbuilding industry, its strategic location as a key hub in the South China Sea has led the US Navy to contract US-owned firms to operate maintenance and repair facilities in the country.

The Agila Subic Shipyard in Subic Bay, where the USS Benfold arrived four days after losing power and was repaired in July and August, was formerly operated by Hanjin Heavy Industries Philippines (HHIC-Phil) and is now owned by New York-based Cerberus Capital Management.

Colorado-based defence contractor Vectrus (now V2X after a merger) provides services at the site, which features a 500-metre long dock and forms part of the growing network of overseas facilities supporting US naval operations in the region.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Marcos’ Brics trip is ‘low-risk opportunity’ for Philippines to make new friends
item.description:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr is set to be the first Philippine leader to join the Brics Summit in New Delhi this weekend – presenting him with the perfect “low-risk opportunity” to engage the grouping as Manila continues to diversify its ties, analysts say.

“The president seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient and capable of delivering prosperity to our people,” Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Analyn Ratonel said in a press briefing on Wednesday.

“This participation is a strategic opportunity to monitor emerging economic frameworks and to represent the priorities and perspectives of the region, while directly engaging leaders of major emerging economies.”
item.content:encoded:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr is set to be the first Philippine leader to join the Brics Summit in New Delhi this weekend – presenting him with the perfect “low-risk opportunity” to engage the grouping as Manila continues to diversify its ties, analysts say.

“The president seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient and capable of delivering prosperity to our people,” Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Analyn Ratonel said in a press briefing on Wednesday.

“This participation is a strategic opportunity to monitor emerging economic frameworks and to represent the priorities and perspectives of the region, while directly engaging leaders of major emerging economies.”

Brics, an international organisation formed in 2009 of emerging economies, currently counts Brazil, Russia, India, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates among its members.

While Marcos is attending the event in his capacity as Asean chair, he is also scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and business executives on the sidelines. Issues to be discussed include the progress of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership, a review of the implementation of an action plan for 2025 to 2029, and a follow-up with business leaders on the US$5.8 billion investment pledges Marcos secured during a state visit to India in August last year.

Analysts say the summit is Marcos’ chance to engage Brics members and diversify beyond its traditional ties with the US amid geopolitical tensions with China. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also expected to be attending, marking his first trip to India in seven years.

“The Asean chairship provides President Marcos with a relatively low-risk opportunity to engage Brics more closely without necessarily signalling that the Philippines is already moving towards membership or changing its broader strategic orientation,” said Enrico Gloria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

The engagement was “not particularly unusual” given that Association of Southeast Asian Nations members already have varying degrees of ties with Brics, he said. Indonesia is a full member and Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam are partner countries. “For the Philippines, this is less as choosing another geopolitical camp and more as a way for it to continue diversifying its partnerships.”

‘Friends to all’

Marcos’ attendance reflected his “friends to all and enemy to none” stance on foreign policy, said Chester Cabalza, founder and president of the Manila-based think tank International Development and Security Cooperation. Under Marcos, the Philippines has signed defence pacts with countries such as Japan, Canada, New Zealand and France.

“Marcos should not ignore this opportunity, not only because he represents Asean, but also due to India’s benevolent acts to the Philippines. The Philippines has India to thank for the Brahmos missiles,” he said. “The growing economic potential of Brics is unprecedented in terms of its energy and AI global outputs.”

For a smaller power such as the Philippines, “expanding the number of countries and institutions it can work with increases its room to manoeuvre”, Gloria said.

Last year, Marcos said he was open to considering Brics membership for the Philippines. But this visit appeared to be “exploratory rather than preparatory”, Gloria said, adding it was not “evidence that Manila is already moving towards a formal plan of accession”.

There is an important difference between being open to something and having made it a foreign-policy objective. Marcos himself framed it last year largely in terms of giving the Philippines more options, rather than announcing an intention to join,” he said.

This is a good chance to re-engage China and India amid uncertainties from the global oil crisis, according to Cabalza. “Manila should learn from India’s non-alignment policy even as Delhi experienced a territorial rift with Beijing in 2000,” he said. “Navigating this tedious diplomatic stunt is important for a country that needs to bring home barrels of oil, employment through investments, and latest AI protocols.”

Despite the finalisation of the code of conduct in the South China Sea remaining an Asean priority, it was unlikely that Marcos would tackle China on maritime issues, he added. “He is going to India as Asean chair, so Marcos’ policy recommendations and contributions to the conversation must attribute to the needs of Asean. He is a statesman from Southeast Asia and not only of the Philippines in that summit.”

Beyond India

One of the most consequential goals of Marcos’ visit would be a deepening engagement with India, both analysts said.

“⁠Following up on the Indian investment commitments should certainly be one of the most tangible objectives of the visit,” Gloria said. “A meeting with Prime Minister Modi offers an important opportunity to assess how much of that potential can actually move towards implementation.”

Manila can also explore further partnerships with India – especially as it looks to strengthen its position as a hub for diversified supply chains. One possibility is the multi-country Pax Silica initiative to secure global supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical minerals.

“This could help move the conversation beyond individual investment pledges towards a more strategic discussion of how Philippine-Indian economic cooperation can contribute to more resilient and diversified regional supply chains,” Gloria said.

Predicting that India would be the “future second-largest economy of the world”, Cabalza said it would be good to “enhance our ties to secure investments in agriculture, business process outsourcing, medical and spaceport ventures”.

However, he cautioned that the Philippines should not focus solely on India as the forum presented a chance for Manila to develop a diverse range of partners beyond traditionally aligned states.

“One weakness of Philippine foreign relations historically has been the concentration of our diplomatic emphasis and economic attention on a relatively small number of major partners. A more multipolar world requires the Philippines to develop a multipolar diplomatic portfolio as well,” he said.

“As the current Asean chair, the Philippines is poised to leverage that institutional power not just for the region but for its own interests as well to diversify existing partnerships.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why AI experts are ‘freaked out’ over safety fears ahead of Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
A flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing, and declining visibility into model safety has sparked fresh alarm over the US artificial intelligence boom, igniting calls from some experts to slow down development – even as critics warn that deceleration risks surrendering America’s technological lead to China.

The mounting concerns come just weeks before President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump are set to meet for a high-stakes summit in Washington.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a private company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, according to a Friday report from Bloomberg.
item.content:encoded:
A flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing, and declining visibility into model safety has sparked fresh alarm over the US artificial intelligence boom, igniting calls from some experts to slow down development – even as critics warn that deceleration risks surrendering America’s technological lead to China.

The mounting concerns come just weeks before President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump are set to meet for a high-stakes summit in Washington.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a private company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, according to a Friday report from Bloomberg.

OpenAI may coordinate the slowdown with other leading AI laboratories, though some firms may decline to participate, the report said, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Altman’s remarks underscored a growing reckoning in Silicon Valley over the risks of rapid AI advancement.

[Industry leaders are] racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives

Julie Steele, OpenAI

Paul Christiano, a prominent AI safety researcher who recently joined OpenAI’s non-profit board to serve on its safety and security committee, warned on Thursday of a “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term” based on the current trajectory of the technology.

In a Thursday post on X that drew more than 1.5 million views and 10,000 likes, OpenAI safety team member Julie Steele wrote in a personal capacity: “I also think we need to slow down.”

Steele cited a viral post from former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon, who said earlier this week that he had resigned from Anthropic because both industry leaders were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.

Political momentum is also building. US Senator Bernie Sanders pledged on Thursday to introduce legislation to “pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence altogether”.

Safety alarms intensify at US labs

The urgency behind these warnings has been heightened by growing security breaches and monitoring difficulties across the industry.

Anthropic said on Wednesday that an early version of its flagship Claude Opus 4.6 model gained unauthorised access to a third-party computer system during testing in January. The incident, which went undetected during a previous company-wide audit, marks the fourth time an Anthropic model has breached security boundaries.

Meanwhile, OpenAI said last week that GPT-6 Astra – its first model to reach what it called a “critical” level of cybersecurity capabilities – was harder to monitor than its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol.

If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents

Ben Hayum, Centre for a New American Security

Security analysts warned that as models became more capable, developers could be sacrificing internal visibility for performance.

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said AI labs in both the US and China faced intense market incentives to push boundaries, “even if this means diminishing control or legibility”.

Theo Bearman, a researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, cautioned that cutting back on chain-of-thought monitoring could trigger a “race-to-the-bottom dynamic” across the industry.

Ben Hayum, a research assistant for the Technology and National Security Programme at the Centre for a New American Security, said: “The fact that the Hugging Face incident happened, and then right afterwards, [OpenAI is] releasing a model that’s harder to monitor – that’s why so many people are freaked out.”

He added that if “substantial gains in internal processing continue without external visibility, AI model alignment becomes a lot harder from the get-go in terms of creating a safe model”.

Analysts also warned of heightened risks as labs pursue recursive self-improvement, a milestone where AI models autonomously build and refine their own successors in an accelerating feedback loop.

“If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents,” Hayum said.

“These are national security threats to America, China and the globe.”

However, pushback against calls to slow down remains fierce, driven by fears of ceding ground to Beijing.

Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham argued on X on Thursday that if China held the lead in AI, researchers would not have the freedom to sound public alarms about potential threats.

Others contended that America’s current lead provided a buffer for a pause.

“Given how far behind China is on compute and how dependent Chinese progress is on US capabilities, pacing AI progress in America would not immediately concede the lead,” said Konstantin Pilz, co-founder of Centre for Technology and Statecraft, on social media.

Pre-summit tensions heighten

The safety concerns come at a delicate time for diplomatic relations between Washington and Beijing.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to lead bilateral talks on AI governance ahead of Xi’s visit to Washington later this month, with agenda items expected to include joint frameworks for monitoring AI-driven cyber threats.

Speaking in Dallas, Texas, on Tuesday, Bessent accused Chinese developers of freeloading on US breakthroughs through model distillation, a common industry technique where smaller AI systems are trained using outputs from larger ones.

“The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation,” Bessent said. “So, the Chinese distil our models and they can never get ahead of us.”

On the same day, three US federal agencies accused major Chinese developers – including DeepSeek, Alibaba Group Holding, Moonshot AI and Z.ai – of conducting aggressive, large-scale distillation “likely with Chinese government awareness”.

China’s Ministry of Commerce on Wednesday called the accusations factually and legally groundless, accusing Washington of using safety and intellectual property concerns to consolidate computing power and maintain a technological monopoly.

Anthropic on Thursday said in a report that Chinese AI companies DeepSeek and MoonShot re-routed users’ queries to Claude, passing off the generated answers as output from their own models.

Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

item.title: [SCMP] Fresh photos offer clearest view yet of China’s ‘WZ-X’ spy drone
item.description:
Fresh clues are emerging about a new type of Chinese drone being developed as a long-range intelligence and surveillance platform intended to operate deep inside contested airspace.

New photographs circulated on Chinese internet forums earlier this month that appear to show the massive drone in the air, offering much clearer views of its wing shape than earlier images. The original source of the photos and exactly where they were taken have not been independently verified.

Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist on Chinese military aviation, said the photographs showed the clearest view yet of the aircraft’s serrated trailing edge – a sawtooth-like shape along the rear of the wing characteristic of stealth design. He added that the aircraft appeared to have been flown in daylight, suggesting such flights might have reached a degree of normality.
item.content:encoded:
Fresh clues are emerging about a new type of Chinese drone being developed as a long-range intelligence and surveillance platform intended to operate deep inside contested airspace.

New photographs circulated on Chinese internet forums earlier this month that appear to show the massive drone in the air, offering much clearer views of its wing shape than earlier images. The original source of the photos and exactly where they were taken have not been independently verified.

Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist on Chinese military aviation, said the photographs showed the clearest view yet of the aircraft’s serrated trailing edge – a sawtooth-like shape along the rear of the wing characteristic of stealth design. He added that the aircraft appeared to have been flown in daylight, suggesting such flights might have reached a degree of normality.

Rupprecht said he was “100 per cent certain” the photographs showed what military aviation watchers have dubbed the “WZ-X”, citing its dimensions, proportions and other visible details. Beijing has not publicly confirmed the aircraft’s designation, purpose or specifications.

The aircraft was first publicly identified by US defence website TWZ in satellite imagery from May last year showing the Chinese air force’s Malan test facility in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Its estimated wingspan of around 52 metres (170 feet) is comparable to that of a US B-2 stealth bomber.

Rupprecht said the aircraft was designed as an intercontinental high-altitude, long-endurance (Hale) intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) drone – a platform intended to operate deep inside defended airspace and function as an advanced communications relay node.

He likened its probable role to that of the RQ-180 – a secretive US high-altitude stealth flying-wing drone believed to be designed for reconnaissance inside defended airspace – describing the Chinese aircraft as an “RQ-180 XXL”.

He stressed that the comparison was about the expected mission and likely sensor role rather than proven performance, saying it remained unclear whether the WZ-X’s larger airframe translated into greater altitude, range or endurance.

Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said the WZ-X was likely intended as a strategic high-altitude reconnaissance platform.

Compared with smaller medium-altitude, long-endurance drones, large Hale aircraft could offer advantages in speed, survivability and capacity for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance payloads, according to Bosack, a former US Air Force drone maintenance unit commander who worked on MQ-9 Reaper strike-capable drones.

“The speed comes from the larger engine and allows the aircraft to get to its target faster,” he said. “The survivability comes from its ability to fly higher than traditional air-defence systems can detect and reach.”

He added that the WZ-X’s airframe appeared to be shaped to minimise its radar signature. Its high operating altitude could protect it from many conventional air-defence threats, he said.

Bosack said a practical challenge would be shelter and maintenance, since keeping it out of satellite view would require sufficient hangar space.

But he cautioned that size and design alone would not determine whether the aircraft became operationally useful.

“Airframes like this are meaningless without the systems they carry,” Bosack said. “However, if they can achieve the right flight profile and carry the most useful ISR equipment, then they can stay operationally relevant for decades.”

“Simply put, until we know what sensors or other payloads the Chinese will put into the aircraft, we cannot really determine how useful it will be.”

Other key details remain uncertain, including the aircraft’s inlet configuration, engine count, sensor fit and whether more than one airframe has been built.

Bosack said the drone’s ability to contribute to real-time operations would depend on whether China could move large amounts of sensor data quickly and securely across the battlespace.

Without that, he said, the aircraft could be more useful for collecting intelligence for later analysis than directly supporting fast-moving combat operations.

He also considered a strike role unlikely, arguing that weapons would detract from its more useful reconnaissance mission.

Tate Nurkin, founder of OTH Intelligence Group, also sees the WZ-X mainly as an intelligence and communications platform rather than a strike aircraft, pointing to its potential for wide-area maritime surveillance, target identification and tracking, as well as data relay.

The WZ-X could fit into a broader People’s Liberation Army effort to expand and integrate specialised uncrewed reconnaissance systems. Last month, Chinese state media showed the new GJ-3A armed reconnaissance drone operating alongside WZ-10 and WZ-7 systems, with the three drone types described as providing intelligence support across the PLA.

“Everything points towards networking, joint and inter-service interoperability,” Rupprecht said, adding that the WZ-X could initially complement and eventually replace the WZ-7 and WZ-10 while performing similar missions in more demanding environments.

Open-source research has linked the Malan facility in far western China to the PLA Air Force’s 178th UAV Brigade and identified it as a major testing and training facility for unmanned aerial vehicles.

Rupprecht described Malan as the Chinese air force’s principal drone test centre, saying the WZ-X’s presence there clearly showed the programme’s importance.

Western China, which falls within the PLA’s Western Theatre Command and includes the frontier with India, could serve both as a testing area and as an early environment for evaluating the drone in scenarios involving India, according to Rupprecht.

He said operations around Taiwan were unlikely to be a priority for the WZ-X, given the island’s proximity to mainland China.

“For Taiwan you don’t need such a range and endurance – it’s almost on the doorstep,” he said.

Given the WZ-X’s likely reach, Rupprecht said the South China Sea, waters around Japan and the Korean peninsula, and potentially the eastern Pacific were other possible operational theatres for the drone.

Nurkin placed greater emphasis on the western Pacific, arguing that the aircraft appeared to be tailored for the “longer ranges, better air defences, [and] more complex maritime environment” of a broader regional conflict. He noted that while Taiwan itself was nearby, a crisis over the island could expand “north to Japan, east to Guam, and south to the Philippine Sea and South China Sea”.

In such a contested environment, a stealthy uncrewed aircraft capable of long-range operations could bolster China’s existing surveillance network.

For now, the WZ-X is known mainly through imagery and analyst assessments rather than official information. Its significance may depend less on size than on the sensors and communications systems it ultimately carries.

item.title: [SCMP] What’s a Northern Metropolis-like project doing in Malaysia? Lessons for Hong Kong?
item.description:
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.

Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.

Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours.

Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure.

Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025.

Covering an area more than four times the size of Singapore, the JS-SEZ aims to generate 260 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$63.9 billion) for Johor’s regional economy by 2030 and create more than 20,000 high-skilled jobs, anchored by the coming 4km Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link designed to slash travel times and cement cross-strait integration.

For Malaysia, the early trajectory of Hong Kong and Shenzhen remains the foundational blueprint.

Lee Ting Han, Johor’s state executive councillor for investment and trade, told the South China Morning Post that despite distinct political frameworks, the wealth gap between Singapore and Johor mirrored the historic economic disparity between Hong Kong and Shenzhen.

“Similarly, it is pretty much like the early days of Hong Kong and Shenzhen, where the economic disparity between the two regions was so wide … what we are trying to do now is see whether there’s a way for us from a business standpoint to make it more integrated from trade relationships to investment culture,” Lee said.

He acknowledged that building the JS-SEZ presented unique regulatory challenges because Johor and Singapore operated as sovereign nations without an overarching central authority such as Beijing to coordinate rules.

However, Johor is studying how Shenzhen strategically transitioned over decades from labour-intensive assembly to capital- and technology-intensive hubs by leveraging Hong Kong capital to build home-grown tech giants in the same vein as Huawei Technologies and DJI.

As Asia’s premier financial and technology centres construct massive border-spanning growth corridors, Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis and Malaysia’s JS-SEZ offer a compelling case study in mutual learning.

While Malaysia looks to emulate Hong Kong’s long-standing success in frictionless border flows and joint state-directed planning, the city stands to learn key lessons from Johor’s aggressive strategy in nurturing talent pipelines and deploying state-backed infrastructure to secure a low-cost, high-reliability energy grid for power-hungry tech industries.

Key to Johor’s rapid rise is its approach to energy, an area where Hong Kong could draw valuable operational insights. Highlighting the power requirements of data centres, Lee noted that Malaysia’s utilities were largely state-backed.

This allows the government to take a long-term, strategic view by investing heavily in power infrastructure upfront, insulating critical digital hubs from the short-term profit pressures faced by purely private, commercial utility entities.

Malaysia adopted a forward-looking approach by making heavy infrastructure investments ahead of the cycle.

Chew Chong-sin, a former Mengkibol state assemblyman who has analysed the region’s economic integration, noted that by combining Singapore’s global financial and connectivity hub status with Johor’s land, energy, and industrial capacity, the zone aimed to mirror Shenzhen’s early evolution into a technology powerhouse.

However, he cautioned that significant operational hurdles persisted – most notably easing severe bottlenecking at the world’s second-busiest land checkpoint and resolving head-on competition in ports and logistics – even as the coming RTS Link aimed to streamline cross-border mobility by 2027.

Crucially, the zone was positioning itself to absorb global supply chain diversification, offering a neutral, disaster-free base for multinationals and mainland Chinese enterprises looking to de-risk, Chew said.

He added that this momentum had already drawn increased interest from Hong Kong firms, including sustainable aviation fuel producers and hospitality enterprises.

As Malaysia and Singapore finalise a comprehensive 10-year master plan, he said that the zone’s ultimate success would depend on maintaining the strict execution discipline needed to translate high-level blueprints into lasting economic integration.

To spur investment ahead of its full master plan launch in late 2026, authorities introduced sweeping tax incentives starting January 2025.

Firms deploying at least 500 million ringgit in high-growth fields such as AI, quantum computing and aerospace enjoy a 5 per cent preferential corporate tax rate for years, paired with stamp duty waivers.

These incentives have caught international attention.

A representative from a Mexico-based construction and information technology enterprise, who did not wish to be named, confirmed to the SCMP that the company would visit Malaysia to explore data centre sites, citing the country’s strong connectivity within Asean, widespread English proficiency and attractive tax environment.

Following stops in Kuala Lumpur and coming visits to Johor, he commended Malaysia’s proactive tech push.

Turning to Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis, however, the representative observed that while the city retained distinct institutional advantages, its position within China imposed inherent geopolitical limitations when manufacturing high-end, sensitive semiconductor chips.

The Northern Metropolis has been touted repeatedly as a top priority for Hong Kong’s administration, capped most recently by a visit from Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, who underscored Beijing’s call to accelerate construction.

The megaproject aims to transform 30,000 hectares into a major housing hub and an economic growth engine.

Both the Northern Metropolis and the JS-SEZ are strategically positioning themselves as multifaceted growth engines that integrate international education hubs, hi-tech innovation corridors and vibrant ecotourism circles.

Joining the call for deeper integration, Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers Hong Kong, said the city could take reference from Johor as a benchmark for cross-border development by aligning its land-grant policies with Shenzhen and leveraging universities to spearhead innovation.

She noted that Johor’s experience showed how robust research and technology ecosystems relied heavily on close synergies with academic institutions.

To build a sustainable tech ecosystem, Lee urged authorities to synchronise housing and talent policies with project completion timelines, anticipating a resurgence in demand as new infrastructure came online.

Given the intensive energy requirements of advanced technology and data centres, she recommended that the government initiate joint feasibility studies with mainland Chinese authorities on cross-border electricity supply to secure a reliable, green power source for the city’s tech sector.

Echoing the push for seamless integration, former lawmaker Edward Lau Kwok-fan argued that Hong Kong should draw inspiration from the JS-SEZ by speeding up the implementation of bespoke legislation for the Northern Metropolis to unlock the fluid movement of people, goods, capital and data.

He also called on higher education institutions to take greater initiative.

“I feel universities have not done enough yet. In the future, universities could evolve towards an industry-oriented development path,” said Lau, a member of the Advisory Committee on the Northern Metropolis.

“Universities need to reflect. There is a need to rethink course offerings and review academic programmes going forward.”

In response, Hong Kong’s Development Bureau said that the Northern Metropolis operated as a strategic cross-boundary hub under the “one country, two systems” governing principle, utilising coming Hetao-specific legislation to facilitate fluid cross-border resource sharing within the Greater Bay Area.

The bureau highlighted that by pairing the city’s five global top-100 universities and a planned 1,000-hectare university district with Shenzhen’s industrial scale, Hong Kong provided a platform, backed by common law, capable of rapidly converting lab discoveries into mass production.

The Education Bureau also said in a reply that it was encouraging University Grants Committee-funded universities to revamp their academic offerings, backed by a fund launched in 2023 to drive digital teaching reforms.

The Chinese University of Hong Kong said in a reply that it offered AI degree programmes across its engineering and science faculties, which delivered structured training to foster AI talent equipped for real-world innovation and academic research.

The SCMP also reached out to the University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

Under the 2025-28 triennial planning cycle, local universities were introducing 27 new undergraduate degree programmes tailored to STEAM fields, the bureau said.

STEAM refers to an educational approach that combines science, technology, engineering, the arts and maths.

Addressing Hong Kong’s internal bottlenecks, lawmaker Aaron Bok Kwok-ming, a former president of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers (HKIE), stressed that the city had to aggressively tackle its ongoing engineering talent shortage similarly to Malaysia.

To supply future high-value talent for the JS-SEZ, the Johor Talent Development Council acts as a centralised talent engine by partnering with universities, institutions and agencies to deliver industry-aligned upskilling, matching programmes and specialised training.

Bok called for targeted manpower forecasts, particularly in electronic engineering, to pinpoint exact deficit areas as Hong Kong advanced its innovation ambitions.

He urged government leaders to conduct official, comprehensive surveys rather than relying on industry estimates, while establishing structured pathways to entice overseas Hong Kong engineers back home and expanding domestic university training.

According to a manpower forecast report by Hong Kong’s Construction Industry Council released in 2023, the sector is expected to face a shortage of about 6,000 to 6,500 professionals by 2027, with civil, mechanical, structural and environmental engineering listed among the most severely affected specialisms.

Drawing on the forecast report, the HKIE noted in 2023 that the city would face a shortfall of about 3,000 professional engineers over the five years through 2027, stressing that engineers played an indispensable role in supporting the government’s push for new industrialisation and biotechnology.

This deficit is already affecting local businesses. Some tech companies previously said that while they struggled to find veteran talent, such as experienced electronics engineers, locally in Hong Kong, they could easily recruit skilled professionals on the mainland.

Addressing these industry concerns over projected workforce shortages, including the estimated shortfall of 3,000 engineers, engineer and former technology minister Alfred Sit Wing-hang said that emerging technologies such as AI, robotics and building information modelling required more sophisticated technical expertise rather than diluted entry criteria.

Sit added that as Hong Kong’s economic landscape underwent a structural shift towards advanced manufacturing and technology-driven industries, local universities and professional bodies were actively overhauling their training frameworks.

AI had increasingly become a core component of undergraduate engineering curricula, while new certification programmes were being developed to upskill mid-career professionals in fields such as smart industrial engineering and automation, he said.

On the energy front, lawmaker and energy sector expert Chan Siu-hung noted that Hong Kong already possessed top-tier infrastructure for data centres and computing hubs, but suggested the government could accelerate the roll-out of power infrastructure blueprints to match coming industrial investments.

On the city’s digital expansion, he noted that major development zones such as the Lok Ma Chau Loop and the San Tin Technopole were well positioned, with strong power supply nodes.

Responding to queries on energy security, the Environment and Ecology Bureau said that the government had signed Scheme of Control Agreements (SCAs) with the city’s two power companies.

Under these agreements, the suppliers are obliged to support the development of Hong Kong including the Northern Metropolis, by providing, operating and maintaining sufficient electricity-related facilities to meet the needs of various industries.

Chan stressed that actual energy demand would ultimately depend on incoming corporate investments.

“To ensure long-term energy security, Hong Kong’s two power suppliers need to finalise power agreements with mainland supply, securing cross-boundary supply options while advancing low-carbon energy goals,” he said.

“Officials should provide clearer and earlier timelines for these infrastructure plans to give operators certainty.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump threatens Taiwan’s representative office, sparking debate over island’s US policy
item.description:
Taiwan’s representative office is among a list of entities US President Donald Trump has threatened to sue as part of his crusade against a progressive American think tank, triggering debate about the island’s US policy ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month.

Trump named the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office (Tecro) in a social media post on Monday attacking the Centre for American Progress, a prominent left-leaning Washington think tank, over a report disputing his claims about the effect of National Guard deployments on violent crime.

Trump called the think tank a “radical left scam” and threatened to seek US$5 billion in damages, adding that he was “strongly considering” including some of its donors in the lawsuit.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan’s representative office is among a list of entities US President Donald Trump has threatened to sue as part of his crusade against a progressive American think tank, triggering debate about the island’s US policy ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month.

Trump named the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office (Tecro) in a social media post on Monday attacking the Centre for American Progress, a prominent left-leaning Washington think tank, over a report disputing his claims about the effect of National Guard deployments on violent crime.

Trump called the think tank a “radical left scam” and threatened to seek US$5 billion in damages, adding that he was “strongly considering” including some of its donors in the lawsuit.

He named Tecro – Taiwan’s de facto embassy in the US – alongside the Japanese embassy, the Korea Foundation and the embassy of the United Arab Emirates as foreign supporters of the think tank.

The remarks have raised questions in Taiwan about whether Taipei’s funding of US think tanks has become a political liability under Trump, particularly ahead of his expected summit with Xi.

Chen I-hsin, head of the culture and communications committee of the Kuomintang, Taiwan’s main opposition party, described Trump’s remarks as an “unusual diplomatic warning”.

He questioned the value of using taxpayers’ money to support an institution strongly critical of the US leader, only for Taiwan to be singled out by Trump.

“[Taiwan’s] foreign ministry must immediately explain how much taxpayer money is still being provided to CAP since Trump returned to the White House,” Chen said.

He acknowledged that Taipei’s cooperation with US think tanks across the political spectrum predated the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) return to power in 2016, but said “diplomacy required adjusting to political changes”.

Chen said that if the DPP government continued providing substantial funding to institutions closely associated with US Democrats and strongly critical of Trump, it raised questions about whether Taipei’s diplomatic strategy had become unbalanced.

“Taiwan-US relations must not pay the price for the DPP’s misguided political bet,” he said, adding that the government should explain the situation to the public.

Taiwan’s foreign ministry defended the practice, saying it and its overseas missions had long worked with major US think tanks and academic institutions across the political spectrum.

It said the cooperation supported research into Indo-Pacific security, supply-chain resilience and critical technologies, while improving Americans’ understanding of Taiwan and the island’s ties with the US.

“Such cooperation does not involve Taiwan in US local politics and should not be turned into an issue for political manipulation in Taiwan,” it said.

The ministry added that Taipei would continue deepening cooperation with the Trump administration on the basis of mutual respect and mutual benefit.

Taiwan has funded prominent Washington think tanks for years as part of efforts to build support in the United States.

A 2020 investigation by The American Prospect magazine identified the Centre for American Progress, Brookings Institution, Centre for a New American Security, Centre for Strategic and International Studies and Hudson Institute as recipients of Taiwanese funding.

The report questioned whether researchers adequately disclosed their institutions’ Taiwanese funding when advocating stronger security and economic ties between Washington and Taipei.

Taipei later rejected suggestions that its funding influenced research, saying it respected academic freedom and that such programmes promoted scholarly exchanges and expert discussion.

Data from the Washington-based Think Tank Funding Tracker showed Taiwanese entities provided about US$6.77 million to 25 American think tanks between 2019 and 2024.

International relations and strategic studies scholar James Yifan Chen said Taipei still needed relationships with US think tanks given its reliance on Washington’s support, but should ensure its outreach was politically balanced.

“For over a decade, the DPP has relied heavily on US support … and often seeks partnerships with American think tanks that share similar values,” Chen said, adding that such an approach risked unsettling Trump and his Republican allies.

“Without formal ties, Taiwan must adopt a more balanced approach, building bipartisan relationships to avoid future embarrassments,” he said.

Chen added that Taiwan should cultivate ties across the US political spectrum and allocate its resources more strategically.

“Taiwan must avoid actions that could complicate the situation in the lead-up to the Trump-Xi summit,” he said.

Chen said he believed the planned September 24 meeting in Washington was “unlikely to provide much room for transactional bargaining” between Trump and Xi.

Instead, Xi was likely to seek to stabilise relations and offer incentives that aligned with Trump’s desire to strengthen the US economy ahead of the midterm elections, he said.

Dennis Lu-chung Weng, an associate professor of political science at Sam Houston State University in Texas, said Taipei should focus less on whether funding the Centre for American Progress was right or wrong and more on whether the broader political atmosphere in Washington was shifting ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting.

He said Trump’s decision to name Tecro was “not a positive development” because the US leader appeared to be ramping up the pressure from attacking the think tank’s work to drawing attention to those supporting the institution.

“For Trump, negotiations often begin well before anyone sits down at the negotiating table,” Weng said. “Public statements, legal threats and even naming the other side’s supporters can themselves form part of the negotiating process.”

There was no evidence Trump would take action against Tecro, Weng stressed, but if the list was not random, being named could be a political signal that Taiwan had entered his field of vision.

The real concern would be if the island were incorporated into Trump’s broader political calculations over US-China relations, Weng said.

“That would not be something that could simply be resolved with money.”

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. The United States, like most nations, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but is opposed to any forcible change to the status quo and is committed to providing arms for its defence.

item.title: [SCMP] US Navy plans compact Silent Anvil torpedo as China’s submarine fleet surges
item.description:
As China expands its submarine fleet, the US Navy is looking to develop a compact air-launched torpedo that could enable more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to attack submarines from farther away.

The US Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information – a step towards development – to industry in late August for the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT).
