While air-launching a torpedo from stand-off range is not new – the US Navy already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC) – the SAA-LT would be much smaller.
item.content:encoded:
As China expands its submarine fleet, the US Navy is looking to develop a compact air-launched torpedo that could enable more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to attack submarines from farther away.

The US Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information – a step towards development – to industry in late August for the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT).

While air-launching a torpedo from stand-off range is not new – the US Navy already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC) – the SAA-LT would be much smaller.

HAAWC adds a glide kit to a Mark 54 lightweight torpedo and can be launched by P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft from altitudes of up to 30,000 feet (9,140 metres).

According to the request for information, the navy wants the new weapon to weigh up to 268lbs (122kg) while measuring up to 70 inches (178cm) long and 7.5 inches (19cm) in diameter – dimensions intended to broaden the range of aircraft that could carry it.

The requirements also envisage that Silent Anvil would be compatible with aircraft carrier storage and handling systems, potentially allowing carrier-based platforms to field the weapon.

The US Navy said it was considering two approaches: a new integrated weapon designed to glide into the water before homing acoustically on its target, or a glide kit fitted to an existing torpedo.

The glide system could receive targeting updates during flight, helping it to release the torpedo closer to the submarine’s expected location. Once in the water, the torpedo would use its own acoustic sensor to find and attack the target.

The document does not mention China, nor does it name any potential adversary. But it comes as Beijing expands and modernises its submarine fleet amid intensifying US-China military competition in the western Pacific.

Peter Jones, a retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral and an adjunct professor with the Naval Studies Group at UNSW Canberra, said Silent Anvil could potentially enable many more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to serve as delivery platforms for weapons.

“The overall effect will be a more responsive anti-submarine capability,” Jones said. “For an adversary submariner, it means that any air platform could be a weapon carrier.”

But Jones said the Silent Anvil’s usefulness would also depend on whether the weapon could be produced cheaply enough to be widely deployed, while the aircraft carrying it would still rely on air, surface and underwater systems to find submarines.

Lyle Goldstein, director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities, said spreading the mission across more platforms could be particularly valuable because specialised US anti-submarine warfare aircraft such as the P-8 were few in number.

Large, slow anti-submarine warfare aircraft could struggle to operate in the vast and highly contested airspace of the Asia-Pacific, potentially increasing the value of drones operating from “very remote locations under austere conditions”, he added.

While separating detection platforms from those that attack submarines could make better use of resources, it could also complicate operations, Goldstein observed, citing the enormous distances involved, attempts to jam communications and attacks on logistics nodes.

James Holmes, a professor of maritime strategy at the US Naval War College who was speaking in a personal capacity, said that while the Silent Anvil concept “shows a lot of promise”, its effectiveness would have to be shown in practice.

“The difficulty here is ensuring connectivity among elements of the force,” Holmes said, especially as China’s “systems destruction warfare” concept involved disrupting the networks that allowed an adversary’s forces to operate together, including through electronic warfare.

The push to broaden US options for attacking submarines comes as Beijing rapidly builds up its undersea fleet.

Rear Admiral Mike Brookes, head of the US Office of Naval Intelligence, told a congressional commission in March that China could have up to 80 submarines by 2035, roughly half of them nuclear-powered – a major shift for a force that has historically relied heavily on conventionally powered boats.

The build-up is not only about numbers. China is also developing new submarine designs.

The South China Morning Post reported in July that satellite imagery and expert analysis indicated a previously unidentified attack submarine at Shanghai’s Jiangnan Shipyard. Its propulsion type remains uncertain.

Meanwhile, another next-generation nuclear-powered design has been spotted at Bohai Shipyard in Liaoning province, northeast China.

According to Goldstein, China’s newer nuclear-powered attack submarines could pose a growing challenge by operating farther into the central and eastern Pacific. “As this challenge grows, the US will be forced to devote more effort to the anti-submarine threat.”

Holmes observed that the undersea competition could increasingly resemble the Cold War rivalry between the navies of the US and the then Soviet Union, particularly in relation to a potential conflict involving Taiwan.

He compared the first island chain – an arc of islands from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines that underpins the US security strategy in the region – to the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, a key Cold War passage for Soviet submarines entering the Atlantic.

Holmes described both as geographic barriers to a wider ocean. “We are back to the future,” he said.

According to Holmes, the Luzon Strait and the Bashi Channel south of Taiwan are obvious routes for People’s Liberation Army Navy submarines seeking access to the western Pacific.

The depth and underwater conditions of these waterways would make them difficult places for submarine hunters, while frequent rough weather could further complicate operations above the surface, he said.

If successfully developed, Silent Anvil would be “highly relevant” in such a scenario, in his view. “Any system that would help seal up the PLA Navy’s access to the western Pacific would help the US and its allies stiffen a ‘denial defence’,” Holmes said.

Goldstein said he expected the US Navy to be closely coordinating potential anti-submarine operations with Australia and especially Japan, including through sharing technology and tactics.

Any conflict could require large stocks of anti-submarine weapons at forward bases in those countries, he said, but those bases and logistics nodes could be vulnerable to Chinese missile and drone strikes.

Companies have until September 29 to respond to the request, which calls for a complete system demonstration within 18 months of a development agreement, followed by production of about 180 prototype weapons over the following three years.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore MPs back ministerial pay rise, but agree money alone won’t lure talent
item.description:
While Singapore’s officials are among the highest-paid in the world, money alone cannot attract the brightest leaders to public service, lawmakers have said during a debate on the increase in ministerial salaries – a move supported by both opposition and ruling party MPs.

The parliamentary discussion on Thursday, which saw MPs share their personal reflections on stepping into public office, followed an announced rise in ministerial salary, which Prime Minister Lawrence Wong insisted was necessary for leadership renewal and to keep pace with the private sector.

Benchmark salaries of Wong’s cabinet will be increased by more than 60 per cent, ranging from S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) to S$3.6 million annually. Ministers will receive a one-off rise of up to 9 per cent next month, with subsequent increments subject to individual performance and responsibilities.
item.content:encoded:
While Singapore’s officials are among the highest-paid in the world, money alone cannot attract the brightest leaders to public service, lawmakers have said during a debate on the increase in ministerial salaries – a move supported by both opposition and ruling party MPs.

The parliamentary discussion on Thursday, which saw MPs share their personal reflections on stepping into public office, followed an announced rise in ministerial salary, which Prime Minister Lawrence Wong insisted was necessary for leadership renewal and to keep pace with the private sector.

Benchmark salaries of Wong’s cabinet will be increased by more than 60 per cent, ranging from S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) to S$3.6 million annually. Ministers will receive a one-off rise of up to 9 per cent next month, with subsequent increments subject to individual performance and responsibilities.

Singapore last adjusted the salaries of political holders in 2012, slashing wages by more than 35 per cent. A recommendation to increase the pay following a 2017 review was not adopted.

“If too many capable people conclude that political service asks for sacrifices which are just too great, then over time we will have fewer people prepared to step forward,” Wong said as he rounded up the debate that lasted over 3½ hours.

“Eventually, the quality of our leadership will suffer and Singapore will suffer the consequences.”

He called it a “mistaken framework” that the purpose of the salary structure was to entice people into politics with money since “motivation to serve” and “responding to the call” had to come first.

“We have to persuade good people that Singapore needs them, that the work matters, that they can make a difference. Then, if someone is prepared to step forward, remuneration becomes a practical consideration,” Wong said.

Earlier, opposition Workers’ Party chief Pritam Singh questioned if the city state’s high earners in the private sector were deterred from politics by lower pay or whether the issue was political responsibilities.

He argued that most of Singapore’s cabinet continued to be fielded from the public sector, while “only a small handful” chose to leave the private sector for politics.

“For some, it would not be out of order to suggest that no amount of money will persuade them to trade their suits and ties for grass-roots activities and to immerse themselves in municipal concerns and the rough and tumble of politics,” he said.

Singh in parliament reiterated his party’s view that ministers’ salaries should be a multiple of an MP’s allowance instead of pegged to the median wage of the top 1,000 earners in Singapore, with a discount. The approach of WP – the only opposition party in parliament – would have resulted in more modest increases over time, he said.

Wong argued that the WP’s formula would arrive at a similar figure and if the salary was benchmarked with inflation, a higher sum would be derived.

“For all intents and purposes, within this term of government, we agree on the implementation approach. Beyond that, we will have to consider the circumstances then,” Wong said, noting that another independent review would be done in five years.

Wong also countered the argument that Singapore’s office holders were among the highest earners in the world, saying political office holders in many countries were given pensions, allowances, housing and other benefits beyond their official salary package.

As prime minister, Wong’s salary would be increased from S$2.2 million to S$3.6 million. He pledged to donate the increment to good causes for five years and said on Thursday that he would not keep the tax benefits from his donation.

Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng, a former doctor and medical entrepreneur, shared his personal experience of giving up his career as group CEO and managing director of IHH Healthcare to enter politics in 2020, at the age of 55.

Tan said on Thursday that he made the move after a “growing inner realisation” that his experience in the private sector could be put to good use to give back to the country. He added that no realistic level of ministerial salary could have matched what he was earning in the private sector.

On attracting future talent, Tan said: “If we make entry into the public service come at too high a personal cost for too many capable Singaporeans, then over time we will indeed narrow the pool from which our country can draw its leaders and, members of the House, that would be a far greater cost than any salary debate.”

Singapore’s ministerial salary model ensured that its leaders were “not incentivised to look elsewhere” and act with citizens’ best interests in mind, said Christopher de Souza, a lawmaker from the ruling People’s Action Party.

Prolonged wage stagnation may lead political office holders to view their time in office as a stepping stone for their professional careers, he said, citing examples of state leaders from the United States and the United Kingdom who earned large sums from assets and corporate deals after leaving office.

“If politicians know that their future careers may depend on relationships built while in office, the public will inevitably wonder whether today’s decisions are made solely in the national interest, or whether tomorrow’s opportunities are also at the back of the minds of their leaders,” he said.

Several MPs raised concerns regarding negative public sentiment over ministerial pay increases and some asked for more information to be made public on how ministers’ performances were reviewed.

Wong said he understood the concerns, but there was never going to be a “politically convenient time” to adjust salaries.

“If every difficult circumstance becomes a reason not to act, then we will keep putting the issue off, and there will come a point where restraint ceases to be prudence and becomes neglect,” he said, adding that leadership renewal was urgent.

On how ministers’ performance bonuses were distributed, he cautioned against the assessment being made into a public popularity contest and said the cabinet was a team that Singaporeans should judge based on how the government as a whole performed.

“If we fall short, Singaporeans can choose another team to govern. That is the final accountability in our system,” Wong said.

The pay bump reignited a long-standing debate on the thorny issue, with opposition parties voicing swift criticism. Some pointed out ongoing economic uncertainty and rising unemployment rates, while others criticised the salary framework.

Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said the argument of recruiting and retaining talent was justifiable from a human resource perspective.

He said the amounts would, however, appear “eye-watering” to the public and raise questions about “other forms of inspiration” to serve the people.

“Even without the pay rises, political appointees still earn more than enough to afford a very, very comfortable standard of living.”

He suggested that indicators such as total fertility rate and progress on climate issues be included in the assessment for compensation for political office holders.

Currently, ministers’ salaries include a national bonus, which is linked to socio-economic indicators such as the growth rate of residents’ median income and Singapore’s real gross domestic product.

item.title: [SCMP] J-50 designers reveal leapfrog tech for China’s next-gen stealth fighters
item.description:
China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.

The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies.
item.content:encoded:
China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.

The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies.

China’s future fighters, including the J-50 and J-36, are considered rivals to the US Air Force’s sixth-generation main fighter programme, the F-47, being developed by Boeing.

The lead researcher is chief flight-control designer Zhang Dong at the institute, and his team’s paper – rare for its public details – was published in a peer-reviewed journal Aircraft Design in August.

China’s next-generation stealth fighter programmes were undergoing a “leapfrog transformation from being able to fly steadily to being able to win in combat”, wrote Zhang and his colleagues.

Zhang’s study presents a future of pilots handing over control during periods of extreme workload or incapacitation, quantum navigation technologies supporting operations in satellite-denied environments and crewed fighters coordinating attack, reconnaissance and protection missions with reconfigurable wingman drones.

The team’s institute is part of the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China, which oversees much of the country’s aircraft research and development.

Its subsidiary, Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group, is also developing the J-36 fighter, widely regarded as another candidate for China’s next-generation sixth-generation combat aircraft.

In 2025, an investigation by defence news website, The War Zone, using satellite imagery found that the Chengdu J-36 and the Shenyang J-50 aircraft were both based at an experimental military airfield near Lop Nur, a highly secretive site for aerospace test flights that has often been compared to the United States’ Area 51.

Their simultaneous presence at the same base suggested that China’s military was actively supporting the parallel development of the two programmes.

Zhang’s paper presents a rare technological road map for future combat aircraft, describing a fundamental restructuring of the flight-control system from a device concerned mainly with flight quality into a core enabler of collaborative engagement, intelligent manoeuvre and mission effectiveness.

The change reflected what the authors described as three successive eras of air combat.

In the earlier “energy manoeuvrability” era, victory depended heavily on physical manoeuvring performance in close-range combat, while flight-control systems were largely closed and centralised, with specialised hardware and software designed mainly to keep the aircraft stable, controllable and responsive to pilot inputs.

The rise of long-range radar, stealth shaping and precision-guided weapons shifted combat towards “information manoeuvrability”, where detecting, tracking and attacking an opponent before being detected became increasingly important.

Fifth-generation aircraft such as the F-22 and J-20 use full-authority digital fly-by-wire systems and increasingly integrate flight control with fire-control and propulsion systems through high-speed data links.

The authors argued that the next phase was “cognitive manoeuvrability”, in which artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and distributed networking allowed air combat to move from platform-versus-platform competition towards system-level contests involving manned-unmanned formations.

This changes what flight control is expected to do.

“The functional positioning of the flight control system is undergoing a fundamental restructuring – from a platform controller merely pursuing flight quality to a core enabler of collaborative engagement management, intelligent manoeuvre decision-making and closed-loop mission effectiveness,” Zhang and his co-authors wrote.

The first major capability is autonomous flight control.

Instead of making pilots constantly turn high-level battle plans into precise stick movements, the new system would let on-board intelligent algorithms do that job automatically, translating tactical orders into smooth, continuous flight actions while keeping the aircraft safely within its physical limits, even during extreme manoeuvres.

The aircraft would constantly monitor its own health by fusing data from sensors such as inertial navigation, airspeed indicators, control-surface positions and engine performance.

This would allow it to assess its flight state, estimate remaining manoeuvrability and detect potential problems before they develop into emergencies.

The system could then automatically adjust control settings and redistribute on-board resources while strictly enforcing safety boundaries to avoid stalls, loss of control or stuck control surfaces.

In particularly stressful situations, the aircraft could take over from the pilot.

The paper proposes allocating control authority between humans and autonomous systems so that pilots can spend less effort on low-level aircraft handling and more on battlefield assessment and tactical decisions.

During periods of excessive workload or if a pilot loses the ability to control the aircraft, the system could take control and continue executing the intended tactical task while prioritising flight safety.

The second major change concerns navigation.

Future combat aircraft may need to operate when satellite navigation is jammed, disrupted or unavailable, prompting the researchers to identify quantum inertial navigation, visual navigation, geomagnetic navigation and terrain matching as potential technologies for passive autonomous navigation.

The paper proposes combining data from various sensors to reduce errors and prevent failures caused by the degradation or loss of any single sensor under severe electromagnetic interference.

Quantum inertial navigation is therefore presented as part of a broader effort to give aircraft an independent sense of movement and position, rather than as a replacement for GPS.

The study framed these technologies as areas requiring further engineering research and implementation, rather than saying a quantum navigation system had already been deployed on a Chinese fighter.

The biggest shift, however, may come from the way multiple aircraft work together.

Future formations could pair crewed fighters acting as command nodes with uncrewed wingmen assigned to reconnaissance, attack and protection roles. Flight-control systems would coordinate their positions, routes, electromagnetic spectrum use and weapons-launch windows while dynamically allocating tasks between aircraft.

The authors saw this as more than a traditional formation controlled by a single leader.

If an aircraft suffered a malfunction or combat damage and left the formation, the remaining aircraft could automatically reorganise, replace the missing node and redistribute its unfinished tasks.

The system used consensus-based coordination and a dynamic “virtual leader” replacement mechanism to maintain autonomous operation without relying on a permanent central node.

Zhang and his team said single-aircraft autonomous control guaranteed survival in complex environments, while swarm coordination delivered multiplied combat effectiveness.

The paper pointed towards a more heterogeneous air-combat network rather than a simple arrangement of one crewed fighter and several identical drones.

It further highlighted large collaborative wingmen alongside various aircraft and autonomous platforms, suggesting a future architecture in which crewed fighters, larger unmanned aircraft and smaller autonomous systems could perform different functions within the same network.

Aircraft such as the Chinese Y-20 transport aircraft, the J-20 fighter and even the H-20 stealth strategic bomber, which is believed to be under development, could potentially form part of such a combat network.

However, Zhang and his team did not say whether the “combat group”, or the crewed “lead aircraft” and unmanned wingmen, would consist mainly of large numbers of drones or a combination of the larger aircraft described above.

The Shenyang Aircraft Corporation and the paper’s authors did not respond to a request for comment.

Based on the paper’s publicly available discussion, the researchers suggested retaining conventional systems engineering as the safety backbone while using intelligent tools for tasks such as parameter optimisation, test expansion, automated testing and defect detection, with early trials conducted on lower-cost uncrewed platforms before broader adoption in major aircraft.

But the researchers do not advocate handing the aircraft’s most safety-critical functions directly to artificial intelligence (AI).

Instead, they identified a basic engineering conflict between intelligence and flight safety.

Data-driven algorithms can be difficult to explain and verify, and they might not apply in every situation, especially in extreme scenarios.

Applying such systems directly to the innermost control loops could therefore introduce unpredictable risks.

The proposed solution was a layered architecture.

“Engineering practice widely adopts a hybrid architecture with a closed core and open periphery,” the team wrote, allowing high-reliability, real-time functions to remain tightly controlled while more flexible software functions could be upgraded and connected across different platforms.

Under this model, the inner loop would retain conventional, highly deterministic controls for functions such as attitude stabilisation, control-surface actuation and hard flight-envelope protection.

AI would operate mainly in the outer loop, handling tactical decision-making, trajectory optimisation, multi-aircraft coordination and payload adaptation, while rigid safeguards would constrain its commands so that its recommendations remain inside a safe operating envelope.

The researchers called for further work on open layered architecture, verifiable intelligent flight control and cross-domain cooperative control, supported by large-scale simulation and flight-test data to improve the robustness and verifiability of intelligent models.

item.title: [SCMP] Young Chinese turn to Mao Zedong for life advice, 50 years after his death
item.description:
When you are denied a pay rise, when you feel anxious about your children’s education, or when you are alienated by colleagues, Chairman Mao can help.

At least, that is what China’s online influencers and their hundreds of thousands of followers believe.

Wednesday marks the 50th anniversary of the death of Mao Zedong, founding father of the People’s Republic of China. Chinese authorities have not announced any plans to mark the date, as former state leaders are usually commemorated on the anniversaries of their birth.
item.content:encoded:
When you are denied a pay rise, when you feel anxious about your children’s education, or when you are alienated by colleagues, Chairman Mao can help.

At least, that is what China’s online influencers and their hundreds of thousands of followers believe.

Wednesday marks the 50th anniversary of the death of Mao Zedong, founding father of the People’s Republic of China. Chinese authorities have not announced any plans to mark the date, as former state leaders are usually commemorated on the anniversaries of their birth.

The only special arrangement in place is at the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall in Beijing, which will open for an extra three hours on Wednesday. Visiting slots for the week are fully booked.

Despite the official silence ahead of the anniversary, it is hard to ignore the quiet comeback of Mao’s popularity in the country.

In recent years, younger generations of Chinese have rediscovered Mao as their life coach. They organise online book clubs devoted to his works, spread the gospel through artificial intelligence-narrated videos, and affectionately refer to him as jiaoyuan, or “teacher”, a title Mao himself once said he preferred.

His views are regularly cited in times of US-China tensions. Last year, when the Trump administration imposed a 104 per cent tariff on Chinese goods, social media users searched for the term jiaoyuan, described imperialism as a “paper tiger” – one of Mao’s best-known slogans – and quoted his collection of speeches, On Protracted War.

While much of this youthful sentiment aligns with China’s official narrative about Mao as a symbol of national independence, especially in the face of US-led international pressure, experts say Beijing is also wary that Mao’s teachings could feed into scepticism about the country’s economic policies and its interpretation of Marxism.

Mao in youth culture

For Mao’s most vocal online admirers, the former state leader is a symbol of resilience, courage and dedication to the common people.

One blogger on the arts and culture forum Douban praised Mao’s selflessness, especially the fact that he sent his own son to the battlefield.

“He stood with us, the people, at all times,” she wrote.

The 29-year-old blogger, who asked to be referred to only by her surname Liu, describes herself as an “ordinary company worker”. She said she had read most of Mao’s works and applied them to her own life.

“Don’t regard a mistake as merely a disgrace; see it as an asset,” she said, quoting the late leader. She added that this perspective had taught her not to criticise herself too harshly.

I believe [Mao’s] spirit in heaven can bless young students like us, help us make progress and achieve our ideals

Li Muqi, Chinese university student

Young people can also be spotted paying tribute to Mao at a giant monument in Changsha, Hunan province. Li Muqi, a second-year student at Hunan Normal University, has made a habit of visiting the enormous statue before final exams to pray for good luck.

“I believe his spirit in heaven can bless young students like us, help us make progress and achieve our ideals,” Li said.

According to public data, the number of annual visitors to the site has more than tripled in about a decade, from 5.88 million in 2016 to 19 million last year.

It is hard to estimate the number of Mao’s young followers in China today, but a glimpse is possible through growing library loans and merchandise sales. At Beijing’s prestigious Tsinghua University, the Selected Works of Mao Zedong topped the library loan list last year, open records show.

On Taobao, one of China’s largest online shopping platforms, a shop selling enamel mugs with Mao’s portrait sold more than 20,000 units in the past year.

Wealth gap and nationalism

The deeper reason for the interest in Mao is that young people are becoming increasingly disillusioned by today’s China and cannot achieve their aspirations, according to analysts.

In June 2023, the official urban unemployment rate for young people aged 16 to 24 hit a record high of 21.3 per cent. Fearful for their futures, university graduates have started joking that they have to “degrade themselves” and consider blue-collar jobs with low pay.

“I think a lot of people have realised that this isn’t something that could simply be solved with the cake being made bigger,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University in Australia.

He said that Mao’s theories on class struggle and conflict were still relevant today, as young people facing immense pressure, a wealth gap and few employment opportunities sought an explanation or simply comfort.

This has been accompanied by a rise in nationalism in recent years. Many admire Mao for his foresight in areas such as the development of nuclear weapons, satellites and the industrialisation of inland provinces – achievements that have helped China compete and defend itself against outside forces.

During recent US-China tensions, members of the public have regularly cited Mao’s teachings.

For example, a Baidu blog post from last year stated that thanks to the former leader’s strategy, China “holds the ace” for winning the trade war. Despite tariffs, China has developed its domestic industry chain, made alliances with other countries and used rare earths to counterstrike – all moves out of Mao’s playbook on protracted war, according to the blogger.

An April commentary in the Monthly Review, a New York-based independent socialist magazine, said Mao’s legacy offered a “powerful counternarrative to the Western-centric story of globalisation”.

“He represents the possibility of an alternative path to modernity, one that does not require submission to the economic and political dictates of Washington.”

Mao reimagined

Rana Mitter, S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, noted that young people’s interpretation of Mao’s teachings generally did not include the violence of the Cultural Revolution.

When asked about the Cultural Revolution, Douban blogger Liu said she had mainly read Mao’s works to see the logic of his writing, how he worked and his attitude towards life, and she had not done “systematic research on historic events”.

Rebecca Karl, professor of history at New York University, said that for young people, the Cultural Revolution “reads as a liberatory moment”, rather than the “doom and gloom that we know from mainstream narrative convention and state repudiation”.

One reason young people have an incomplete view of Mao is due to censorship.

The Mao era came to an end with his death in 1976. In the years that followed, his legacy was officially defined by the Communist Party.

A 1981 party resolution under Deng Xiaoping, China’s leader at the time, established the basic framework: Mao was credited with major achievements and with laying the foundations of modern China, but his later rule was heavily criticised, particularly for the Cultural Revolution, which was described as a “catastrophe”.

Under President Xi Jinping, the emphasis has shifted towards more recognition of Mao’s achievements. Xi argued in 2013 that Mao’s three decades of rule “could not be repudiated” by the reform era.

Tiptoeing around Mao

Chinese authorities are prepared to tackle anyone who deviates from the official assessment of Mao’s legacy, and the government censors those who openly criticise him.

But at the same time, Beijing has been careful not to let Mao-related discussions get out of hand, especially those concerning his more radical ideas and the Cultural Revolution.

Analysts said that while the Mao revival among young people would not grow into a larger movement, it would persist as a form of self-expression.

“His return signifies that the fundamental questions he posed about China’s path are not relics of a bygone era. The questions of class, of social justice, and of who truly holds power in society have not been resolved by decades of market reforms … The revolutionary agenda, it seems, remains unfinished,” the Monthly Review commentary said.

Gao, the professor of Chinese studies, said the trend was a collection of mixed feelings mostly confined to the digital realm, and it would not be allowed to develop into something larger.

However, facing the problems of today, young people turn to Mao because “there’s no new path to take”, according to Gao.

“When the entire world is changing – and even chaotic – there’s no alternative narrative,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Indo-Chinese cuisine in Hong Kong: a delicious dialogue of cultures and flavours
item.description:
On September 12 and 13, world leaders and ambassadors are due to gather in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit, with President Xi Jinping expected to be among them – his first visit to India since 2019. It is a moment of cautious optimism in a relationship that has see-sawed between tension and thaw for the better part of a decade, marked by such events as the 2017 Doklam (Donglang) stand-off and the 2020 clashes in the Galwan valley.

But as politicians cook up deals and diplomacy, two chefs in Hong Kong would rather let the food do the talking. In July, chef Palash Mitra of Prince and the Peacock and chef Theign Phan of Grand Majestic Sichuan fired up their tandoors and woks, trading notes on the almost 2,000-year-old conversation their cuisines have been engaged in, long before anyone put it on an agenda.

Growing up in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state in eastern India, Mitra never thought of Chinese food as a separate cuisine. It was simply stitched into the city’s culinary fabric.
item.content:encoded:
On September 12 and 13, world leaders and ambassadors are due to gather in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit, with President Xi Jinping expected to be among them – his first visit to India since 2019. It is a moment of cautious optimism in a relationship that has see-sawed between tension and thaw for the better part of a decade, marked by such events as the 2017 Doklam (Donglang) stand-off and the 2020 clashes in the Galwan valley.

But as politicians cook up deals and diplomacy, two chefs in Hong Kong would rather let the food do the talking. In July, chef Palash Mitra of Prince and the Peacock and chef Theign Phan of Grand Majestic Sichuan fired up their tandoors and woks, trading notes on the almost 2,000-year-old conversation their cuisines have been engaged in, long before anyone put it on an agenda.

Growing up in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state in eastern India, Mitra never thought of Chinese food as a separate cuisine. It was simply stitched into the city’s culinary fabric.

He remembers the Chinese food carts his family would visit on special occasions, and “Shubhon”, the man behind the wok, whose real name was Chen Shiobin. By day, Shubhon worked at a rifle factory; by night, he sold street bites, peddling in fluent Bengali, bargaining at the market in Bengali, laughing in Bengali.

“He was as much a part of Kolkata as the tram lines and the Durga Puja pandals. He was simply one of us,” says Mitra.

It’s easy to think of Indian and Chinese gastronomies as detached empires. But beneath the surface, a dialogue has been under way for more than a millennium. On ancient maps, the two are interwoven through the maritime lanes of the spice trade and the mountain passes of the Silk Road. It is believed that India initiated the exchange, sending black pepper to China during the first two centuries AD. Later, the favour was returned: China dispatched cassia bark and star anise along the same routes. By the time Hakka and Cantonese settlers arrived in Kolkata – then named Calcutta – more than 200 years ago, and adapted their woks to local ingredients to give birth to a composite cuisine now beloved across the subcontinent, Chinese and Indian communities had been using food as the language of negotiation for generations.

“Indo-Chinese is not a hybrid that belongs nowhere,” Mitra asserts. “It belongs specifically to Kolkata, a city that has always absorbed the world and made it its own.”

Global trade had shaped Kolkata for centuries. Portuguese merchants brought chillies, potatoes and cashews in the 1500s, and the English East India Company followed in the 1600s, chasing the spice trade. By the time the city was established, in 1690, other settlers, such as Armenians, had already brought their own kitchens and their own gods.

Kolkata’s Chinese community, concentrated in Tangra, the “new” Chinatown, peaked at 40,000 around the time of World War II. Settlers had arrived in waves, starting in the late 18th century, first making a home in Tiretta Bazaar, the “old” Chinatown, and then again throughout the 19th century and early 20th century, fleeing war and invasion. Many worked in the tanning industry, a profession that higher-caste Hindus considered “polluting”, leaving a niche that the Hakka filled. As tanneries in the Tangra neighbourhood closed or relocated over the years, the community increasingly turned to food to sustain their livelihoods.

Like many new immigrants, the Chinese adapted their cuisine, adding more chillies, more garlic and more ginger to suit Indian palates, while keeping the non-negotiables – wok, high heat and soy sauce – close to the hearth. A menu at an Indo-Chinese restaurant is what Mitra calls “gloriously Calcuttan”. While early Kolkata institutions such as Eau Chew pioneered the genre in the 1920s, the now-classic Hakka wheat noodles dish was later popularised by the grass-roots, family-run kitchens of Tangra. In 1975 came chicken Manchurian, invented at the Cricket Club of India, in Mumbai, when the Kolkata-born chef Nelson Wang paired the Indian trinity of ginger, garlic and green chilli with soy sauce and cornflour instead of garam masala. Chilli paneer – cubes of firm cheese fried with peppers and green chilli – emerged in the late 20th century as a vegetarian adaptation of familiar Indo-Chinese poultry recipes.

Mitra carried those memories with him when he arrived in Hong Kong. “It was only when I was dining at Luk Yu Tea House that I realised chilli chicken did not exist in China,” he says. “[Chicken] Manchurian was an Indian invention. Hakka noodles, as we knew them, did not belong to any province on a map [of China]. Instead, I found dim sum and Cantonese broths.”

It was the culinary equivalent of an American landing in Hong Kong and discovering fortune cookies were never Chinese to begin with. “Looking back, I laugh, because I had unknowingly grown up loving a cuisine that bore very little resemblance to the Chinese food I encountered in Hong Kong. Living on both sides of that divide has been a rare gift,” he reflects.

Phan speaks that same dialect of living between cultures – born in Malaysia, raised in Singapore, now cooking Sichuan food in Hong Kong. She recalls a childhood of tucking into roti prata at hawker centres, fish-head curries with her father and banana-leaf meals where she learned to eat with her hands.

“[Indian food] was always bold, flavourful and communal,” she says. “It was only after I started cooking professionally and travelling that I realised how incredibly diverse Indian cuisine is. What I knew growing up was just a small glimpse.”

Phan’s father is Hakka, so learning about the Kolkata community resonated with her. She had seen the same dynamic play out in Peranakan cuisine, born from Chinese-Malay intermarriage.

“Neither cuisine was created because people wanted to invent something new; they developed naturally because communities settled in a new place and began cooking with what was around them, while holding onto parts of their own identity,” she says.

At a time when a quick scroll on social media can (virtually) transport you to a Chongqing hotpot joint, it’s easy to forget the ingredients themselves have already travelled farther. While huajiao (Sichuan pepper) is native to Sichuan province, chilli peppers arrived from Mesoamerica. It took centuries of seafaring and cross-continental trade to bring them together in a single pot.

Mala, one of Sichuan’s most famous flavour profiles, is defined by the chillies that hit the tongue first, delivering a building burn that lingers, and the huajiao that numbs the tongue, a tingling that feels almost electric. It’s a dialogue between two different kinds of fire, connected through ancient routes.

But just as it would be a mistake to generalise Indian food as “curry” – a British catch-all for a whole universe of Indian cooking – it would be equally reductive to sum up Sichuan cuisine, which has 24 official flavour profiles, such as the sweet, sour, salty, savoury, spicy and numbing guaiwei (“strange flavour”) and the fish-free yuxiang (“fish-fragrant”), as just mala.

With such vast and layered traditions on both sides, how do two chefs even begin to find common ground? “Both cuisines understand the importance of balance,” says Phan. “Even when a dish is spicy, it’s never just about heat. You’re looking for aroma, depth, acidity, texture and fragrance all working together.”

In Indian cookery, this plays out in the methodical blooming of whole spices in oil before adding aromatics and garam masalas. In Sichuan fare, the same instinct runs through layers of aromatics and the slow heat of chillies and peppercorns.

Both traditions also share a deep understanding of fermentation – the funky depth of doubanjiang (fermented broad-bean paste) meets the sharp tang of Indian pickles and kasundi (fermented mustard). More importantly, they are unafraid of fire. “Whether it’s a tandoor or a blazing wok, both cuisines rely on high heat to create smokiness, caramelisation and complexity,” Mitra adds.

When the two chefs travelled through India together earlier this year, these parallels became tangible, and the trip became the foundation for two four-hands dinners at Prince and the Peacock and Grand Majestic Sichuan. In Mumbai, Phan ordered crab cooked two ways and found herself naming Sichuan flavour profiles: garlic paste and fragrant-spicy. “I could taste cardamom, peppercorns, cassia bark, coriander seeds – not just chilli, but layers of dry spices working through the sauce,” she says.

In hotel restaurants across the country, the international menus told the same story: Sichuan stir-fried vegetables, triple Sichuan fried rice (an Indo-Chinese dish with “Manchurian” gravy), kung pao prawns, mapo tofu. “It really shows India’s love of Sichuan food – the flavours have been embraced so naturally,” says Phan.

For Mitra, the trip was also a homecoming: “I probably ate Hakka noodles almost every day we were in India.”

Mitra’s cravings naturally found their way onto his four-hands menu – but with a twist. During recipe trials in Jamnagar, in Gujarat state, he was making a bowl of Hakka noodles when a leftover Goan xacuti spice blend caught his eye. He added a little without thinking and found that “the coconut rounded everything out, while the stone flower brought an earthy note that worked surprisingly well with the soy [sauce] and chilli” – and so the spice blend stayed. Both flavours are products of migration and adaptation; xacuti carries Portuguese influence into Goa, while Hakka noodles carry Chinese technique into Kolkata.

Chilli paneer was another classic discussed from the start. “We always knew we wanted chilli paneer on the menu because it’s such an iconic Indo-Chinese dish,” Mitra says. But Prince and the Peacock doesn’t have the kind of set-up that produces wok hei (“breath of the wok”), so he turned to the grill. Paneer hits the hot metal with a hiss; onion and capsicum blister and pop as the skewers turn. “It still tastes recognisably like chilli paneer, but the grill gives it a different character,” he says. It’s the same spirit that built Tangra’s kitchens: when you don’t have the right tool, you invent a new way to use the one in front of you.

At Grand Majestic Sichuan, Phan had the woks to spice things up. In Mumbai, she had a Bombay duck chilli fry and thought about how to translate its fragrant heat, sweetness and savouriness through a Sichuan lens for the collaboration, eventually landing on the flavours of kung pao. What emerged keeps the crisp-fried fish and the punchy chilli of the original, but reroutes it through the sweet-sour-nutty dialect of kung pao.

Other dishes in their four-hands collaboration, such as the chilled soup of chaas and tangerine peel, look forwards, rather than backwards. Chaas, a spiced buttermilk drink meant to cool the palate, takes on a faint bitterness and citrus fragrance from the dried tangerine peel, a combination Mitra and Phan describe as “completely new”. It is a dish that requires both chefs in the same kitchen, with no particular interest in staying inside the lines.

“Sharing a meal creates a different kind of connection,” says Mitra. “Food has always travelled more freely than politics.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s export machine strengthens in August as US critiques trade imbalance
item.description:
China’s exports continued to beat expectations in August, buoyed by strong demand for tech products and pre-Christmas orders that offset severe weather disruptions, though analysts warned the country’s widening trade imbalances remained a concern among Western policymakers.

The country’s exports rose by 25 per cent year on year to US$401.44 billion last month, according to Chinese customs data released on Tuesday. The reading was above a forecast of 21.93 per cent growth from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. That compared with 23.9 per cent growth in July.

China also saw imports grow by 28.2 per cent last month to US$282.36 billion, slightly above the Wind poll’s projections of 28.07 per cent growth.
item.content:encoded:
China’s exports continued to beat expectations in August, buoyed by strong demand for tech products and pre-Christmas orders that offset severe weather disruptions, though analysts warned the country’s widening trade imbalances remained a concern among Western policymakers.

The country’s exports rose by 25 per cent year on year to US$401.44 billion last month, according to Chinese customs data released on Tuesday. The reading was above a forecast of 21.93 per cent growth from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. That compared with 23.9 per cent growth in July.

China also saw imports grow by 28.2 per cent last month to US$282.36 billion, slightly above the Wind poll’s projections of 28.07 per cent growth.

That brought China’s trade surplus to US$119.09 billion last month, up from US$112.5 billion in July. This marked the fourth consecutive month the surplus had stayed above US$100 billion.

China’s export sector has remained resilient this year, as the global artificial intelligence boom and energy security worries linked to regional conflicts – including the US-Israel war on Iran – have driven up shipments of goods as well as prices.

Exports have also benefited from seasonal pre-Christmas orders, though a series of typhoons last month caused widespread delays at Shanghai’s two major container ports.

Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said that demand related to AI offset the effects of adverse weather, with high-priced tech shipments boosting export figures, while tariff uncertainty continued to front-load US import demand.

However, looking ahead, Xing said he expected overall export growth to slow later in the year due to a higher base, noting exports may be close to their peak and fourth-quarter growth “may not be so strong”.

Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, also noted that tech-related export categories outperformed in August. “The trade data came in broadly in line with expectations, and illustrates that external demand remains strong.”

He added he expected China’s balance of trade to keep growing, with another record trade surplus likely by the end of this year. The cumulative surplus had already reached US$805.51 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up about 3 per cent from the same period last year, customs data showed.

That figure, which hit a record US$1.2 trillion last year, has drawn intensified scrutiny from the West and prompted trade restrictions over Beijing’s industrial policy.

Speaking publicly after a meeting of Group of 20 finance ministers last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called China’s current account surplus “unsustainable” and cited opposition from Beijing as the reason the group failed to issue a unanimous statement.

As China continues to rely on exports to support the economy, trade imbalance has become an area of discussion among policymakers, said Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.

He added that while the recent appreciation of the Japanese yen and South Korean won had built up pressure on the yuan to appreciate, exchange rate adjustment would likely be modest this year, with limited impact on trade imbalances.

President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington later this month, with trade, AI and the Iran war expected to be high on the agenda.

In August, China’s exports to the United States rose 34.4 per cent year on year, against a low base for the same period last year.

Exports to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, China’s largest trading partner by bloc, rose by 30.21 per cent year on year, while shipments to members of the European Union increased by 6.61 per cent.

The world’s second-largest economy is taking steps to further boost trade with Southeast Asia. The 134km (83-mile) Pinglu Canal is set to open to navigation next week, linking south China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region to Vietnam and other countries in the region via the Gulf of Tonkin, also known as the Beibu Gulf.

Meanwhile, the EU’s trade deficit with China has become a point of contention for Brussels. Amid marathon trade talks with their Chinese counterparts at the end of June, the bloc’s trade officials set a three-month deadline for the two sides to make “tangible progress” in disputes spanning several areas.

EU policymakers and business leaders have expressed fears that cheap Chinese imports – aided by hefty state subsidies – are helping to deindustrialise swathes of the continent’s manufacturing economy.

Separated by product category, the data showed tech-related exports continued to rise as automobile exports slowed.

Shipments of integrated circuits fell by 7.92 per cent year on year in volume terms last month but surged by 129.83 per cent in value – driven by higher prices amid a memory chip shortage fuelled by a global AI infrastructure buildout. The pace improved upon July’s 116.57 per cent growth, as well as June’s 121.9 per cent growth rate.

Outbound shipments of automatic data-processing equipment and related components also jumped last month, growing by 76.52 per cent year on year. Export growth for automobiles, however, was 43 per cent in value terms, down from the 60 per cent rate recorded in July.

China’s rare earth exports fell by 18.25 per cent year on year by volume, as Beijing continues to exert tight control over shipments of the minerals, which are essential to the production of a range of hi-tech products.

Meanwhile, imports came in a little softer than expected, Song said.

Both the import volume and value of automobiles dropped in August, falling by 50 and 32 per cent, respectively.

“China’s import profile is undergoing a clear structural shift in autos, where heavy domestic competition has also driven a sharp drop in demand for foreign imports,” Song said.

The country’s crude oil imports reached US$22.72 billion last month, down 8.85 per cent year on year in value terms, while shipments fell by 23.36 per cent.

Among emerging economies, China’s imports from Africa slowed to just 3.7 per cent year on year compared with a 25 per cent surge in July. Last week, Xi paid a state visit to Egypt, his first in 10 years, aimed at boosting economic and trade ties.

item.title: [SCMP] Red tape, high cost: can Hong Kong’s new yacht scheme chart a smoother course?
item.description:
Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip.

It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements.

“If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip.

It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements.

“If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said.

“If I have to do a massive round of work just to sail for one or two days, I might as well sail in Hong Kong.”

He added that he would rather take a commercial ferry to Dongao for a holiday.

Still, the 66-year-old veteran mariner gave the voyage a score of 60 out of 100 and viewed it as a worthwhile test run.

Yu was among 139 participants aboard 16 yachts from Hong Kong and Macau that sailed to Dongao under the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme. Launched in June, the scheme allows eligible Hong Kong and Macau vessels to enter designated Guangdong waters for tourism.

The voyage, which took place over the weekend, was the scheme’s largest cross-border flotilla to date. It gave visitors a taste of the island’s seafood, hotel suites and natural scenery.

An eventful voyage

Early on August 29, the flotilla left the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club in Causeway Bay for Dongao, about 36 nautical miles (53.7km) southwest of the city.

The journey took between 6½ and 8½ hours, depending on the yacht’s speed.

For participants such as 60-year-old financial executive Noel Chan and his 16-year-old son Nigel, it was family time. Chan sailed his 45-foot cruiser, Rampage, in 15-knot winds, while the pair chatted and shared drinks on deck.

“The wind speed was very good, conditions were great,” Nigel Chan said.

Mabel Tsim, an IT professional and sailor, described the eight-hour journey as a stress-relieving bonding experience.

She compared Dongao Island’s idyllic setting and sea views with those of a Southeast Asian resort in Thailand or Bali, Indonesia.

“For us as crew members, we focus on the journey itself,” she said. “The destination is a place for leisure, but more importantly, the process is sailing … For city dwellers, it is very stress-relieving.”

But hardware limitations soon became apparent. Immigration procedures at the designated port on Guishan Island took about 20 minutes – visitors entered a building, went upstairs for home return permit and baggage checks, then waited downstairs while officers checked vessel documents.

However, there was only one yacht berth, meaning vessels had to circle at sea for about 15 minutes while waiting for the previous yacht to clear.

One yacht suffered an incident at the port when its propeller broke off and sank to the seabed.

After navigating intermittent rain, the fleet arrived at Dongao, an island heavily reliant on mainland families visiting at weekends. But its temporary pontoons proved inadequate, with one yacht running aground twice in shallow water.

In the end, 13 of the 16 yachts stayed on the island for one night, while the rest remained for two.

Before setting sail, a yacht typically had to spend thousands of Hong Kong dollars to meet government requirements, including a US$1,500 vessel inspection and 3,000 yuan (US$447) in clearance fees, excluding hotel, food and other expenses.

For some participants, the time and expense were still worthwhile.

“I think out of 100 marks, I would say 85 to 90, so no such complaint … [the mainland is] really, really helpful for this [scheme] … [they] didn’t give you any hassle,” Noel Chan said.

His son Nigel compared the cost of sailing to Zhuhai with a friend’s experience in the United Kingdom.

“It’s 100 per cent more affordable, and it’s a much more pleasant experience,” he said.

While committed sailors and industry advocates regard the scheme’s early problems as necessary growing pains on the path to a world-class Greater Bay Area maritime economy, more pragmatic yacht owners remain divided over whether sailing north is worth the effort.

The yacht economy

For those with a team to navigate the administrative hurdles, the value proposition can be striking. Noel Chan said he spent just several thousand yuan on Marriott sea-view suites and other expenses for his group of 12.

He said the trip cost a fraction of a comparable stay in Hong Kong, and voiced concern that it could lead to a further outflow of Hong Kong consumer spending to the mainland.

“You go to Hong Kong, have a bad dinner, you spend that money already. So I think it’s a big challenge [for the] Hong Kong economy,” he said. “The money moved here again by sea instead of Hong Kong cars going [through the northbound vehicle scheme].”

The flotilla was a boon for some hotels.

A representative from the island’s five-star Gree Dongao Hotel said that the flotilla booked nearly 70 rooms, filling the 268-room property on August 29.

The hotel is part of the state-owned Zhuhai Gree Group, which has invested about 4 billion yuan since 2009 to develop a high-end hotel cluster on Dongao. The cluster also includes a 257-room Marriott and the cliffside Alila resort, which has 103 suites and is already attracting Hong Kong yachting people.

Dongfa Seafood Restaurant co-owner Zhou Shunfang, 60, marvelled at the flotilla but said she had not seen an influx of high-spending yacht guests. She suspected touts had intercepted them at the pier before they discovered her long-established restaurant.

Charting a smoother course

Liao Kai, president of the Zhuhai Yacht Association, said about 50 yachts had obtained temporary nationality certificates, allowing them to use the scheme to travel to the Greater Bay Area.

Participants broadly agreed that the cross-border experience would require major upgrades to both its policy framework and physical infrastructure before it could unlock the full economic potential of Greater Bay Area waters.

At the policy level, reducing the barriers to entry is crucial. The Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club had called for cross-border costs to be harmonised, vice-commodore Joseph Chu said. He suggested that northbound fees should be cut from thousands of Hong Kong dollars to match the nominal HK$58 charged for southbound vessels.

He argued that equalising the fees would turn special expeditions into more frequent trips, similar to Hong Kong residents travelling to Shenzhen for afternoon tea before returning home.

Yu echoed the call for less bureaucracy. He urged authorities across the border to drop the allegedly redundant “temporary nationality certificate” and accept surveys carried out by Hong Kong-approved professionals, rather than requiring separate and costly mainland inspections.

Workarounds to reduce costs are also emerging. Liao said traditional commercial shipping agencies had charged tens of thousands of dollars for customs clearance, prompting the Zhuhai Yacht Association to set up a dedicated agency to deal with paperwork. The move helped reduce outbound clearance fees to around 3,000 yuan for the flotilla.

On the water, relatively simple logistical changes could reduce delays. Noel Chan recommended staggered arrival times for yachts at clearance ports such as Guishan, to prevent bottlenecks that leave vessels circling offshore.

Tsim said authorities should find a way to process several boats at once. She also called for less rigid point-to-point travel rules, allowing yachts to visit more than one destination on the same itinerary.

Infrastructure remains a major constraint. Both Yu and Noel Chan said robust floating moorings, and more of them, were urgently needed at destinations such as Dongao Island to stop yachts having to “double park” in unsafe conditions.

Gao Jun, an associate professor at Sun Yat-sen University’s school of tourism management, said Zhuhai needed to improve tourist spending opportunities and amenities to extend the value chain beyond its 20-year manufacturing base in Pingsha.

By taking advantage of new self-navigating repair policies in Jinwan, cross-border access points and related services, Zhuhai aims to capture longer-term value from yacht maintenance and berthing, rather than relying solely on weekend tourism.

Liao said four yachts had successfully sailed to Jinwan, undergone major repairs and returned to Hong Kong since the self-navigating vessel repair policy was launched in March.

He added that more than 20 other vessels were applying to use the service.

Industry leaders urged patience. Chu compared the scheme’s early administrative and infrastructure problems with the chaotic early days of Hong Kong International Airport before it developed into a global aviation hub.

Stakeholders are now preparing for the anticipated launch of southbound travel.

Liao said he had heard from local authorities that the southbound scheme might open in September.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Chelsea football shirts are making Hong Kong fans nervous about crypto laws
item.description:
English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws.

Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses.

Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws.

Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses.

Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong.

Only two stablecoin issuers are currently licensed in Hong Kong – Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC.

Ahead of the enactment of the Stablecoins Ordinance on August 1, 2025, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned on its website that “it will be illegal for any person to … actively market the issue of unlicensed [fiat-referenced stablecoins] to the public”.

Winnie Choi, a Chelsea fan of 12 years, was among those worried about breaking the law.

“After looking up the law, I still do not understand whether it is a problem to wear the jersey,” she said.

Choi suggested that the HKMA issue a clear, “down-to-earth” guideline on whether wearing the shirt with the USDC logo constituted promotion.

Danny*, a club supporter for more than 20 years, said ordinary football fans would not have the awareness to identify if the shirt promoted an unregulated stablecoin.

“If I wear it, who will enforce the law? Will I be arrested by police?” he said.

Danny said he would not buy the new jersey until authorities clarified whether it was legal to wear it.

Hammer Chung, owner of football apparel shop DirectSoccer in Mong Kok, said he was unsure whether it was legal to sell replica jerseys with the USDC logo.

He added that he hoped regulators would clarify the matter.

But Chung noted that many of the kits for other football clubs that he sold also bore the logos of illegal gambling websites.

“Are we also promoting for them by selling the shirts?” he said.

The HKMA said it would not comment on individual cases, but noted the ordinance prohibited the “active marketing” or advertising of unauthorised stablecoin activity in Hong Kong.

Whether an act constituted actively marketing to the public was determined on a case-by-case basis, a spokesman said.

Factors considered by the HKMA included the languages used in the marketing messages, whether they targeted people living in the city, whether a Hong Kong domain name was used and whether a detailed marketing plan was in place to promote the activity.

A specific exemption was provided to publishers and live broadcasters who merely published content created by others, as long as they satisfied the relevant conditions set out in the provision and considered the relevant facts and circumstances, he said.

Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung expressed concerns that fans donning the new Chelsea shirt in public could be “problematic”, as it all depended on how the HKMA defined active marketing.

“There are so many grey areas,” he said, adding that he dared not wear T-shirts sporting the logos of unlicensed crypto trading platforms after the licensing regime was put in place by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC).

Li said USDC was the second-largest stablecoin in the world, and it was ridiculous that it was labelled as “unlicensed” under local legislation.

He also said it was difficult to regulate the promotion of cryptocurrencies within a certain jurisdiction in the age of the internet because they were issued globally. “How can you say something legal in other countries is illegal here?”

The ordinance provides an exemption for promoting unlicensed stablecoins across various media and digital platforms, including live broadcasts, provided the person did not devise and exercised no control over the content of the advertisement.

“A group of players on TV is wearing [shirts with] this logo … it’s impossible that it isn’t an advertisement. We’re looking at them the entire game, right?” Li said.

Tanna Chong, head of public policy at VerifyVASP, a digital assets compliance company, called for enhanced consumer protection through disclaimers before every match, similar to warning messages in moneylending advertisements.

“They would be clear reminders that the programme contains these materials [about cryptocurrency], and that those companies actually do not have a licence in Hong Kong,” she said.

Chong, who helped draft the ordinance during her time in government, said there was no hard and fast rule to define active marketing, noting that it was a concept determined on a case-by-case basis considering various contextual factors.

She said neither Circle nor Chelsea had control over the broadcasting of matches in Hong Kong, which involved a deal between NowTV and the Premier League, and had not actively implemented a marketing campaign in the city.

Circle was not “by way of business providing services” in the city either, she added.

She also reassured fans that there was no problem with wearing the Blues’ shirt with the USDC logo, as wearers were not the service provider.

“Unless [the wearer] is a Circle employee walking down the street in a Chelsea jersey. In that case, you need to establish that Circle instructed him to wear it with the intent of targeting a Hong Kong audience,” she said.

An HKT spokesman said Now TV strictly complied with all relevant Hong Kong laws and regulations.

The South China Morning Post has reached out to Circle and Chelsea FC for comment.

The West London club’s latest deal followed a collective agreement by all 20 Premier League clubs to phase out front-of-shirt gambling sponsors. But the Blues are not the first team to partner with the crypto sector.

OKX and Kraken, both virtual asset trading platforms unlicensed in Hong Kong, are the sleeve sponsors of Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur.

Chelsea itself also partnered with crypto platform BingX, which is also unlicensed in Hong Kong, for an official training kit front sponsorship.

During their visit to the city last month, Chelsea players wore the training kit with the BingX logo during an open training session at Kai Tak Stadium.

Players from City and Spurs also wore kits sporting the OKX and Kraken logos during their friendlies in Hong Kong in August this year and July last year, respectively.

Similar clauses regulating the promotion of unlicensed virtual asset trading platforms are present in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance.

The SFC said it would not comment on specific cases. It added that it would take into account all marketing and advertising activities in their totality in considering the appropriate course of action.

Kraken said that it maintained jurisdiction-specific controls designed to ensure its activities complied with applicable local laws.

The trading platform also stressed that its partnership with Tottenham Hotspur was a global brand sponsorship.

It did not reflect an offer, solicitation or promotion of Kraken’s virtual asset trading services in jurisdictions where those activities were restricted, it added.

The SCMP has reached out to Manchester City, OKX, Tottenham Hotspur and BingX for comment.

*Name changed at interviewee’s request.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore investigates racism related to China-Nepal disaster, Air India investment
item.description:
Police are investigating “shameful” racist and xenophobic online comments about the China-Nepal disaster and Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday.

Mr Shanmugam told reporters that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information will also ask social media platforms to remove comments that breach guidelines.

“The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” added Mr Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security.
item.content:encoded:
Police are investigating “shameful” racist and xenophobic online comments about the China-Nepal disaster and Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday.

Mr Shanmugam told reporters that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information will also ask social media platforms to remove comments that breach guidelines.

“The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” added Mr Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security.

“I have asked police to look into these comments.”

Under CNA’s social media moderation policy, users who post hate speech, racist or offensive comments are blocked from commenting on CNA’s social media pages.

In cases where such comments are widespread and persistent, CNA may totally turn off comments on its posts, as it did for several news posts related to the China-Nepal disaster.

MP Alex Yam (People’s Action Party) also called out such comments earlier this week, describing them as “not just racist” but “downright heartless”.

Nine Singaporeans remain missing after devastating floods caused massive destruction in Nepal on August 26.

Mr Shanmugam gave several examples of racist remarks made online about the missing Singaporeans, including “no, they are not our own” and “all ABNNs look the same”. He noted that “ABNN” is a derogatory term for Indians.

More than a thousand people died in the disaster and Singaporeans remain unaccounted for, he said, yet such remarks continued to circulate online.

Mr Shanmugam added that most Singaporeans do not share these views, pointing to more than S$3 million (US$2.4 million) raised by the Singapore Red Cross for relief efforts in Nepal.

“Singaporeans are generous, across all races. And it is important that we don’t allow a minority to poison the entire well.”

Racist backlash over Air India investment

Meanwhile, news that Air India is seeking fresh equity from shareholders, including SIA, has sparked a new wave of “anti-Indian, racist ranting” online, such as “references to snakes, curry, prata, black magic”, Mr Shanmugam said.

An “online mob” has also attacked various parties, including the CEO and senior management of Temasek, over their ethnicity. Temasek is the majority shareholder of Singapore Airlines.

“It has been said that because the CEO is of Indian ethnicity, he would favour Air India. In the eyes of these people, the CEO’s sin is that he is of Indian ethnicity, even though he is as Singaporean as any of us, he was born here, studied here. That is nasty and libellous,” Mr Shanmugam said.

“But for this online mob, however, all of that, the facts don’t matter. What matters is their racism and their own prejudices. If we allow this, in future, everyone can be attacked for their decisions based on their ethnicities.

I’ve decided to call out these people because you see what is happening in other countries. First, a minority says these nasty things, slowly it becomes normalised, then it becomes mainstream, and political and community leaders will say it

Singapore’s Senior Minister K Shanmugam

“These people should be unmasked and dealt with rather than be allowed to hide behind online anonymity.”

Singapore is not exempt from “latent racism”, Mr Shanmugam said, adding that authorities have taken a “tough line” to protect the country’s multiracial, multi-religious fabric and preserve social harmony.

“I’ve decided to call out these people because you see what is happening in other countries. First, a minority says these nasty things; slowly it becomes normalised; then it becomes mainstream, and political and community leaders will say it,” he added.

“Public discourse is then debased. Social harmony is affected. Violence against people of a different skin colour and different religion becomes acceptable.”

Racist comments, particularly against Indians in Singapore, have grown more frequent of late, with some originating and “fanned from overseas”, Mr Shanmugam said.

“We are a very small multiracial, multi-ethnic country. If we are divided along racial or religious lines, we will lose the unity that has made Singapore strong. There will be feelings of ill will, suspicion, and we will all suffer,” he added.

“We should not tolerate this. This is not who we are as Singaporeans.”

Temasek’s role in SIA’s decisions

A Reuters report last month cited sources as saying that Air India is seeking a further US$1.5 billion in support from owners Tata Sons and SIA, just months after it posted a record annual loss.

An SIA spokesperson said last week that the board would “carefully consider any requests for additional capital from Air India, taking into consideration the group’s other capital requirements and Air India’s business strategy”.

Workers’ Party MP Kenneth Tiong said in a Facebook post on August 26 that he would not support nor expect any future use of Temasek’s funds to “prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines”.

Whether it is SIA or Temasek that “writes the cheque”, there will be a “significant impact” on Temasek, he wrote.
