“No one, least of all Singaporeans, owes Air India a living … if Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek’s.”

Mr Shanmugam said it is SIA’s responsibility to assess its investments in Air India against the resources it has for its “long-term growth and profitability”.

“Any decision to invest in Air India lies with SIA, and Temasek as a shareholder in SIA, along with other shareholders, will expect SIA to make its investment decisions responsibly.”

Temasek is accountable to the government for its overall portfolio and long-term performance, Mr Shanmugam said, but not for individual investment decisions of its portfolio companies.

“Temasek and its subsidiaries decide how to invest across a wide portfolio with investments of varied risks and varied time horizons. Once governments or politicians start directing individual investment decisions, commercial discipline will be compromised,” he added.

“Decisions will become politicised – shaped by political considerations, rather than commercial judgment. In the end, Singaporeans will bear the cost.”

The government’s general principle is not to intervene in individual investment decisions or pressure companies on how to invest, Mr Shanmugam added.

Its role is to ensure professional management in Temasek, and then provide Temasek and its portfolio companies with the “political cover and the confidence which will allow them to make properly considered commercial decisions, free from untoward pressures”.

Temasek and many of its portfolio companies, including SIA, Sembcorp, Singtel and CapitaLand, have made substantial investments in India over the years, Mr Shanmugam said.

“Temasek’s website says that 43 per cent, nearly half, of its country exposure is to the Americas and China, and seven per cent is in India. But its website also says that India has in fact been its best-performing market over the last decade,” he said.

“Mr Tiong is entitled to his views. He is entitled, like any other Singaporean, to ask questions about SIA and Temasek.

“But neither his views, nor that of any minister, or any other MP, should substitute for the commercial judgment of SIA’s management and board of directors – boards which have knowledgeable and independent members, and management which has professionals whose primary responsibility is to consider and make these decisions.”

Asked by a reporter to respond to Mr Tiong’s statement that no one “owes Air India a living”, Mr Shanmugam said: “I think he ought to do his homework and look at SIA’s letter and the facts that I put out today, and ask if he is being responsible.”

This article was first published by CNA: Police investigating ‘shameful’ racist online comments about Nepal-Tibet disaster, Air India: SM Shanmugam - CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Social media must join the fight against teen suicides
item.description:
As we observe World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, the global community reflects on a sobering reality: suicide remains a leading cause of death among young people. Every year, more than 720,000 people die by suicide – each life a story cut short, a family shattered, a community left to grapple with unbearable loss.

In Hong Kong, the Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention (CSRP) at the University of Hong Kong estimates last year’s suicide rate at 13.0 per 100,000 in the population – a slight improvement from 13.8 in 2024. But let me be clear: this is no cause for complacency. The rate among our young people, particularly boys, remains stubbornly high, and that is where my deepest concern lies.

We can no longer afford to ignore the role of social media in the mental health crisis facing our teenagers. Social media has become the landscape of modern adolescence. In the United States, reports indicate that up to 95 per cent of adolescents use social media, with over one-third reporting near-constant use. For young people, these digital spaces are not merely entertainment – they are where identities are formed, relationships are navigated and self-worth is measured.
item.content:encoded:
As we observe World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, the global community reflects on a sobering reality: suicide remains a leading cause of death among young people. Every year, more than 720,000 people die by suicide – each life a story cut short, a family shattered, a community left to grapple with unbearable loss.

In Hong Kong, the Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention (CSRP) at the University of Hong Kong estimates last year’s suicide rate at 13.0 per 100,000 in the population – a slight improvement from 13.8 in 2024. But let me be clear: this is no cause for complacency. The rate among our young people, particularly boys, remains stubbornly high, and that is where my deepest concern lies.

We can no longer afford to ignore the role of social media in the mental health crisis facing our teenagers. Social media has become the landscape of modern adolescence. In the United States, reports indicate that up to 95 per cent of adolescents use social media, with over one-third reporting near-constant use. For young people, these digital spaces are not merely entertainment – they are where identities are formed, relationships are navigated and self-worth is measured.

Their impact on mental health deserves attention. For decades, my team at the CSRP has tracked the data, studied the patterns and advocated for evidence-based solutions. The evidence is overwhelming. Excessive use of social media is correlated with poor mental health and deteriorating family relationships. The causes of youth suicide are complex – home and school problems are major, intertwined contributors – but the digital environment has become a significant amplifier of distress.

We have long known that irresponsible media reporting can trigger the Werther effect – where sensational coverage of suicide leads to imitative behaviour. Social media has made this problem exponentially more complicated. A single post, whether a careless comment or misguided “awareness” message, can reach thousands of vulnerable young people instantly. Specificity in describing methods or locations – even when framed as a warning – drives contagion risk.

Yet the responsibility does not rest solely with individuals. The platforms design their algorithms to maximise engagement, often at the expense of well-being. The recent US$18 billion settlement by Meta Platforms – agreeing to examine its algorithm design to improve mental health among young users – should be a wake-up call for the industry.

The tragic case of American Sophie Rottenberg, who ended her life after months of confiding in a ChatGPT therapist, illustrates the dangers of unregulated digital environments. In our work on chatbot development, we have observed that overly empathetic responses can inadvertently reinforce a user’s negative thoughts, create a dangerous feedback loop and validate harmful ideation.

For years, we have partnered with local media to promote safe reporting practices. But the landscape has shifted dramatically. Passive audiences have become content creators. The old guidelines were not designed for this reality. That is why, with the support of The Better Hong Kong Foundation, we worked with the Hong Kong Press Council to produce an updated 2026 edition. For the first time, we have incorporated targeted guidance for social media alongside traditional recommendations.

So, what does responsible social media use look like? First, pause before posting. If your post describes methods, means or locations in specific detail, do not share it. Do not speculate on causes or spread rumours. Always obtain consent before sharing someone else’s experience with suicide.

Second, promote hope, not despair. Whenever suicide is mentioned, attach help-seeking resources. These can make a tangible difference. Share recovery stories that highlight coping strategies and resilience.

Third, use mindful language. Avoid phrases that frame suicide as noble, peaceful or an act of empowerment. Such framing normalises it for at-risk individuals. Describe the pain, not the act.

But individual action is not enough. We must hold platform operators accountable. With their sophisticated algorithms, these companies have the ability to identify at-risk users – the same algorithms that deliver personalised advertisements can be repurposed for early detection and intervention. Platforms worry that intervening might affect traffic volume. But we cannot accept profit motives as a justification for inaction.

Platforms should detect and remove harmful content using automated tools, but they must route flagged items to human moderators before removal to avoid overreach. They should deprioritise borderline high-risk content in recommendation feeds while reserving outright restriction for clear violations like content that promotes suicide methods, pacts or graphic acts. They must act swiftly against cyberbullying, which remains a major class of harmful content. And they should pin help resources prominently alongside sensitive posts.

I am pleased Meta has suggested a two-hour daily limit for young users and content filtering for children under 15. These are potentially effective measures. But we need systemic change.

Our government has committed to continuing the three-tier system to support mental health in secondary and upper-primary schools. That is welcome. However, I must highlight a critical point often overlooked: by our estimates, about 75 per cent of suicides occur among those who do not have depressive symptoms. By focusing solely on depression, we are missing most of those at risk. This is a central reason our suicide rate remains stubbornly high despite increased mental health awareness.

To truly move the needle, we must think beyond clinical interventions. We must promote a healthy lifestyle: a balanced diet, regular exercise and adequate sleep are all essential. We must make schools and homes safe places where young people feel valued and supported. And we must give them something to look forward to – a meaningful future, hope and a strong support network.

There is no silver bullet to solving the suicide problem among teenagers. The path forward is difficult and requires coordinated effort across families, schools, governments and technology companies. But it is not impossible. We have seen progress: the rate has come down from 13.8 to 13.0. That shows our efforts are working. We just cannot afford to ease up.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline.

You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s ‘Tesla imitators’ have a new mission: build affordable humanoid robots for consumers
item.description:
When Nio CEO William Li outlined earnings prospects for the Shanghai-based carmaker in March, he could not help but liken the automotive business to the development of robots.

“I think robotics will represent a natural extension of our carmaking capabilities and business acumen,” Li told reporters at a media briefing after Nio posted its first-ever quarterly profits for the three months ending December.

“Don’t you think that every car we produce in the future will actually be a robot? Its perception, decision-making, and execution will all be based on artificial intelligence.”
item.content:encoded:
When Nio CEO William Li outlined earnings prospects for the Shanghai-based carmaker in March, he could not help but liken the automotive business to the development of robots.

“I think robotics will represent a natural extension of our carmaking capabilities and business acumen,” Li told reporters at a media briefing after Nio posted its first-ever quarterly profits for the three months ending December.

“Don’t you think that every car we produce in the future will actually be a robot? Its perception, decision-making, and execution will all be based on artificial intelligence.”

While Li has adopted a “latecomer” strategy in robotics to avoid potential big losses in early-stage investment, he is convinced that robotics and carmaking have synergistic benefits.

The premium cars Nio is building already embody perception, decision-making and control systems – similar to those of robots.

That perspective on the future of mobility, buoyed by rapid growth of physical AI, is typical of the more than 10 Chinese manufacturers of intelligent vehicles that have ventured into robotics.

These players, from BYD – the world’s largest electric vehicle (EV) maker – to Stellantis-backed Leapmotor, are once again being labelled as Tesla imitators because the US carmaker is accelerating commercialisation of its humanoid robot Optimus.

Some of the Chinese firms – with clear-cut time frames to begin production and deliveries of self-developed robots – could compete against Elon Musk’s Tesla on an equal footing in robotics, buoyed by government support, an integrated supply chain and consumer willingness to embrace new technologies, according to analysts.

“AI’s enhanced role in cars provides a catalyst to automotive companies’ diversification into robotics,” said Qian Kang, owner of a vehicle circuit board factory in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “More importantly, Tesla’s business scope and model is inspiring Chinese companies to explore embodied AI.”

The robotics sector has supply chain synergy with smart EV production because key components like cameras and radar, as well as software, are needed for both.

Other key parts, from motors to heat control systems, are strongholds for automotive firms but also actively sought after by robot builders.

Chinese EV maker Xpeng and autonomous driving technology developer Baidu got off to an early start in building robots. Five years ago, they offered a sneak peek into their vision of the future of mobility, underscoring the role of robotics technology.

In August 2021, when Baidu founder and CEO Robin Li Yanhong unveiled a prototype “robocar”, he said that in the future “a car will be equivalent to a robot”.

The two-seat vehicle looked like something out of a science fiction movie. It had no steering wheel or pedals, featured two retractable doors, and the cockpit was dominated by a large curved intelligent display and a control pad.

A month later, Guangzhou-based Xpeng announced its plan to release a four-legged robot pony for children, banking on its design and manufacturing capabilities to churn out robotic products equipped with power modules, motion controls, intelligent navigation, and emotional interaction capabilities.

Today, Chinese carmakers are viewed as strong rivals to Tesla as they meld the latest AI technologies with mobility, industry officials and analysts said.

In December, Musk endorsed Xpeng’s Iron humanoid robot on social media while predicting Chinese companies would ­dominate the global robotics market alongside Tesla.

Tesla has yet to sell any of its Optimus humanoid robots, and Musk is now transforming the EV maker from a hardware-centric business into a ­physical AI firm.

Tesla has halted production of its Model S and Model X cars at its plant in Fremont, California, and instead will build humanoid robots in the facility.

In April, Tesla’s China president, Allan Wang Hao, said the company’s Shanghai Gigafactory had the potential to produce humanoid robots, taking advantage of the mainland’s complete supply chain and advanced manufacturing techniques.

The contest between Chinese carmakers and Tesla in humanoid robots takes on broader importance in the context of the heated China-US tech rivalry.

The two countries are battling for supremacy in a number of fields, with humanoid robotics one of the key areas where Beijing and Washington hope their companies can establish global dominance.

Thanks to the country’s diverse supply chain and large production scale, upstream Chinese suppliers could make high-quality, cost-efficient and innovative components for various types of robots, including humanoids, according to Lu Hancheng, former director of the Shenzhen-based Gaogong Robot Industry Research Institute.

Mainland China was now home to more than 150 humanoid robot makers, according to the National Development and Reform Commission. They delivered 97 per cent of the total humanlike robots on the global market in the first half of the year, according to Morgan Stanley.

Early this year, the US bank predicted that the global humanoid market would achieve US$7.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2050.

Morgan Stanley also forecast in July that China’s humanoid robot shipments could hit 446,000 units by 2030, jumping nearly ninefold from about 50,000 units this year, spurred by competition to reach deployment scale and to close the real-world data feedback loop.

Among the Chinese carmakers diversifying into robotics, BYD and Xpeng are now under the spotlight due to their development and manufacturing heft as their mass production plans draw near.

At the end of July, BYD said in a statement to the South China Morning Post that its first humanoid robots would debut in August at the firm’s Di Space experience centres, but that timetable has now been delayed.

In June, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice-president, predicted that China would become the first market to “see full commercialisation of humanoid robots”.

However, automotive giants do not just see themselves as just making robots to sell on the open market. They also aim to achieve a high level of automation in production by gaining experience in embodied AI technology.

In late July, BYD formed a strategic partnership with Chinese robotics start-up PaXini Tech to deploy robots in manufacturing. The carmaker will create real-world industrial environments for the robots, generating operating data to help train embodied AI models.

Xpeng’s robotics subsidiary Dogotix received US$900 million in its latest round of financing last month, which valued it at US$6.3 billion. The fundraising, which attracted Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the SCMP, and IDG Capital, marked the biggest single private-equity deal involving a Chinese robotics maker.

The company said it planned to begin producing its Iron humanoid robots at the end of 2026, targeting an initial volume of 1,000 units, to be deployed as sales assistants at its domestic showrooms.

Iron runs on the firm’s Vision-Language-Action 2.0 AI model. Unlike older systems that translate images into text-based code before executing a movement, the newer model allows the robot’s neural network to convert visual data directly into motion, improving task efficiency and reducing information loss.

Xpeng CEO He Xiaopeng said in November that the company aimed to sell 1 million robots annually by 2030, when costs would be brought down to a level to make the products affordable for household use.

Rivals Li Auto, Xiaomi and Leapmotor have all ramped up the development of humanoid robots, which are expected to perform tasks such as factory work and elderly care.

Since early 2024, Chery Automobile has been working with AI company Aimoga to develop Mornine, a humanoid robot capable of understanding natural language and interpreting human intentions.

At the World Robot Conference in Beijing last month, the industry’s mindset had firmly pivoted towards real-world application ramp-up, Goldman Sachs said.

“While demonstrations of locomotion and entertainment still attract interest, discussions are now centred on quantifiable metrics such as task performance, success rates, throughput, and payback periods, reflecting a healthy maturation of the sector,” the bank said in a research report. “Logistics sorting has emerged as one of the most visible early commercialisation directions.”

Shao Yu, chief economist with the Sci-tech Innovation Centre at Fudan University’s School of Management, said tech industries, propelled by government support and an influx of private capital, were acting as the major growth driver for the Chinese economy.

Shao added that tech sectors, from advanced semiconductors to embodied AI, would sustain their strength over a period of time despite worries of an AI-generated bubble.

“With the trend of innovation, more investment will be made to those hi-tech areas to reflect the K-shaped structure of the Chinese economy,” Shao said. “The crux point is how to leverage hi-tech companies and products to benefit society as a whole.”

A K-shaped divergence refers to China’s economic structure, where hi-tech manufacturing and exports are thriving while consumption, property and traditional industries are experiencing slower growth.

But Xu Mingqi, a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, threw a wet blanket over investors’ expectations for quick returns from investing in physical AI.

Real benefits from AI won’t be achieved quickly

Xu Mingqi, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences

“No AI technology with material impact on people’s lifestyle has been in sight yet,” he told reporters in a media briefing this month. “Real benefits from AI won’t be achieved quickly and it will still turn out to be a long drawn-out process.”

item.title: [SCMP] Golden years: in Southeast Asia, growing old is big business
item.description:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.
item.content:encoded:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.

Carers wheeled and walked eight fellow residents to the dining table before breaking into song. Goaded into a speech, Fung kept it brief: “I’m very happy to be here.”

The home, a refurbished two-storey bungalow, is one of a growing number of assisted living facilities springing up as Singapore’s population ages. The city state officially became a “super-aged” society this year, with more than one-fifth of its population over 65.

These facilities offer a much-needed middle ground for older people who can no longer live independently but do not require the round-the-clock medical care of a nursing home.

Staff help residents with daily tasks such as dispensing medication and writing letters, while some facilities include memory care units for those experiencing cognitive decline.

Assisted living is a nascent but fast-growing segment of Singapore’s multibillion-dollar silver economy. The government has provided more than 1,100 such flats since 2021, and private real estate operators are also increasingly entering the market.

For residents like Fung, what matters most is feeling part of a community, keeping their independence and being treated with dignity. Despite her early-stage osteoporosis, she moves around the home without a walking frame, sometimes forgoing afternoon sessions of mahjong to journal in her room instead.

“I’m fitting in little by little – I’ve learned to get to know more of the residents and our different timetables,” she said. “I told my family I’ll probably stay here until the time comes.”

For fellow resident Soo Soo Cheng, 90, her single room is a world away from the six-bedded ward she shared at her previous nursing home. “It was like a dormitory and nothing private like this. I was getting really uncomfortable,” she said.

Now she spends her days in a bright orange armchair by the window, walking frame within reach, while carers take care of tasks like printing copies of bills and helping her to bed when her spine acts up.

“I’m thankful for a place like this, where I can do things on my own and yet never have a dull moment,” she said. “Time seems to fly.”

A middle ground

Southeast Asia is ageing rapidly and its social welfare systems are increasingly grappling with a thorny question: what happens to the people who can no longer manage entirely on their own, but do not need a hospital bed?

Assisted living – offering medical and social care scalable to residents’ needs – has emerged as an answer.

It was designed for people whose needs fell somewhere between the intensive clinical care of a nursing home and what a domestic helper, who cannot reasonably be expected to manage a medical emergency, could provide, said Janice Chia, founder of Ageing Asia, a Singapore-based social enterprise focused on the business of growing old.

In Singapore, more people are ageing alone – an estimated 83,000 by 2030, according to the Ministry of Health – while shrinking family sizes are increasing the caregiving burden shouldered by adult children.

“Assisted living provides independence and privacy without the seeming unpopular burden of managing foreign domestic helpers,” said Kelvin Tan, who heads the applied ageing studies programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

Options in the city state range from government-run flats to private luxury apartments, with monthly bills ranging anywhere from three to five figures, depending on location, room size and level of care required.

In 2021, Singapore introduced community care flats aiming to support independent ageing in a social environment. Five such projects have launched so far.

The Housing Development Board announced in July that from its sixth project, launching in October, the eligibility age for assisted-living public housing estates would be lowered from 65 to 55, alongside lower fees aimed at improving affordability.

Estimated fees for a 15-year lease – currently S$40,000 to S$49,000 (US$31,400 to US$38,500) for a basic package – will drop to between S$26,000 and S$28,000 from next year, according to Vanguard Healthcare, which operates the developments.

“The cost is a big advantage for average Singaporeans looking for an accessible offer,” Tan said.

Private operators are also scaling up their operations. St Bernadette Lifestyle Village, which runs eight facilities island-wide, offers a mid-tier option priced from S$3,000 to S$6,000 a month.

Care homes were “less a business venture than a necessity”, said founder Belinda Wee, who has observed elderly residents growing unsettled in nursing homes due to a lack of socialising. About 80 residents lived in St Bernadette’s homes last year, up from 19 in 2023.

Well-heeled pensioners gained a luxury option last month with the opening of Perennial Living, a S$260 million, 195,000 sq ft development in northeastern Singapore featuring a hydrotherapy pool, a traditional Chinese medicine clinic and a karaoke lounge.

A basic package for a 330 sq ft studio flat starts at S$8,000 a month, while a 565 sq ft two-bedder costs more than S$13,000.

The hefty price tag has raised concerns about the affordability of retirement, though experts note the project is aimed squarely at the upper end of the market.

Chia said its prices should be viewed in the category of premium hospitality and care, rather than general assisted living.

Sign-ups have been gradual and interest has been “positive”, according to Perennial Holding’s chief executive Pua Seck Guan, who projected a 30 per cent occupancy rate after a year and 80 per cent after two.

More new entrants were expected to join the assisted living sector, Chia said, as Singapore’s shift from live-in caregiving to mainstream services gave firms the confidence to invest. But she urged regulators to pace approvals carefully given the dearth of healthcare workers.

Singapore needed to recruit about 6,000 nurses, healthcare professionals and support staff every year to meet demand, the Health Ministry said in 2024. It previously estimated that a healthcare workforce of 82,000 would be needed by 2030.

“This figure is the one worth dwelling on, because it shows care capability cannot simply be commissioned. Sites can be approved considerably faster than carers can be trained, deployed and retained,” Chia said.

Ageing in luxury

With its circular driveway and plush lobby, Perennial Living looks more like an upscale hotel than a home for the elderly.

The development aimed to set a “new benchmark for senior living in Singapore”, Pua said – reflecting a surge in luxury senior living facilities across Asia as operators recognise their target demographic wants more than just care and medical services.

More than US$500 billion is expected to pour into the silver economy across six Southeast Asian markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines – by 2030, according to Ageing Asia.

Retirees today were wealthier, healthier and more assertive than any generation before them, the social enterprise said in a report released last month, making the business of ageing the Asia-Pacific’s “largest commercial opportunity”.

“Baby boomers, the biggest savers of all generations, have spent their lives making choices and are expected to hold onto that autonomy into their older age,” it said.

At Homerly International Senior Living in Thailand, residents walk long, tree-lined avenues within a large, serene gated community, accompanied by nurses, with their pets padding along behind them. The resort, which provides assisted living and nursing care, is one of hundreds of retirement communities popping up across a country with abundant land and a growing healthcare workforce.

A month’s stay – including round-the-clock medical care, physiotherapy, pool villas shaded by trees and two staff members in attendance – starts at US$2,200, with the top-end pool villas commanding a price tag of around US$4,500.

“Here you’re not a patient, you are a resident. We treat people with dignity,” general manager Rene Pisters said. “You have somebody with you all the time if you need it and the feeling that if something happens to you, there is a nurse sitting here.”

Malaysia is seeing a similar boom in luxury homes for the elderly, driven by changing expectations of ageing, according to N. Raaj Selvarajan, group chairman of regional healthcare infrastructure investor Hemrish Group and founder of its flagship senior living brand Sukha Golden.

Residents increasingly wanted privacy, wellness and access to care without the institutional feel traditionally associated with elderly care, he said.

Demand for its luxury Sukha Senior Resort has surged since it opened in March last year – all rooms are fully occupied, with interested residents placed on a waiting list.

Capitalising on the boom, Selvarajan said plans to expand regionally were under way, with projects in Indonesia and Vietnam in the pipeline. “The opportunity is not simply that Asia is ageing; it is that people want to age differently,” he said.

Crossing borders

For Singaporeans who feel priced out of their own super-aged society, homes for the elderly have become an unlikely engine of Malaysia and Thailand’s recent tourism boom, as families shop for similar care standards at a fraction of the cost.

The Straits Resorts Medini, a retirement home in Johor just a 15-minute drive from the border, has built its business around Singaporean demand.

“Consistent and encouraging” is how founder Elvira Tan describes cross-border interest in the facility, which offers rooms from S$4,300 a month, bundling in personalised care and grooming services, arts activities and social programmes.

Industry insiders expect the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Rapid Transit System Link, set to open in January, to further boost demand.

“You can obtain the most expensive level of care in Malaysia for about one-third the price of the same level of care in Singapore,” said Kashif Ansari, group CEO of real estate market intelligence group Juwai IQI.

Cultural familiarity and the absence of a language barrier eased the transition for would-be residents considering homes across the causeway, he added.

“Families with a senior who needs potentially years or even more than a decade of care, naturally want the highest quality service and the lowest cost they can possibly obtain,” he said. “Malaysia has a real competitive advantage in this sector and operators hope to make the most of it.”

Money goes further in Thailand too. Facilities in Bangkok and Chiang Mai are attracting a growing number of Asian retirees, including from Singapore and Hong Kong, looking for care comparable to what they can get at home at a fraction of the cost.

Thailand hopes the care and wellness industry will become a defining part of its economy in the years ahead, as more people grow old and spend money on a curated retirement.

Care standards were high, Homerly’s Pisters said, adding that his company helped elderly residents with bureaucratic hurdles such as visas and bank accounts.

“The demand is huge, and it will only get bigger,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s youth job crisis is driving graduates to German vocational apprenticeships
item.description:
Two years ago, Yuki Liu was a university student in the northern Chinese province of Hebei, studying traditional Chinese music and the pipa – a pear-shaped Chinese lute – weighing the usual paths considered by her peers: postgraduate degree or civil service exam.

Today, her day begins at 1am in Germany.

While many people sleep, she is already working as an apprentice at an industrial bakery in a small town outside Stuttgart in the country’s southwest, preparing the shop for the morning rush.
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago, Yuki Liu was a university student in the northern Chinese province of Hebei, studying traditional Chinese music and the pipa – a pear-shaped Chinese lute – weighing the usual paths considered by her peers: postgraduate degree or civil service exam.

Today, her day begins at 1am in Germany.

While many people sleep, she is already working as an apprentice at an industrial bakery in a small town outside Stuttgart in the country’s southwest, preparing the shop for the morning rush.

The turning point for Liu came as she approached graduation and grew increasingly unsure about the path her studies could offer her in China. “With a music degree, your only option is to teach,” she said. “Otherwise you starve.”

Liu came across Germany’s apprenticeship system almost by happenstance, discovering a path that the musician had never imagined: becoming a blue-collar worker in Europe’s largest economy.

Liu is among a growing number of young Chinese turning to Ausbildung, Germany’s dual vocational training system, as an alternative to an increasingly competitive graduate job market at home and as a potential route to staying in Europe. Many applicants, like her, already hold university degrees or have worked for well-known companies.

On Chinese social media, the pitch is straightforward: little upfront cost and the prospect of a job at the end. Apprentices are employed by a company in Germany and paid a training allowance while attending a state vocational school tuition-free. Most stay on as regular employees once they qualify.

Back in China, there is a popular cultural refrain that students and degree-holders often use to describe how hard it is to find a job: “graduation means unemployment”.

A record 12.7 million students graduated from Chinese universities this year, up 480,000 from 2025. Unemployment among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, rose to 17.9 per cent in July – an 11-month high.

For some, Ausbildung – literally translated as “education”, “training” or “apprenticeship” – offers more than a pay cheque. It is also one of the cheaper routes to relocating abroad, particularly for those looking to escape a working culture epitomised by a notorious “996” schedule – working from 9am to 9pm, six days a week.

Social media has helped fuel the appeal. Liu recalled a video on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – featuring a philosophy postgraduate student who had dropped out and moved to Germany to train as a gardener, listing what he found different about working there: no rat race, no overtime and no office politics. The video drew thousands of likes, with viewers asking in the comments how they could follow a similar path.

The financial incentives also blunt some reluctance towards blue-collar work. Workers in Germany with a recognised vocational qualification earned about €4,125 (US$4,800) a month before tax in April 2025, according to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office – roughly five times the average pay of production workers in China last year, data from the National Bureau of Statistics shows.

“You can really feel it: far more people are talking about it than before,” said Emilie Xie, a former media worker in China who is now applying to become a carer in Germany.

However, for some, reality often hits harder than the online pitch.

Lin Chenxi runs a youth hostel in Hamburg and helps place Chinese apprentices with German employers, supporting them after they arrive. “Only about a third of the students we placed made it through,” she said. “The other two-thirds either got weeded out or lost heart and left.”

The language, Lin said, can be the biggest hurdle. She explained how applicants need a B1 proficiency level in German – an intermediate stage in which they can handle everyday situations and communicate familiar topics – but many appear to have drilled their way through the German language exam in China, and they arrive unable to hold a conversation.

I feel like a screw on an assembly line

Yuki Liu

The promise of plentiful jobs can also be misleading. Germany lacked enough qualified workers to fill 369,500 skilled jobs in 2025, according to the German Economic Institute, with nursing among the hardest-hit professions. Some of the roles that are more accessible to Chinese applicants are said to include care work, baking and kitchen jobs.

“I feel like a screw on an assembly line,” Liu said, explaining how she spends about six hours every workday sorting deliveries and two hours making products. In nearly a year, she lamented, she had never taken a single item from raw ingredients to a finished loaf.

Apprentices spend about three years on a training allowance that averages €1,238 a month before tax, according to the Federal Statistical Office, with smaller firms typically paying less. Liu takes home €873, of which €680 goes towards rent. She said she is already considering her next restart, possibly by pursuing another apprenticeship.

Those realities may help explain the gap between the buzz on Chinese social media and the number actually taking the route. Germany counted 573 Chinese nationals in dual vocational training in 2024, up from 282 in 2020, according to the Federal Institute for Vocational Education and Training.

The figures exclude nursing and other school-based programmes that attract many more Chinese applicants. Still, the overall number remains a fraction of China’s outbound workforce.

For Emilie Xie, though, none of this has changed her mind. “A degree isn’t hard currency any more,” she said. “It has become consumption, not an investment.”

Xie graduated from Hengshui High School – famed for its gruelling exam drilling – and went on to study at a university in Beijing. It was a path once seen as a ticket to a comfortable career. She worked in media before deciding to retrain herself.

Xie said she deliberately chose care work: the sector is short-staffed, relatively easy to enter and – she believed – harder for artificial intelligence to replace. She said she knew the job meant changing adult diapers and cleaning up after people, but she said she was ready for it.

For his part, Willie Wei had an advantage many other students lacked: he studied German as an undergraduate before dropping out of a journalism master’s degree programme in Beijing. He was hired by a large care provider for disabled people in Saxony on a regular employee contract, rather than an apprentice wage, with 32 days of paid leave and what he said was one of the better salaries in the sector.

“Things are falling into place, step by step,” he said, revealing his plan to apply for German citizenship once he qualifies.

Even so, looking back on his journey through the Ausbildung system, Wei said he would have preferred to have taken an academic path through a university – a route that he said he still may consider in the future.

item.title: [SCMP] Family firms power China’s economy – but what happens when the heirs refuse the throne?
item.description:
Many Chinese tend to label the offspring of the country’s nouveau riche private business founders with the pejorative “fuerdai”, literally “second-generation rich”.

They are seen as scions, waiting in the wings to inherit their family’s enterprises and the massive wealth their parents oversaw, a life in the lap of luxury guaranteed.

In reality, many of these transitions are plagued by a clash between generations, as the younger generation is unwilling – or unable – to keep the family business going, let alone allow it to thrive.
item.content:encoded:
Many Chinese tend to label the offspring of the country’s nouveau riche private business founders with the pejorative “fuerdai”, literally “second-generation rich”.

They are seen as scions, waiting in the wings to inherit their family’s enterprises and the massive wealth their parents oversaw, a life in the lap of luxury guaranteed.

In reality, many of these transitions are plagued by a clash between generations, as the younger generation is unwilling – or unable – to keep the family business going, let alone allow it to thrive.

The private sector, the backbone of China’s economy and employment, is now facing a growing succession crisis – one which may see businesses wind down or fold, observers warn, as family matters threaten to send broader tremors throughout the country.

In regions like China’s eastern Zhejiang province, a major economic centre, questions over inheritance are becoming more pressing.

“I cannot – and probably should not – take over from my father,” said Li Fante, whose family’s factory, like many other businesses in Zhejiang’s city of Wenling, has maintained steady profits.

However, he said the work was neither exciting nor lucrative enough to lure him in.

“We may not do as well as our parents have done, and the business is boring,” Li said.

There is no consensus over how to run a business. So why bother?

Li Fante, Wenling, Zhejiang province

When Li’s parents were approaching 70 years old, he said he made an agreement with them to wind down the family business, which produces rubber and plastic parts, after more than 30 years in the trade.

He said that disagreements in the family had contributed to the decision.

“For us, taking over from our fathers means the beginning of endless quarrels and clashes,” he said. “There is no consensus over how to run a business. So why bother?

“Business drive and acumen may not automatically pass from one generation to the next.”

Li, who is in his early 30s, used the proceeds from the sale of the factory’s land and its assets to invest in stocks and Shanghai property.

Although ostensibly a family matter, Li’s decision – and those taking place among wealthy households across the country – could impact the future of China’s private sector, which accounts for 60 per cent of gross domestic product and 80 per cent of urban employment.

More than 85 per cent of the country’s private enterprises are family-run, according to data from the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, and Zhejiang is a major site of succession debates.

The province is one of China’s richest, and its private sector contributes 70 per cent of local GDP and employs many of its residents.

The average age of founders from Zhejiang’s top 100 biggest private enterprises was 64 years old, according to a 2025 report from the local government.

“This means enterprises entering the succession phase are not isolated ones, but a huge swathe of the most vibrant and productive part of China’s private economy,” provincial authorities said.

Data from Wenling’s United Front Work Department showed that, in 2025, close to 60 per cent of local private firms with an annual industrial output of 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million) were in need of “urgent succession planning” to ensure continuity in operations as their founders reached 60 years old.

Of 114 private firms surveyed throughout Ningbo and neighbouring cities, including Wenling, 90 were still led by their founders, some aged 70 or older, and about 60 firms had neither a designated successor nor any second-generation family members in management.

Only 10 companies of the 114 covered in the survey, conducted between 2023 and 2025 by Ningbo University of Finance and Economics (NBUFE), had come under the control of the second generation.

A related NBUFE survey also found close to 20 per cent of the second-generation members of the 114 firms explicitly declined to take over, while 45 per cent remain undecided or prefer to pursue a career other than their family’s business.

Su Saier, a deputy professor at NBUFE who led the survey, said most private entrepreneurs in Ningbo – and across Zhejiang broadly – showed limited awareness of succession planning and lacked systematic, long-term arrangements.

“Founders have limited willingness to ‘relinquish’ control and there is also a lack of resilience and entrepreneurial drive among their children,” she said.

The risks of investment reduction, business closures and broader impact on the economy have researchers worried.

“The succession and continuity of private enterprises is no longer a family matter, but a question of regional economic vitality and industrial ecology,” Su warned.

“This is particularly true in regions known for their private sector that are China’s economic pillars, like Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Guangdong, where numerous private firms are embedded in industrial and supply-chain networks.

“If succession is not smooth at one enterprise, it could put employment, upstream and downstream production and even the broader industrial ecosystem on the line,” she said.

Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing, likened family-operated factories to capillaries in the massive Chinese economy.

“These factories may not be massive conglomerates themselves, but collectively they could be foundational to the Chinese manufacturing ecosystem,” Tang said.

“They usually specialise in a single component, or a minor link in the supply and production chain, that larger manufacturers usually outsource. If they shut down as their founders grey, the resilience and cost-effectiveness of Chinese manufacturing may be at stake going forward.”

Li, from the family factory in Wenling, agreed.

“The ageing of founders at many factories that do not have a successor may mean potential supply disruptions,” he said.

His family factory was one of many producers established in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It now sells moulded plastic auto parts to carmakers like Geely and BYD.

Handling succession is not just a test for business owners, but also a challenge for local cadres. If businesses in their jurisdictions wither, officials will have to tackle the subsequent impact on sentiment, jobs and fiscal income.

In one recent example, listed kitchenware maker Zhejiang Meida sold a controlling stake to an outside bidder for 1.29 billion yuan in July after its 85-year-old founder failed to convince his children to take over the business. Its stock price subsequently fell.

Meida is one of the largest listed firms in its home base of Haining, and employs thousands of workers. Local officials have stepped in following the sudden announcement to save local jobs and retain the local production base, according to people there familiar with the matter.

The succession issue has also caught the attention of top policymakers in recent years, with some viewing it as an issue that will make or break the future of the private sector of the world’s second-largest economy.

A 2023 Communist Party policy statement on promoting the private economy noted the need for “mentoring and guidance” for the younger generation of private entrepreneurs to ensure “orderly handover and succession”.

A dedicated law on the private economy, in effect since May 2025, requires qualified private entities to establish and improve their modern corporate governance system as an institutional foundation for sustainability and intergenerational succession.

Specific proposals, like recruiting professional managers to help run and modernise family businesses, have been raised.

But Li said this would not help much.

“By design, the founding family retains ownership, while professional managers brought in from the outside can leverage their knowledge and management skills to grow the company and get paid with salary, bonus and shares,” he said. “This idea sounds good on paper.

“The crux of the issue is that for a small family business, nothing is institutionalised,” he added.

“Many business decisions still rest on the founder’s experience, risk-taking, personal connections and even intuition and gut feeling. There is no business model. How can one modernise such a business?”

But NBUFE’s Su argued that to make more private businesses more sustainable, the test was how to transform them, regardless of who sat at the helm.

Succession is becoming the sternest test for Zhejiang businesses, and everyone has a stake in it to address the challenges

Zhejiang Daily

“The challenge goes beyond whether the second generation is willing to take over or not, but rather whether modern governance transformation can replace the founder’s personal abilities, experience and authority and adapt the company to the competitive environment of the new era.

“The key is who can drive the company’s sustainable development.”

Some high-profile examples can provide a model for such a transition.

On August 17, Li Shufu, founder of auto giant Geely Auto, put his long-time deputy An Conghui in the driving seat of the 345-billion-yuan business empire, passing over his children.

“The most feasible approach is to retain the advantages of the ‘family system’ so that shares can be held by the family, but management positions should be opened to the public, as much as possible to talent outside the family,” wrote Zhejiang Daily – a press organ of the provincial government – in a commentary piece following Li Shufu’s retirement.

“The goal is a modern enterprise system with clear property rights, well-defined boundaries between family and business executives for a sound corporate governance structure.”

Officials in the province are determined to tackle the issue, as time appears to be running out.

“The first generation of Zhejiang entrepreneurs who rose to prominence after the reform and opening-up since the 1980s are now seniors. For them – and local officials and governments as well – handing over the business has become a sword hanging overhead, and the window of time is steadily closing,” Zhejiang Daily said.

“Succession is becoming the sternest test for Zhejiang businesses, and everyone has a stake in it to address the challenges.”

item.title: [SCMP] Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
item.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
item.content:encoded:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.

But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.

While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.

That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.

Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.

“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”

The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.

Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another

Seth Goldstein, Morningstar

Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.

While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.

“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.

The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.

Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.

The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.

“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.

Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.

Can Tesla do without China?

At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.

Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.

Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.

Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.

Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.

China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.

“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.

“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”

Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.

Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.

Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.

Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.

And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.

The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised

Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney

Between Washington and Beijing

Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.

Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.

Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.

The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.

But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.

Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.

How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.

“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”

She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”

Tesla lays the first bricks

Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.

It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.

Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.

CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.

Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.

“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.

Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.

SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.

Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.

However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.

While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.

Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’

However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.

“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”

Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.

A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.

Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.

“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.

Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.

Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.

These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.

Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.

“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.

Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.

“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

item.title: [SCMP] 5 years after sweeping ban, China’s tutoring industry still bleeding parents dry
item.description:
Yin Yue, a mother with a 15-year-old daughter, feels like after-school academic tutoring is everywhere again in Guangzhou, the city where she lives in southern China.

Five years ago, China launched a sweeping crackdown that drove much of the industry out of sight. But prep centres had quietly begun popping up again in popular commercial areas across the city, said Yin, a pharmaceutical sales manager in her 40s.

In Guangzhou’s shopping malls, these centres are now among the busiest tenants, pulling in crowds of parents and schoolchildren on weekends and weekday evenings, according to Yin. During the summer and winter holidays, they sometimes get so busy that nearby shops and restaurants see an uptick in business.
item.content:encoded:
Yin Yue, a mother with a 15-year-old daughter, feels like after-school academic tutoring is everywhere again in Guangzhou, the city where she lives in southern China.

Five years ago, China launched a sweeping crackdown that drove much of the industry out of sight. But prep centres had quietly begun popping up again in popular commercial areas across the city, said Yin, a pharmaceutical sales manager in her 40s.

In Guangzhou’s shopping malls, these centres are now among the busiest tenants, pulling in crowds of parents and schoolchildren on weekends and weekday evenings, according to Yin. During the summer and winter holidays, they sometimes get so busy that nearby shops and restaurants see an uptick in business.

That would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago. In 2021, Beijing launched its “double reduction” campaign to outlaw for-profit tutoring in core school subjects such as maths and English, aiming to stamp out an academic rat race that was leading parents to spend eye-watering sums on extra classes for their children.

Thousands of providers closed or were forced to restructure during the intense national enforcement campaign that followed, as the authorities introduced tough punishments for tutors found operating without a licence.

Yet the crackdown did not dampen the intense competition in the country’s education system – or the demand for extra tutoring that it feeds. And that has allowed the industry to gradually make a comeback, aided by a pause in intensive, high-profile national clampdown campaigns.

Everyone is still locked in the same relentless race, spending just as much as before

Yin Yue, mother based in Guangdong province

Recent surveys and interviews with parents in major Chinese cities suggest that families across the country continue to spend heavily on after-school academic tutoring, even at a time when China’s uncertain job market and property downturn are dampening overall household consumption growth.

Yin’s daughter starts high school next month. To help her get a head-start on next semester’s curriculum, Yin spent more than 11,500 yuan (US$1,700) to send her on an intensive 12-day course covering maths, physics, chemistry and English.

In total, Yin said her family had spent close to 70,000 yuan on tutoring over the past year. She felt the extra classes were vital to help her daughter keep up with her peers – after all, they all had private tutors too.

“The stronger the students, the more their parents spend,” Yin said. “Everyone is still locked in the same relentless race, spending just as much as before.”

A survey of more than 2,100 parents in Zhongshan, another city in southern China, conducted by the Southern Metropolis Daily and released in late August, also found that after-school classes were still the norm.

Nearly 70 per cent of the parents surveyed said their children were currently attending subject-based after-school tutoring, while about another 20 per cent said they planned to arrange extra classes for them. Only 8.75 per cent said they had no plans for after-school tutoring.

More than 60 per cent of respondents said they spent at least 1,000 yuan per month on after-school tutoring, with 6.45 per cent spending over 5,000 yuan. This represents a big chunk of a typical household budget, given that Zhongshan’s per capita disposable income was about 35,000 yuan in the first half of 2026, according to official data.

The top three reasons parents gave for paying for tutoring were that their children were struggling to keep up with school coursework, the intense competition for admission to high schools and universities, and the fact that other students were also taking extra classes, according to the survey.

Among affluent Chinese families, the spending on tutoring can be far larger.

“In my son’s class, parents spend an average of 10,000 yuan a month on tutoring,” said Guan Jing, a parent based in Beijing.

Louis Tan, who runs a manufacturing business in Shenzhen, said he had budgeted 300,000 to 500,000 yuan for academic tutoring over the next three years, as his daughter prepared to take China’s national university entrance exams.

He had also set aside another 500,000 yuan for art classes, because his daughter hoped to attend China’s prestigious Central Academy of Fine Arts, Tan added.

“When I was young, a kid from a poor background could stand out on natural talent alone,” said Tan, who grew up in a poor rural community in southwestern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. “Today, they have to compete against peers getting tonnes of extra coaching.”

If everyone else is taking after-school tutoring classes and your child doesn’t, she falls behind

Zhang Liang, father based in Hubei province

Families in smaller cities are also feeling the pressure. In Jingshan, a county-level city in central China’s Hubei province, truck driver Zhang Liang said he had spent more than 10,000 yuan a semester on tutoring for his 9-year-old daughter, plus 2,800 yuan for 14 days of summer classes.

The costs are a burden for the family, which earns about 15,000 yuan a month, but Zhang feels the classes are important for his daughter’s future.

“If everyone else is taking after-school tutoring classes and yours doesn’t, she falls behind,” Zhang said. He worries that his kidney stones could one day stop him from driving long-haul trucks, leaving the family unable to afford the tutoring fees.

Education appears to be one of the few non-negotiable spending categories for Chinese households at a time of heightened economic uncertainty. China’s per capita consumption rose 3.7 per cent in the first half of the year, while spending on education, culture and recreation increased 4.9 per cent, according to official data.

Between 2020 and 2025, education, culture and recreation spending in China grew 71.7 per cent, National Bureau of Statistics data showed.

Xiong Bingqi, director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute, said the core problem was the intense competition for places at China’s top schools, which extended from senior high school through to university. The fight for school places helps explain the resilience of demand for private tutoring, according to Xiong.

item.title: [SCMP] Economist Lan Xiaohuan on the balancing act needed to boost China’s consumption
item.description:
Lan Xiaohuan is a professor of economics at China Europe International Business School. His book, How China Works: An Introduction to China’s State-led Economic Development, has sold millions of copies in China and has been translated into multiple languages.

Here, he discusses the economic realities behind China’s record trade surplus, the case for a stronger social safety net, and how public data infrastructure shapes the artificial intelligence race with the United States.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Lan Xiaohuan is a professor of economics at China Europe International Business School. His book, How China Works: An Introduction to China’s State-led Economic Development, has sold millions of copies in China and has been translated into multiple languages.

Here, he discusses the economic realities behind China’s record trade surplus, the case for a stronger social safety net, and how public data infrastructure shapes the artificial intelligence race with the United States.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

Since you wrote How China Works, the global and domestic environments have both evolved. What are the most critical shifts and developments for China? If you were to add a new chapter to the book to reflect these changes, what would be its central theme?

I would not add a new chapter; I would write an entirely new book. It’s not that there aren’t new issues, but rather addressing them requires a new framework.

Domestically, the decline of the real estate market and the rapid rise of manufacturing and technology are significant shifts. My new book would likely focus on China’s industry and technology.

But actually, I think the most consequential changes are external: the impact of the pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, the energy shocks regarding Iran, and shifting political dynamics in the United States. In comparison, China’s domestic baseline has remained relatively stable.

How China Works explains to the world how to view China. I’ve also thought about writing a book explaining to Chinese people how to view the world. Historically, global world views have been dominated by a North Atlantic, Euramerican perspective. So what is the world from a Chinese perspective? In terms of economics, that would mean looking more closely at Southeast Asia, Central Asia and Russia, where we share closer relations but don’t yet have a systematic understanding of them.

Amid a property market downturn, how can local governments secure new, stable streams of income?

Fiscal pressure can’t be solved by money alone, nor by changing the development model alone; it needs both. Current policy adjustments – such as relaxing special local government bond quotas and easing bank credit – help refinance old debts with new ones to prevent defaults. This is meant to help buy time.

Long-term fiscal sustainability is not only about increasing income – it requires aligning expenditure with income. Past local government spending was too high. It’s unrealistic to expect land revenue to support such a large amount of spending, or to expect other revenue sources to plug the fiscal deficit left by the property market downturn. There aren’t any long-term sustainable revenue sources that can directly replace land finance.

Therefore, I think a reasonable approach is tax reforms in the long term, alongside spending cuts. Much of China’s core infrastructure – high-speed rail networks, urban undergrounds, major city expansions, and so on – has already been completed, so these kinds of local government expenditures will naturally decline.

Local governments might still want to launch new projects, such as building airports, but their finances might not allow it. Investment remains a major engine of economic growth, but its share is not as large as before, nor should it be.

For tax reforms, perhaps it’s not exactly about increasing local government revenue, but about making the distribution of the tax burden more reasonable, such as through adjustments to the value-added tax and consumption tax. But how exactly should they be adjusted? Even a fraction of a percentage point difference in tax rates carries major consequences. So while scholars have offered various opinions, these proposals mean little until implemented.

Creating a strong social security system is what the government should do, and it shouldn’t be linked to consumption

You mentioned that investment’s share as a growth driver must decline. Given the slow pace of rebalancing so far, what structural changes are needed for Beijing to boost domestic demand and bring household consumption in line with global benchmarks?

There are two ways to increase income: raise wages, or raise property and asset income. In terms of wages, most citizens do not receive income from their labour from the state; they are employed by private enterprises. The state cannot simply mandate private sector wage hikes, it can only optimise the business environment in hopes that employment wages improve.
