For property and assets, this requires stabilising property values, improving financial asset performance and unlocking the latent value of rural land, such as through asset revitalisation.

The main thing that the government can do directly is to step up social security and strengthen spending on education, healthcare and pension security. China’s current savings rate is relatively high, so hopefully these measures can help reduce the savings rate and increase consumption.

But I hold a slightly different view from many economists on this issue, in that I think public welfare spending should be expanded regardless of whether it boosts consumption. Creating a strong social security system is what the government should do, and it shouldn’t be linked to consumption. Whether that triggers consumer spending is outside direct policy control, as citizens have a right to maintain a high savings rate even with a robust safety net.

The transition to raise consumption is a long-term process. Household consumption currently accounts for around 40 per cent of GDP in China.

In the United States, it accounts for around 70 per cent. But the number is so high because it is driven by housing, healthcare and education expenses. In China, healthcare and education – which form the bulk of service consumption – are not priced according to the market and are pretty affordable. In the US, healthcare and college tuition are relatively expensive. Do we really want to depend on this to drive consumption? I don’t think so.

Germany and Japan are better international benchmarks, with household consumption at around 50 to 55 per cent of their economies. But if China raises its consumption share by one percentage point per year, the rebalancing will still take over a decade.

Weak household consumption and industrial overcapacity have also driven China’s trade surplus to record highs. Beijing has signalled that it wants to rebalance these trade flows, but how successful can it be if demand remains anaemic?

China’s trade surplus issue isn’t just about weak domestic demand and overcapacity – it also requires a willing buyer. China cannot force foreign markets to purchase its goods. One country’s exports and another country’s imports are two sides of the same coin. The surplus arises because foreign markets genuinely need these goods and demand is substantial.

While foreign markets do want to restrict Chinese imports, what they really want is for China to set up factories there to sell the goods directly, while creating jobs and facilitating technology transfers. Trade barriers can’t restrict demand, they can only aim to take a cut of the profits and redistribute them.

From China’s side, imports will surely expand, especially as the appreciation of the yuan makes foreign goods and services cheaper. But whether this expansion is driven by goods or services is still uncertain.

Raising goods imports might be difficult. The things that China wants – such as graphics processing units and lithography equipment – others won’t sell. What else are we supposed to buy? American cars? That is hardly realistic.

Customs data – including the US$1.2 trillion trade surplus – only represents trade-in goods and has significant limitations.

Supply chains have become extremely complex. Many goods recorded as imports from Europe, Canada, Mexico and Southeast Asia might actually come from China, and vice versa. Goods that China imports that might not appear to come from the US or the European Union could actually be from these places too.

Importing more services is possible, but it is difficult to calculate. For example, spending money while travelling overseas and sending children abroad to study count as importing services, but customs doesn’t track this. It can only be calculated through foreign exchange data. The current account surplus theoretically includes services, but service data is more complicated in reality. It’s hard to say who holds the trade surplus for services.

China’s services imports have also been constrained by external political factors, such as strict visa policies or restricted access to certain educational programmes in the US. The fact that there are fewer Chinese students studying in the US now, that’s completely caused by the US themselves. Chinese people genuinely want to buy – previously goods, now services – but frankly, imports are severely restricted.

Many people have noted that data has now become a new factor of production, with some comparing it to oil. What’s your view on this?

Data as oil is just one analogy. I think it’s probably outdated now in the age of AI, though many data dispute rulings still work on the logic of this analogy.

But data is different from oil. First, if you extract it, that does not stop me from extracting it too – oil does not work that way. If there is oil under a piece of land, your extraction precludes mine. Data does not have that problem; we can both use it.

Second, oil is a natural resource – either you have it or you do not. Data availability, however, can be generated by policy. The data exists; it is simply a matter of whether you allow access. If you adjust usage policies – as Europe has done by relaxing certain rules – a vast amount of data suddenly becomes accessible. Therefore, the critical factor with data is what the law dictates: how much is recognised, what can be used, and under what restrictions. I think that regulatory boundary is the primary constraint.

Oil is a very tangible resource, so ownership is easy to determine. If it is under my land, the oil belongs to me. Data ownership is not nearly as simple. How do we regulate this? A unified model has yet to emerge globally, and it is difficult to see how one will.

There are other analogies to compare data to, and each one reveals different characteristics. For example, data is also inherently a product of labour. Let’s say you drive an electric vehicle. You’re constantly contributing your data to autonomous driving. The more you drive, the more data you contribute, but you don’t get paid for it – that’s frustrating. You continuously generate data for others to use, but you don’t receive corresponding compensation for the data generated by your actions, while others profit from this data.

Frankly speaking, when it comes to the development path of artificial intelligence, only China and the United States are relevant right now

How will this unique role of data affect the development of AI across different regions and their economies?

Frankly speaking, when it comes to the development path of artificial intelligence, only China and the United States are relevant right now. Other countries lack foundational models. Europe has a presence but faces real structural headwinds, including strict data rules.

The primary differentiator, then, boils down to who controls the data. In China, many core data assets are public property, meaning a wider variety of market participants can develop applications on top of them. In the US, however, commercial data holders always command a share of AI revenues.

Take the legal sector as an example. In China, legal data repositories are provided directly by the government via the Supreme People’s Court, allowing anyone to access them. In contrast, the US market is dominated by two private data vendors, so data is more expensive to access. The two vendors are also developing their own AI tools, making it difficult for independent developers to enter the space.

Similarly, Chinese municipalities and state-owned enterprises accumulate vast amounts of smart city and intelligent transport data. If held as private property, this data would be commercialised for profit. But if it is treated as basic infrastructure, the data owners do not extract direct profits from it.

From the perspective of benefiting AI development, accessible, high-quality data – not completely free, but requiring just a nominal cost – is definitely more beneficial for applications. Think about the many companies in China developing autonomous driving systems: a significant reason is the relatively readily available underlying data, thanks to the infrastructure built by the government in the early stages. You don’t just need vehicle data, you also need various other data like road data and traffic light data. It needs to form a complete ecosystem, and I think you can’t do without public data.

How close then is China to catching up with the US in the AI and tech race? In which areas is China leading, and where does it remain most vulnerable?

Whether China catches up or surpasses the US in AI development is not important. What matters is which country can better utilise AI and leverage it for its own economy. The US leads in foundational models and computing power. But does this constitute a guaranteed advantage for the industry? Not necessarily. It also depends on electricity availability, data access, as well as the industry to which you apply it and the results it generates.

For instance, the US excels in applications of AI in legal and financial fields. But for manufacturing, there are a few constraints. If a factory has not undergone digital transformation, or if its data is fragmented, practical application remains far off.

AI models are universally applicable; the key is whether your infrastructure is ready – meaning whether your data is structured and your workflows are prepared. This is a new challenge for everyone, but I think China’s manufacturing sector has more application potential than the US.

Cost is also a significant factor when it comes to widespread use for industry applications, and American models are considerably more expensive. Ultimately, the market will find a compromise in terms of cost-effectiveness.

Some have voiced concerns that advanced tech sectors like AI and humanoid robotics are at risk of “involution” in China. What are your thoughts on this, and how can policymakers prevent these strategic industries from falling into the same hyper-competitive trap?

Robotics are pretty competitive right now, but that’s not a risk yet. Humanoid robotics are still a long way off – the GPT moment for robots hasn’t arrived yet, so everyone thinks there’s still opportunities.

Involution happens when the technological path is already set, and everyone rushes in. In the photovoltaic sector, for example, the playbook is clear. Companies expand capacity aggressively along established pathways while making incremental technical refinements. But for humanoid robots, the approach remains undefined. The industry is still in an exploratory phase. There’s no overcapacity now since robots aren’t widely used yet. Having hundreds of firms enter a sector at this stage is more of an exploration rather than involution.

In contrast, I think AI large language models have already reached their limits in terms of competition. The “war of a hundred models” has consolidated because small firms cannot sustain the immense capital expenditures required for AI computing. The market has naturally winnowed down to a handful of players.

Regarding policy guidance, I think these industries are still too young. Policymakers must understand what they are regulating. For instance, policies for the photovoltaic sector are relatively easy to formulate because the crux of the problem is already known. But right now, for sectors like humanoid robots, even some industry insiders cannot yet predict where the technology will land.

While policymakers and entrepreneurs express optimism regarding technology, there is palpable public anxiety around AI, given stagnant wage growth and elevated youth unemployment. How worried should we be?

I think worrying is pointless because we have reached a point of no return. AI is here to stay, and we simply have to accept it. While many economists argue that AI will cause unemployment but simultaneously create new jobs, I am sceptical of how this rebalancing will play out.

There is likely to be significant demand for manual labour – which AI cannot replace for the time being – but displaced white-collar workers are probably unwilling and unable to take on these roles.

And actually, even manual labour faces risks of displacement. I recently spoke with representatives from a major logistics company who shared that the number of delivery riders is falling as networks and systems are optimised with AI. If short-distance truck transport also becomes unmanned in the future, then another group of jobs will disappear.

The immediate problem is university graduates, because entry-level jobs are increasingly hard to find. This is the case around the world. I don’t think China has reached a point where you can’t find work yet. There will always be work, even if it’s food delivery, but these are not the roles graduates seek. Or appropriate jobs may exist, but they are often not in first-tier cities or the graduates’ hometowns, which are usually the two preferred locations.

Though at present, even with unemployment, basic survival is not threatened for most because general economic conditions have improved. Even if young people go home to “lie flat” and rely on their parents, they won’t go hungry. But I think the biggest and most important problem with AI is the erosion of a sense of purpose. Even if basic needs are met, people will begin to ask whether there is any meaning in this way of living.

My imagination is limited, and I don’t know what new jobs will emerge. New types of demand will certainly appear, but I am sceptical that this will translate into a net increase in employment or successfully lower the unemployment rate on a macro level.

How then should governments manage the risks that AI brings to employment?

This brings us back to the same issue of social security. The issue is heavily discussed by academics around the world, but the shock has not yet reached a scale that forces major policy intervention in any country.

In extreme scenarios, people have proposed a universal basic income, but that requires even greater fiscal expenditure. The AI economy cannot sustain itself if workers lose their incomes and can no longer consume.

If everyone lost their jobs overnight, the solution might be clearer – universal basic income. The difficulty lies in the transition: many will lose their livelihoods while a small group becomes exceptionally wealthy. Taxing this wealth and creating alternative employment during this transition period will be difficult for any country. But we are not yet at that point, and you cannot mobilise state resources without an immediate crisis.

And even if we were to reach that point, it will be a completely different world. It’s hard to imagine what that would look like – our relationship with AI, how to tax AI and robots, and so on. These will all change.

But for that to happen, AI must enter the physical world. We need to see functioning, general-purpose robots first, and we are not there yet. While AI has progressed rapidly over the past six months, the marginal rate of development appears to be slowing. We have seen multiple cycles of AI optimism over the past half-century, but only recently did we see a breakthrough. It remains possible that artificial general intelligence or functional robotics will never truly materialise.

item.title: [SCMP] Openness must not be sacrificed in US science and tech policy on China
item.description:
When President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his planned September 24 visit – his first state-level visit to Washington in more than a decade – artificial intelligence is expected to be near the top of the agenda. Both administrations are preparing for their first formal dialogue on AI.

Washington has framed much of that conversation around the need for tighter controls on sensitive technologies. That framing is the problem.

For much of the debate over US science and technology policy towards China, Washington has been stuck on a false choice between engagement (scientific exchange, international students and collaborative research) and security (export controls, research restrictions and visa limits). The real choice is between indiscriminate restriction and disciplined risk management.
item.content:encoded:
When President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his planned September 24 visit – his first state-level visit to Washington in more than a decade – artificial intelligence is expected to be near the top of the agenda. Both administrations are preparing for their first formal dialogue on AI.

Washington has framed much of that conversation around the need for tighter controls on sensitive technologies. That framing is the problem.

For much of the debate over US science and technology policy towards China, Washington has been stuck on a false choice between engagement (scientific exchange, international students and collaborative research) and security (export controls, research restrictions and visa limits). The real choice is between indiscriminate restriction and disciplined risk management.

The security concerns are genuine. Some advanced technologies have clear military or intelligence applications. Universities must take seriously undisclosed affiliations, conflicts of commitment and improper technology transfer. Federal research security policy already requires extensive disclosure of appointments, foreign support, affiliations and potential conflicts of interest and commitment. Advanced computing, semiconductors, quantum science, biotechnology and AI all raise legitimate national security questions, largely because so much of the work is dual-use[end optional trim.

But acknowledging those risks does not require treating every interaction with China as equally dangerous. The challenge is to protect what truly matters without damaging the openness that has long been one of America’s greatest scientific strengths.

Smart openness starts from a simple premise: technologies are not equally sensitive and not every Chinese institution carries the same risk. Military-relevant quantum sensing is not cooperation in basic mathematics or astrophysics. A researcher who conceals ties to a defence laboratory has little in common with a Chinese graduate student studying theoretical chemistry.

Policymakers should ask not only what a measure prevents China from obtaining, but what it costs the US in lost talent, weaker collaboration, slower innovation and incentives for other countries to reduce their dependence on American technology. That calculation is too often missing.

Policy too often blurs those distinctions. Once national security becomes the primary lens for nearly every scientific interaction with China, agencies and universities turn deeply risk-averse. Restrictions spread, compliance burdens grow and institutions abandon perfectly legal activities because they look politically risky.

The result can be self-defeating: measures meant to protect American technological leadership can erode elements of the research system that produce it. Research Caroline Wagner and I conducted for the Quincy Institute has argued that a more sustainable approach would distinguish genuine security risks from ordinary international scientific collaboration, rather than treat broad categories of China-related activity as inherently suspect.

American pre-eminence in science was built in substantial part on imported knowledge and talent. The National Science Board reports that foreign-born workers accounted for 43 per cent of the US science and engineering workforce at the doctorate level in 2021; among foreign-born science and engineering workers, China is one of the two leading countries of origin.

Chinese students and researchers have made tangible contributions to American science and technology. China has also gained substantially from its access to the US research ecosystem, and concerns about technology transfer are well founded. Policy has to hold both facts at once.

Washington should begin by defining critical technologies more narrowly and updating those definitions regularly. Controls should focus on identifiable capabilities with plausible national security consequences, not on sprawling categories like “AI” or “biotechnology.” A “small yard, high fence” approach works only if the yard stays small.

The government should also build a genuinely tiered framework for international research collaboration. The most sensitive technologies, and institutions closely tied to China’s military and security apparatus, warrant heightened scrutiny or outright prohibition. Dual-use research should proceed under disclosure rules, access controls and institutional review. Fundamental research outside those categories should remain open.

Washington should move away from nationality-based screening as well. Visa and research-access decisions should turn on affiliations, research fields, access to controlled information and disclosure records – not on citizenship or country of birth. A Chinese passport is not evidence of a security threat.

Universities receiving substantial federal funding should maintain serious research-security capabilities, conduct due diligence on sensitive collaborations and enforce disclosure requirements. In return, universities need clearer and more consistent federal rules. Institutions should not be punished after the fact because a government assessment shifted.

Washington also needs a firmer distinction between disclosure violations and espionage. Researchers who hide material foreign affiliations or funding should face consequences. But a disclosure failure is not by itself proof of illicit technology transfer.

The United States should treat talent attraction as a national security asset. Foreign students who earn advanced American degrees in important scientific and engineering fields deserve clearer pathways to stay, subject to appropriate screening. It makes little strategic sense to educate exceptional people, then push them to build their careers elsewhere.

The importance of this talent pool is particularly evident in advanced science and engineering: more than half of doctorate-level computer and mathematical scientists and engineers working in the US were born abroad. In the competition for scientific talent, the ability to attract and retain such researchers is one of America’s most important structural advantages.

Finally, major restrictions should face a competitiveness test. Policymakers should ask not only what a measure prevents China from obtaining, but what it costs the US in lost talent, weaker collaboration, slower innovation and incentives for other countries to reduce their dependence on American technology. That calculation is too often missing.

The competition runs deeper than technology. It is a contest over where the world’s best scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs choose to build their careers, and openness remains a decisive American advantage. Access to China’s talent pool has real strategic value.

The US does not have to choose between security and openness, though it does have to get better at both. A good place to start is by re-energising the US-China Science and Technology Cooperation Agreement, revised and extended for five years in December 2024. The amended agreement already comes close to the model we need: it limits government-to-government cooperation to basic research while adding stronger safeguards concerning national security, intellectual property, transparency, data reciprocity, and researcher safety and security.

Rather than retreat from scientific engagement, Washington should build on it, drawing sharper lines around genuinely sensitive technologies while preserving room for collaboration where the risks are manageable.

The measure of a successful China policy is not how many doors America can close. It is whether the country can protect what needs protecting without sacrificing the openness, international talent and collaboration that have long been among its greatest sources of strength.

item.title: [SCMP] Heading to America to bridge the gap in US-China relations
item.description:
Before boarding my flight to Boston late last month, I spent the better part of three days doing something I never imagined I would do in more than 30 years of covering China: scrubbing my phone. Old emails, screenshots, WeChat threads that might be read the wrong way, anything that could be misconstrued in an airport interview room – all deleted, just in case.

I was not being paranoid. I was following advice now routinely passed among Chinese travellers to the United States: carry a clean phone, or better yet, a burner. American officials, academics and business travellers headed into China have long been told the same thing. Two sets of citizens, one shared instinct – that what is on your phone could get you into trouble on the other side.

As it turned out, my entry into the US was swift and unremarkable. No locked room, no confiscated devices, none of the horror stories that have circulated among Chinese academics in recent years. The gap between what I feared and what happened was, in miniature, what I have spent 35 years writing about: the gap between perception and reality in US-China relations. It is also the reason I am here.
item.content:encoded:
Before boarding my flight to Boston late last month, I spent the better part of three days doing something I never imagined I would do in more than 30 years of covering China: scrubbing my phone. Old emails, screenshots, WeChat threads that might be read the wrong way, anything that could be misconstrued in an airport interview room – all deleted, just in case.

I was not being paranoid. I was following advice now routinely passed among Chinese travellers to the United States: carry a clean phone, or better yet, a burner. American officials, academics and business travellers headed into China have long been told the same thing. Two sets of citizens, one shared instinct – that what is on your phone could get you into trouble on the other side.

As it turned out, my entry into the US was swift and unremarkable. No locked room, no confiscated devices, none of the horror stories that have circulated among Chinese academics in recent years. The gap between what I feared and what happened was, in miniature, what I have spent 35 years writing about: the gap between perception and reality in US-China relations. It is also the reason I am here.

Beginning this month, I take up a one-year appointment as a senior visiting scholar at the Rajawali Foundation Institute for Asia at the Harvard Kennedy School. My purpose is straightforward to state and harder to fulfil: to sit down with American thought leaders across the political spectrum and ask them where they think this relationship is headed, and whether conflict is as inevitable as it now appears.

To understand why this question matters so much, a brief look back is useful. The relationship began its current downward spiral in 2018, when the first Trump administration launched its opening salvo in the trade war. At the time, the confrontation felt sudden and jarring. It was not, in fact, sudden at all. Grievances had been quietly accumulating for decades across government, industry, trade, academia, science and technology. What changed in 2018 was that those grievances finally found their outlet.

Layered on top were structural anxieties. In Washington, there is the perceived erosion of American primacy in manufacturing and superpower status. In Beijing, there is a mirror-image worry: that a declining but still-dominant America, unwilling to accept the reality of a rising China, is bent on containing its development, through tariffs, technology export controls and alliances built for that purpose.

That mutual anxiety, in turn, fed less rational forces on both sides of the Pacific: incomplete narratives, hostile rhetoric, rumour dressed as fact, all doing damage to how each public sees the other. In Washington, there is a wry observation that American politicians agree on almost nothing except the need to get tough on China. In China, public sentiment towards the US has turned sour.

The goodwill accumulated over decades of engagement has largely evaporated, replaced by mutual suspicion and precaution – of which my scrubbed phone is a small but telling example.

None of this is to dismiss the seriousness of the moment. In the past fortnight alone, US Treasury officials have floated the possibility of sanctioning Chinese banks over their dealings with Iran, a suggestion that drew a sharp pushback from Beijing.

Long Guoqiang, deputy director general of the Development Research Centre of the State Council, a leading government think tank, captured the prevailing mood in Beijing when he warned recently that the US remains “the biggest external source of uncertainty affecting China’s path to modernisation”. He argues that American containment of China will persist and intensify over the long run, notwithstanding the trade war truce.

Long’s warning is not wrong. But a truce, however temporary, is also an opening. After their Beijing summit in May, President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are set to meet three more times this year: Xi is expected in Washington later this month, with further encounters likely on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and G20 leaders’ meetings in November and December.

Much of the coverage of these meetings will, understandably, focus on tangible deliverables – deals on trade, investment, technology. But Beijing and Washington might also use the moment to look at the bigger picture, along three tracks that receive far less airtime than they should.

On global challenges, can both powers still cooperate on climate change and future pandemics, even if the current US administration shows little enthusiasm for the former?

On engagement, law enforcement cooperation – against transnational crime, the booming scam-centre operations along China’s periphery, and the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals into North America – is a shining example. Quiet cooperation on precursor chemicals continued even through the worst of the trade war, proof that narrow, mutually beneficial arrangements can survive broader hostility when both sides see a direct interest in results.

I am a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict

And on global regulation, can the two governments find common ground in governing artificial intelligence, space and other emerging technologies?

Right now, discourse in both capitals dwells overwhelmingly on the negative. Far less is said about where cooperation remains not just possible but necessary.

That is what I intend to spend the next year finding out. I am, by long habit of observation, a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict. From Cambridge, I plan to reach beyond the think tanks most familiar to a China watcher, including into quarters not typically friendly to Beijing’s view of the world, setting aside my instincts and assumptions as best I can.

What will I find by the time this fellowship ends? I do not know. But having spent three decades chronicling how perception so often diverges from reality in this relationship, I remain hopeful that reality, properly examined, still leaves room for two great powers to coexist – durably, and peacefully – for everyone’s sake.

item.title: [SCMP] Exclusive: The Boar brings authentic British pub experience to Hong Kong’s Central
item.description:
If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening.

“I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.”

Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s.

If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening.

“I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.”

Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s.

With five restaurants already in his portfolio, the British restaurateur is finally opening something that connects him to his roots, but with a name that pays homage to his time in both Hong Kong and Britain. “Boars are the largest land mammals in Hong Kong, but you can also find them all around the UK,” explains Richardson. “Here, they’re kind of loved, aren’t they? You walk up The Peak, and people are super excited to see a little family of boars walking around. I quite enjoy it.”

Behind the pass, he has brought on two British chefs with fine-dining pedigrees: executive chef Graham Long, who has worked in Michelin-rated kitchens across London and launched culinary concepts for luxury hotels in Hong Kong. Day-to-day kitchen operations are run by head chef Jake Bennett, who cut his teeth at several Simon Rogan restaurants, including three-Michelin-star L’Enclume in Britain’s Lake District. Most recently, he was at The Baker and The Bottleman, in Wan Chai.

“I jumped on board as soon as I found out [Richardson was opening a pub],” says Long. He recalls how the pair began brainstorming the making of The Boar over a few pints.

“I’ve always felt that pubs were missing in Hong Kong to a degree. You’d think there would be more, given Hong Kong’s history and the expat community that’s here.”

Despite its name, however, the pub and dining room will not be serving wild boar. In Hong Kong, it’s illegal to kill or capture the animal. In Britain, they were hunted to extinction several hundred years ago, before being reintroduced into the ecosystem in recent decades by farms. “I’ve cooked it professionally before. It’s not that common any more, but we used to get it from our game dealer. I actually prefer normal pork, to be honest, but it’s nice,” Long admits.

So, if boar is not on the menu, what is? Classic pub grub, of course, including Welsh rarebit, sticky toffee pudding and pork cheek and lobster pie, as well as courses that speak to British sensibilities, such as Eton mess and coronation chicken salad.

With both chefs coming from haute-cuisine backgrounds, the dishes reflect their technical discipline. “We want to make the best version of everything. Yes, we’re going to do fish and chips, but we want to make sure it’s the best fish and chips we can possibly do,” Long explains.

As for their Scotch eggs, these will be made with British sausage meat, black pudding and Japanese eggs, then fried to order. “You know, nothing beats a Scotch egg. Hopefully, nothing will beat our Scotch egg,” says Long.

The Boar will offer two menus, with “downstairs” serving casual bites such as prawn cocktail toast, the signature BLT sandwich, Guinness and treacle bread with salted English butter, broccoli and Stichelton tart, and more, while “upstairs” hosts a more formal dining format, with celeriac and mushroom Wellington, roasted turbot chop, baked Chilean sea bass and chargrilled rib-eye steak to look forward to. (Sunday roasts are in the works, too.) “It’s where we get to have a little bit more fun, be a bit more chef-y, have a few more luxury ingredients and a more sit-down experience,” says Long.

One of the highlights of the upstairs menu is the roasted duck, dry-aged for two weeks in-house – no short cuts, all processed by the Boar team – and served with buttered turnips, carrots, a sauce of port and citrus, and toller’s pie, a play on the timeless shepherd’s pie in reference to the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a medium-sized gun-dog breed traditionally trained by hunters to find, flush out and retrieve shot game.

Moving into Flaming Frango’s old space on Elgin Street, the two-storey location, with an expansive ground floor and quirky structural nooks, has just the right bones to make it feel like a British pub – but Richardson has a fresher take in mind.

“We want it to feel more like a modern pub, because we feel it would be unjust to try and transport something you’d find from the laneways in London [to Hong Kong] – that would be too theatrical,” says Richardson. Instead, he explains he was inspired by his favourite pub, The Pelican, a Michelin Bib Gourmand spot in London’s Notting Hill neighbourhood.

“It’s a totally different experience from what people might know of the pub world, but the aesthetics, the feel, is that,” he says. “So, downstairs, think brighter colours and nice wood textures, but lots of nods to the things you might recognise from a pub back home, like the way we do the edgings on the tables and footrests and textures. And then when you move upstairs, this will have a different feel – more green, a bit more opulent.”

For Long and Richardson, The Boar is more than just another restaurant opening. “I spent most of my adult life in London and, generally, when I wasn’t working in a kitchen, I was in a pub,” recalls Long, whose time in the city included a stint at two-Michelin-star Pied à Terre, then helmed by Shane Osborn.

“Wherever you grow up, everyone has their local pub,” Long says. “[A pub is] shaped by the community that it’s in.”

Richardson agrees: “When I’m back home [in Britain, the go-to pub is] just wherever my friends are.”

Creating that sense of community here in Hong Kong – where both restaurateur and chef have settled, and for not an insignificant amount of time – is top of their minds when it comes to shaping the destination. “We let the food, the drinks and the genuine hospitality speak for themselves,” says Richardson, adding that every visit to The Boar “feels like coming home”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s shrinking population may be a blessing, not a curse
item.description:
There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president.

But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead.

While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60.
item.content:encoded:
There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president.

But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead.

While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60.

The reaction was swift and familiar: China will grow old before it grows rich, its workforce will hollow out, its pension system will buckle, its ascent will end.

Some concerns are warranted. If 2.1 children per woman is the population replacement rate, then those countries with the lowest birth rates – China at 0.63, Japan at 0.6, and South Korea at 0.46 – are projected by 2050 to experience population declines of 20-30 per cent relative to 2023; their share of the population aged 65 and over to reach 30-40 per cent; and older workers (aged 45 and over) to comprise 60 per cent of the labour force.

But that’s not the whole story. In fact, much of it is missing, and the alarm has outrun the analysis. “What if the historical evidence tells us that collapsing birth rates, paradoxically, are good for the economy,” economist Joeri Schasfoort asks in his YouTube channel, “because they force companies to innovate?”

He was referring to a groundbreaking paper, “Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy”, which was published in July by the National Bureau of Economic Research in the United States and has attracted widespread interest in academic and policymaking circles.

The four economists – Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne and Andrew Scott – studied seven decades of demographic change across more than 100 countries and 722 American local labour markets. They find that countries where birth rates fell earlier and further did not grow more slowly. Rather, they grew faster per head, and total output did not decline.

Something is compensating for the missing hands. The authors argue that it’s technology

“Contrary to the widespread expectation that these trends hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings,” they wrote.

They found that these patterns could not be explained by educational upgrading and other likely factors. Rather, they reflected “the endogenous, labour-saving response of technology to the scarcity of younger workers”.

The size of the effect is striking. A country with a birth rate one percentage point lower in 1950 saw income per working-age adult roughly a quarter higher 50 years later, or about half a percentage point (0.46 per cent) of additional growth every year, compounding across two generations. The same pattern appears in American regions, measured through wages.

There is an obvious mathematical objection: the same output divided among fewer workers naturally produces a higher figure per worker. But the study finds no meaningful decline in total output either. Something is compensating for the missing hands.

The authors argue that it’s technology. When young workers become scarce and expensive, employers buy machines. Economies with falling birth rates register faster productivity growth, heavier investment in equipment, a shift of employment from labour-intensive industries towards research-intensive ones, and more patenting in automation. The productivity gains are large enough to offset the lost labour entirely.

The most persuasive test uses the second world war. Military casualties fell overwhelmingly on young men; civilian casualties fell across all ages. Fifty years later, countries that lost population to civilian deaths were poorer per head. Those that lost young men were measurably richer. It is not population loss that damages an economy, but the wrong kind of it.

As the economists wrote: “Exploiting cross-country variation in WWII military and civilian deaths, we find that declines in younger population, rather than population size per se, drive our results [of productivity and growth].”

China’s record is consistent with this. It does not have a labour shortage; rather the opposite. Youth unemployment reached 17.9 per cent in July as a record 12.7 million graduates entered the market. That is an argument for patience rather than panic: the cohorts that will genuinely be scarce are yet to come.

Its factories installed 295,000 industrial robots in 2024 – 54 per cent of the global total – bringing the operational stock past two million units, the largest anywhere. Robot density rose 17 per cent in a single year, and Chinese manufacturers outsold foreign suppliers at home for the first time. That’s 166 robots per 10,000 employees, according to China’s statistics bureau. Robotics, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing sit at the centre of the 15th five-year plan. The economy grew by 5 per cent last year on a record trade surplus.

None of these neglect genuine problems. The state pension fund for urban workers may be exhausted by the middle of the next decade. In 2023, 11 of 31 provinces were running deficits. But that is a question of who pays, not whether the wealth exists. If output holds steady while the workforce shrinks, the resources are there. Moving them from prosperous coastal provinces to depleted industrial ones is a political task, not a demographic one.

The researchers themselves are cautious. The decline in China, they note, will be faster and larger than anything in their data, and their evidence for the technological mechanism is indirect. Or, as Schasfoort has observed, their findings describe the past and may not predict the future.

However, that caution cuts both ways. The pessimistic case rests entirely on projections. The optimistic case rests on what has actually occurred across 70 years and most of the world.

China now contemplates spending an estimated 180 billion yuan (US$26.76 billion) this year alone to lift the birth rate – subsidies, free preschool, funded fertility treatment. Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore have all tried variations of this, with more generous provisions and greater personal freedom. All have failed.

The focus should be on preparing for a smaller, older, more automated workforce than trying to get women to have more babies when most other socio-economic factors cause them to have fewer or no children.

Demography is not destiny. Beijing should focus on fighting the right war – advancing technology on all fronts.

item.title: [SCMP] From Ohio to Hong Kong: former NBA player Bryant Austin’s basketball journey
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Lima, Ohio, a small city in the United States, to high-school sweethearts, in 1987. My childhood was split between the inner city and my great-grandparents’ farm: livestock, a wood-burning furnace, the whole thing. Although both my parents had been athletes, I never saw them in their prime. Instead, I watched my older sister. My parents split up when I was six or seven, and we moved to Columbus. My mum worked four jobs to support us. Money was tight, but there were constants: Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan films, and a meal at a Chinese restaurant as a reward when I did well at school.

AT MY GRANDFATHER’S house, I’d sit for hours watching old VHS basketball tapes. There was Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan. One clip stayed with me – a young Kobe Bryant growing up in Italy, speaking Italian, playing basketball on the other side of the world (his father played for an Italian team). Something shifted in me. I started to dream of playing overseas. I was also quietly obsessed with Asia. I watched anime, drew constantly – it felt like a world I couldn’t explain to anyone in Ohio. Every year, our teacher asked us what our top three ambitions were. Mine never changed: professional basketball player, marine biologist, or lawyer. In that order. I was already manifesting it.

MY SISTER IS two years older than me, and she was my hero before I knew what that meant. At school, she protected me from bullies, from older boys who wanted to jump me. When I was 13, a group of men broke into our home and held our family hostage at gunpoint for hours. While two of them left to move what they had stolen, one stayed behind. My sister – 15, maybe 16 then – wrestled the gun away from him. She shot him in the face. She saved all of us.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Lima, Ohio, a small city in the United States, to high-school sweethearts, in 1987. My childhood was split between the inner city and my great-grandparents’ farm: livestock, a wood-burning furnace, the whole thing. Although both my parents had been athletes, I never saw them in their prime. Instead, I watched my older sister. My parents split up when I was six or seven, and we moved to Columbus. My mum worked four jobs to support us. Money was tight, but there were constants: Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan films, and a meal at a Chinese restaurant as a reward when I did well at school.

AT MY GRANDFATHER’S house, I’d sit for hours watching old VHS basketball tapes. There was Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan. One clip stayed with me – a young Kobe Bryant growing up in Italy, speaking Italian, playing basketball on the other side of the world (his father played for an Italian team). Something shifted in me. I started to dream of playing overseas. I was also quietly obsessed with Asia. I watched anime, drew constantly – it felt like a world I couldn’t explain to anyone in Ohio. Every year, our teacher asked us what our top three ambitions were. Mine never changed: professional basketball player, marine biologist, or lawyer. In that order. I was already manifesting it.

MY SISTER IS two years older than me, and she was my hero before I knew what that meant. At school, she protected me from bullies, from older boys who wanted to jump me. When I was 13, a group of men broke into our home and held our family hostage at gunpoint for hours. While two of them left to move what they had stolen, one stayed behind. My sister – 15, maybe 16 then – wrestled the gun away from him. She shot him in the face. She saved all of us.

I WASN’T AN immediate star. I have always been super-introverted, and had anxiety interacting with crowds and fans. I didn’t make varsity until my senior year. No one was knocking down my door offering scholarships. So, I started clicking through university websites, cold-emailing coaches. That’s how mundane it was. I ended up playing at Notre Dame College, then Columbus State and Indiana Tech. After graduating, I played in the professional minor leagues, but it wasn’t enough.

MY TURNING POINT was a high-profile tournament in Portsmouth, Virginia, where I was up against players from Duke, Kentucky, North Carolina – the big blue-blood universities. I didn’t just hold my own; I dominated. There was a rage in me, the accumulated weight of being overlooked for years. My trainer and mentor, Greg “Radar” Williamson, spent two years helping me prepare for that moment.

BY THE END, three NBA (National Basketball Association) agents were competing to represent me: Andre Buck, who worked with LeBron James; Sean Rooks, who had played alongside Kobe and Shaq (Shaquille O’Neal); and John Spencer, who had a past playing in Hong Kong’s A1 Division against Yao Ming and China’s national team. I signed with John. At the time, I didn’t realise how significant he would become to me.

AT 25, I WAS drafted into the NBA Development League by the Fort Wayne Mad Ants. It was overwhelming. You’re meeting Magic Johnson and all these star players. So, on one side, you’re starstruck and on the other side, you’re thinking, “I’m supposed to be here.”

I BROKE MY thumb the day before training camp. I decided to play through it without a cast because the NBA is so cutthroat, I couldn’t risk losing my shot. I also had a newborn son at home and no room for excuses. That season, I was also working as an overnight carer for disabled adults and as a substitute teacher. Three jobs, one broken thumb, a new baby. On the court, I was playing beside Khris Middleton, who would go on to become an NBA All-Star. I was proud, exhausted and watching every penny.

AT THE END of that season, the team president, Jeff Potter, sat me down and was honest with me. He advised me to go overseas, build my profile and then come back, as I wasn’t getting much court time alongside so many more experienced players. John Spencer helped me get a contract in Israel. And when I landed in Tel Aviv (in October 2013), I was in heaven. I had an apartment right by the sea. The city was beautiful: new culture, new language, new food. Then came the blood clot.

I PLAYED THROUGH what I thought was a severe calf strain for a month – it felt like my leg was being sawn off – but ego and pride refused to let me sit it out. I had developed a blood clot in my leg and then one in my lung and didn’t know it. The pain started in my chest, and nearly ended everything – not just my career, but my life.

I WAS BACK home in the US (by December 2013), had almost died and was injecting blood thinners daily. The doctors told me I couldn’t play. I was depressed for six months. I didn’t talk to many people, I just retreated into myself and stopped training. I’d fought all those years to have my name on that jersey. Having it taken away so suddenly left me in a dark place. Then, a new drug, Xarelto, appeared and gave my cardiologist enough confidence to clear me. That same week (in April 2014), without knowing any of this, John Spencer called out of nowhere and asked if I’d go to Hong Kong. The league had been closed to American imports since the 2008 financial crisis, but had just reopened and the money was good. I call that timing a call from God.

I STEPPED OFF the plane into the heat and humidity, and looked up at the skyline. Instantly, I fell completely in love. I saw bamboo scaffolding around glass towers and felt like I’d walked onto a Rush Hour set. Apparently, I was all over the local media. My American teammate, Reggie Johnson, had full culture shock; the density, the noise, strangers staring at two tall black guys on trains and in lifts. But I didn’t mind any of it. It felt like arriving somewhere I’d been dreaming of since I was a kid.

THE BASKETBALL SYSTEM in Hong Kong is unlike anywhere else; it’s fast-paced and kind of chaotic. We won the championship with the Eastern Long Lions (now Hong Kong Eastern) team. I flew my mum over for the final and we celebrated with champagne.

IN AUGUST 2014, I went to Bangkok to party for a week, to celebrate my Hong Kong championship with my close friend and NBA G League teammate, Tommy Smith, who works with me today. I asked to train with his team to stay sharp between nights out. They begged me to stay and I said yes. I played in the Thai Super League season, and then for an Indonesian team in Surabaya.

INSTEAD OF GOING back to the US, I realised that life had a plan for me in Asia, and specifically in Hong Kong – it always drew me in. Now, I play forward and point guard for Chongde Flying Eagle here in the A1 Division. When I first got here, the Hong Kong fans were crazy, following me around, asking for autographs, photos. I just love that they love basketball as much as I do. I started a basketball academy with just five kids. I’d turn up in my jersey on the street courts of Southorn Playground, Nathan Road and Victoria Park, and ask to join games. Kids would clock who I was and ask if I coached. That’s how my academy, League MVP, started – organically.

TODAY, OUR TEAM works with up to 150 local boys as well as international students here on holiday camps. We’ve worked with refugee children from Africa, India and Pakistan. One of the players I coached, Hong Kong-born David Muoka, became the first from the city to be drafted into the NBA.

WHAT I WANT for Hong Kong basketball is more visibility, more opportunity. There’s talent here. It just needs investment, time and belief. Hong Kong is an underdog, but there are a lot of passionate players, and I want them to win.

MY SON IS 13 now. Every summer, he comes over from Ohio. I wake him early – he hates it – and we’re in the gym by 5am. I never forced basketball on him, but once he chose it, I made it clear: no short cuts. We train hard, then we enjoy the city – Disneyland, Ocean Park, beaches, hotpot, the MTR. I push him to explore independently; this city is safe enough to do that.

TWELVE YEARS AFTER I arrived, Hong Kong is home – not a posting, or a chapter. I’m 38, still playing, still growing my business, still up early doing weights – my life is kind of consumed by basketball. I’m manifesting my end game – the best is yet to come. And I know I want to be here when the next kid from a Hong Kong court makes it somewhere nobody expected, and gives the city another reason to believe.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Nancy Kwan’s enduring legacy, six decades after the release of The World of Suzie Wong – interview
item.description:
To many, Nancy Kwan Ka-shen is the actress who rose to international stardom for her role in the 1960 film The World of Suzie Wong, based on the book of the same name, about a sex worker in Wan Chai who meets a wealthy American (played by William Holden). Kwan’s story, however, is far richer than any single role.

From breaking barriers for Asian actors in Hollywood and standing her ground in an industry that was rigid and often prejudiced, to founding her own ballet studio, producing films and television advertisements across Southeast Asia, and starring in more than 50 films spanning decades, she has lived a life of relentless creativity, resilience and grace.

Now 87, Kwan’s path to celebrity was as serendipitous as it was extraordinary. In August 1959, she stumbled upon a casting call for The World of Suzie Wong.
item.content:encoded:
To many, Nancy Kwan Ka-shen is the actress who rose to international stardom for her role in the 1960 film The World of Suzie Wong, based on the book of the same name, about a sex worker in Wan Chai who meets a wealthy American (played by William Holden). Kwan’s story, however, is far richer than any single role.

From breaking barriers for Asian actors in Hollywood and standing her ground in an industry that was rigid and often prejudiced, to founding her own ballet studio, producing films and television advertisements across Southeast Asia, and starring in more than 50 films spanning decades, she has lived a life of relentless creativity, resilience and grace.

Now 87, Kwan’s path to celebrity was as serendipitous as it was extraordinary. In August 1959, she stumbled upon a casting call for The World of Suzie Wong.

“I thought it was dreadful because all I did was giggle,” she tells me over a FaceTime call from her home in Los Angeles, in the United States. “I was really quite silly. I was surprised I got a job at all. But they seemed to like it, so I ended up in Hollywood doing more screen tests. Eventually, I got the role.”

Initially, France Nuyen had been cast, but when the French-American actress withdrew, Kwan’s ballet-trained poise and expressive presence made her the perfect replacement. The film catapulted her to global fame, subtly transforming Hollywood’s perception of Asian women at a time when “yellowface” – casting non-Asian actors in make-up to portray Asian characters – was still widespread.

Even decades later, her magnetism remains palpable. Behind her, a poster of Suzie Wong seems almost to lean towards the camera, a reminder that the character and the woman who portrayed her remain inseparable in the public memory. Yet Kwan’s memoir, last year’s The World of Nancy Kwan, reveals a keen awareness of her own agency, her understanding that her story is as much about heritage and personal resilience as it is about fame.

Born in 1939 to Kwan Wing-hong, a prominent, Cambridge-educated Chinese architect, and Marquita Scott, a British model and aspiring actress who would leave the family before the start of World War II but later reconnect with her daughter in the US, Nancy grew up in a family whose legacy was intertwined with Hong Kong’s development and global affairs.

Her great-grandfather, Kwan Yuen-cheung, was the city’s first Western-trained dentist; her great-grandmother, Lai Amui, survived the mainland’s Taiping rebellion (1850-64) to become one of the first Western-trained nurses in Hong Kong. Her great-uncle Kwan King-leung studied alongside Dr Sun Yat-sen and later served as physician to the Empress Dowager of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911). “I don’t know if great-uncle Kwan King-leung’s friendship with Dr Sun Yat-sen endured, but I think it is extraordinary that the man who is considered the father of modern China spent his formative years in the Kwan household,” Kwan writes in her memoir.

Kwan also recalls how, although she has only hazy memories of it, her father (who later remarried) had to hide her and her brother in wicker baskets to travel to Macau by boat and then onwards to mainland China to flee the war after Japan’s attack on Hong Kong in 1941 – an event remembered locally as “Black Christmas”.

Later, Kwan learned that her father had served covertly with the British Army Aid Group, assisting soldiers stranded behind enemy lines in their escape from Japanese forces. Some media have even described him as a “Chinese James Bond”. The family returned to Hong Kong in 1945, resuming their lives amid the city’s post-war recovery.

Hollywood was never Kwan’s first passion. Ballet had captivated her from childhood, and she trained in Britain, attending the prestigious Royal Ballet School, in London.

“I’ve always continued with ballet,” she says. “Then I branched out – jazz and other kinds of dance. Nowadays, I take tai chi.”

That disciplined movement would define her screen presence, most memorably in Flower Drum Song (1961).

“Hermes Pan, the choreographer, told us, ‘Don’t dance like this; this is jazz.’ We did jazz because that’s what the piece called for. It was all about keeping ballet at bay,” she recalls, a glimmer of mischief in her eyes.

At the time of filming, Kwan had no idea how historic the movie would become.

“I just thought, ‘Oh, Flower Drum Song, all great.’ But it was the first time a major Hollywood studio made a film with a mostly Asian cast – that was a real achievement. I didn’t know the business that well back then,” she admits. “It wasn’t until my friend [the late Chinese-American actor] Benson Fong told me, ‘Nancy, this is the first time they’re making a film with an all-Asian cast,’ that I thought, ‘Wow, OK, this is bigger than I realised.’ It was very exciting.”

Decades later, that trail-blazing spirit echoed in the meteoric success of Crazy Rich Asians, the 2018 film adapted from Kevin Kwan’s 2013 novel, starring a predominantly Asian cast and capturing the global imagination. The connection is more than thematic: Kevin is Nancy’s cousin.

“Nancy really paved the way for me to pursue my own creativity,” Kevin, 53, tells me over the phone. “The first time I saw her in Flower Drum Song, I could hardly believe my eyes – just this glamorous creature in my own family. It was always inspiring.”

He fondly remembers the rare glimpses of authentic Hong Kong and the nuanced female characters Nancy brought to the screen. He recalls her performance in the late-1980s miniseries Noble House, adapted from the James Clavell novel, that was shot in Hong Kong, which also starred Pierce Brosnan and Deborah Raffin, as it offered him an immersive look at his heritage.

“It was remarkable to see her playing a sassy, empowered secretary, and years later, seeing her in Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story [1993] as Lee’s boss was another milestone,” he says. “She was there at every significant stage, paving the way for younger talent, for stories like my own.”

Kevin attributes her success to her perseverance.

“She never gave up, no matter the hardships or controversies. She was the first woman to return to Hong Kong and run her own film studio, and she got through everything with determination. Even now, in her 80s, she carries herself with the energy and poise of someone decades younger – not just physically, but in spirit,” he says.

Nancy navigated Hollywood’s entrenched racial attitudes, which often reduced Asian actors to exoticised caricatures. She admired Anna May Wong – considered to be the first Chinese-American film star in Hollywood, in the 20s – and her ability to get through the barriers she faced.

“I didn’t know much about her until I came to Hollywood and found out she was really the first Asian actress from Los Angeles,” Nancy recalls. “I think I met her niece – she comes to a lot of my screenings and book signings – a very lovely girl. I read up on Anna May Wong and even did a documentary about her, doing the voice-over, so I learned a lot about the struggles she faced, especially when they didn’t use Asian actors – they used Caucasians dressed up as Asians, like Luise Rainer in The Good Earth [1937]. She was trying to work during that era, and it was very difficult. When we did Flower Drum Song, the producer told me [Wong] was going to have a role, and I was so excited to work with her. Sadly, she passed away just a few weeks before filming.”

Private life and career are intertwined in Kwan’s reflections. Decades spent in Los Angeles, a brief return to Hong Kong to manage her father’s company and the routines of long-term partnership and care illustrate a life shaped by both focus and balance.

“I came back when my father was ill and, sadly, he passed away,” she recalls. “After that, I was offered the chance to run a company in Hong Kong. I thought, ‘Why not?’ But I quickly realised it wasn’t for me. Being a CEO meant more lunches and meetings than actual work – I wanted to be on the ground, doing things myself. By then, my son was ready to start high school, so that’s why I moved back to Los Angeles.”

Her memoir is filled with vivid, intimate stories of Hollywood encounters. She recounts her then-boyfriend Maximilian Schell, in a fit of jealous rage, hurling his “Best Actor” Oscar at her, and the time she turned down the lead opposite Elvis Presley in Blue Hawaii (1961).

“I was asked to meet someone at Paramount Studios about a film,” she recalls. “I didn’t know it was Elvis. I walk onto this empty stage, and then suddenly, he appears with a few of his friends. He sat me down and sang the ‘Hawaiian Wedding Song’ – I was floored. He was such an entertainer. Of course, I applauded and made a fool of myself.”

Despite the allure, Kwan politely declined. “I told them I’d already signed for Flower Drum Song. Both roles were historic in their own way, but I felt committed to this one,” she says.

She fondly remembers meeting Ursula Andress, who casually mentioned she was about to star in a “B” movie called “007” with Sean Connery, and her own friendship with Bruce Lee, whom she first met in Hong Kong and grew close to while filming The Wrecking Crew (1968), for which he served as martial-arts adviser.

“He was going to teach Sharon [Tate] and me some kung fu for a fight scene. That’s how I got to know Bruce quite well. We would hang out at the house, and he often told me about his plans to return to Hong Kong and make martial-arts films,” she remembers.

That now-famous fight scene between Tate and Kwan is immortalised in Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 film, Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, in which Margot Robbie, playing Tate, is shown watching that exact scene in a cinema. In her memoir, Kwan also reflects on Tate’s kind nature and tragic death, revealing the personal impact it had on her.

The memoir confronts other heartbreaks. Kwan opens up about the loss of her son and “best friend”, Bernie Pock, whom she shared with her first husband, Peter Pock.

Born in Austria and raised in Hong Kong, Bernie was fluent in Cantonese, adored and mastered martial arts and was described as wise beyond his years. Known for his kindness – he once sheltered a homeless boy – Bernie was a stunt performer in Los Angeles when he was diagnosed with Aids, contracted from a woman he loved and later married, before he died, in 1996, aged 33.

Even in the shadow of loss, Bernie refused to let their story end in tragedy. Together with Kwan and her new husband, Vienna-born actor and producer Norbert Meisel, now aged 96, the family completed a final project: Rebellious (also known as The Biker Poet), a 1995 film about a biker discovering himself, a testament to Bernie’s creativity and enduring spirit.

In the years since, Kwan has devoted herself to Aids awareness advocacy, channelling her grief into purpose. She also wrote Celebration of a Life: Memories of My Son (1997), a memoir that honours Bernie and preserves his memory.

Arthur Dong, the Oscar-nominated filmmaker and American Book Award-winning author of Forbidden City, USA (2014), has interviewed Kwan on many occasions over the past 20 years. He recalls the magnetic presence she brought to every set.

“Nancy candidly confronts the xenophobic and sexist attitudes that once branded her a ‘real-life China doll’, despite the pivotal influence of producer and mentor Ray Stark, who promoted her as a ‘girl of many nations’.”

Kwan became a symbol of possibility for actors navigating Hollywood’s rigid and often Eurocentric standards.

“I am from the East and West. My father is Chinese, my mother is English, and bringing that together … I feel very proud. The world is getting smaller, we recognise each other more and I wish I had even more cultural roots to embrace. It’s a wonderful thing,” she reflects.

“Nancy was among the most beautifully photographed women of the 60s,” notes Dong.

“That she was biracial made her worldwide popularity even more historic, particularly in the image- and race-conscious world of entertainment.”

Her pragmatism has always stood out to him. “In 2004, when I asked her to sum up the roller-coaster trajectory of her career, she replied, ‘What’s fair in life? There’s no fairness. As an actor, you have to keep that in mind; otherwise, you might as well not be in this business. Nothing lasts forever. Times change.’”

Even in her mid-80s, Kwan retains vitality and joy. Asked what she does to relax, she replies, “Probably tai chi, meditation […] that is the way I am.”

Her energy and elegance are palpable. “I’ve been in the business a long time now. I made my mark in the 60s, and now it’s [the mid-2020s]. It’s been a long journey, and I’ve met so many people along the way. Many Asian actors I know are still working, thank goodness, and television has opened up opportunities for them.”

Any advice for budding artists? “Just work hard,” she says. “Do what you can, steadily. Go out there. The film business is changing, too.”

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Thailand’s bid to wire the world’s AI revolution
item.description:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
In the rush to build an AI future, semiconductors are the silicon rock stars that soak up all the applause. Yet behind the curtain, an unglamorous stagehand is doing much of the heavy lifting.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the copper-laced panels inside every mobile phone, car key fob, digital camera and data-centre server rack on Earth. Without them, even the most advanced AI chip would be useless, unable to process even a single line of code.

This year alone, more than 1 million square metres (10.8 million sq ft) of PCBs will roll out of WellTek Electronics’ factory in Ayutthaya – just one company’s contribution to Thailand’s scramble for an edge in the global tech supply chain.

“They are essential to our daily life. They are in all electronics you are using,” said WellTek founder Jennifer Deng, who established the Thai subsidiary of her China-based Jiangxi Welgao Electronics in Ayutthaya two years ago.

Thailand is now Southeast Asia’s No 1 producer of PCBs – often described as the nervous system of modern electronics, channelling essential signals through increasingly complex arrays of semiconductors, resistors and capacitors – and the fifth largest in the world.

Deng’s US$75 million WellTek plant, built in under a year, is the first of two planned for Ayutthaya, a major Thai industrial zone once dominated by Japanese carmakers and global electronics giants, now being rewired for the artificial intelligence age.

Circuitous success

Malaysia may lead the field in lucrative semiconductors and Vietnam in electronics assembly, but PCBs give Thailand its competitive advantage in Southeast Asia’s race for tech relevance.

Its rise in this niche owes as much to the trade wars triggered by Washington as it does to the smart timing of Thai authorities in welcoming global companies seeking new bases away from the tariff line of fire.

“The market demanded movement to Thailand,” Deng told This Week in Asia from WellTek’s Ayutthaya headquarters, where workers in crisp company polo shirts hustled down corridors beneath posters bearing the mantra “Conscience and Altruism”.

Over the next few years, Deng not only wants to build a second factory but treble output to more than 3.6 million square metres (38.8 million sq ft) of PCBs per year.

Thailand’s existing PCB industry gave it a head start over rivals, she said, explaining that “Europeans and Americans all requested we are outside of China, and our main partners are here in Thailand.”

Narit Therdsteerasukdi, secretary general of Thailand’s government-run Board of Investment, told an investor forum on Wednesday that the country was at a “turning point”.

Investment in the PCB and electronics component sector topped US$10 billion over the past three years, he revealed, calling this proof of how Thailand should pivot its economy.

“We need to restructure our economy … and the electronic industry, especially PCBs, is a very good example [of how to do it],” he said. “The key question is where do we go from here?”

For Narit, the country’s future growth depends on climbing the value chain, backed by a higher-skilled workforce trained for the AI age.

Printed fortunes

PCBs are a rare success story in a decade of patchy industrial policy that has left Thailand a regional growth laggard.

Many of the ideas floated to accelerate growth through new manufacturing chains and a splurge of foreign investment have been delayed, watered down or scrapped entirely on contact with the reality of delivering big infrastructure projects in a politically febrile kingdom.

Trade dispute and fuel-price spikes from distant wars have further hurt an economy that expanded just 2.4 per cent last year – a relative crawl compared with Vietnam’s 8 per cent.

Yet around 60 per cent of all new investment into Southeast Asia’s PCB industry has flowed into Thailand since 2023, according to the Thailand Printed Circuit Association.

Phutana Daoruang, the association’s general manager, said Thailand already had the PCB infrastructure, built up by a dozen or so Taiwanese firms, when Donald Trump’s first presidency fired the starting gun on companies fleeing US tariffs.

Thailand’s location and logistics networks, tax breaks, industrial estates and skilled workforce allowed the new factories to plug straight into electronics clusters like Ayutthaya, with the upgraded deep-sea port at Laem Chabang – a two-hour drive away – providing a maritime gateway to China.

“We pitched to compete with Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam as the fundamental infrastructure was already here,” Phutana told This Week in Asia.

“Thailand is quite suitable, we are quite strong in logistics and electricity supply is stable – especially compared with Vietnam and Malaysia.”

There are now around 50 PCB companies in the country, forming a sector that meets a modest 5 per cent of world demand but is eager to capture more of a global market forecast to reach US$100 billion in the coming years.

The ambition is to export eight to 10 times more PCBs than Thailand currently does – reaching roughly US$18 billion to US$25 billion in trade volume and a 20 per cent global market share.

Lofty as that sounds, it may not be impossible given the trillions of dollars flowing into data centres that need increasingly complex layers of PCBs.

“It’s quite complicated and uses very specialised material,” Phutana said of PCB manufacturing. “Thailand has the fundamentals to do it.”

Running hot

AI has changed the stakes for PCB manufacturers. A PCB destined for use with an AI accelerator card – roughly the size of a sheet of A4 paper – is a very different beast from the boards that are found inside car key fobs.

Densely layered with winding copper traces that resemble an illuminated cityscape from above, these boards must survive extreme heat and power loads while shuttling vastly more data at far higher speeds, providing the physical foundations for the AI chips crunching numbers across the region’s data centres.
