“Both leaders need to please a domestic audience. Pushing a line that a leader is tough is always popular, especially when it does not cost the taxpayer anything,” Lankov said.

“I do not think there is any amount of protest that Japan can make that will change how Russia represents World War II. That is especially the case now as Russia emphasises victory over Japan at the same time as it is improving relations with North Korea and China.”

Brown said that any lingering hopes that Moscow and Tokyo might come to some agreement on joint development of the southern Kuril Islands – as appeared possible when former prime minister Shinzo Abe met Putin on several occasions a decade ago – had vanished.

“This must be a major disappointment to Russia because even this year it had hoped that it would be able to make progress on this issue with Takaichi, in part because she was Abe’s protege,” he said.

“But as is so often the way with Russia, they pushed harder when they detected softness and that very quickly killed off any engagement on the issue.”

item.title: [SCMP] Japan’s China-facing military build-up confronts labour, budget and political limits
item.description:
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the third of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines the various challenges confronting Japan in its bid to expand its military.

Driven by the growing risk that a conflict over Taiwan could draw Tokyo into a high-intensity confrontation with Beijing, Japan is pursuing its most ambitious military transformation since World War II.

Tokyo is acquiring long-range missiles, embracing drones and expanding defence partnerships stretching from Canberra to London.
item.content:encoded:
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the third of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines the various challenges confronting Japan in its bid to expand its military.

Driven by the growing risk that a conflict over Taiwan could draw Tokyo into a high-intensity confrontation with Beijing, Japan is pursuing its most ambitious military transformation since World War II.

Tokyo is acquiring long-range missiles, embracing drones and expanding defence partnerships stretching from Canberra to London.

Yet, analysts say some of the toughest obstacles to the transformation may lie at home.

As Tokyo prepares to revise its strategic security documents by year’s end, its historic military build-up must contend with growing constraints.

These include a shrinking pool of military recruits, an ageing population, mounting fiscal pressures, an industrial base struggling to expand and lingering questions over how far the Japanese public would support the use of its ascendant military power.

Together, the pressures raise a fundamental question about the next phase of Japan’s transformation: not simply how much military capability Tokyo can acquire but whether the country has the economic, human and political resources to sustain it, especially if a prolonged regional conflict were to erupt over Taiwan.

According to Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, acquiring the hardware is only one part of building an effective force.

“Japan may acquire increasingly sophisticated weapons without necessarily developing the manpower and institutional capacity required to operate them effectively,” Matsuoka said.

She warned that the mismatch could create a “hardware-capability gap”, with sophisticated equipment outpacing the ability of Japan’s Self-Defence Forces (SDF) to translate it into operational capacity.

Understaffed, outdated

The first test is therefore whether Japan can find enough people to operate the force it is building.

The country’s declining birth rate is shrinking the pool of potential recruits while a tight labour market forces the SDF to compete with private employers.

Recruitment improved in the 2025 financial year, but the SDF still had only 217,701 personnel against an authorised 247,154 at the end of March – a staffing rate of 88.1 per cent.

Defence ministry projections released in February suggested that, without corrective measures, personnel numbers could fall from about 220,000 to about 130,000 by 2045.

Tokyo is responding with better pay and working conditions as it turns to uncrewed systems and automation to do more with fewer personnel.

But the ministry itself acknowledges that strengthening recruitment and retention alone will not be enough.

The shortages could become particularly consequential in a contingency over Taiwan. Japan’s southwestern islands lie close to the potential conflict zone and the SDF could face demands to defend Japanese territory while maintaining operations under sustained pressure.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Filling the ranks, however, is only part of the problem for Tokyo. The force itself may also have to change.

Rintaro Inoue, a research fellow specialising in Japanese defence strategy and industry at the Institute of Geoeconomics as well as a PhD candidate at Keio University, said the challenge went beyond recruitment.

“In order to deter China from initiating a conflict in the region, the [Japan Self-Defence Force] will need to significantly change its force composition,” he said.

For instance, preparing for high-end warfare could require Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force to shift resources from some existing vessels and crewed patrol aircraft towards Aegis destroyers, uncrewed vessels and sensors, Inoue said.

Meanwhile the Ground Self-Defence Force may need to reduce its reliance on infantry, tanks and artillery as it expands missile forces, he added.

Internal organisational politics, resistance from local governments concerned about the economic impact of base closures and continuing demand for disaster-relief operations could make such changes difficult.

The structural problems are emerging even as the amount of money Tokyo is committing to defence keeps climbing.

The defence ministry has requested a record ¥8.9 trillion (US$55.7 billion) for the financial year 2027 – its 15th consecutive annual increase in defence requests.

In addition, officials have indicated that the figure could ultimately rise to about ¥10 trillion once the revision of Japan’s three main security documents is completed by the end of the year.

But spending more does not necessarily mean Japan can buy proportionately more military capability.

Matsuoka said the financial burden should not be measured merely by the initial cost of acquiring weapons. New systems bring long-term spending on personnel, maintenance, training, ammunition, infrastructure, upgrades and eventual replacement.

Once incorporated into the SDF, such capabilities could also become politically and strategically complicated to give up, potentially locking Japan into “a long-term cycle of defence spending that is increasingly difficult to sustain”, she said.

Japan says it has already reached its goal of spending about 2 per cent of gross domestic product on defence ahead of schedule. But sustaining that level, let alone substantially exceeding it, could prove harder.

High debt, weak yen

Darren Tay, head of Asia-Pacific country risk at BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, said the 2 per cent level itself was affordable but would become more difficult to sustain as Japan’s enormous stock of government debt was refinanced at higher interest rates.

National debt servicing is budgeted at ¥31.3 trillion in financial year 2026 and, under one finance ministry scenario, would reach ¥41.3 trillion by financial year 2029.

Tay identified debt servicing as the biggest economic constraint on Japan’s defence ambitions, ahead of demographics or procurement inflation.

BMI expects the government’s effective borrowing cost to rise to about 2.4 per cent by 2035 as older, near-zero-yield bonds mature and are refinanced at higher rates.

That would force defence, social-security spending and interest payments to compete for the same government revenue, Tay said.

At the same time, the weak yen is eroding the defence budget’s purchasing power. Much of the equipment Tokyo buys from the US is priced in dollars, meaning depreciation raises its cost in yen.

According to Tay, procurement planning underpinning the five-year build-up had assumed an exchange rate of about ¥108 to the dollar.

Moving towards defence spending of 3.5 per cent of GDP would therefore be of a “different order of difficulty”, Tay said, while reaching 5 per cent would require painful trade-offs with other public spending and was unrealistic without an acute geopolitical crisis directly involving Japan.

Fiscal constraints could thus force Japan to scale back what it can afford to buy.

“The more likely outcome is not a further rise in the budget but quietly accepting what is effectively a smaller defence budget,” Tay added. “Japan ends up buying less rather than paying whatever it takes.”

Inoue framed the dilemma differently. Given Japan’s security environment, Tokyo might have little choice but to spend more, he said, making the question whether the country was willing to bear the cost.

Sustaining a prolonged conflict

The Sanae Takaichi administration has sought to ease the burden by promoting a “virtuous cycle between defence and the economy”, including investment in dual-use technologies and expanded weapons exports that could lower unit costs.

Inoue described the objective as optimistic, saying the actual savings were likely to be limited.

Even if Tokyo finds the money to buy the force it wants, sustaining it through a prolonged conflict poses another challenge.

Japan’s defence industry has historically been structured to supply the SDF in relatively small quantities rather than replenish weapons at wartime rates.

Companies have withdrawn from parts of the sector, while limited production runs have contributed to high unit costs and made it harder to maintain suppliers and skilled workers.

Tokyo is trying to reverse that decline by improving conditions for contractors, attracting new entrants and expanding weapons exports, potentially increasing production volumes and spreading costs across larger orders.

Nevertheless, Tay said, the economic benefits would be “real but modest” this decade.

“The bigger pay-off is keeping Japan’s industry technologically capable and its equipment supply secure”, rather than substantially relieving pressure on the defence budget, he added.

Japan is also expanding ammunition production, shoring up supply chains and pursuing joint production with allies and partners.

Still, the defence ministry has acknowledged shortcomings in its ability to sustain operations, prioritising ammunition, fuel, equipment availability and hardened facilities.

Building stockpiles before a crisis is one challenge; replacing missiles, repairing damaged equipment and maintaining production as fighting continues is another.

And while hardware can be manufactured, public resolve cannot automatically be assumed.

Matsuoka cautioned against equating a growing public acceptance of a stronger SDF with a willingness to fight.

“There is an important distinction between support for strengthening defence in principle and support for actually using military force,” she said.

Acceptance of higher defence spending and new weapons would not necessarily mean the public would accept Japanese forces taking part directly in a war, suffering casualties or conducting operations that could expose Japan to retaliation, Matsuoka added.

“The build-up has therefore shifted the debate away from the traditional question of whether Japan should possess military power towards the more consequential question of how and under what circumstances that power should be used.”

The distinction is particularly important regarding Taiwan.

Japan’s stated mission is to defend its own territory rather than Taiwan itself, but its proximity to the island, the presence of major US bases and the strategic importance of its southwestern islands mean a cross-strait conflict could force Tokyo to make decisions on how far and under what legal circumstances the SDF should be involved.

Regional reactions

Takaichi brought the question directly into the Taiwan debate last November when she said a contingency involving mainland Chinese warships and the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation”, a legal designation that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence under certain circumstances.

The prime minister’s remarks drew a strong reaction from Beijing, which called them a violation of Tokyo’s Article 9 – the war-renouncing clause of Japan’s constitution that constrains the use of military force.

Beijing could raise the cost of Japan’s transformation through tighter controls on rare earths and dual-use materials, Inoue said.

However, such pressure could reinforce Japanese threat perceptions and accelerate efforts to reduce Tokyo’s economic dependence on China.

Other than the reaction from Beijing, Japan’s transformation also depends on regional acceptance of its growing military role.

Inoue said Japan enjoyed considerable support, pointing to renewed military training with South Korea and wider defence cooperation with Southeast Asia.

Matsuoka was more muted, describing the receptivity as “conditional rather than unlimited”.

“We should distinguish between welcoming Japan as a security partner and welcoming Japanese military expansion,” she said.

Southeast Asian states may welcome Tokyo’s security assistance without necessarily supporting unrestricted military expansion.

Furthermore, historical concerns could become more salient if Tokyo’s posture were perceived as increasingly autonomous or offensive, she said.

Despite such constraints, Matsuoka said Japan’s defence transformation was becoming more difficult to reverse.

Institutions, budgets, procurement programmes and alliance arrangements were being built around a particular conception of the regional security environment, she noted, giving the transformation a structural staying power that could extend beyond any single government.

But threat perceptions themselves are mutable. A major improvement in Sino-Japanese relations, shifts in US policy, economic pressure, domestic political change or declining public willingness to bear defence costs could all alter the trajectory, she said.

The opposite outcome is also possible: a self-reinforcing cycle in which Japanese capabilities intended to bolster deterrence reinforce Beijing’s perception of Japanese militarisation, prompting Chinese responses that further strengthen Tokyo’s perception of threat.

“Japan’s challenge is not only to strengthen deterrence but also to avoid a security strategy in which military expansion becomes the default answer to every deterioration in the regional security environment,” Matsuoka said.

item.title: [SCMP] Houthi offensive on Bab el-Mandeb Strait threatens new Red Sea shipping crisis
item.description:
A battle for control of Yemen’s coastal plains overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, launched on Friday by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, is rapidly intensifying into an all-out war with Saudi-backed government forces.

A wave of Houthi missile and drone strikes launched against four cities in southern Saudi Arabia early on Tuesday, injuring 73 civilians, may prove to be the tipping point in the conflict, analysts say.

Coinciding with an escalating battle of attrition between the United States and Iran for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthi air strikes are widely viewed as a precursor to a parallel conflict with Saudi Arabia for dominance over the Red Sea.
item.content:encoded:
A battle for control of Yemen’s coastal plains overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, launched on Friday by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, is rapidly intensifying into an all-out war with Saudi-backed government forces.

A wave of Houthi missile and drone strikes launched against four cities in southern Saudi Arabia early on Tuesday, injuring 73 civilians, may prove to be the tipping point in the conflict, analysts say.

Coinciding with an escalating battle of attrition between the United States and Iran for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthi air strikes are widely viewed as a precursor to a parallel conflict with Saudi Arabia for dominance over the Red Sea.

As with Hormuz, the intense fighting in Yemen’s Taiz and Hodeidah governorates is expected to strangle maritime traffic using the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Indian Ocean to Europe via the Suez Canal.

A Houthi embargo imposed in July on Saudi shipping transiting the strait has forced the kingdom to divert oil exports from Red Sea ports to Asia around Africa, adding thousands of kilometres and associated costs to tanker voyages.

“We are looking at both the return of Houthi cross-border attacks into Saudi Arabia and the resumption of the group’s efforts to bring a virtual halt to Red Sea shipping,” said Adam Baron, a veteran Yemen analyst and fellow with the future security programme at the Washington-based think tank New America.

The economic and political fallout of this escalation risked “further shaking the wider region”, particularly as it effectively underlined the potential capacity of the Iran-led axis of resistance to “squeeze US-aligned Gulf states from both sides of the Arabian Peninsula”, Baron said.

Analysts said it was unclear how much of a role Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps played in the Houthi push to decisively change the balance of power in Yemen following four years of relative peace.

According to Baron, the escalation instead underlined the extent to which it remained in the Houthis’ interests – both as an autonomous force and as part of the axis of resistance – to “maintain a demonstrable capacity to shut down Bab el-Mandeb”.

Particularly in light of the situation in Hormuz, “this remains a key point of leverage for Iran’s wider regional network”, he said.

However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed no such doubts about Tehran’s involvement.

“The Houthis, in many ways, are agents and proxies of the Iranians,” Rubio told reporters in Washington on Tuesday. “I think behind some of this is clearly the Iranian hand.”

Speaking in Moscow on Tuesday, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Farhan bin Faisal refrained from directly pointing fingers at the Islamic Republic, but warned the Houthi militia that it had embarked on a course of action whose consequences “it will not be able to handle”.

While Farhan reiterated the kingdom’s openness to a negotiated political settlement in Yemen, he stressed that Saudi Arabia “will not hesitate to defend ourselves and we will not hesitate to protect our interests”.

The strident tone of his remarks led many Saudi analysts to conclude that Riyadh was preparing to ditch its long-standing policy of containment in Yemen in favour of establishing military deterrence against Houthi aggression.

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political commentator reputedly close to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said he expected the kingdom to “respond aggressively and continue its strong support of the Yemeni government forces”.

Analysts note that the competing factions making up the internationally recognised government forces were currently at their strongest since Yemen’s civil war erupted in 2014.

A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year after Houthi rebels seized swathes of northern and western Yemen, with the conflict ending in stalemate in 2022.

The UN-sponsored political road map agreed upon at the time failed to produce the desired settlement, despite lengthy mediation efforts by neighbouring Oman, because of incessant jockeying for position between the Houthis and rival elements within the Yemeni government camp.

Southern separatists backed by the United Arab Emirates went on the offensive in southern and eastern Yemen late last year, leading to the UAE’s expulsion from the country in December – and an unprecedented rift between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.

Since then, Riyadh has worked to consolidate anti-Houthi groups under a unified command. This force benefits from Saudi intelligence, better weaponry and advanced drones that have proven especially effective in repelling recent rebel ground assaults.

Pro-government forces have responded to the Houthi offensive in Taiz and Hodeidah by counter-attacking at strategic points across multiple fronts – a tactic aimed at drawing Houthi forces away from the Red Sea coast.

On the other hand, the Houthi offensive may be intended to prevent operations against Houthi-controlled areas along the western coast, according to Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, a Brussels-based non-profit organisation focused on conflict prevention and resolution.

Amid widespread rumours of a government offensive to retake the key Red Sea port of Hodeidah, Houthi operations could pull government forces away from their coastal positions and reinforce Houthi defences in the mountains overlooking the western coast.

In an advisory published by the International Crisis Group on Tuesday, Nagi said the Houthis appeared intent on seizing high ground on the western coastal plain and areas near Mokha port and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This would expand their control over terrain overlooking the coast, putting them in a stronger position to target transiting shipping.

By staging this ground assault alongside cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia and maritime operations against Saudi-linked shipping, the Houthis were “seeking to demonstrate the ability to operate simultaneously across multiple fronts”, Nagi said.

They also hoped to project an image of strength after suffering losses to government-aligned forces using advanced drones in recent weeks.

Nagi warned the scale of reinforcements in weapons and manpower on both sides suggested the current battle “may well morph into a prolonged confrontation”.

Continued escalation could open additional fronts. In particular, the Yemeni government, with Saudi support, “may see an advantage in expanding military operations” to force the Houthis to disperse their forces and stretch their capabilities, rather than allowing them to concentrate their resources on the Taiz and western coastal fronts.

With both sides eyeing momentous territorial gains, Baron described the line between brinkmanship and aiming to make decisive gains as “quite thin”.

Both the Houthis and their adversaries now “broadly assess that a return to fighting is in their interest”, he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Could China sanction US for illegal international seabed mining? A study says yes
item.description:
For decades, the United States has used economic and financial restrictions as major foreign policy tools.

But as China and other countries gain greater economic and technological strength, they are also acquiring more ways to push back against US actions, with deep-sea mining possibly becoming a testing ground for that shift.

China could join other countries in taking coordinated countermeasures, including sanctions against companies, if the US proceeds with seabed mining in violation of international law, according to Bian Yongmin, a professor of international law at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, the United States has used economic and financial restrictions as major foreign policy tools.

But as China and other countries gain greater economic and technological strength, they are also acquiring more ways to push back against US actions, with deep-sea mining possibly becoming a testing ground for that shift.

China could join other countries in taking coordinated countermeasures, including sanctions against companies, if the US proceeds with seabed mining in violation of international law, according to Bian Yongmin, a professor of international law at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing.

“[However,] if the United States insists on ignoring international law, it would indeed be difficult to restrain them,” said a Beijing-based international law expert familiar with the proposal who asked not to be named, citing the sensitivity of the matter.

Bian’s analysis was published in the June issue of the peer-reviewed China-based Pacific Journal.

The US remained bound by customary international law governing global seabed resources, despite not being a party to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), the professor wrote.

The Donald Trump administration has been moving from policy to concrete preparations for seabed mineral development after issuing an executive order in April last year promoting offshore critical-mineral extraction and subsequently advancing proposed lease sales in Pacific waters.

On July 16, the Marine Minerals Administration, an agency within the US Interior Department, published a proposed leasing notice for a potential mineral lease sale offshore American Samoa, with a proposed sale date of November 19 this year.

On August 17, the agency issued another proposed leasing notice for potential mineral leases offshore the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, with a proposed sale date of December 16.

Even though the US was not a member of Unclos did not mean Washington had a free hand on the international seabed, Bian wrote.

Several principles contained in Part XI of Unclos had developed into customary international law, she added, including the principle that the international seabed was the “common heritage of mankind”, the obligation to protect the marine environment and the requirement that benefits from seabed mineral resources be shared internationally.

In addition, the US’ own past conduct could weaken any argument that it had consistently rejected those rules, Bian said.

In 1970, Washington voted in favour of a UN General Assembly declaration recognising the seabed beyond national jurisdiction as the common heritage of mankind. It later supported arrangements recognising benefit-sharing from deep-sea mineral development.

Bian argued that the US could not, therefore, simply invoke its non-party status to Unclos to escape customary rules it had previously accepted.

The legal question is likely to hinge on how US-authorised mining is ultimately carried out, including whether it appropriates international seabed resources, causes serious environmental harm or allows mining operators to retain benefits that should be shared, according to Bian’s study.

The Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a mineral-rich seabed area in the northeast Pacific, covers about 4.5 million sq km (1.74 million square miles) and is estimated to contain about 21 billion tonnes of polymetallic nodules rich in nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese.

The Metals Company, a Canadian firm, has an American subsidiary that applied this year for a US deep-sea mining permit to operate in the zone.

The zone lies on the seabed of the high seas, and companies and organisations holding exploration licences there have agreed to follow mining rules set by the International Seabed Authority, according to Bian’s research.

The deep ocean is particularly sensitive because polymetallic nodules can take millions of years to form, and experimental mining has been found to leave lasting ecological effects.

For China, the issue creates a tension between defending the multilateral system and protecting access to critical minerals, with Beijing already deeply involved in international seabed development.

“If the United States starts mining first, China may follow,” the unnamed expert said, adding that this was an industry view rather than a personal one.

That said, China’s response would not necessarily mirror the US’ approach, according to Bian’s analysis.

China could conduct seabed mining while continuing to work with the International Seabed Authority and following existing multilateral principles on the common heritage of mankind, benefit-sharing and environmental protection, Bian wrote.

China has multiple exploration contracts in the international seabed area and capabilities in deep-sea equipment, mining machinery and mineral processing, with Chinese participants including China Minmetals Corporation and the China Ocean Mineral Resources Research and Development Association.

Other countries are pursuing their own approaches, although they differ in scope and legal circumstances.

According to Bian’s research, exploration licences in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone are also held by Belgium’s Global Sea Mineral Resources, Norway’s Loke and Green Minerals, Germany’s Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources, France’s French Research Institute for Exploitation of the Sea, Kiribati’s Marawa Research and Exploration Ltd, South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and UK Seabed Resources.

“If the United States unilaterally authorises mining, it cannot take the zone, part of the zone or other areas of the international seabed for itself or improperly prevent other countries from legally mining in the area,” Bian wrote in her study.

The unnamed expert said that “Japan and the United States have already signed an agreement to develop rare earth resources on Japan’s continental shelf, which I think is an attempt that faces relatively fewer legal obstacles”.

“The European Union, because of environmental concerns, may not begin deep-sea mining in the foreseeable short term,” the expert said, adding that “India’s technology is not up to it”, when asked about the South Asian country.

But the most immediate response to a US breach would still be negotiation and consultation, the professor said.

Coordinated action could follow if diplomacy failed.

Bian wrote that countries firmly committed to upholding the multilateral mechanism for deep-sea mining could at least refuse to cooperate with American mining companies.

They could also avoid buying deep-sea mineral products sold by American deep-sea mining companies and their processed products, she wrote.

“Companies such as Apple, Google, Microsoft and BMW have promised not to purchase deep-sea minerals in their supply chains.”

And even if American companies obtained permission, mining could not begin immediately.

“Seabed mining is highly risky,” Bian said. “Even if American companies obtained permission, it could not be implemented immediately. I estimate that environmental impact assessments and other procedures will take a lot of time.”

She also said environmental impacts could affect market demand for seabed minerals.

“If the environmental impact is really significant, this kind of mineral may be resisted to a certain extent by the market,” Bian added. “People are reluctant to be associated with problematic products, just as they resist forced-labour products.”

item.title: [SCMP] How some grey-market crypto ATMs in Hong Kong can turn users into fraud victims
item.description:
Inside a tiny self-service laundromat in Quarry Bay in the east of Hong Kong Island, next to a wall of washing machines, stands a waist-high cryptocurrency terminal with signs reading “Elon Musk recommends Dogecoin” and “Buy bitcoin in one minute”.

In order to obtain Dogecoin through the ATM, customers feed Hong Kong dollar notes into a slot and scan a QR code. The equivalent amount in cryptocurrency is then credited into their digital wallet.

Such machines have proliferated across the city in recent years as interest in cryptocurrencies has risen. Many are installed at 24-hour unstaffed shops such as laundromats and claw-machine arcades.
item.content:encoded:
Inside a tiny self-service laundromat in Quarry Bay in the east of Hong Kong Island, next to a wall of washing machines, stands a waist-high cryptocurrency terminal with signs reading “Elon Musk recommends Dogecoin” and “Buy bitcoin in one minute”.

In order to obtain Dogecoin through the ATM, customers feed Hong Kong dollar notes into a slot and scan a QR code. The equivalent amount in cryptocurrency is then credited into their digital wallet.

Such machines have proliferated across the city in recent years as interest in cryptocurrencies has risen. Many are installed at 24-hour unstaffed shops such as laundromats and claw-machine arcades.

As of 2024, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) found about 200 virtual asset retailers in the city, which included such ATMs.

According to Coin ATM Radar, a global geographical tracker, there are currently 236 crypto ATMs in Hong Kong – concentrated in Mong Kok, Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai and Quarry Bay – offering a dozen different types of cryptocurrencies.

However, these ATMs operate in a legal grey area, with the city still in the process of setting up a regulatory regime for over-the-counter cryptocurrency trading.

Potential tools in financial scams

Some lawmakers and industry insiders warned people of the potential investment risks associated with scams, weak consumer protection and money laundering that ATMs posed.

Legislator Johnny Ng Kit-chong said scams involving ATM cryptocurrency transfers were growing increasingly common across the world and often took two forms.

The first was through fraudulent machines that accepted cash but did not dispense any crypto, or vice versa. The second was through human actors, such as when fraudsters posed as officials or wooed targets romantically to get them to transfer cash or crypto through a fake ATM controlled by the scammers.

“Because blockchain-backed transactions are irreversible and ATMs lack robust verification, recovering these funds is nearly impossible,” Ng said.

Two operators, Coinhero and Coinunit, claim to be running Asia’s largest crypto network. A check on their websites found that Coinhero lists its transaction fees online and offers customer support via WhatsApp, email and an actual flagship store in Causeway Bay, while Coinunit’s only channel is a web contact form.

Another operator is Canada-based Localcoin. Its CEO, Tristan Fong, said the company had 30 ATMs in Hong Kong and operated consumer protection controls remotely.

“We have best-in-class, real-time on-and-off-chain transaction monitoring tools that can be deployed anywhere on earth,” he said.

Fong acknowledged the risks of money laundering and scams but noted that other financial services also faced such risks. His company monitored transactions and issued scam warnings to combat illicit activity.

Fong welcomed the city’s planned regulation and dialogue with lawmakers on rules for the sector.

“Clear rules in Hong Kong would protect consumers, raise standards across the industry, and benefit operators with the ability to implement strong and sophisticated controls,” he said.

“We look forward to reviewing the framework when it is published. We will comply fully with any new requirements.”

The South China Morning Post has reached out to Coinhero for comment.

Regulatory proposal in the works

In response to queries from the SCMP, the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau said it was finalising legislative proposals with the SFC to regulate virtual asset dealers, including crypto ATM operators, virtual asset custodians and advisory and management service providers.

“We are now finalising the legislative proposals, with a target of introducing the relevant bill into the Legislative Council later this year,” it said.

The bureau stressed that operators should also “comply with other applicable laws and regulations in Hong Kong”.

Andrew Fei, a partner at law firm King & Wood, said that even without a dedicated virtual asset dealer licensing regime, ATM operators remained bound by the city’s existing statutes, including criminal laws.

But a specific licence would impose more robust consumer protection, know-your-customer standards, financial resources, risk management and other requirements to help ensure that crypto ATMs were operated in a safe and compliant manner, he added.

Fei said shop owners who allowed crypto ATMs on their premises appeared to have straightforward commercial motives, such as drawing foot traffic, and their legal exposure hinged on what they “reasonably suspected” or knew about the operators’ legitimacy.

“For criminal liability to attach to shop owners that merely allow the ATMs to be placed in their premises, they would need to have at least some knowledge or suspicion that the ATM operator is doing something illegal,” Fei said.

“If they don’t know or suspect anything, then I don’t think the shop owner would be criminally liable.”

He suggested that regulators establish an orderly timeline to allow existing market participants to prepare for and obtain the new virtual asset dealing licence before the regime formally comes into effect, to avoid disruption of existing client-facing activities, especially those carried out by financial institutions.

Singapore bans crypto ATMs. Other jurisdictions such as Australia allow such services, despite the government’s warning in 2025 that such machines are “one of the highest risk money laundering channels”.

Future demand and legitimacy of crypto operators

Syed Musheer Ahmed, the founder of Advisory FinStep Asia, a fintech, crypto, and virtual asset advisory firm, said customers of cryptocurrency ATMs in Hong Kong could be small-amount crypto investors, or visitors from jurisdictions where crypto trading was forbidden.

“The broader crypto exchange activities globally have come down in the past six months,” Ahmed said, noting that the retail interest for local investors could have gone down.

As of Friday, one bitcoin traded at about US$80,630.

An SCMP reporter who observed the Quarry Bay laundromat for three hours on a weekday afternoon found that not a single person used the ATM.

Fong of LocalCoin said demand for cash-to-crypto transactions had cooled in Hong Kong, with both transaction volumes and average sizes declining. But he argued ATMs were still useful for consumers seeking quick access to digital assets.

“We’ve also seen ever-growing numbers of fake crypto exchange websites,” he said. “Concerns about these websites also drive first-time crypto buyers to our machines, because their physical presence in a trusted retail location creates a high level of comfort.”

Leon Liu, a researcher at the blockchain network Tron, said the location of the ATMs was not incidental, as laundromats and claw machine arcades were typically unstaffed and opened round the clock – a business model that minimised the cost of running ATMs.

But Jack Poon, professor of practice in fintech and entrepreneurial finance at Polytechnic University, warned that unstaffed machines could be platforms for money laundering, as users had no way of knowing whether the cryptocurrency they received came from a legitimate source or illegal activity.

He also pointed to the collapse of cryptocurrency platform JPEX, which allegedly committed the city’s biggest financial fraud involving HK$1.6 billion (US$204.1 million) and more than 2,700 victims in 2023, as a cautionary precedent for what happened when an operator had no accountable presence in the city.

“A lot of people put money in there without protection. When the operator pulled the plug, a lot of people suffered,” he said. “It was very difficult for Hong Kong law enforcement or regulators to help investors recover their money because the entity was not even in Hong Kong.”

According to police, 969 cryptocurrency-related cases were recorded in the first six months of this year, with losses totalling HK$2.68 billion. Those losses amounted to 77.9 per cent of the figure in all of 2025.

The number of cases declined by 11.1 per cent to 2,234 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the figure in 2024 was 2,513, a 26.4 per cent drop from 3,415 in 2023. Losses in 2025 totalled HK$3.44 billion, down by 1.7 per cent from 2024.

Police did not record the breakdown of cases related only to crypto ATMs.

item.title: [SCMP] Silver linings: in Southeast Asia, ageing is big business
item.description:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.
item.content:encoded:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.

Carers wheeled and walked eight fellow residents to the dining table before breaking into song. Goaded into a speech, Fung kept it brief: “I’m very happy to be here.”

The home, a refurbished two-storey bungalow, is one of a growing number of assisted living facilities springing up as Singapore’s population ages. The city state officially became a “super-aged” society this year, with more than one-fifth of its population over 65.

These facilities offer a much-needed middle ground for older people who can no longer live independently but do not require the round-the-clock medical care of a nursing home.

Staff help residents with daily tasks such as dispensing medication and writing letters, while some facilities include memory care units for those experiencing cognitive decline.

Assisted living is a nascent but fast-growing segment of Singapore’s multibillion-dollar silver economy. The government has provided more than 1,100 such flats since 2021, and private real estate operators are also increasingly entering the market.

For residents like Fung, what matters most is feeling part of a community, keeping their independence and being treated with dignity. Despite her early-stage osteoporosis, she moves around the home without a walking frame, sometimes forgoing afternoon sessions of mahjong to journal in her room instead.

“I’m fitting in little by little – I’ve learned to get to know more of the residents and our different timetables,” she said. “I told my family I’ll probably stay here until the time comes.”

For fellow resident Soo Soo Cheng, 90, her single room is a world away from the six-bedded ward she shared at her previous nursing home. “It was like a dormitory and nothing private like this. I was getting really uncomfortable,” she said.

Now she spends her days in a bright orange armchair by the window, walking frame within reach, while carers take care of tasks like printing copies of bills and helping her to bed when her spine acts up.

“I’m thankful for a place like this, where I can do things on my own and yet never have a dull moment,” she said. “Time seems to fly.”

A middle ground

Southeast Asia is ageing rapidly and its social welfare systems are increasingly grappling with a thorny question: what happens to the people who can no longer manage entirely on their own, but do not need a hospital bed?

Assisted living – offering medical and social care scalable to residents’ needs – has emerged as an answer.

It was designed for people whose needs fell somewhere between the intensive clinical care of a nursing home and what a domestic helper, who cannot reasonably be expected to manage a medical emergency, could provide, said Janice Chia, founder of Ageing Asia, a Singapore-based social enterprise focused on the business of growing old.

In Singapore, more people are ageing alone – an estimated 83,000 by 2030, according to the Ministry of Health – while shrinking family sizes are increasing the caregiving burden shouldered by adult children.

“Assisted living provides independence and privacy without the seeming unpopular burden of managing foreign domestic helpers,” said Kelvin Tan, who heads the applied ageing studies programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

Options in the city state range from government-run flats to private luxury apartments, with monthly bills ranging anywhere from three to five figures, depending on location, room size and level of care required.

In 2021, Singapore introduced community care flats aiming to support independent ageing in a social environment. Five such projects have launched so far.

The Housing Development Board announced in July that from its sixth project, launching in October, the eligibility age for assisted-living public housing estates would be lowered from 65 to 55, alongside lower fees aimed at improving affordability.

Estimated fees for a 15-year lease – currently S$40,000 to S$49,000 (US$31,400 to US$38,500) for a basic package – will drop to between S$26,000 and S$28,000 from next year, according to Vanguard Healthcare, which operates the developments.

“The cost is a big advantage for average Singaporeans looking for an accessible offer,” Tan said.

Private operators are also scaling up their operations. St Bernadette Lifestyle Village, which runs eight facilities island-wide, offers a mid-tier option priced from S$3,000 to S$6,000 a month.

Care homes were “less a business venture than a necessity”, said founder Belinda Wee, who has observed elderly residents growing unsettled in nursing homes due to a lack of socialising. About 80 residents lived in St Bernadette’s homes last year, up from 19 in 2023.

Well-heeled pensioners gained a luxury option last month with the opening of Perennial Living, a S$260 million, 195,000 sq ft development in northeastern Singapore featuring a hydrotherapy pool, a traditional Chinese medicine clinic and a karaoke lounge.

A basic package for a 330 sq ft studio flat starts at S$8,000 a month, while a 565 sq ft two-bedder costs more than S$13,000.

The hefty price tag has raised concerns about the affordability of retirement, though experts note the project is aimed squarely at the upper end of the market.

Chia said its prices should be viewed in the category of premium hospitality and care, rather than general assisted living.

Sign-ups have been gradual and interest has been “positive”, according to Perennial Holding’s chief executive Pua Seck Guan, who projected a 30 per cent occupancy rate after a year and 80 per cent after two.

More new entrants were expected to join the assisted living sector, Chia said, as Singapore’s shift from live-in caregiving to mainstream services gave firms the confidence to invest. But she urged regulators to pace approvals carefully given the dearth of healthcare workers.

Singapore needed to recruit about 6,000 nurses, healthcare professionals and support staff every year to meet demand, the Health Ministry said in 2024. It previously estimated that a healthcare workforce of 82,000 would be needed by 2030.

“This figure is the one worth dwelling on, because it shows care capability cannot simply be commissioned. Sites can be approved considerably faster than carers can be trained, deployed and retained,” Chia said.

Ageing in luxury

With its circular driveway and plush lobby, Perennial Living looks more like an upscale hotel than a home for the elderly.

The development aimed to set a “new benchmark for senior living in Singapore”, Pua said – reflecting a surge in luxury senior living facilities across Asia as operators recognise their target demographic wants more than just care and medical services.

More than US$500 billion is expected to pour into the silver economy across six Southeast Asian markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines – by 2030, according to Ageing Asia.

Retirees today were wealthier, healthier and more assertive than any generation before them, the social enterprise said in a report released last month, making the business of ageing the Asia-Pacific’s “largest commercial opportunity”.

“Baby boomers, the biggest savers of all generations, have spent their lives making choices and are expected to hold onto that autonomy into their older age,” it said.

At Homerly International Senior Living in Thailand, residents walk long, tree-lined avenues within a large, serene gated community, accompanied by nurses, with their pets padding along behind them. The resort, which provides assisted living and nursing care, is one of hundreds of retirement communities popping up across a country with abundant land and a growing healthcare workforce.

A month’s stay – including round-the-clock medical care, physiotherapy, pool villas shaded by trees and two staff members in attendance – starts at US$2,200, with the top-end pool villas commanding a price tag of around US$4,500.

“Here you’re not a patient, you are a resident. We treat people with dignity,” general manager Rene Pisters said. “You have somebody with you all the time if you need it and the feeling that if something happens to you, there is a nurse sitting here.”

Malaysia is seeing a similar boom in luxury homes for the elderly, driven by changing expectations of ageing, according to N. Raaj Selvarajan, group chairman of regional healthcare infrastructure investor Hemrish Group and founder of its flagship senior living brand Sukha Golden.

Residents increasingly wanted privacy, wellness and access to care without the institutional feel traditionally associated with elderly care, he said.

Demand for its luxury Sukha Senior Resort has surged since it opened in March last year – all rooms are fully occupied, with interested residents placed on a waiting list.

Capitalising on the boom, Selvarajan said plans to expand regionally were under way, with projects in Indonesia and Vietnam in the pipeline. “The opportunity is not simply that Asia is ageing; it is that people want to age differently,” he said.

Crossing borders

For Singaporeans who feel priced out of their own super-aged society, homes for the elderly have become an unlikely engine of Malaysia and Thailand’s recent tourism boom, as families shop for similar care standards at a fraction of the cost.

The Straits Resorts Medini, a retirement home in Johor just a 15-minute drive from the border, has built its business around Singaporean demand.

“Consistent and encouraging” is how founder Elvira Tan describes cross-border interest in the facility, which offers rooms from S$4,300 a month, bundling in personalised care and grooming services, arts activities and social programmes.

Industry insiders expect the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Rapid Transit System Link, set to open in January, to further boost demand.

“You can obtain the most expensive level of care in Malaysia for about one-third the price of the same level of care in Singapore,” said Kashif Ansari, group CEO of real estate market intelligence group Juwai IQI.

Cultural familiarity and the absence of a language barrier eased the transition for would-be residents considering homes across the causeway, he added.

“Families with a senior who needs potentially years or even more than a decade of care, naturally want the highest quality service and the lowest cost they can possibly obtain,” he said. “Malaysia has a real competitive advantage in this sector and operators hope to make the most of it.”

Money goes further in Thailand too. Facilities in Bangkok and Chiang Mai are attracting a growing number of Asian retirees, including from Singapore and Hong Kong, looking for care comparable to what they can get at home at a fraction of the cost.

Thailand hopes the care and wellness industry will become a defining part of its economy in the years ahead, as more people grow old and spend money on a curated retirement.

Care standards were high, Homerly’s Pisters said, adding that his company helped elderly residents with bureaucratic hurdles such as visas and bank accounts.

“The demand is huge, and it will only get bigger,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Her nude became a sticker: Hong Kong women say image abuse thrives despite law
item.description:
Five years after a nude photo was taken without her consent, a woman opened Instagram to find the image had been turned into a sticker and sent back to her in a chat.

Terrified that the sticker could already be circulating widely, the victim reached out to Emilia Wong Yue-kiu, a women’s rights activist and adult content creator who advocates for bodily autonomy.

But Wong was pessimistic that reporting the case would help, noting it was just one of countless similar messages for help she had received in recent years.
item.content:encoded:
Five years after a nude photo was taken without her consent, a woman opened Instagram to find the image had been turned into a sticker and sent back to her in a chat.

Terrified that the sticker could already be circulating widely, the victim reached out to Emilia Wong Yue-kiu, a women’s rights activist and adult content creator who advocates for bodily autonomy.

But Wong was pessimistic that reporting the case would help, noting it was just one of countless similar messages for help she had received in recent years.

“Senders of the sticker may not even know where they got it from, and have no idea who the girl is, but they sent it around nonetheless. What offence did they commit then?” she said.

Advocates say Hong Kong’s voyeurism laws have been insufficient to tackle the circulation of intimate images obtained without consent and the surreptitious online chat rooms where members post such images.

They are urging city authorities to establish faster takedown mechanisms to better protect victims.

Legal framework and enforcement gaps

Hong Kong’s laws against voyeurism – encompassing four main offences – were enacted nearly five years ago in October 2021, to plug a legal loophole in tackling acts such as upskirting and revenge porn.

These four offences are voyeurism, unlawful recording or observation of intimate parts, publication of images originating from the two aforementioned acts, as well as the publication or threatened publication of intimate images without consent.

Official data obtained by the South China Morning Post shows that among the four voyeurism-related offences, the number of prosecutions in relation to arrests per year for publishing or threatening to publish intimate images without consent has been the lowest.

Between October 2021 and March this year, authorities recorded 545 cases, made 258 arrests, launched 46 prosecutions and secured 33 convictions.

That means only 17.8 per cent of arrests for this offence led to prosecutions over that period.

Cheryl Yip Cheuk-yi, advocacy officer at the Association Concerning Sexual Violence Against Women, said her organisation’s experience with victims and its work to take down intimate images have shown that the need to prove an intention to cause distress, humiliation or alarm to the photographed individual under the law was a high threshold to reach.

For cases involving online groups where people share or leak intimate images taken without consent, she said proving that someone who did not take the image – and may not know the person depicted – intended to cause distress could be difficult.

“Perhaps they were thinking that this is a leaked image, and I’m merely sharing it with other people. The requirement to prove their motive may not be something that could be handled here,” Yip said.

She added that subtle browbeating could also be challenged in courts, citing an example of someone saying “see you on a forum”, which a victim might interpret as a threat to post intimate photos but which could be dismissed as not constituting a threat.

The advocacy officer also described the legality of resharing intimate images obtained without consent that a person did not take as a “grey area”, saying the law offered little clarity on such actions.

Data from the organisation’s sexual violence victim support service showed that 63.3 per cent of image-based cases – 178 out of 281 – between 2019 and 2023 involved repeated incidents rather than one-off occurrences.

Yip suggested city authorities reference the United Kingdom, which created a specific offence for sharing such images without consent, even if there was no malicious intent involved.

“No matter what a person’s intention may be, publishing or threatening to publish intimate images without their consent would create the same level of harm,” Yip said.

Legal interpretations and limits

But barrister Michelle Wong Lap-yan, who has advised victims of sexual violence, said it did not matter whether the person knew the victim or whether the person had taken the image in voyeurism-related cases.

“One of the guilty mental elements regarding the unconsented publication of intimate photos taken without the victim's consent is that the person is reckless as to whether the image originated from the commission of the unconsented taking of intimate photos,” Wong said.

For example, if a photo showed clear signs of being taken without consent – such as an upskirt image inside an MTR train – a person ignoring those circumstances could be found reckless in court, she said.

The barrister added that publishing intimate images that were taken with consent, but without authorisation for publication, was also a crime.

But in the case of a non-consensual nude photo turned into a sticker and circulated, Wong admitted that it could be difficult for prosecutors to prove whether one could deduce that the photo was taken without consent, as well as the circumstances around how the sticker was sent and circulated.

Advancing technology poses new threats

Both Yip and activist Wong highlighted advancing technology as another threat – both in surreptitious filming equipment and in the increasingly elusive nature of online chat groups where such images are circulated.

The latter, especially, has made collecting evidence for a case and taking down non-consensual images more difficult than before, according to both advocates.

Wong said filming equipment has become much more sophisticated and accessible in the five years since the law took effect, making filming equipment ever harder to detect, but much easier to obtain.

For instance, hidden cameras could be fitted on shoes or inside bags, while some appear as accessories placed near phone cameras that would refract the lens so as to film in 360 degrees.

Wong said many of these tools were sold on e-commerce platforms for less than HK$100 (US$12.75).

Other tools included software that keeps phone screens blank to view, despite a filming function being switched on.

“With these, one can simply take a bag and place it underneath a girl’s skirt for upskirting,” Wong said. “You don’t even need to point a phone at the person to take photos.”

While online chat rooms for sharing explicit sexual content were not new to Hong Kong, Yip and Wong said these groups have increasingly hidden their activities behind layers of evasive mechanisms to avoid detection and potential criminal liability.

Activist Wong, who uncovered an upskirting group with tens of thousands of local members in 2018, said the scale of such groups had greatly shrunk since the voyeurism laws came into place, with group administrators making access to illicit photos more secretive.

Unlike the large, publicly accessible groups with boisterous discussions and doxxing she had uncovered eight years ago, these groups now have only a few thousand members, compared with tens of thousands in the past, she said.

Some required referrals from trusted members before admitting newcomers and used cryptocurrency for payments, Wong added.

Chat room organisers have also adopted self-destructing messaging methods, which have become widely popular in recent years.

“They would now put out really descriptive prompts about a video they would post, then say they would upload it for five minutes before the content was deleted. If members could catch that window, they could see it,” Wong explained.

Wong added that bans on online discussion within the groups were effectively another way to evade criminal liability, as there would be no trace of individual members commenting on shared images or requesting payment details for access.

Yip said some groups were no longer run by individual administrators but by bots or other built-in systems, making it more difficult for her organisation to request the removal of images or prove they had been posted.

Directly posting intimate images on forums or publicly accessible online messaging groups has in fact become rare, according to Ip.

“Now, they would post a link, which would be connected to a bot once clicked. Users would have to type some keywords to access the non-consensual image. This is a grey area, as they could say they had never posted the picture,” the officer explained.

Faster takedowns are urged

Yip called on Hong Kong authorities to establish faster mechanisms for removing non-consensual content to strengthen protections for victims, some of whom may be reluctant to enter lengthy judicial processes that can take years.

The officer said that, for most victims reporting cases to non-governmental organisations or the police, the most pressing concern was stopping the circulation of their images.

Expedited civil-law channels for removing non-consensual intimate images online exist in some overseas jurisdictions.

Singapore launched its Online Safety Commission in June. The commission can issue removal directions and restrict perpetrators’ accounts, with legal authority over online platforms, administrators, internet access providers and app distribution services.

Various Canadian provinces also provide for civil claims and urgent court orders to remove images.

Activist Wong said Hong Kong could draw on these overseas mechanisms, but cautioned that authorities would need to address how any system would operate on foreign platforms and within jurisdictional limits, given that online activity easily crosses legal borders.

Yip noted that, to her knowledge, Hong Kong authorities had not invoked a court disposal order available under the law to require a person to take steps to remove the intimate image concerned at any stage of legal proceedings.

“As an NGO, we have no legal authority to demand these platforms take any action. If these orders are issued with legal power, these platforms have to follow up,” Yip said.

Barrister Wong said online platforms were not subject to a specific statutory duty to pre-screen user content. Their civil liability for non-consensual intimate images would arise only if they were notified of the content and failed to remove it promptly.

“But whether it is effective against foreign platforms is questionable. Primary criminal responsibility rests with the individual uploader under the Crimes Ordinance,” Wong said, noting that city courts had warned of the need to balance freedom of expression against platform liability.

But activist Wong said Hong Kong society could not simply rely on the law to address the invasive threat posed by upskirting and image leaks, and that a broader cultural shift in attitudes towards women was needed.

“This is intrinsically bullying, which cannot be reversed by law. We need women’s social status to rise, better sex education and less taboo on discussing sex,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Born to Fly’ documents Hong Kong-born Rahul Sharma’s world record 566km run across Sri Lanka
item.description:
In January 2025, Rahul Sharma ran his first marathon, in Mumbai, India. Months later, he learned of British ultra-endurance athlete William Goodge, who ran across Australia in 35 days, a journey of 3,800km (2,361 miles).

It was all the encouragement the then 24-year-old needed to up his game. Within weeks, the Melbourne-based exercise physiologist had rallied two of his best friends and decided on a goal: he would run 566km (352 miles) from Point Pedro, the northernmost point of Sri Lanka, to Dondra Head, at its southern tip, in six days.

None of the trio – Sharma, Ali Khajeian and Ben Lawson – knew the first thing about ultra-running. But that wasn’t going to stop them.
item.content:encoded:
In January 2025, Rahul Sharma ran his first marathon, in Mumbai, India. Months later, he learned of British ultra-endurance athlete William Goodge, who ran across Australia in 35 days, a journey of 3,800km (2,361 miles).

It was all the encouragement the then 24-year-old needed to up his game. Within weeks, the Melbourne-based exercise physiologist had rallied two of his best friends and decided on a goal: he would run 566km (352 miles) from Point Pedro, the northernmost point of Sri Lanka, to Dondra Head, at its southern tip, in six days.

None of the trio – Sharma, Ali Khajeian and Ben Lawson – knew the first thing about ultra-running. But that wasn’t going to stop them.

“I try my best not to be cocky, but it’s just not who I am,” Sharma admits in Born to Fly, a newly released documentary that charts his Sri Lanka run. “I have a big head.”

But why Sri Lanka?

“We didn’t want to follow a blueprint. We wanted to find a country that had never been done before,” says Sharma. Sri Lanka it was then, although, it is not strictly true that no one had attempted it previously; in 2023, Irishman Chris Rickard, assisted by two friends on bicycles, ran a slightly longer route between the same two points in Sri Lanka, in just under 12 days.

Born and raised in Hong Kong, Sharma played cricket from a young age, and represented the city’s under-19 team. He stepped away from the sport after a series of injuries.

Having moved to Australia, he started running to help in his recovery from the injuries, and the activity quickly became something more all-consuming.

Challenging himself to run the length of a country wasn’t just a vanity project, though. Driven by a childhood friend’s battle with leukaemia, Sharma aimed to raise A$20,000 (US$13,100) for the Children’s Cancer Institute (CCI), a Sydney-based research organisation.

Eventually, the dates were set: December 24 to 30, 2025.

Lawson, 25, a journalism major who lived with Sharma while the latter trained, liaised with sponsors, the media and the CCI. He also worked closely with Sharma’s coach to ensure that the runner was getting the optimal amount of nutrients, hydration and rest in between training sessions. Lawson came to know Sharma inside out.

But as the day neared, both Sharma’s friends, who had helped map out his entire journey, had to pull out of the actual trip to Sri Lanka for personal reasons.

“It was a hard conversation and, honestly, I didn’t think that Rahul would have that level of understanding,” says Khajeian, who, like Lawson, nevertheless stayed involved in the project, and would direct and produce Born to Fly. “I know internally he was crashing out. But on the outside, he was very understanding and very mature. It just brought us closer to each other.”

Sharma brought in another friend, Mohammed Abdullah, a Sri Lankan who happened to be in the country at the time.

“Rahul is like an older brother figure to me, so this project was important to me because it was important to him,” says Mohammed.

Lawson passed on elaborate spreadsheets to Mohammed for use in tracking Sharma’s heart rate, meals and water intake during his attempt. Meanwhile, Khajeian promised to stay awake in Melbourne, which is four-and-a-half hours ahead of Sri Lanka, to instruct Mohammed and the videographers on capturing the right shots for social media and the planned documentary.

“He’s very artistically gifted,” Sharma says of Khajeian, 23, who has a degree in finance and is behind several of the social-media reels made for Ebb&Flo, the Australian running club started by Sharma. “I always told him that it was my dream to buy him out of a corporate job because he’s just too gifted to be sitting at a desk.”

Finally in Sri Lanka, Sharma spent almost every waking minute of the six days of the attempt on his feet, stopping only to eat and sleep for three hours per night, initially, in a camper van with a malfunctioning air-conditioner. While he ran, his entourage, which included Mohammed, a physiotherapist, two cameramen and the driver, followed in the camper van.

With temperatures soaring, the conditions were brutal.

“I blacked out on the second day. I have no memory of it,” Sharma says. At one point, he tried to remove his socks only to discover the rubber grips had melted and fused to his skin. They had to be cut off with scissors.

Mohammed and Lawson, who were monitoring Sharma’s heart rate and pace, the latter remotely from Australia, suggested he finish in seven days instead of six.

“There was a lot of colourful language,” Sharma recalls. “I was just lashing out at the team, telling them it was not an option.”

Lawson, Khajeian and Mohammed understood their friend’s frustration.

“One of the things we have become very good at as a group is separating our relationship as colleagues from our relationship as friends,” says Lawson. “So I knew that Rahul’s anger at me wasn’t a personal attack on me.”

From day three, Sharma slept during the day and ran through the night and early morning, to beat the heat. But the challenges kept coming.

An old injury returned in his left knee, becoming “the worst physical pain” he ever felt, he says, akin to two knives stabbing into his Achilles tendon with every step. Painkillers could only do so much, so Sharma and his physiotherapist fell into a different rhythm: every five minutes, he would stop, get restrapped and sprayed down to dull the pain, then continue to run.

“My physio had sleepless nights. My whole team was working so hard for me to be able to run,” Sharma says. Mohammed even blacked out from the stress at one point on the final day. “It would’ve been selfish of me to stop or slow down.”

Before his sixth and final day, Sharma was told by his father that several priests were praying for him. “Son, tomorrow you will fly,” he told Sharma over the phone, words that would inspire the title of Khajeian’s documentary. Spiritually revived, Sharma’s pace picked up on that last day.

Born to Fly’s most affecting moment is when Sharma arrives at Dondra Head. He collapses, bursting into tears as loved ones gather around him.

“It wasn’t just the physical pain,” he explains. “I put my team through hell. I didn’t see my friends, but they still came to support me. I hadn’t seen my dad in nine months. We raised money for cancer. We did all of this, and for it to just finish in six days …”

Six days, 13 hours and 22 minutes, to be exact – a time that earned Sharma recognition by the World Book of Records as the “fastest man to run from northernmost point to southernmost point of Sri Lanka”, all 566km of it. He also succeeded in raising the A$20,000 for the CCI.

Khajeian, who says it took him more than a month to put the two-hour documentary together, has been especially inspired by Sharma’s feat: “It has made me realise that the only thing standing between me and my goals is myself.”

Says Sharma, “I don’t know how fulfilled I would be if I was still playing cricket. I never got that feeling of, ‘This is what I was born to do.’ With running, everything just feels right.”

His next goal is to tackle a 1,000km route in Nepal. “I’ve done one world record at 24. It’ll be two at 25, if I’m eyeing to be the greatest of all time.”

Eventually, though, “I want to build a brand or open clinics through which I can help the community”, says Sharma.

“If I can choose to have a world record within eight months, you can choose to do the same in any walk of life.”

item.title: [SCMP] Taiwan waits for its new F-16s, still stuck in Hawaii after a fortnight’s delay
item.description:
The first two F-16 Block 70 fighters bought by Taipei from the United States have yet to reach Taiwan, after spending more than two weeks in Hawaii for reasons that remain unclear.

The aircraft, which were expected to arrive at Taiwan’s Chihhang Air Base in late August, were spotted preparing for departure at Joint Base Pearl Harbour-Hickam on Monday, raising expectations that the fighters were finally about to resume their journey.

But the two single-seat F-16Cs, numbered 6727 and 6728, apparently did not leave Hawaii, with witnesses saying they taxied towards the runway before returning to the apron.
item.content:encoded:
The first two F-16 Block 70 fighters bought by Taipei from the United States have yet to reach Taiwan, after spending more than two weeks in Hawaii for reasons that remain unclear.

The aircraft, which were expected to arrive at Taiwan’s Chihhang Air Base in late August, were spotted preparing for departure at Joint Base Pearl Harbour-Hickam on Monday, raising expectations that the fighters were finally about to resume their journey.

But the two single-seat F-16Cs, numbered 6727 and 6728, apparently did not leave Hawaii, with witnesses saying they taxied towards the runway before returning to the apron.

It was the latest twist in the long-awaited delivery of the aircraft, which arrived in Hawaii on August 21 after leaving the continental United States with aerial refuelling support from US Air Force KC-135 tankers.

The pair had been expected to continue to Guam after refuelling and servicing before making the final leg to Taiwan. Instead, they have remained at Hickam, with reports suggesting an earlier attempt to leave Hawaii was also aborted.

Neither the US side nor Taiwan’s air force has publicly explained why the aircraft have been held up for so long, fuelling speculation among military and aviation enthusiasts that technical problems may have emerged.

Some local reports have cited military sources as saying the aircraft encountered “minor problems” that required adjustments in Hawaii. Poor weather along the trans-Pacific route and around Taiwan has also been cited as a possible factor.

Neither explanation has been officially confirmed.

Michael Bosack, a former US Air Force officer and director of the Parley Policy Institute, said maintenance, tanker problems, aircrew health or weather could have caused the delay, but a maintenance issue was the most likely explanation.

Even a routine warning could force an aircraft to return for inspection, he said. If a more serious defect was discovered, repairs would have to be followed by further checks and a post-maintenance safety flight before the aircraft could continue.

“All it would take is one of the aircraft to be ‘hard broke’ … to stop the transit,” Bosack said, adding that problems could emerge even in newly delivered aircraft once they had been flown for some time.

Another possible factor was aerial refuelling, with a maintenance problem involving the designated tanker or limited tanker availability potentially disrupting the flight plan, Bosack noted.

Aircrew health could also have played a role, particularly if one or more pilots became unwell, he said, adding that he considered weather to be less likely as it would take “extreme conditions” to prevent the flights.

However, Taipei-based military analyst Erich Shih said weather could have been a significant factor, with Hurricane Lowell bringing heavy rain, strong winds and high waves to Hawaii and conditions along the westbound route remaining unstable.

“Monday may have offered the only recent window for the ferry flight, as conditions in Hawaii were barely acceptable and Taiwan’s weather had improved after days of heavy rain,” Shih said.

But US commanders may have decided not to take any risks, he said, adding that this might explain why the two fighters entered a taxiway connecting Hickam with Honolulu airport before being recalled and the mission cancelled.

One military enthusiast questioned why two newly built aircraft would require such a lengthy stay in Hawaii if only routine adjustments were involved.

“The point now is not when they will fly back, but why newly delivered aircraft have encountered problems and what kind of defects would require such a long time to fix,” the enthusiast said.

Other disappointed military fans have also complained about the repeated delays in the programme, which has already fallen well behind its original delivery schedule.

“Taiwan has spent a huge amount of money buying so many aircraft, but has yet to receive even one, while [the military] keeps asking for more money,” one online commenter wrote.

Others were more cautious, noting that ferrying fighter jets across the Pacific was a complex operation involving weather, aerial refuelling, maintenance and coordination between several bases. Flight safety should take priority over meeting a delivery date, they said.

Taiwan’s air force has declined to give a firm arrival date, saying the arrangements remain subject to notification from the US side.

“We are waiting too,” an air force official said on Monday when asked about the delivery, while thanking the public for its interest.

Mounting delivery pressures

The uncertainty comes as the entire F-16 Block 70 programme faces mounting pressure over its delivery schedule.

Washington approved the sale of 66 newly built F-16 Block 70 fighters to Taiwan in 2019, for more than NT$247.2 billion (US$7.6 billion).

The order comprises 56 single-seat F-16Cs and 10 twin-seat F-16Ds, which will primarily be stationed at the Chihhang base in the eastern county of Taitung and operated by the air force’s Seventh Tactical Fighter Wing.

Deliveries were originally scheduled to begin in 2023, with all 66 aircraft due by the end of this year. But production line relocation, Covid-19 supply-chain disruptions, software issues and more recent flight-testing problems have pushed procurement well behind schedule.

Wellington Koo Li-hsiung, the Taiwanese defence minister, said earlier this year that US contractor Lockheed Martin was producing 46 single-seat and 10 twin-seat F-16V Block 70 fighters for Taiwan. He did not give an update on the remaining 10 aircraft.

Koo later acknowledged that the original completion target would not be met but has stopped short of saying whether all the remaining aircraft could be delivered by next year or 2028.

The new fighters will significantly expand an F-16 fleet that is at the centre of Taiwan’s air defences as the People’s Liberation Army increases aerial operations around the island.

Once all 66 fighters are delivered, they will join 139 older F-16A/B Block 20 aircraft that Taiwan has upgraded to the F-16V standard, giving the island more than 200 F-16s and making it one of the world’s largest operators of the type.

The Block 70 aircraft are also fitted with conformal fuel tanks, giving them greater range and endurance than Taiwan’s older F-16s.
