Even so, moving fighter aircraft across the Pacific remains a complicated undertaking, requiring careful coordination of weather, aerial refuelling and servicing, as well as stopovers.

Based on Taiwan’s previous F-16 deliveries, the new fighters are expected to stop in Guam before continuing to Taitung. The Hawaii-Guam leg takes about eight hours and 20 minutes, while the flight from Guam to Taiwan takes roughly four hours and 40 minutes.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force for reunification. The United States, like most nations, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but is opposed to any forcible change to the status quo and is committed to providing arms for its defence.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines wants to be a global semiconductor giant by 2030. Can it get there?
item.description:
The Philippines has launched a five-year road map to expand its share of the global semiconductor and electronics sector, but capacity challenges and political stability are potential stumbling blocks, analysts say.

The Philippine Semiconductor and Electronics Industry road map, launched by the Philippines’ Semiconductor and Electronics Industry Advisory Council (SEIAC) on September 2, aims to grow annual exports of chips and electronics to US$110 billion by 2030, and move beyond manufacturing and assembly into higher-end operations.

SEIAC chief and executive secretary Ralph Recto said the goal was to transition to chip design, engineering, research and innovation to boost regional competitiveness.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines has launched a five-year road map to expand its share of the global semiconductor and electronics sector, but capacity challenges and political stability are potential stumbling blocks, analysts say.

The Philippine Semiconductor and Electronics Industry road map, launched by the Philippines’ Semiconductor and Electronics Industry Advisory Council (SEIAC) on September 2, aims to grow annual exports of chips and electronics to US$110 billion by 2030, and move beyond manufacturing and assembly into higher-end operations.

SEIAC chief and executive secretary Ralph Recto said the goal was to transition to chip design, engineering, research and innovation to boost regional competitiveness.

One target is raising the Philippines’ share of global assembly, testing and packaging – already the country’s top semiconductor activities – from 4 per cent to 7 per cent by 2030.

Other goals include growing the country’s share of the global electronics manufacturing services market from less than 1 per cent to 4 per cent and building an integrated circuit design sector that generates US$2 billion to US$3 billion in annual exports.

This expansion would translate to opportunities beyond factories, including jobs in engineering, research, design and other highly skilled fields, Recto said.

Over 60 per cent of the Philippines’ current merchandise exports are from the semiconductor and electronics industry, which generates over US$45 billion annually.

The industry is also being eyed as a major driver of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a US-Japan-Philippines infrastructure initiative and economic hub.

“Whether we act or not, this industry will continue to expand. And we must grow with it. That is the direction President [Ferdinand] Marcos Jnr has set for us,” Recto said.

The SEIAC chairman said the government would focus on removing barriers – such as skilled worker shortages, gaps in power, water and logistics infrastructure, slow permitting and regulatory bottlenecks.

All technical working groups would be held to specific targets and timelines, he said. “A road map is only as good as its execution. We have enough good plans in government. What the industry needs from us now are results.”

Explicit strategy

Josef Yap, a senior research fellow at the Ateneo School of Government, said the road map turned previous recommendations into a “much more explicit industrial upgrading strategy”.

It addressed a larger portion of the value chain and connected semiconductor policy to related sectors such as AI, data centres, consumer electronics, clean energy, infrastructure corridors, economic zones and international partnerships.

“This makes the road map more ambitious as an instrument of economic transformation,” he said.

Lawrence Dacuycuy, a professor of economics at the De La Salle University, said the US$110 billion export target was “possible but highly ambitious”. Electronics exports in 2025 hit US$49.64 billion – meaning a compound annual growth of over 17 per cent for five years would be needed to reach the mark.

The most “credible” target would be raising its global assembly, testing and packaging (ATP) share, due to its established base, he said. But here, the Philippines faces stiff competition from neighbours Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and India.

“Achieving 7 per cent would require the Philippines to outperform the current forecast and expand faster than global ATP capacity growth … This is especially challenging because Vietnam is projected to increase its share from 1 per cent to 8 per cent, and Malaysia from 7 to 9 per cent,” Dacuycuy said.

“The key is to strengthen the country’s supply chains … and design an investment architecture that would support upgrades, advanced manufacturing, diversification and financing.”

Though not the first, the road map was the Philippines’ “most ambitious and sophisticated one yet”, said Lianne Angelico Depante, a doctoral researcher at Tokyo’s National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies.

Its strength lay in recognising the need to build infrastructure such as national laboratories for design, advanced packaging and lab-scale fabrication. “The focus on building capabilities is an important shift in the way we think about industrial policy compared to before,” he said.

But the real test would be “whether we can actually implement it effectively and consistently,” he said. “This is where the Philippines has historically struggled.”

Bigger picture

To succeed, Manila should take a “whole-of-government” approach by developing related sectors and exploring more holistic financing, the analysts say.

Instead of being dependent on foreign direct investments, the industry should look to “embedded reciprocity”, Yap said. “The central policy question is not simply how to attract foreign investment, but how to convert the presence of [multinational corporations] into domestic … capabilities.”

State funding, such as sovereign wealth fund Maharlika Investment, could potentially play a role, particularly for projects that private capital may consider too risky or long-term, according to Depante.

“But ultimately, this will depend on whether the government has the risk appetite … because, in an industry like semiconductors, the willingness to take calculated risks is what determines whether a country remains in low-value activities or successfully moves up the value chain,” he said.

Krista Danielle Yu, an economics professor at the De La Salle University, said the government should prioritise talent development. “Without talent, investors will not come. The road map looks at the talent pipeline in the higher education part, when in reality, it should start as early as elementary school.”

She also stressed the importance of developing stable and cheaper sources of energy. The Philippines’ power rates are the highest in Southeast Asia, according to the Department of Energy.

“Industrial water costs about three times what it does in Malaysia. Logistics is also more expensive compared to other Asean countries,” she said.

To move up the value chain, the focus had to go beyond semiconductor firms, Depante said. “We also need to develop the industries that support them, from chemicals, metals, equipment, logistics and power to other upstream and downstream activities.”

Clark, a central hub in the Luzon Economic Corridor, could potentially play that role, concentrating all forms of support around it, he said.

Most importantly, the survival of the road map will depend on how it weathers leadership changes, according to Depante.

Launched with less than two years in the Marcos administration, the road map could be disrupted by shifting priorities under the next presidency.

“If we genuinely believe that semiconductors and electronics can be a strategic industry for the Philippines … then we need to build institutions and a policy consensus that can survive beyond any single administration.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan is digging in to deter – and withstand – a conflict over Taiwan
item.description:
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the second of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Tokyo is building military resilience within its territory.

Japan’s recent purchase of a former Nippon Steel site to build a sprawling new defence hub points to a deeper shift in Tokyo’s preparations for a potential Taiwan conflict: it is increasingly planning not only for how to deter a war, but also for how to sustain the fight if deterrence fails.

The planned complex in Kure, Hiroshima prefecture – already home to one of Japan’s major naval bases – is intended to combine military facilities, logistics and defence production, concentrating several of the functions Tokyo would need to sustain its forces during a prolonged conflict.
item.content:encoded:
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the second of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Tokyo is building military resilience within its territory.

Japan’s recent purchase of a former Nippon Steel site to build a sprawling new defence hub points to a deeper shift in Tokyo’s preparations for a potential Taiwan conflict: it is increasingly planning not only for how to deter a war, but also for how to sustain the fight if deterrence fails.

The planned complex in Kure, Hiroshima prefecture – already home to one of Japan’s major naval bases – is intended to combine military facilities, logistics and defence production, concentrating several of the functions Tokyo would need to sustain its forces during a prolonged conflict.

Four years into a sweeping defence build-up, experts say that emphasis on endurance reflects a grim conclusion taking hold in Japanese defence planning: preparing for a Taiwan crisis increasingly means preparing to defend Japan itself.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made that concern unusually explicit last November, saying a Taiwan contingency involving warships and the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan – potentially allowing its Self-Defence Forces (SDF) to act even if Japan itself had not come under direct attack.

The geopolitical stakes far exceed the 110km (68 miles) separating Taiwan from Japan’s westernmost territory. Taiwan lies along vital Japanese sea lines of communication and at the centre of the first island chain, close to Japan’s southwestern islands and key US military installations.

Should Beijing gain control, it could significantly strengthen the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) operational position around Japan and its access to the western Pacific.

But the more immediate concern is what could happen during a war over the island.

Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not see Taiwan as a sovereign state but are opposed to any forcible change to the cross-strait status quo.

US forces operating from bases in Japan could play a central role in a Taiwan conflict, potentially placing those facilities – and Japan itself – in Beijing’s crosshairs.

For a country whose post-war security policy has been built around constitutional pacifism and an exclusively defence-oriented posture, preparing to absorb and fight through such attacks marks a profound shift in military thinking.

That pivot is likely to shape revisions to Japan’s National Security Strategy, National Defence Strategy and Defence Buildup Programme, which the government has brought forward to this year, just four years after the present documents were adopted.

The timing shows how quickly Japan’s defence transformation is moving. Tokyo is updating its three strategic documents a year ahead of schedule in response to what Takaichi described as “new ways of warfare” and a growing need to prepare for protracted conflict – developments she said were “accelerating across multiple domains”.

That shift is also reflected in successive increases in military spending. The defence ministry is seeking 8.9 trillion yen (US$55.7 billion) for fiscal 2027, which would mark another record defence budget. The request identifies “sustained response capabilities” as one of three main pillars, alongside responding to “new ways of warfare” and strengthening the foundations of defence capability, including the defence production and technology base.

Yet Tokyo draws an important line around what those preparations are intended to achieve.

Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo and a former Japanese defence ministry official, said the strategic review was intended to strengthen Japan’s ability to defend its own territory, “not to promote an active Japanese role in a contingency over Taiwan”.

But Japan’s stated mission is different from the question of what kind of war its Self-Defence Forces are preparing to fight.

Analysts say the capabilities being assembled suggest Japanese planners expect bases and communications to come under attack while forces must remain operational as ammunition, fuel and equipment are depleted.

Ogi said that because of Taiwan’s proximity and the strategic importance of Japan’s southwestern islands, a cross-strait conflict could spill over into an armed attack on Japan, depending on Beijing’s decisions.

Japan’s concern over Taiwan is not new. Masashi Murano, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said Tokyo had been shifting its military centre of gravity southwest since issuing its 2010 National Defence Programme Guidelines. What had changed were its assumptions about how a conflict with Beijing would unfold.

Murano said Japanese bases, ports and radar sites would probably come under large-scale missile attack in the opening phase of a conflict, while the PLA’s ability to strike US and Japanese forces and bases across the region could hamper US efforts to reinforce Japan.

The more resilient those sites became, however, the harder it would be for Chinese planners to assume an opening barrage could quickly suppress Japan’s ability to fight or support US operations. By raising the prospect of a longer and costlier conflict, that resilience itself becomes a form of deterrence.

This calculation is driving Tokyo towards weapons that can survive, disperse and impose costs despite the PLA’s numerical advantage.

Uncrewed systems could also help offset Japan’s manpower constraints. Murano said SDF personnel numbers were likely to decline, making affordable systems essential for fielding forces in greater numbers.

The remote southwestern Nansei Islands are central to that strategy. For Murano, they are both territory to defend and positions from which dispersed surveillance systems, anti-ship missiles and one-way attack drones could threaten People’s Liberation Army forces moving through chokepoints between the East China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean.

“Southwest island defence, long-range fires and Japan-US integration should be understood not as separate elements but as a single structure,” Murano said.

Michael Bosack, founder and director of the Parley Policy Institute in Melbourne, said Taiwan’s proximity to Japan would become even more significant as relatively cheap uncrewed systems proliferated. In a conflict, such systems could threaten ports, supply lines and commercial shipping – a particular vulnerability for trade-dependent Japan.

Japan’s emerging Shield – Synchronised, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defence – concept reflects similar thinking, combining longer- and shorter-range missiles with large numbers of unmanned systems to target enemy forces at different distances as they approach Japan’s remote islands.

Murano cautioned against relying too heavily on lessons from Ukraine, noting Beijing’s large missile arsenal and expanding bomber force. For Japan, he said, “the far more serious problem is the lack of an effective capability to counter PLA bombers” – particularly given vulnerable Japanese airfields and the PLA’s numerical advantage in combat aircraft.

But denying access to a rival force is only part of the challenge. Japan is also preparing to keep fighting after taking losses.

The defence ministry has acknowledged shortfalls in the availability of ammunition, fuel and equipment for sustained operations, which is why Tokyo is expanding stockpiles and hardening facilities, including by moving key command centres underground.

The Ground Self-Defence Force is also reorganising its logistics system to centralise the management of ammunition, fuel and other supplies, enabling their more flexible distribution in a contingency.

Bosack said that combining concealment, dispersal and hardening – hiding assets, spreading them across sites and reinforcing facilities against attack – could frustrate Beijing’s operational planning, but warned that “Japan’s transparency in its security practice introduces additional risk”.

PLA planners could glean information about new ammunition, fuel and weapons storage simply by following defence ministry engagement with local communities, he said, helping them update potential target lists.

For Murano, Japan’s stockpiling, acquisition of affordable uncrewed systems and pursuit of force survivability are “all premised on a protracted war of attrition lasting months”.

But he cautioned that preparing for a prolonged war would require more than stockpiling – Japan would also need a “defence innovation cycle” that rapidly fed battlefield lessons back into weapons and tactics, rather than treating sustainability simply as a question of how much ammunition had been stockpiled beforehand.

Tokyo is already experimenting with faster equipment procurement. Less than three months after seeking interceptor drones in June, the defence ministry’s procurement agency selected Terra Drone’s Terra B1 and signed a mass production contract for delivery to the Maritime Self-Defence Force.

Joint operations

Surviving PLA strikes would mean little if the SDF could no longer coordinate its operations, however. This realisation is driving changes in how Japanese and US forces plan to command operations during a potential crisis.

The Japan SDF Joint Operations Command (JJOC), established in March 2025, created a permanent headquarters for joint operations, while Washington is turning US Forces Japan (USFJ) into a more operational “warfighting” headquarters. USFJ commander Lieutenant General Stephen Jost said in July that about 215 personnel had been added since the transformation began, including around 100 recent arrivals working to develop bilateral command procedures with the JJOC. The expanded headquarters now had enough personnel to sustain round-the-clock operations across key functions, Jost said.

Tokyo is also investing in space capabilities, cyberdefence and resilient communications networks to maintain its ability to detect targets and transmit information should infrastructure and command nodes come under attack.

Murano said Japan should develop greater independence in the “kill chains” – systems used to find, track and strike targets – supporting its long-range weapons, rather than relying entirely on US systems. With the SDF becoming more dependent on unmanned platforms, he said, resilient space-based communications would become particularly important.

That emphasis on resilience extends beyond the military. Tokyo is developing shelters in parts of the southwestern islands and plans its first field exercise next year to practise evacuating residents from remote Okinawan islands, including Yonaguni, in a military contingency.

The measures underline how planning for a Taiwan conflict encompasses not only keeping the SDF in the fight but protecting civilians if hostilities reach Japanese territory.

And Japan’s ability to remain operational would have consequences beyond the defence of its own territory.

Murano cautioned that the phrase “a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency” did not mean the SDF would necessarily be assigned a mission to defend Taiwan.

But Japan would be a critical platform for US forces that did.

If Japanese military infrastructure were disabled or Tokyo were coerced into dropping out early, Murano warned, the US would struggle to effectively support and defend Taiwan.

The PLA’s ability to strike Japanese and US targets across the region could therefore serve not only to physically disrupt their operations but also to exert “psychological coercion” aimed at making Tokyo drop out early – “before the war begins, if possible”, Murano said.

That makes the line between preparing to defend Japan and preparing for a Taiwan conflict increasingly difficult to draw.

For Bosack, planning around a scenario in which Japan remains untouched makes little sense.

“There may only be one scenario where Japan makes it through unscathed, and a thousand where it doesn’t,” he said.

Preparing for those scenarios requires more than making the SDF itself resilient. A prolonged conflict could rapidly consume missiles, drones and ammunition, while damaged equipment would need repair or replacement.

That brings Tokyo’s acquisition of the Kure site back into the equation. The defence ministry signed the contract with Nippon Steel in late August to acquire the former Setouchi Works site, where the planned hub is intended to combine equipment maintenance and manufacturing, logistics and operational facilities. The ministry has said integrating those functions will help increase the sustainability of SDF operations.

The development comes as the Japanese government is also considering a greater state role in defence production, including government-owned facilities operated by private companies.

The approach reflects a problem that stockpiling alone cannot solve: a prolonged conflict would require Japan to replenish weapons and ammunition, and repair damaged equipment. Tokyo increasingly describes its defence production and technology base as “defence capability itself”.

Beijing, however, sees the transformation very differently.

Responding to Japan’s 2026 defence white paper last month, the defence ministry in Beijing accused Tokyo of hyping the “China threat” to justify easing post-war restraints on its military, pointing to the accelerated revision of the three strategic documents, rising defence spending and longer-range strike capabilities.

Chinese officials have repeatedly described Japan’s trajectory as “remilitarisation” and warned of a revival of militarism, while accusing Tokyo of interfering in Beijing’s internal affairs over Taiwan.

Tokyo rejects that characterisation, maintaining that the capabilities it is acquiring are intended to deter attacks and defend Japanese territory.

For Ogi, the central task of the review is organisational rather than conceptual: integrating the missiles, drones and other capabilities envisaged in Japan’s 2022 defence strategy documents into how the SDF is structured and fights.

Tokyo may insist its military is not being built to defend Taiwan. But its preparations suggest that a war over the island could force Japan to withstand missile attacks, disrupted communications and months of high-intensity attrition simply to defend itself.

Stronger Japanese capabilities would in turn make Beijing “more hesitant to expand a conflict into Japanese territory”, Ogi said, and indirectly, make a successful PLA takeover of Taiwan more difficult.

For Bosack, that is ultimately the logic behind Japan’s preparations.

“At best, it deters China,” he said. “At worst, it prepares Japan for a conflict that will inevitably impact the country in significant ways.”

item.title: [SCMP] In Singapore, malls for shopping only are going out of style
item.description:
While the announcement last week of the closure of a 40-year-old mall in Singapore’s Marina Bay district for redevelopment has caused an outpouring of sentiment among shoppers and tenants, experts say the prime real estate has to be updated into a mixed-use site to survive in the city state.

Last Monday, property developer Singapore Land Group (SingLand) said in a statement that Marina Square, which was completed in 1986, would close on March 31 for a redevelopment that would include features such as luxury residences, serviced apartments and offices with a gross floor area of more than 360,000 sq m.

The revamp, slated for completion in 2031, will have a 304-key hotel that will place guests close to the Marina Bay area, and Marina Square will be refreshed into a four-storey shopping centre offering a wider variety of food and drink options and pet-friendly environments, according to SingLand.
item.content:encoded:
While the announcement last week of the closure of a 40-year-old mall in Singapore’s Marina Bay district for redevelopment has caused an outpouring of sentiment among shoppers and tenants, experts say the prime real estate has to be updated into a mixed-use site to survive in the city state.

Last Monday, property developer Singapore Land Group (SingLand) said in a statement that Marina Square, which was completed in 1986, would close on March 31 for a redevelopment that would include features such as luxury residences, serviced apartments and offices with a gross floor area of more than 360,000 sq m.

The revamp, slated for completion in 2031, will have a 304-key hotel that will place guests close to the Marina Bay area, and Marina Square will be refreshed into a four-storey shopping centre offering a wider variety of food and drink options and pet-friendly environments, according to SingLand.

Three new towers will be integrated into the site, including a 49-storey residential tower hosting 204 luxury homes, while offices will occupy eight floors of a new mixed-use tower, providing around 13,000 sq m of lettable space.

Local media reported that the news of Marina Square’s closure came with disappointment from shoppers and tenants alike. Parents lamented the loss of the shopping centre known for its indoor playgrounds and children’s retail outlets, while tenants said they were shocked by the short notice.

Retail experts point out that consumers today are increasingly seeking experiences, community and connection, and this shift is fuelling the growth of mixed-use developments around the world.

Speaking to This Week in Asia, Tina Qiu, partner and head of Southeast Asia and China at PLP Architecture, the development’s master planner and lead designer alongside local firm DP Architects, noted that the current Marina Square mall was built in the 80s, before much of the iconic Marina Bay precinct had come into existence.

“It was really quite unique of its time because it was the only object there. But in the last 40 years, everything around it to the south of the bay has really been developed,” said Qiu.

Marina Bay was built through a decades-long land reclamation and water management project that transformed open sea and docking points into a modern downtown financial and lifestyle district. The iconic Marina Bay Sands building was opened in 2010.

Qiu noted Marina Square was built in an “introverted” way since malls were then designed to keep shoppers inside the building and the focus was internal attractions like department stores, bowling alleys and cinema complexes, without much connection to pedestrians walking on the street.

“It remained quite by itself, tucked away. Meanwhile, it holds this massive jewel [of being] in the centre of this bay front,” Qiu said.

Without any rejuvenation, the mall would have struggled to keep up with everything else happening around Marina Bay, and there was a need to prepare for the next 40 years to stay relevant, she added.

The revamped mall will have better wayfinding, sports facilities like padel courts, a botanic loop, gardens, covered bridges linking it to other buildings in the area like the coming NS Square and places for members of the public to sit.

Marina Square is the latest example in Singapore of a shopping centre being redeveloped to offer a wider range of amenities. Union Square along Havelock Road is slated to become a mixed-use landmark with offices, retail, and luxury residences, while Tanglin Shopping Centre near Orchard Road is slated for a similar transformation.

These projects are being upgraded with support from the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s (URA) Strategic Development Incentive (SDI) Scheme, which encourages the rejuvenation of older commercial buildings in some areas into innovative developments that will transform the surrounding urban environment.

The scheme allows developers to apply for customised planning parameters, including higher density allowances to the gross floor area and gross plot ratio, permission to change land use, like introducing residential or hotel components into commercial areas and greater flexibility for taller or distinct architectural building profiles.

Experts noted that such upgrades in Singapore reflected a global shift to mixed-use developments for shoppers, homeowners and office tenants to enjoy a more diversified experience.

Seshan Ramaswami, an associate professor of Marketing Education at Singapore Management University, called the redevelopment of Marina Square “another little chipping off of the traditional bricks-and-mortar shopping model”, which was based on large malls, department stores as anchor tenants and a huge array of specialty stores.

In recent years, several major department stores in Singapore, including John Little, Robinsons and Metro, have either ceased or wound down their operations due to evolving lifestyle trends.

Ramaswami likened modern retailing to a real estate business where a developer would build what would generate the greatest value in returns over the long term.

“Increasingly, all physical retail is facing very powerful competition from e-commerce outlets across the world. And then, in Singapore, there is also the proliferation of physical malls built up over the last decades. Some estimate that over 50 new malls have been developed in Singapore since 2000,” Ramaswami said, noting that every town in Singapore had its own mall with similar offerings.

“The attractiveness of centrally located malls in the Orchard and central business district area has reduced considerably consequently,” he added.

Sona Aggarwal, managing director and head of retail sales and strategy in Asia-Pacific at Cushman & Wakefield, noted that for asset owners too, mixed-use developments offered the added advantage of diversified income streams and greater resilience across market cycles.

“By integrating retail with residential, office and hospitality components, these developments can generate consistent footfall throughout the week, benefiting retailers while enhancing the overall appeal and long-term value of the asset,” said Aggarwal.

She noted that across Asia, many of the most successful retail destinations were now part of large-scale mixed-use developments that integrated retail, offices, hotels, residences and public spaces into a single, connected precinct.

These included Bangkok’s IconSiam and One Bangkok, Omotesando Hills in Tokyo and Taikoo Li in Shanghai, which combined retail with lifestyle, cultural and public space elements to create vibrant urban precincts, Aggarwal noted.

She pointed out that particularly in land-scarce Singapore, mixed-use developments enhanced land productivity and created stronger and more consistent footfall.

“As consumer preferences continue to change, the modern mall is no longer just a place for commercial transactions, but a destination for community, connection and shared experiences,” Aggarwal said.

Sulian Tan-Wijaya, executive director and head of retail at Savills Singapore, noted that what made Singapore unique was the “level of government orchestration”.

“Through precise planning incentives like the SDI scheme, Singapore’s URA pushes developers to think about urban renewal, sustainability and community placemaking much faster than market forces alone would dictate,” Tan-Wijaya said.

She also noted that the Marina Square example showed redevelopment no longer meant demolition since the plan was to retain the existing retail podium structure, which would minimise the project’s carbon footprint.

“It shows that cities can radically reinvent themselves for the next century without erasing their architectural heritage or destroying the environment,” said Tan-Wijaya.

Helen Kuan, a regular at Marina Square, said she had been going to the mall since it opened, when it was the largest shopping centre in the country. With about 59,000 sq m of retail space at the time, it was said to be the largest shopping complex in Southeast Asia.

Kuan, a retired regional human resources director, recalled family outings at the mall when her children were young.

“Now that it will be redeveloped, I’m going to miss it but it’s for the good of the future and its expansion. I’m looking forward to seeing the new Marina Square,” said Kuan.

item.title: [SCMP] Angkor Wat marathon: 6,500 runners race through Cambodia’s ancient Khmer empire
item.description:
Under the cloak of darkness, runners gather in their hundreds at the entrance to the Angkor Wat temple complex, in Cambodia’s Siem Reap. They wait in groups, stretching muscles to pumping house music while a little way off, apsara dancers and traditional Khmer musicians help lift the early-morning energy.

Volunteers, many of whom have been at the site since 2am, hand out bottles of water to a crowd of runners and spectators that started arriving at 3.30am, ahead of the staggered starts of the 11th Angkor Empire Marathon.

From a small stage framed by the stone carvings of mythical Nagas at the main-road end of the causeway that crosses the moat to Angkor Wat, two emcees shout out motivational phrases in Khmer and English.
item.content:encoded:
Under the cloak of darkness, runners gather in their hundreds at the entrance to the Angkor Wat temple complex, in Cambodia’s Siem Reap. They wait in groups, stretching muscles to pumping house music while a little way off, apsara dancers and traditional Khmer musicians help lift the early-morning energy.

Volunteers, many of whom have been at the site since 2am, hand out bottles of water to a crowd of runners and spectators that started arriving at 3.30am, ahead of the staggered starts of the 11th Angkor Empire Marathon.

From a small stage framed by the stone carvings of mythical Nagas at the main-road end of the causeway that crosses the moat to Angkor Wat, two emcees shout out motivational phrases in Khmer and English.

As the clock ticks down to 4.30am and the start of the first of four races – the full, 42km (26 miles) marathon – pacers make their way to the starting line, competitive racers cramming in behind, waiting for the klaxon to sound. With minutes to go, dignitaries deliver speeches from a stage, wishing competitors luck, thanking sponsors and praising the event’s success over the years.

“Angkor Wat always has such a special vibe, so it will be exciting to run among all of the ancient temples,” says Christine Hellington, 32, an Australian who recently moved from Cambodia to Vietnam and is competing in her first marathon. “I’m hoping the atmosphere will help push me through, so I can actually finish it.”

National Olympic Committee of Cambodia (NOCC) president Thong Khon, Chinese ambassador Wang Wenbin and NOCC secretary general Vath Chamroeun together light a torch with a blazing flame to officially open the event, then the klaxon sounds and the runners set off towards Siem Reap city, roared on by spectators young and old, who are lining the road.

For many competitors, such as Hellington (who did manage to complete the 42km, in five hours and 34 minutes), this marathon’s appeal isn’t just about finishing. Unlike conventional city races, in which competitors run in the shadow of skyscrapers and urban landmarks, here, runners spend much of the course among the temples, settlements and reservoirs that once formed the heart of the Khmer Empire (802-1431).

According to Thong Khon, the 11th Angkor Empire Marathon (which took place on August 2) saw a 25 per cent increase in the number of competitors compared with last year. Of the 6,500 total, 1,050 were international runners hailing from 51 countries, with the bulk having come from China, Japan and Britain.

Over the two days before the races, entrants were required to visit the Royal Angkor Resort, on the outskirts of Siem Reap, to collect their race gear: their race number – mine was 7008; a T-shirt; a drawstring bag; and a lanyard. Here, the competitive spirit was already being stirred, with pre-race activities ranging from football target practice to mini runs, as well as games and freebies dished out by sponsors. Volunteers and officials were in attendance to offer advice and encouragement.

At 4.30am on the day itself, 1,000 people set off on the full marathon. At 5.30am, another 1,000 took on the half-marathon, and the 10km (six miles) attracted 3,000 runners, who set off at 5.40am. The final 1,500 took part in a 3km (1.9 miles) fun run, and set off at 5.50am. Each route started and ended on the road at the entrance to the Angkor Wat complex.

The 42km route led deep into the Unesco-crowned Angkor Archaeological Park, passing Ta Prohm – the temple featured in the 2001 film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider – and sacred Srah Srang, a vast reservoir known as the “Royal Bath”. The runners pushed through the ancient capital of Angkor Thom, home to the multifaced Bayon temple, and past some of the park’s lesser-known places of worship, including East Mebon, Pre Rup, Banteay Kdei, Prasat Top and Ta Keo, all of which took on an unearthly aspect in the mist. With a section through Siem Reap city and another through a traditional village, Preah Dak, where the smell of num banh chok – the Khmer breakfast dish of rice noodles – wafted through the air, it’s easy to see how the race made it onto Forbes Travel Guide’s “12 Marathons Worth Travelling For in 2026” list, rubbing shoulders with China’s Great Wall Marathon and the Boston Marathon, in the United States.

Clutching his finisher’s medal, Vann Chan Thada seems energised after having completed his second Angkor Empire Marathon, in four hours and 55 minutes.

“The marathon was really challenging with the [searing heat], but it was really exciting with the views on the route that we ran,” says the 25-year-old Cambodian. “Running through the ancient temples gave me a different vibe compared with running in the city. We ran in the early morning under the tree-lined shade, and the sunrise with the temples made us feel like we were running through the golden era of ancient Angkor.”

The 10km race is timed to begin as the sun starts to peek from behind Angkor Wat. In addition to serious athletes, families and groups of friends are taking part, chatting, laughing, stopping to snap selfies and cheer each other on along the way. The 10km is the perfect option, in other words, for beginners such as me.

The seasoned racers storm ahead at the sound of the klaxon, leaving us more casual runners space to take in our surroundings and shoot photos before setting off.

Rays of sunlight pierce a high canopy dripping with cooling condensation along the road from Angkor Wat to Angkor Thom’s South Gate. Mist hovers above waterways and the silhouettes of temples suddenly emerge from the treetops, creating a whimsical atmosphere that feels as though it’s been lifted from a fairy tale.

Dawn is also when nature springs to life, the treetops alive with birdsong and the faint morning call of gibbons. Unperturbed by the pounding feet of thousands of runners, mischievous macaques join spectators on the sidelines, snatching discarded water bottles from the road with which to rehydrate.

Crossing the finish line to energising cheers in one hour and 34 minutes leaves me just enough time to compose myself before English expat Jim Thompson, 46 and dripping in sweat, does the same.

“I’ve run before in very uninspiring places, but the key difference is that this race has the temples of Angkor Wat as a sublime backdrop to your achievement of running,” says Thompson, who is no stranger to the experience, having competed in the Angkor Wat International Half Marathon in 2013 and 2014. The longer-established half marathon is a separate NOCC event that takes place around the temples in December each year.

“The setting in ancient Angkor Wat is the No 1 highlight; the way that the temples slowly emerge from the darkness into the dawn, and all the while this beautiful mist appears in the sunlight, raining back down onto the runners. All of the other participants were a definite highlight, too, spurring you on to the finish.”

The Angkor Empire Marathon was launched in 2014 as an international event designed to promote Siem Reap and the Angkor Archaeological Park as a destination for sports tourism while contributing to charitable and community initiatives.

This year’s marathon came at a challenging time for Cambodia’s tourism sector, which is struggling to rebuild international visitor numbers after the Covid-19 pandemic. Figures from the Ministry of Tourism reveal the nation welcomed 1.75 million international arrivals in the first half of 2026, marking a 47.9 per cent year-on-year decline, the dramatic drop attributed to the closure of land borders with Thailand due to the ongoing conflict between the two nations; the Middle East war and its impact on airfares; and the negative publicity regarding online scam centres operating in Cambodia.

Angkor Enterprise recorded a 31.69 per cent drop in ticket sales for the Angkor Archaeological Park during the same period, highlighting the importance of finding new ways to draw visitors to Siem Reap.

The return of thousands of runners to Angkor Wat offered a welcome boost, a renewed energy having been injected into the city during the race weekend. Restaurants and bars were bustling and shopkeepers engaged in lively bartering to sell their wares.

Tuk-tuk driver Mr Chai secured a steady flow of customers throughout the marathon weekend, he says: “Business has been very quiet lately, so it has been good to be busy and see so many people at the temples again.”

Furthermore, proceeds from the Angkor Empire Marathon and Angkor Wat International Half Marathon directly benefit children’s hospitals, landmine victims and disability support organisations, and the Cambodian Red Cross, among other humanitarian initiatives.

Athletic pursuits in the days of the Khmer Empire – as depicted in bas-relief on the walls of Angkor Wat – served a dual purpose, being a form of military preparation for soldiers as well as a major element of social entertainment. Likewise, today’s Angkor Wat runs are bifunctional: helping to revitalise the local tourism industry while raising funds for charitable causes.

The entry fee for the full marathon for international competitors this year was US$75. It was US$65 for the half marathon, US$50 for the 10km and US$25 for the fun run, with tickets available at checkpointspot.asia. The 31st Angkor Wat International Half Marathon will take place on December 6; to register, click here. The date for the 12th Angkor Empire Marathon has not yet been set, although a different event – the Marathon Trail Angkor, which is a series of off-road runs – is scheduled for January 23, 2027; to register, click here

The writer was hosted by Angkor Village Hotel, in Siem Reap

item.title: [SCMP] Can Japan, South Korea move past the ‘comfort women’ issue?
item.description:
South Korean citizens’ groups have called for the abuse of wartime “comfort women” to be recognised by Unesco, as analysts say the ongoing feud between Seoul and Tokyo threatens to upset recent improvements in their relations.

They also suggest that the two nations would benefit from working together at a time of unprecedented regional and global security and economic challenges, although they admit that may be impossible.

On Sunday, a coalition of South Korean citizens’ groups called on the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation to move forward with the listing of documents about wartime comfort women on its Memory of the World Register.
item.content:encoded:
South Korean citizens’ groups have called for the abuse of wartime “comfort women” to be recognised by Unesco, as analysts say the ongoing feud between Seoul and Tokyo threatens to upset recent improvements in their relations.

They also suggest that the two nations would benefit from working together at a time of unprecedented regional and global security and economic challenges, although they admit that may be impossible.

On Sunday, a coalition of South Korean citizens’ groups called on the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation to move forward with the listing of documents about wartime comfort women on its Memory of the World Register.

The request was made at a press conference in Seoul more than a decade after groups from eight countries first requested that Unesco collate and preserve victims’ testimonies and other paperwork related to the sexual slavery of women from across Asia imposed by Japanese troops.

It comes after the Korean Supreme Court on August 12 dismissed an appeal by Japan’s Nippon Steel against a lower-court ruling in South Korea that ordered the company to pay 80 million Korean won (US$59,528) to the family of the late Min Moon-sik for forced labour in 1942. The previous month, Unesco passed a resolution at its World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan insisting that Japan present the “whole history” of forced labourers – including more than 1,500 Koreans – who worked during Japan’s colonial era at a mine on the Japanese island of Sado.

More than 80 years after the end of the second world war, it is unlikely that the two nations will see eye-to-eye on their shared history – and particularly the years of Japan’s often brutal occupation of the Korean peninsula in the early decades of the last century, according to analysts.

“I do not think it will ever be possible to have a bilateral alliance in the usual sense between the two nations,” said Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo’s Waseda University. “Friendship might be possible, but even that will not be easy.”

Japan was at fault for failing to apologise to the nascent Korean nation immediately after its surrender in 1945 and for not immediately offering to provide compensation for its 35 years of colonial rule, Shigemura said. It was not until 1965 that the two countries normalised diplomatic relations and Tokyo paid US$300 million in compensation to Seoul.

“Japan should have reflected more carefully on its behaviour sooner after the war and emphasised that we were adopting a constitution committed to peace,” he said. “But on the other hand, I think there are still many people in Japan who consider themselves to be superior to Koreans and that we actually helped to modernise their society.”

Equally, some in Korea blamed Japan for virtually all the nation’s problems and to this day insisted that Tokyo intended to expand its military so it could invade and reoccupy the Korean peninsula again, Shigemura said.

“There have been failures on both sides, and that is why I am not optimistic that the relationship will ever be really strong.”

Robert Dujarric, co-director of the Institute of Contemporary Asian Studies at the Tokyo campus of Temple University, likened the relationship to the similarly troubled ties between England and Ireland. The two countries have had disagreements over past sectarian violence in Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK, and Dublin calling for a vote to allow the Northern Irish to decide on reunification.

“I do not think Japan and South Korea will ever be able to have what I would call ‘normal’ relations,” he said. “There will always be irritants, so the question is how the two governments control those situations to make sure they do not degenerate.”

Dujarric said he hoped that the Japanese government would not comment on the Unesco documents request, although he expressed concern that conservative groups in Japan would be unable to let go of the opportunity to criticise their neighbour.

Criticising the request and becoming embroiled in debates on the other historical issues would only escalate the rivalry and potentially return the relationship to the lows it experienced in 2018 and 2019, when the row over the sovereignty of Korean-held Dokdo island came to the fore, and a Korean warship locked its radar onto a Japanese maritime patrol aircraft.

On the trade front, Japan imposed new restrictions on exports of key materials critical to South Korea’s semiconductor industry in 2019, triggering a swift boycott by Korean consumers of Japanese goods before the end of the same year. Political leaders in both capitals have in subsequent years worked hard to smooth ruffled feathers, a task arguably made easier by the worsening security situation over North Korea and their separate deepening trade disputes with the US.

In 2019, then-president Moon Jae-in also angered Japan when he reversed the December 2015 “final and irreversible” agreement to settle the comfort women dispute, under which Japan made a formal apology and acknowledged the suffering of the women. Tokyo also paid 1 billion yen (US$8.3 million) that was meant to be disbursed to the former comfort women through a foundation.

“China and North Korea are security problems that both Japan and South Korea have to face up to, but that situation has been made worse by questions over their alliances with this US administration and the trade tariffs that Washington has imposed on its two most important Asian allies,” Dujarric said.

“Seoul and Tokyo are not short of challenges and enemies, so it would clearly be in their best interests to work together,” he said. “Relations are OK at the moment, but there is always potential for something to happen that upsets that – like a Japanese politician going to the Yasukuni Shrine.”

Yasukuni is the last resting place of Japan’s nearly 2.5 million war dead and is controversial because it also honours the memories of 14 Class A war criminals. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi most recently visited the shrine on August 12, the anniversary of Tokyo’s surrender at the end of the war.

“I hope they can continue to muddle through,” Dujarric said.

Yuji Hosaka, a professor of political science at Korea University in Sejong city and an adviser to the South Korean government on Japan relations, is also pessimistic about the relationship and fears that Tokyo is going to be disappointed if it is holding out hope that the comfort women issue will come to a natural end when the last surviving victim dies.

“There are many groups in South Korea that were not satisfied with the 2015 comfort women agreement, and one of the survivors, Lee Yong-soo, is still very active in promoting their campaign,” said Hosaka.

“I met her recently, and it is clear that she has great power to push the citizens’ movement forward,” he said, pointing out that there were just five former comfort women alive today.

“I recently met another woman who told me that her mother was also a victim, and she said she was committed to continuing the movement even after the last of them has died,” he said.

The South Korean government of President Lee Jae Myung was presently “quiet” on the issue of historical issues with Japan, Hosaka said, but behind the scenes they were being “very helpful” to victims of Tokyo’s colonial rule.

item.title: [SCMP] How Tokyo is widening regional defence ties to complicate Beijing’s Taiwan calculus
item.description:
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the first of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Japan is building a network of partnerships to strengthen its strategic endurance.

Japan is rapidly building a web of defence partnerships spanning the Indo-Pacific and beyond, a move that may bolster its ability to withstand a prolonged armed conflict over Taiwan and complicate Beijing’s calculations.

The push was on display in Australia last month, where Tokyo and Canberra moved to deepen cooperation, ranging from defence planning and advanced weapons development to the construction and sustainment of Japanese-designed warships.
item.content:encoded:
The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the first of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Japan is building a network of partnerships to strengthen its strategic endurance.

Japan is rapidly building a web of defence partnerships spanning the Indo-Pacific and beyond, a move that may bolster its ability to withstand a prolonged armed conflict over Taiwan and complicate Beijing’s calculations.

The push was on display in Australia last month, where Tokyo and Canberra moved to deepen cooperation, ranging from defence planning and advanced weapons development to the construction and sustainment of Japanese-designed warships.

But the deepening relationship with Australia is only part of a much broader shift.

With Taiwan increasingly shaping its defence planning, Japan is connecting regional military ties with defence-industrial and technological partnerships across North America and Europe.

The United States is Japan’s only treaty ally and security cornerstone, and Tokyo is looking to other countries to complement that relationship: from operational and logistical cooperation with Australia and the Philippines to weapons production, intelligence and more secure supply chains farther afield.

Analysts say the aim is not to create a Nato-style coalition committed to fighting alongside Japan but to give Tokyo greater capacity to sustain a prolonged crisis.

For Beijing, that could mean having to calculate not only Japan’s own military strength in a Taiwan conflict but also the wider network of countries that could help keep its forces supplied, its economy resilient and its defence industry running.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

According to Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, Tokyo’s growing defence partnerships could make it harder for Beijing to “isolate or exhaust Japan” in a Taiwan contingency, even though European partners would be unlikely to fight the People’s Liberation Army directly.

“A wider network of partners could give Japan more options and make it harder for China to pressure Japan into accepting an early settlement,” Matsuoka said.

The question of how much support Japan could draw upon has become more salient since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said last November that an attack by Beijing on Taiwan involving military force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” – a legal designation that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence under certain circumstances.

Beijing said the remarks implied possible “armed intervention in the Taiwan Strait” and demanded they be retracted, contributing to a sharp deterioration in Sino-Japanese relations and renewed attention to Tokyo’s potential role in a conflict.

Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at Warwick University, described Tokyo’s approach as a three-layered strategy: strengthening Japan’s own capabilities, integrating more deeply with the United States and building complementary ties with like-minded American allies and partners.

The first two remain at the core, Hughes said, meaning the blossoming relationships with regional partners and Nato member states are not intended to replace the US alliance.

Celine Pajon, head of Japan research at the French Institute of International Relations, echoed that analysis.

“Japan is not trying to replace the US alliance,” Pajon said. “It is trying to make itself less dependent on any single partner.”

For decades, the region’s US-led security architecture followed a “hub-and-spokes” model, with Washington at the centre of separate alliances with Japan, Australia and the Philippines.

Tokyo is now connecting those spokes through bilateral and minilateral arrangements while building ties beyond the traditional US alliance system.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi referred to the shift at the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, describing Japan’s ambition as turning individual security relationships from “points into lines, and from lines into planes”.

Koizumi said this went beyond military access and exercises.

Asking what would happen if “necessary items run short and logistics are cut off” during a crisis, he called for partners to cooperate more closely on defence production, maintenance and sustainment.

That thinking is reflected in work on the coming revision of Japan’s three main security documents.

Defence ministry planning material calls for a “multilayered web of cooperation” spanning bilateral and minilateral frameworks, including the US alliance, Japan-US-Australia-Philippines cooperation and the Global Combat Air Programme.

Such convergence is particularly advanced in Japan’s relationship with Australia, where cooperation increasingly spans operations, defence planning, advanced technology, production and sustainment.

Under a defence coordination framework established in December, the countries have deepened cooperation across operations, intelligence, technology and industry.

On August 18, they agreed to let Japan use Australian ranges to test next-generation long-range precision-strike and autonomous systems, including those linked to its hypersonic missile programme.

The talks also highlighted successful field trials under Boobook, the countries’ first jointly funded defence research project, involving laser technology.

Meanwhile, Australia’s decision to acquire Japan’s upgraded Mogami-class frigate is creating plans to build and sustain the warships locally.

The tempo of cooperation has also accelerated sharply. Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles said he and Koizumi had met seven times over the past 12 months, while bilateral exercises were increasing “at a really significant rate”.

The relationship is also becoming a platform for wider regional partnerships. Japan, Australia and New Zealand launched trilateral defence-ministerial talks in May, while Japan, Australia and Indonesia held their first trilateral defence ministers’ meeting on August 26, agreeing to advance three-way cooperation across the Indo-Pacific.

Japan is also widening its operational ties with India, with the Japan Air Self-Defence Force set to deploy F-2 fighters there in September for the first time, following earlier Indian Air Force deployments to Japan for joint exercises.

In addition, Tokyo and New Delhi are expanding defence-industrial cooperation, adding another dimension to their deepening security relationship.

But it is in the Philippines, which is also embroiled in a territorial dispute with Beijing, where Tokyo’s push intersects most directly with the geography of a potential Taiwan conflict.

The Philippines’ security calculations have become entwined with Taiwan, with Manila quietly expanding unofficial security contacts with Taipei.

The country’s geography, US alliance and economic interests could make remaining outside a major US-China conflict difficult.

At the same time, Japan, the Philippines and the US have been deploying missile systems close to Taiwan along the first island chain, creating what some analysts describe as a tacit “division of labour” that could constrain the PLA in a conflict over the island.

For instance, Japan is strengthening its Type 12 missile capabilities across its southwestern islands while the Philippines has deployed BrahMos anti-ship missiles and US forces have fielded systems including NMESIS and Typhon. Taiwan sits at the geographical centre of this increasingly distributed architecture.

Those capabilities are being accompanied by agreements aimed at deepening operational and logistical ties. A Japan-Philippines Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement that entered into force in August enables reciprocal logistical support during joint operations and exercises.

It builds on a reciprocal access agreement that makes it easier for Japanese forces to train in the Philippines and conduct rotational deployments, alongside expanding defence equipment and sustainment cooperation.

Beijing views the trend differently.

For Beijing, the significance goes beyond more Japanese forces exercising overseas. Access, logistics and complementary capabilities could help dispersed forces operate across the first island chain, forcing mainland China to account for threats from several directions during a Taiwan contingency.

Responding to Japan’s participation in the Balikatan exercises and growing defence relationship with Manila, Chinese defence ministry spokesman Senior Colonel Jiang Bin accused “certain politicians in Japan and the Philippines” of stepping up “military collusion” and criticised Tokyo for “instigating bloc confrontation and building ‘small circles’”.

Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo, said the emerging minilateral frameworks were intended to help deter Beijing while expanding Japan’s regional security role, amid growing concern about Washington becoming distracted by crises elsewhere.

According to Maslow, the network has three broad objectives: to offset the US’ eroding security role, deter China and expand Japan’s security footprint in the region.

But broadening operational ties across the Indo-Pacific is only one dimension of Japan’s internationalisation. Tokyo is also seeking industrial and technological depth through Europe, Canada and other partners that could help it sustain a prolonged crisis.

Nato has become one avenue for that expansion, with Japan deepening cooperation with the alliance on cyber defence, hybrid threats, technology and defence industry while strengthening bilateral relationships with individual member states.

Japan, Britain and Italy are developing a next-generation fighter under the Global Combat Air Programme, which Canada joined as an observer in July, while France and Germany have expanded bilateral defence cooperation and military engagement with Tokyo.

“GCAP is about much more than building a fighter,” said Pajon, referring to the programme. “It is Japan learning to build defence capabilities internationally.”

But the potential wartime relevance of industrial cooperation extends beyond sophisticated platforms.

Hughes said these links could help Japan maintain a technological edge over China in some areas while reducing overdependence on the US, which has sometimes been less willing to export or license particular technologies.

European partners could also work with Japan on less “exquisite” but militarily useful systems, he said, including massed deployments of drones – equipment they might be able to supply during a regional contingency.

That trend is already visible in rising foreign interest in developing and producing drones and other defence technologies with Japanese industry.

Japan’s liberalisation of defence exports reinforces the process.

Tokyo has increasingly treated equipment transfers, joint development and industrial cooperation as instruments of security policy, particularly in Southeast Asia, where they can create long-term relationships involving training, maintenance, parts and upgrades.

Japan’s Official Security Assistance programme extends that approach by helping strengthen the capabilities of strategically located partners whose territory, waters or surveillance capacity could shape the wider regional environment during a Taiwan contingency. Recipients have included the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia.

Economic security is another component. Tokyo is seeking to reduce vulnerabilities including foreign weapons supplies that could be stretched by competing conflicts and dependence on China for critical materials and components.

Maslow said this reflected a broader conception of national security in Tokyo, with supply-chain resilience, trade and investment increasingly forming part of Japan’s strategic competition with China.

Pajon said that ultimately Japan’s expanding partner network was making China’s strategic environment “more complex and less predictable”, while Maslow similarly argued that Tokyo’s efforts had “complicated China’s security planning”.

In a Taiwan contingency, this means Beijing would have to factor in not only Japan’s own military capabilities but also Tokyo’s access to outside sources of technology, production, intelligence, economic support and political backing as a conflict continued.

Matsuoka described the broader objective as an attempt to build “strategic endurance”, giving Japan greater capacity to withstand the political, economic and military pressures accompanying a prolonged confrontation.

However, there are significant limits to what this network could deliver if deterrence failed.

Hughes said Japanese policymakers were “relatively clear-eyed” about European capabilities, adding that their defence commitments to the Indo-Pacific remained “quite limited and not to be relied on in a potential conflict over Taiwan”.

European submarines or aircraft carriers that sometimes sail to the region might play some role, he said, but more realistic contributions could include economic pressure or European navies assuming greater responsibility in the Indian Ocean, freeing US forces to concentrate on Japan or Taiwan.

Pajon likewise said Europe’s strongest contributions would probably come through diplomacy, sanctions, cyber and information operations, intelligence, capacity-building and selected military deployments rather than large-scale combat operations.

“The real value therefore lies in deterrence through a broader network of capable partners, not in assuming that Europe would provide large-scale military support if deterrence failed,” Pajon said.

Tokyo thus does not need every partner to fight the PLA for its growing network to have strategic value.

Sharing intelligence, producing components, repairing equipment, protecting shipping routes, imposing economic costs or assuming security responsibilities elsewhere could all help Japan sustain a Taiwan contingency.

But that distinction may carry little weight in Beijing, which already regards Tokyo’s expanding security relationships as a form of bloc-building.

China’s foreign ministry said in April that Japan had been “interacting frequently with Nato” in an effort to bring the “non-regional military organisation” into the Asia-Pacific, accusing Tokyo of “provoking confrontation”.

And for most of this year, Chinese state media and spokesmen have lashed out frequently at Japan’s defence push, comparing it with the country’s pre-World War II military build-up.

The perception gap between Tokyo and Beijing risks intensifying an already deepening security dilemma.

“The same network that makes Japan harder to isolate could also deepen the regional arms race,” Matsuoka said.

“From Japan’s perspective, these measures are largely defensive and intended to strengthen deterrence. From China’s perspective, they may look like Japan is becoming part of a wider military coalition.”

item.title: [SCMP] What North Korea’s new warship reveals about Kim’s moves to secure surrounding waters
item.description:
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s promise to unveil more projects in eight months’ time at the launch of the country’s second modern destroyer hints at another major strategic military asset, according to experts.

“The nuclearisation of our navy is being realised, making it increasingly suited, diversified and practical for the use of our deterrent,” Kim said while commissioning the Kang Kon in the southeastern port of Wonsan on Sunday.

Kim was accompanied by his daughter and potential successor, Kim Ju-ae, his wife, Ri Sol-ju, his influential sister, Kim Yo-jong, and other senior officials
item.content:encoded:
North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s promise to unveil more projects in eight months’ time at the launch of the country’s second modern destroyer hints at another major strategic military asset, according to experts.

“The nuclearisation of our navy is being realised, making it increasingly suited, diversified and practical for the use of our deterrent,” Kim said while commissioning the Kang Kon in the southeastern port of Wonsan on Sunday.

Kim was accompanied by his daughter and potential successor, Kim Ju-ae, his wife, Ri Sol-ju, his influential sister, Kim Yo-jong, and other senior officials

“We must make the practical operation of our nuclear combat systems more diverse and effective, and our military activities for maritime defence and war deterrence more explicit, by making our powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent more clear,” he said. “Concerns of the enemies will be surely deepened.”

North Korea was currently carrying out “important plans to strengthen our naval forces”, Kim said without elaborating. “I will demonstrate them to the world once again eight months from now.”

This specific time frame suggests that North Korea could unveil another large-scale asset, such as a submarine capable of carrying submarine-launched ballistic missiles or a nuclear-powered submarine, according to observers.

It could be a “disclosure of progress in the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine, a third destroyer or additional naval bases”, said Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies. Other possibilities included “nuclear torpedoes designed for use by destroyers or improved versions of strategic cruise missiles”.

The commissioning of the Kang Kon came roughly 15 months after the vessel was damaged during its launch in May 2025, and 75 days after the first modern destroyer of the same class, the Choe Hyon, was put into active service in June.

The Choe Hyon is operating in the Yellow Sea off North Korea’s western coast, while the Kang Kon has been deployed in the Sea of Japan off the eastern coast. Both are the North’s most advanced 5,000-tonne destroyers and are equipped with nuclear-capable missiles.

Sovereignty exercise

The back-to-back commissioning of the two destroyers underscored North Korea’s efforts to develop a more diversified and operationally credible naval nuclear deterrent, Kim said.

“This is a clear reality that allows us to measure the speed at which our navy is changing,” he said. The North Korean armed forces’ duty was to “safeguard the absolute security of the state, maintain strategic stability and the balance of power in the region, and deter geopolitical threats”.

The commissioning ceremony came as the United States, South Korea and Japan kicked off their five-day Freedom Edge exercise on Monday in waters off South Korea’s Jeju Island, in a demonstration of their commitment to deterring North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats.

“The fact that the Kang Kon is being officially commissioned into the maritime force of the East Sea, and the information that naval bases are being built in the East Sea, sends an unmistakable signal to our enemies,” Kim said. “Now is the time to exercise our sovereignty directly at sea and underwater as well.”

The East Sea is the name used by both Koreas for the Sea of Japan, off the eastern coast of the Korean peninsula.

Yang said the move appeared to serve multiple purposes: “addressing North Korea’s relatively weaker defensive posture in the East Sea, responding to Japan’s recent moves to strengthen its military capabilities, countering the presence of US aircraft carriers, and potentially taking into consideration expanding maritime military cooperation with Russia”.

Although North Korean state media did not explicitly mention Ju-ae in its report, photographs showing her accompanying her father underlined her position in the hierarchy, Yang said. “Her attendance may be intended as part of her military education and exposure to high-level defence and naval affairs as a potential future successor.”

The commissioning of the Kang Kon, and North Korea’s broader effort to nuclearise its navy, could also be intended to portray the country's ability to secure the Kim family’s bloodline, according to Yang.

“Kim Ju-ae’s visible participation in events alongside senior party, government and military officials may be intended to strengthen her public image and cultivate familiarity and personal affinity, thereby indirectly building support for the future leadership succession,” he said.

Addressing the Kang Kon’s crew, Kim described the destroyer as “one means and capability incorporated into the state nuclear response system”.

“If the adversaries attempt to use force against us, I will order you comrades to use absolute power that will be most lethal to the enemy. You must deliver a devastating retaliatory strike against the enemy at any moment that order is given.”

‘Nuclear for nuclear’

Those remarks amounted to a public declaration that North Korea was “moving towards the operational deployment of a sea-based nuclear response system”, said Lim Eul-chul, a political-science professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.

They also signal efforts to make the country’s maritime nuclear deterrent more practical and diversified, including through the deployment of tactical nuclear-capable cruise missiles, according to Lim.

“This suggests that the vessels are intended to be operated as launch platforms for tactical nuclear-capable multipurpose cruise missiles, or submarine-launched cruise missiles,” Lim said.

“In particular, by designating the East Sea as a major security threat area and forward-deploying the Kang Kon there, North Korea appears to be pursuing an Anti-Access/Area Denial, or A2/AD, strategy aimed at directly deterring South Korean, US and Japanese naval exercises and the deployment of their nuclear assets within the destroyer’s operational range,” he said.

The East Sea is a key approach route for US Navy aircraft carriers and strategic ballistic-missile submarines.

“By explicitly referring to the construction of a blue-water fleet and expansion into distant waters, North Korea is signalling that it intends to continue building larger warships and expanding its naval capabilities,” Lim said.

In his speech, Kim singled out the East Sea as North Korea’s greatest security threat.

“Nowhere else on Earth can you find waters surrounding any country where warships of the opposing side constantly appear, carrying out the movement and deployment of nuclear assets and joint warfare demonstrations without any restrictions, and using them as a stage to track and deter even the legitimate exercise of self-defence,” he said.

“We must respond thoroughly to these threats with highly professional and overwhelming force, possessing the will and sufficient capability to use it.”

By openly declaring the nuclearisation of its warships, Pyongyang was making clear the concept of a “nuclear-for-nuclear” confrontation and showing its intention to directly counter the deployment of US naval forces with a sea-based nuclear deterrent, according to Lim.

“North Korea also sent a strong A2/AD message by saying it would ‘strictly constrain’ US naval forces and force them to make a ‘strategic retreat’. This indicates that Pyongyang does not recognise the maritime superiority that the United States has enjoyed in the East Sea and intends to challenge it,” he added.

The risk of close encounters and accidental clashes with South Korean, US and Japanese vessels is higher now that North Korea is expected to increase patrols and show of force in the Sea of Japan, according to Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification.

“As the East Sea is also a contact zone with the Russian Pacific Fleet, attention must be paid to the possibility that it could become a channel for accumulating open-ocean operational experience through future joint North Korea-Russia naval activities or port calls,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Viral Jennie clip tests limits of South Korea’s AI deepfake laws
item.description:
For a few seconds during Blackpink member Jennie’s headline set at Tokyo’s Summer Sonic festival last month, it looked like something had come undone.

She turned away from the crowd, adjusted herself and then, the moment was gone. But online, the clip never disappeared – and more than 10 million views later, it has become the latest test of South Korea’s fight against AI-enabled sexual abuse.

Fans were quick to cry deepfake, dissecting the footage frame by frame for signs of possible AI manipulation and calling for it to be taken down.
item.content:encoded:
For a few seconds during Blackpink member Jennie’s headline set at Tokyo’s Summer Sonic festival last month, it looked like something had come undone.

She turned away from the crowd, adjusted herself and then, the moment was gone. But online, the clip never disappeared – and more than 10 million views later, it has become the latest test of South Korea’s fight against AI-enabled sexual abuse.

Fans were quick to cry deepfake, dissecting the footage frame by frame for signs of possible AI manipulation and calling for it to be taken down.

The K-pop star’s agency, OA Entertainment, neither confirmed nor denied the clip’s authenticity, merely saying in a statement on August 18 that it had “recently identified ongoing misconduct targeting the artist [Jennie] across online communities and social media platforms”.

It added that it was working with lawyers to pursue civil and criminal action, vowing “no compromise or leniency whatsoever”.

The account believed to have first posted the video has now been suspended, but no official police or prosecutorial follow-up has yet been announced.
