If pursued, the case is set to become a high-profile test of South Korea’s revised deepfake laws. Enacted in 2024, their scope has since been broadened to punish not only those who create or distribute sexually exploitative AI-manipulated material, but also those who possess, save or watch it.

Yet legal experts say a viral clip of disputed authenticity also exposes the practical limits of enforcement, from proving who made it to who knowingly spread it around.

South Korea’s legal framework is “relatively proactive in establishing strong criminal penalties for this kind of abuse”, according to Bang Suk-ho, a senior legal adviser and head of the AI industry centre at Seoul-based law firm Lin LLC.

“But simply strengthening the law does not make crime disappear,” he told This Week in Asia. “If anything, we’re in a phase where technology has led to more crime while making it harder to detect criminals.”

Evolving abuse

South Korea overhauled its legal arsenal against deepfakes two years ago in the wake of public fury over Telegram-based sex crime rings that distributed doctored images of women and girls, including students and servicewomen, via encrypted chat rooms.

The scandal carried echoes of the notorious Nth Room case of 2020, which first exposed how platforms based overseas could be used to produce, sell and blackmail victims with sexually exploitative material.

But the newer deepfake cases were different in one crucial aspect: demonstrating how convincing abuse material can now be conjured from an ordinary photo, then rapidly circulated and viewed by large numbers of people, before anyone – victim or investigator – knew who had made it.

Under amendments to South Korea’s Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes that came into effect in 2024, creating sexually explicit deepfakes carries penalties ranging up to seven years in prison or a fine of 50 million won (US$36,800).

Possessing, purchasing, storing or knowingly viewing such material can carry up to three years in prison or a fine of up to 30 million won.

Campaigners got some of the harsher penalties they were calling for, but the new law also raised difficult questions about proving intent – and how to actually enforce it.

Tougher sentencing rules had pushed prosecutors to seek “increasingly harsher sentences”, which in turn had influenced court decisions, said An Gab-chul, a lawyer at Gammyung Law Firm in Seoul who specialises in sexual crimes.

Yet An said the new measures “often fall short in practice and do not function as effectively as they should”, further arguing that procedures for removing illegal material should be simplified.

The Jennie case shows why. Before any prosecution can begin, investigators need to establish whether the footage was indeed fabricated, trace who posted it first and prove whether those who shared it knew it was fake.

“The apprehension and punishment of offenders is another major problem, as it’s difficult to identify the operators of platforms based overseas,” An said. “Extraditing them may raise conflicts with foreign laws, and overseas servers are outside the jurisdiction of South Korean law.”

That difficulty was borne out in police data presented late last month at a forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea, which showed that authorities had filed 26,697 data requests with foreign messaging services and platform operators but received responses to just 15,466 of them, or 58 per cent. The rest went unanswered.

For An, the more immediate concern is often more basic: identifying who is behind an anonymous account before the evidence disappears.

“The biggest obstacle in online sexual crimes today is preventing suspects from destroying or tampering with evidence,” he said.

“In the case of anonymous accounts, it can take a long time to identify the actual user. Investigators often have to contact operators of overseas servers to determine who is behind an account before the person behind the account shuts it down or destroys evidence.”

In viral celebrity cases like Jennie’s, that delay can be especially damaging, as reposts and screenshots multiply and vanish long before investigators can establish where the material originated.

Still, South Korean courts have shown they can impose prison sentences for AI-generated sexual abuse material when investigators do identify the person responsible.

In June, a man convicted of creating and distributed deepfakes of K-pop girl group Aespa was sentenced to two and a half years in prison, alongside an 80-hour sexual violence treatment programme and a seven-year ban from working with children and adolescents.

Moral disconnect

Criminal penalties alone cannot solve the issue, according to Bang, who finds the psychological side of these offences more unsettling.

Whereas committing a crime in person forces the offender to confront their victim, he argues that screens remove this human element.

“In the virtual world, that awareness of wrongdoing … becomes much weaker, especially among younger people,” Bang said.

“The younger the users, the wider the gap tends to be between their awareness of wrongdoing and the severity of the punishment. As a result, their awareness of the seriousness of these crimes, and of the harm caused to victims, is becoming weaker.”

Last year, deepfake-related offences accounted for 35.2 per cent of all cybersex crimes uncovered by police, or 1,553 cases in total – the single largest category, according to statistics presented at the Amnesty forum.

Of the 3,557 people apprehended in 2025, almost half – 1,761 – were teenagers and over 90 per cent of deepfake suspects were in their teens or twenties.

One case last month involved a teenager being referred to prosecutors after allegedly creating sexually explicit deepfakes using photographs of about 20 girls his age and sharing them on social media.

“So this is not something that can be solved simply by strengthening the law, like an endless game of cat and mouse,” Bang said. “We’ve already seen that from experience.”

This is not something that can be solved simply by strengthening the law, like an endless game of cat and mouse

Bang Suk-ho, AI legal expert

Won Eun-ji has seen it too. As executive director of Team Flame, the investigative group that helped expose the Nth Room digital sex-crimes and blackmail scandal in 2020, she has watched high-profile cases like Jennie’s capture the kind of public attention that ordinary victims rarely receive.

“The government, media and society as a whole are not paying enough attention to this issue,” she said, noting that even today, many investigations only began after victims forced the issue.

“The police and authorities need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities in tracking and investigating such cases.”

Her final point was one she wanted readers to reflect on: that viral moments like the Jennie clip showed the public had a role to play too.

“Most of us may not be perpetrators or victims, but that does not mean we are unrelated to the issue,” Won said.

“Whenever we come across deepfake sexual abuse material, it is important to report it to the platform, and remember that when someone opens up about being victimised, it is important to support them. We shouldn’t just be bystanders.”

Amnesty International Korea framed the challenge in still broader terms, saying the real task ahead was for society to ask “why this violence continues to occur and how we can change the environment in which violence occurs and spreads”.

“Digital sexual violence should be understood as a form of gender-based violence,” the organisation said in a statement.

“We need to address the structural causes that allow such violence to persist, as well as creating change in the digital environment that provides it a platform.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hired, then what? Malaysia’s deaf workers push past entry-level jobs
item.description:
Yap Yee Lin has been serving espresso at a Starbucks in Malaysia since 2012, longer than many of his colleagues have worked anywhere.

But it was only last year, after 13 years with the company, that he was promoted to shift manager at a branch in Kuala Lumpur’s Bangsar Village II.

The wait says less about Yap, who is deaf, than it does about how rare that kind of promotion still is for deaf workers in the Southeast Asian nation – and how much has had to change around him to make it possible.
item.content:encoded:
Yap Yee Lin has been serving espresso at a Starbucks in Malaysia since 2012, longer than many of his colleagues have worked anywhere.

But it was only last year, after 13 years with the company, that he was promoted to shift manager at a branch in Kuala Lumpur’s Bangsar Village II.

The wait says less about Yap, who is deaf, than it does about how rare that kind of promotion still is for deaf workers in the Southeast Asian nation – and how much has had to change around him to make it possible.

Yap, 36, works at what Starbucks calls a Signing Store: an outlet staffed by deaf baristas working alongside colleagues trained in sign language, where visual alarms replace buzzers and dual screens allow staff who cannot hear to confirm an order without it needing to be called out.

The Kuala Lumpur branch was the first of its kind in the world when it opened in 2016 and has since become something of a flagship for corporate inclusion.

“The hearing and the deaf, they are also given the opportunity to be independent and an opportunity for promotion,” Yap said.

Across Malaysia, structured career progression for people with disabilities remains the exception rather than the rule. And it often depends on their employer taking the initiative.

Room to rise

The idea for a Signing Store has its roots in a project that Starbucks began rolling out in 2016 to create job opportunities for people with disabilities, according to Rina Siew, head of sustainability and social impact for Berjaya Food, the licensee that operates Starbucks in Malaysia and Brunei.

At first, deaf recruits were mainly employed as cleaners, but the company soon found that offering routine work with little room for career growth was unsustainable.

Deaf employees wanted to become baristas, Siew said, so the coffee giant worked to make it happen.

“That was how the concept of the Signing Store was born,” she said. “We wanted a place where they could build their careers like all of us here at Starbucks.”

Achieving this meant redesigning the outlets themselves, training hearing staff in Malaysian Sign Language and integrating deaf employees into the same professional-development and performance-review track as everyone else.

“At Starbucks, we have a career progression plan for all partners,” Siew said.

A decade later, the results are clear to see in the company’s organisational structure. Starbucks Malaysia now has its first deaf store manager-in-training, based in Penang, alongside deaf shift managers working in branches across Kuala Lumpur, Johor and Sarawak.

Globally, the company operates more than 26 Signing Stores, including in the United States, Japan, South Korea and China.

Siew said the ultimate goal was to make that level of inclusion the norm rather than the exception, incorporating it into Starbucks everywhere, not just a few designated branches.

Standing in the way of the ambition to hire more workers with disabilities is a lingering workplace stigma, however.

Some employers still viewed deaf staff as less productive, or asked why they should receive the same pay as hearing colleagues, Siew said, adding that there was also a chronic lack of sign language interpreters.

“Interpreters in Malaysia are really scarce,” she told This Week in Asia.

Wong Yi Xiang, 34, knows that struggle all too well. He joined Starbucks six months ago, after a job search hamstrung not by his qualifications, but by communication difficulties.

“My biggest barrier is communication, especially during interviews, because some employers do not understand deaf people,” he said. “All I want is a fair chance to show my work-related skills.”

What Wong really desires from a workplace is simple: hearing colleagues willing to meet him halfway and learn enough sign language to work alongside him as an equal.

Opportunities for deaf people are scarce in Malaysia and many employers who do hire them largely treat it as a quota-filling exercise – a truth Yap knows from firsthand experience.

“It’s difficult for deaf people to look for a job,” he said. “In most places, you only get one or two [deaf employees].”

A place to belong

More than 800,000 people were registered as persons with disabilities in Malaysia in 2024, according to the country’s Department of Statistics, representing 2.4 per cent of the population.

Employment among that group has inched upwards: 4,209 people with disabilities held civil service jobs in 2024, the latest year for which figures are available, up from 3,901 the year before.

Yet the main obstacle remains acceptance and understanding, according to the Malaysian Federation of the Deaf.

Its executive director Mohamad Sazali Shaari, who is himself a member of the deaf community, said deaf jobseekers were still routinely asked to prove their competence before being considered for a role in a way hearing candidates rarely were.

“Limitations arise when colleagues are not accommodating of deaf employees’ communication needs or when there is poor access to information,” he said.

“This can become more difficult in workplaces with high staff turnover, where new colleagues may not understand the support deaf employees need, undermining efforts to build an inclusive workplace.”

Government incentives had helped, Sazali said, but this was not the same as a sense of belonging.

“We will never feel welcome if our needs aren’t in place and sensitivity towards these needs will help to ease our discomfort in society at large,” he said.

Malaysia’s government has said it is pushing for precisely that kind of change in perspective.

At a gathering in December to mark the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, the cabinet minister who oversees social welfare, women’s rights and family development said the country should move away from viewing disabled citizens as a group in need of assistance and start treating them as one capable of contributing, creating and leading.

“This shift requires a change in mindset: from sympathy to respect, from simply giving to empowerment and from assistance to the recognition of rights,” Women, Family and Community Development Minister Nancy Shukri said.

Malaysia is not alone in trying to move disability employment beyond simply getting people into work.

Singapore has set a target of 40 per cent employment among resident people with disabilities aged 15 to 64 by 2030, up from the 34.7 per cent recorded in 2024-25.

Its Ministry of Manpower said in March that 6,800 employers had received government wage support to hire 10,800 residents with disabilities last year, with a separate scheme helping more than 2,400 disabled jobseekers find work over the previous four years.

Even so, officials in the city state have drawn many of the same conclusions Starbucks reached in Malaysia – that getting people through the door is not the same as offering them a place to belong.

“Inclusive workplaces cannot be built on incentives alone,” said Shawn Huang, senior parliamentary secretary for manpower, during a parliamentary meeting about the country’s annual budget, adding that Singapore would also focus on training, employer support and career resilience.

For Yap, helping manage a Signing Store means more than just a pay cheque; it is a way of being accepted by society. After years of seeing deaf workers elsewhere relegated to one or two token roles per company, a shift manager’s badge feels like a quiet victory.

“I really enjoy it [my job],” he said. “There are so many tourists coming here from all over the world. I really thank them for coming to visit our place and it’s a really amazing experience for us.”

Wong, earlier in his career, is thinking about what he can pass on rather than what he has been given.

“I hope to become a coffee master and learn more about coffee,” he said. “I want to share my knowledge about my work and teach other people.”

item.title: [SCMP] Cats and mind-full mechanics: what happens when quantum physics meets the brain
item.description:
Cats are wonderful gymnasts. Their ability to land on their feet – even when dropped upside-down – caught the attention of two of the nineteenth century’s greatest mathematical physicists, Sir George Gabriel Stokes and James Clerk Maxwell.

The remarkable feats of cats inspired these theorists to perform, in the 1850s, legendary experiments in “cat-turning”, as Maxwell later described:

“There is a tradition in Trinity that when I was here I discovered a method of throwing a cat so as not to light on its feet, and that I used to throw cats out of windows,” he wrote.
item.content:encoded:
Cats are wonderful gymnasts. Their ability to land on their feet – even when dropped upside-down – caught the attention of two of the nineteenth century’s greatest mathematical physicists, Sir George Gabriel Stokes and James Clerk Maxwell.

The remarkable feats of cats inspired these theorists to perform, in the 1850s, legendary experiments in “cat-turning”, as Maxwell later described:

“There is a tradition in Trinity that when I was here I discovered a method of throwing a cat so as not to light on its feet, and that I used to throw cats out of windows,” he wrote.

“I had to explain that the proper object of research was to find how quick the cat would turn round, and that the proper method was to let the cat drop on a table or bed from about two inches, and that even then the cat lights on her feet.”

These pioneering experiments in cat-turning were limited by the available technology. High-speed photography revolutionised the subject. Etienne-Jules Marey developed a chronophotographic camera that could record 12 frames per second, and in 1894 he published a classic, delightful series of stop-action photographs that reveal the sequence of actions through which cats reorient themselves on the fly (literally) and stick the landing.

In 1969 a now-classic dynamical model appeared. Even today the subject is not exhausted: a 2026 study began replacing idealised hinges and cylinders with measured properties of a real cat’s spine.

Similarly, human divers and gymnasts learn how to guide themselves, catlike, through routines that reorient their bodies in motion. For the cat much of this control may be reflexive; in a human athlete it can be planned, rehearsed and revised.

These abilities seem, on the face of it, to violate the spirit of Newtonian mechanics, which says that accelerated motion occurs through the action of physical forces, not willpower. That tension, I think, is one reason that cat-turning fascinated Stokes and Maxwell.

A second, more technical reason has to do with the relationship between angular momentum and angular motion. Starting with zero angular momentum and with no external torque, the cat nevertheless changes its orientation. This would be impossible for a rigid body, but by executing a closed loop in its space of possible shapes the cat manages to rotate.

A big part of the reason why classical Newtonian mechanics was difficult to discover, and a big part of why it is such a towering intellectual achievement, is that it required a kind of cognitive dissonance.

Specifically, it required – and still requires – people to reconcile two very different, quasi-contradictory descriptions of motion, both successful and convincing within their domains of application.

There is the “common sense” understanding of movement, in which the concepts of will and purpose are central. This is the way we live our everyday lives: when we reach out to pick something up, we don’t compute forces and accelerations, we just decide to do it.

Then there is classical mechanics proper – austere, rigorously mathematical, and deterministic – from which those concepts are excluded.

Before the mechanical world-view took hold, self-directed motion was often treated as evidence of an animating principle – a soul – absent from inert matter.

Today, science has understood that matter, embodying a system of known, (relatively) simple, mathematically formulated laws, can support the sort of complex emergent behaviour we find in molecular biochemistry, neurobiology and synthetic intelligence. With that understanding, we can bring mind back into mechanics without sacrificing its integrity.

The abilities of cats, divers and gymnasts don’t really evade the laws of physics, of course – if they did, we’d promptly change the laws.

The fruitful way to engage this problem is not to deny the role of mind in mechanics, but rather to welcome it in.

The cat does not invent a new force; it chooses a path in shape space and uses its muscles to redistribute its mass. Ordinary mechanics translates that path into rotation. Thus, to do justice to cat-turning we must enrich mechanics’ vocabulary and its stock of concepts.

We can call this expanded subject – which brings ideas about will, control and goal-seeking behaviour into mechanics – “mind-full mechanics”. Its technical ingredients flourish under names such as biomechanics, control theory and robotics. Mind-full mechanics names the conceptual innovation they share in common.

In mind-full mechanics, we let ourselves assume that our cat, diver or gymnast can change its shape by acts of “will”.

“Will” is the product of minds that have plans aimed at achieving goals, monitor progress, and respond to cues from the external world. Purpose is not a new force; it is a new way of organising forces.

Ordinary mechanics – basically, physics according to Sir Isaac Newton – governs how willed shape changes get translated into motion through space.

Will is not a force. It is a policy for choosing and coordinating forces. To describe the purposive motion, we need both forces and minds. This hybrid approach defines mind-full mechanics. It is how biologists, athletes and trainers generally think about the mechanical issues they deal with.

Allowing for mind and will spices up mechanics considerably. It invites new kinds of questions and permits new kinds of answers.

What degrees of freedom can mind-full acts of will call into play? What kinds of observations can guide good choices? How can feedback help to provide stability? What is the role of practice and learning? How did cats’ abilities evolve, and how can athletes move more efficiently or more beautifully?

Engineers who design machines for transport, manufacturing, or many other purposes practice mind-full mechanics. Consider, for example, what goes into designing a self-driving car. Sensors provide perception, computers implement a control policy, and actuators translate the policy into forces.

The sensors and computers form a narrowly focused mind, while the actuators are like muscles that it activates. Modern “mechanical” engineers learn not only physical mechanics but also control theory, operations research and optimisation.

These playful and practical aspects of mind-full mechanics should not obscure its profundity. It is a big step to connect mind and matter. Here we do just that, concretely and successfully. With feet planted on the ground, then, let us contemplate the clouds. Mind-full mechanics shines a bright light into the murky philosophical question of free will versus determinism.

The fundamental equations of present-day physics suggest that the complete physical state of a closed system fixes its future. But that is rarely the question we are interested in. We usually have only approximate knowledge of a few aspects of the state of a system, and our interest is focused on limited aspects of its behaviour.

For instance, it would be hopelessly difficult, not to mention silly, to try to do psychiatry by evolving the patient’s fundamental wave function. (“How are your gluons arranged today?”)

Usually, we have approximate knowledge of a few aspects of our system, and we want to predict a few aspects of how it is likely to behave. Given only that partial information, many underlying states remain possible, leading to a range of possible macroscopic outcomes that we often describe probabilistically.

Determinism names a property of a dynamical theory: given a complete state of a closed system at one time, the theory prescribes its later state. But an agent never possesses that complete description and, more importantly, does not pose that question.

Its question is not simply “What will happen?” but “What will happen if I do this rather than that?” It has partial information, several available actions, and a goal. It faces a problem of control.

Those alternatives do not contradict determinism. If I perform action A, one consequence follows; if I perform action B, another follows. Deliberation is the physical process through which one of those conditions is made actual. Memories, reasoning and imagined consequences are among the causes that shape the choice. Choice is not outside the causal chain; it is one of its links.

In philosophical language, determinism is an ontological claim, not an epistemic gift. That is, it says something about the ultimate nature of reality, not about our knowledge of reality. Determinism does not imply predictability across all contexts, and it does not erase the inside perspective of an embedded, finitely informed agent.

From outside, an idealised complete description will contain one trajectory. From inside, the agent encounters information, counterfactuals, goals and handles.

For people-oriented questions, physical determinism is rarely a useful language. We can’t know a person’s complete “state of mind” in the sense of physics. And we wouldn’t be able to use that information even if we had it – the calculations required are much too hard.

In practice, if we want to predict how someone will behave, we try to understand their state of mind using concepts like knowledge, motivation and mood and to figure out how their personality will translate that state into action. For the questions at hand, ontological determinism is largely academic.

This applies to our self-awareness, too. Free will is not an illusion, but a useful and legitimate way to understand ourselves. It is very plausible, I think, that free will is how intelligent minds process, and experience, determinism. In short, free will is what determinism looks like from the inside.

The quantum state of a closed system evolves deterministically, just as in classical physics. There is a new wrinkle: no embedded observer can measure everything about the complete quantum state, even in principle, without changing it.

Quantum theory only widens the classical gap between formal description and experienced reality; it does not create it.

Another famous physics cat – Schroedinger’s – dramatises the gap between a complete formal description and an uncertain experienced outcome.

The falling cat dramatises a different gap: between a trajectory described from outside and a future navigated from within. Of the two cats, the falling one may teach us more about free will.

item.title: [SCMP] Young Malaysians brew goal for traditional tuak drink to become national success
item.description:
At Raffly Langi’s family longhouse in Sarawak, on Malaysian Borneo, the tuak rice wine did not come in a branded bottle or a tasting flight.

His aunt has brewed the drink for Gawai, the harvest festival celebrated by Dayak communities, an umbrella term for indigenous groups in Sarawak whose longhouses have long been centres of family, rituals and communal life.

She made it from steamed glutinous rice and a cake called ragi, prepared with rice flour, yeast and spices to kick-start fermentation. Once ready, the tuak was drawn from a jar and served without flavouring.
item.content:encoded:
At Raffly Langi’s family longhouse in Sarawak, on Malaysian Borneo, the tuak rice wine did not come in a branded bottle or a tasting flight.

His aunt has brewed the drink for Gawai, the harvest festival celebrated by Dayak communities, an umbrella term for indigenous groups in Sarawak whose longhouses have long been centres of family, rituals and communal life.

She made it from steamed glutinous rice and a cake called ragi, prepared with rice flour, yeast and spices to kick-start fermentation. Once ready, the tuak was drawn from a jar and served without flavouring.

Years later, 33-year-old Raffly has carried that family recipe to the Klang Valley, the urban region around Kuala Lumpur, where he produces tuak under the brand Tuak Alus and develops modern flavours for drinkers who are unfamiliar with the traditional brew.

Tuak traditionally comes in sweeter indu, or female, and drier laki, or male, versions, but artisan brands now also offer flavours derived from pandan, pineapple and roselle.

The drink can still be bought in Sarawak for US$5 to US$7.50 in an unlabelled plastic or glass bottle, while at Klang Valley pop-ups, producers sell premium bottles and promote brand collaborations and tasting flights, with prices around US$25 or more each.

But as it moves from longhouses into mainstream markets, brewers are confronting a persistent question: how much can tuak be changed before the culture that gives it meaning fades?

Keeping tradition alive

For Raffly and Kuin John, the 39-year-old founder of Tuak Sun Borneo, their craft is inextricably linked to the women who have taught them the drink’s brewing process.

“The basic method of making tuak is something I will always keep because it was taught to me by my mother,” Kuin said.

She makes a traditional ragi from rice flour, ginger, jicama root and pepper, and lets the drink ferment for at least three to four months to give it a deeper character.

“Most importantly, I still respect the traditional taboos and practices passed down from the older generations, [because] even as I modernise the business, these are the parts I don’t want to lose,” Kuin told This Week in Asia.

In Raffly’s case, his aunt is the main inspiration for the drink.

“The way I learned it throughout all the years, it’s always from my auntie. She’s the one that was always making the tuak in the house,” Raffly said.

But preserving that foundation does not mean reproducing every part of her process. Raffly now uses a commercial rice steamer and dehydrator, after batches of ragi dried in the sun repeatedly failed. The machine, he said, was “the key to making the ragi consistent”.

For Raffly, authenticity does not require every ingredient to come from Sarawak.

Alus sources glutinous rice in West Malaysia, where supplies are more readily available, but continues buying Sarawak’s nipah palm sugar, or gula apong, for indu. Unpredictable gula apong stocks have spurred Alus to develop its pandan and sour-plum versions, which require less palm sugar than indu.

“We try to get all the resources from Sarawak, but it’s not efficient for us to maintain production every month,” Raffly said.

His aunt has not insisted that authenticity depends on a particular rice or sugar. “It’s the feeling and the taste of the tuak that make it different,” he said.

Raffly’s business partner, Ayden Chong, 31, was emphatic that their business should not be rigid in adhering to traditional tuak-making.

“There’s a sacrifice and there is adjustment, that we need to make hard decisions … but it is what it is,” he said.

Chong, who hails from Perak, said his first taste of tuak came during a visit to a Sarawak longhouse over a decade ago.

Mindful of tuak’s cultural significance, he said Alus had tried to hire Sarawakians to work in the Klang Valley and create a community around the drink, instead of just marketing it as alcohol.

“I always tell people we are sharing the culture,” he said. “I’m not trying to sell you things.”

With tuak’s rising popularity and commercial potential, some Sarawakian politicians have embraced the drink as a symbol of their state.

At the launch of Borneo Tuak Festival 2026 in the state capital of Kuching last July, Snowdan Lawan, Sarawak’s deputy tourism, creative industry and performing arts minister, described the drink as a “living heritage”, where a family recipe could become a source of income, brewers could build brands and young people could see a future in inherited knowledge.

At the same festival, Gerald Rentap Jabu, the state’s deputy youth, sports and entrepreneur development minister, said building tuak into a recognised Sarawakian product required an ecosystem with quality rice production, research into tuak production and opportunities for young entrepreneurs to develop new products without compromising authenticity.

Licensing gap

As more tuak entrepreneurs seek to expand their business, they say that current legislation poses a stumbling block.

Malaysia’s excise law distinguishes domestic tradition from commerce, defining “native liquor” as customarily made by natives in Sabah and Sarawak for their own consumption and not for commercial use.

Work like fermenting, bottling or adding ingredients to liquor intended for sale is treated as manufacturing, requiring a customs licence tied to specified premises. Retail sales are separately licensed.

For small producers such as Alus, this leaves a gap between home brewing and conventional commerce.

“Pop-ups are still the way because we can’t afford retail,” Chong said. Establishing an approved brewery would require equipment, specialist employees and – by his estimate – an eight-figure investment even before compliance audits.

Alus and other tuak brewers are seeking to partner with established Sarawak distilleries, according to Raffly.

The Royal Malaysian Customs Department has not responded to This Week in Asia’s questions about excise application and licensing requirements for small commercial tuak producers.

Consistency challenge

Micky Vincent, a fermentation researcher who lectures at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak, said the composition of yeast and other microorganisms in ragi would typically affect tuak’s alcohol content, aroma and acidity, making quality results difficult to reproduce.

“This batch might be good and you become the best brewer for the year. But next year … you buy the ragi from the same auntie, it could be a bad one, it could be masam [sour],” he said.

A bioethanol specialist by training, Micky and his students have collected ragi from across Sarawak and isolated about 20 yeast species, retaining five for their ability to produce alcohol and aroma, and suitability for food use.

His method directly applies the selected yeast strains to cooked rice instead of using a traditional ragi cake. His own label “Tuak Bioteknologi Borneo” includes novel flavours like coconut and vanilla.

Micky said commercial producers should document their fermentation and hygiene protocols and analyse alcohol, residual sugar and organic acids before bottling. But standardisation should not require having a single recipe, he added.

“It’s my protocol; it’s their mother’s recipe or tradition. But what we can fight for is the same product.”

SAGO Group, a food innovation platform that organises the Borneo Tuak Festival, convened brewers and other stakeholders in 2024 to draw up a tuak manifesto, proposing reforms covering licensing, food safety, research and market access.

In a joint written response on Tuesday, SAGO founders Arif Abdul Rahman, Ehon Chan and Evelyn Teo said they were unaware of any policy change arising directly from the manifesto.

Because the issues could involve multiple government and other agencies, SAGO had called for coordinated discussions among stakeholders and different licensing tiers proportionate to the scale of producers and risks.

“The most immediate issue remains the absence of a clear and proportionate pathway for small producers to move from home or community-based production into legitimate commercial activity,” they said.

Malaysia’s new generation of tuak producers are not content with just making it big at the national level and are aiming for the global market.

Chong said the Alus sour-plum variety had proved popular with Japanese and Korean customers at the brand’s events, as they were already familiar with plum wines as part of their drinking cultures.

“If you have the skills, the right people, the right place and more equipment, this is actually going global,” said Chong, adding that he and Raffly had not decided on their export plans.

Kuin said: “Exporting tuak is one of my hopes and ambitions, where I can introduce Sun Borneo’s tuak and send it overseas, so more people get to know about tuak as part of Sarawak’s heritage and culture.”

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese students, wary of geopolitics, seek international diplomas without leaving home
item.description:
One Shanghai family made an unconventional choice as they pored over college options this summer: rather than opting for overseas study or one of the many institutions within the borders of the financial centre, they picked a lesser-known university in a third-tier city – a Sino-foreign joint venture they felt would confer career benefits in the long run.

Rose Hu said her son gained admission to the Guangdong Technion–Israel Institute of Technology in the coastal city of Shantou to study mechanical engineering and robotics, a field he was passionate about, and one deemed to have strong job prospects.

“The biggest attraction of this institution to us is where graduates end up,” Hu said. “Most go on to top master’s programmes in the United States, the United Kingdom or Hong Kong, which aligns perfectly with our plan – we’re committed to science, technology, engineering and mathematics and intend for our son to pursue a graduate degree at a renowned university.
item.content:encoded:
One Shanghai family made an unconventional choice as they pored over college options this summer: rather than opting for overseas study or one of the many institutions within the borders of the financial centre, they picked a lesser-known university in a third-tier city – a Sino-foreign joint venture they felt would confer career benefits in the long run.

Rose Hu said her son gained admission to the Guangdong Technion–Israel Institute of Technology in the coastal city of Shantou to study mechanical engineering and robotics, a field he was passionate about, and one deemed to have strong job prospects.

“The biggest attraction of this institution to us is where graduates end up,” Hu said. “Most go on to top master’s programmes in the United States, the United Kingdom or Hong Kong, which aligns perfectly with our plan – we’re committed to science, technology, engineering and mathematics and intend for our son to pursue a graduate degree at a renowned university.

“Tuition is also reasonable for a regular family. If he studied abroad, it could cost 10 times more.”

Hu said studying at the institute cost 100,000 yuan (US$14,826) a year, but those costs would be significantly defrayed with a 40,000-yuan scholarship.

The family made their decision amid a period of explosive growth in higher education joint ventures in China. In May, the Ministry of Education approved more than 80 new joint institutions and over 130 joint programmes at the bachelor’s degree level and above.

That followed a boom last year that saw more than 100 institutions gain approval. By early this year, the national total exceeded 320.

Like Hu’s son, an increasing number of Chinese students are being lured by these programmes, which allow them to earn a relatively cheap international degree without straying far from home, or becoming embroiled in rising geopolitical tensions.

Choosing this institution gives us a clear path in tech-related fields

Rose Hu, Shanghai

The programmes are also seeing growing interest from international students – mainly from countries involved in the Belt and Road Initiative trade development plan, where Chinese companies are investing and hiring more, according to industry insiders. They said the trend could dovetail well with China’s efforts to stimulate its economy and compensate for a drop in domestic student enrolments.

“I think the overall number of Chinese students studying overseas is likely to shrink in the next few years,” said Zhang Wuhua, chairman of Shanghai-headquartered Ambright Education, which operates schools that prepare students for overseas education. “This is not due to diminished interest or need, but largely a measured response to concerns including persistent geopolitical volatility.

“At the same time, the number of students pursuing a ‘study-abroad’ experience through Sino-foreign cooperative programmes and institutions without leaving China will keep growing.”

There were 570,600 Chinese students studying overseas last year, down about 20 per cent from the 2019 peak, according to figures released by the Ministry of Education in April – the first issuance of these numbers since the Covid-19 pandemic.

The emerging alternatives offered by Sino-foreign joint institutions align well with the in-demand academic disciplines of science and engineering, a major consideration for Chinese families focused on job prospects and concerned about the higher risks and less rosy career outlooks faced by those studying overseas.

By the end of last year, engineering programmes accounted for 48 per cent of these cooperative education initiatives, according to a report released by the Hurun Research Institute in June.

Nearly 60 per cent of the Sino-foreign cooperative institutions and programmes that gained approval last year were concentrated in emerging interdisciplinary fields such as artificial intelligence, big data, new energy, bioengineering and advanced manufacturing, Hurun said.

Hu said her son was now studying at the institute in Shantou and was enjoying the “international” experience there. All his lecturers except for one were foreigners.

“Choosing this institution gives us a clear path in tech-related fields: if his academic performance is not outstanding, he will find a job at a technology firm in the Greater Bay Area after graduation, and if he excels, he can pursue a master’s degree at a more prestigious university overseas,” she said.

Sun Yat-sen University’s Lingnan College in Guangzhou launched a full international undergraduate programme taught in English this year. Under its inbound “two plus two” model, students will complete their first two years abroad and then attend Lingnan College for the final two years.

One of the first of its kind, the model is expected to help bring international students to China for the later years of their undergraduate degrees, in contrast to the more common outbound “two plus two” model for Chinese students going abroad.

“The emergence of this model means that China’s international education is gradually shifting, from a one-way flow of ‘students going abroad’ to a ‘two-way flow of educational resources’,” Zhang said.

Lingnan College said in June that the programme was targeting students in countries taking part in the Belt and Road Initiative as a response to “the accelerating overseas expansion of Chinese firms and their urgent need for cross-cultural talent versed in local markets and the Chinese model”.

“The motivation is very practical,” Zhang said. “As Chinese companies expand overseas and increase investment in their countries, local annual salaries are often higher than those offered by Japanese and Korean firms.

“They hope to increase their chances of entering these companies by studying in China, solidifying their language skills, gaining practical social experience and understanding the knowledge structure that Chinese enterprises require.”

These students previously had to choose between Western and Chinese universities, but Zhang said the emergence of Sino-foreign cooperative education means they no longer have to struggle with that choice. For example, if they attended the University of Nottingham Ningbo China, they would receive a University of Nottingham diploma without leaving the country.

Domestic universities were also motivated to launch cooperative programmes, largely as a way to improve their difficult financial situations, said Chu Zhaohui, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Education Sciences.

Chinese students going abroad spend tens of billions of yuan every year – why not keep that spending within the country?

Zhang Wuhua, Ambright Education

At Zhejiang University, for example, tuition fees for regular undergraduate programmes ranged from 5,000 to 6,000 yuan per academic year, but one of its cooperative programmes, the Zhejiang University-University of Edinburgh Institute, charged students from China 160,000 yuan a year.

In addition, local governments also provided financial support for cooperative education, which was something universities could not afford to miss out on.

“Many universities are currently facing financial problems, with some even unable to pay salaries,” Chu said, adding that he believed the rapid expansion of cooperative education in the past couple of years had primarily been driven by government policy.

“This is written into the 15th five-year plan, and there are assessment requirements for universities,” he said.

According to China’s education plan for the period from 2026 to 2030, authorities will encourage high-quality foreign universities specialising in science and engineering to set up cooperative programmes in China, and launch international talent development initiatives for outstanding students.

Zhang said one of the motivations for that drive was the need to boost domestic economic circulation.

“From an economic perspective, Chinese students going abroad spend tens of billions of yuan every year – why not keep that spending within the country?” he said. “And from an educational perspective, it relates to China’s ongoing commitment to opening up.”

And overseas students could help fill lecture theatres.

In an article published in China Higher Education magazine last year, a Ministry of Education official said university enrolment was expected to peak in 2032.

Zhang said: “If we lay the groundwork now, then when the number of Chinese students declines, we will have a large number of overseas students to fill the gap – so this is an arrangement with strategic foresight.”

But he warned that the quality of international students being recruited was a concern.

He said students in Europe or Southeast Asia tended to regard China’s top universities – which Chinese students fought tooth and nail to get into – as safety options, because the admission threshold for international students at Chinese universities was very low.

“They would say, ‘If I can’t get into a local school, then I’ll go to Tsinghua in China’, which is something really sad for our universities,” Zhang said.

The Chinese government launched the China Scholastic Competence Assessment exam for international students at the end of last year.

Zhang said the National Higher Education Entrance Examination taken by domestic high school students was more than twice as difficult, but even so, placement tests at top universities like Nanjing University and Fudan University found that “a large number” of international students scored just 30 to 40 points out of 100 in mathematics.

item.title: [SCMP] Visa policy brings in more foreigners on short-term jobs and HK$20,000 salaries
item.description:
About 80 per cent of the foreign nationals granted working visas under Hong Kong’s General Employment Policy (GEP) last year were hired on short-term contracts, while nearly half of successful applicants earned less than HK$20,000 (US$2,564) a month.

According to the latest Immigration Department data, 31,278 GEP working visas for foreigners were approved last year. Mainland Chinese residents cannot apply to the scheme.

While the figure marked the second consecutive year the scheme had cleared the 30,000-level, the number was still shy of the more than 40,000 recorded annually in 2018 and 2019.
item.content:encoded:
About 80 per cent of the foreign nationals granted working visas under Hong Kong’s General Employment Policy (GEP) last year were hired on short-term contracts, while nearly half of successful applicants earned less than HK$20,000 (US$2,564) a month.

According to the latest Immigration Department data, 31,278 GEP working visas for foreigners were approved last year. Mainland Chinese residents cannot apply to the scheme.

While the figure marked the second consecutive year the scheme had cleared the 30,000-level, the number was still shy of the more than 40,000 recorded annually in 2018 and 2019.

The latest statistics showed that 79.7 per cent of successful candidates, or 24,929, held short-term positions or jobs lasting less than a year. Among those granted visas, 47.5 per cent, or 14,850, were earning below HK$20,000 a month.

The proportion of approved applicants holding short-term contracts last year also marked an increase from 72.1 per cent in 2024 and 64 per cent in 2023.

The data also showed 13,640 GEP visas were approved in the first half of this year, with 68.6 per cent on short-term contracts and 49.8 per cent earning less than HK$20,000.

Alexa Chow Yee-ping, managing director of human resources consultancy ACTS Consulting, attributed the uptick in GEP visa holders taking on short-term work to the government’s mega-events drive to stimulate fresh economic growth.

“As an international city, Hong Kong needs to create its own character to retain its attractiveness and charm. Not just focus on properties and finance. We need [economic] diversification,” she said.

The department said the GEP also had a new “creative industry and performing arts services” category since April 1, with 2,340 applications approved so far.

Chow said such applicants could be performers and crew for mega-events, which also brought valuable experience to local people in event production.

Despite the temporary nature of the jobs, Chow said that such talent still benefited Hong Kong economically as mega-events drove growth in tourism, catering, retail and hospitality.

Earlier this month, the government revealed that about 1.75 million visitors were drawn to more than 130 major events between January and June this year, generating around HK$5.8 billion in spending and contributing HK$3.3 billion to the economy.

In terms of industry, the sports and recreation sector accounted for the highest number of GEP applicant approvals, at 4,517, followed by arts and culture, academic research and education, financial services, and commerce and trade.

Gordon Yau Yick-chung, a sports public relations leader and chairman of concern group Hong Kong Fitness Guide, which closely monitors sports industrialisation, said the actual number of sports events could be higher than the public knew.

“I am not surprised. The figures reflected the trend of more sports competitions held in Hong Kong, to the extent that sometimes we may not notice [a match was held],” he said.

Yau said that apart from recent high-profile friendly matches featuring European football teams, there had been many small and large international sports events and competitions in the city.

Such events included baseball, wrestling and golf as well as emerging sports such as pickleball, he said, adding that some were organised by shopping centres to draw visitors.

He said many of these international competitions hired overseas judges and organisers, while global sports icons invited for commercial events would bring their managers and entourage, creating short-term visa applications.

In terms of location, South Korea accounted for the largest proportion of approved GEP applicants last year, at 17.6 per cent.

The number of South Koreans approved for the visas surpassed 5,500 annually in 2024 and 2025, representing a surge of nearly 85 per cent from 2019.

This momentum also carried into the first half of 2026, with South Korea accounting for the largest number of approved GEP candidates, at 2,226, followed by Japan with 1,974.

Korean Sky Lee Sang-ju, 25, said he came to Hong Kong in 2024 to teach taekwondo at NRG Taekwondo Korea despite not finishing his final year at university.

The 25-year-old said he chose Hong Kong over the United States and Canada because of its lower taxes and better salaries, in addition to its more systematic and well-organised working environment.

He added that his employer had provided him with professional development, including customer relationship management training, something that was rarely offered at traditional taekwondo schools in South Korea.

The vibrant local Korean community and widespread appreciation of K-pop culture among locals had also helped him adapt to life in Hong Kong, Lee said.

“I like Hong Kong, and I hope to stay here in the long term,” he said.

Lee said that after completing his university degree through distance learning, he encouraged classmate Jerry Kim Seong-hun, 26, to come and teach at the same school last year.

Kim said he enjoyed working in Hong Kong as the work culture back home was more “conservative” and stressed seniority.

Chang Hyo-suk, general manager of the Korean Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said he had noticed many more Koreans coming to work in the city in recent years due to the geographical proximity, low taxes and minimal regulations.

He said that many Koreans worked in the city’s trading industry, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises or start-ups.

Roy Ying Fai, co-chair of the Hong Kong Institution of Human Resource Management’s advocacy and policy research committee, attributed the growth to the “Dedicated Team for Attracting Businesses and Talent” government initiative.

The policy, which launched in 2022, seeks to attract talent through the city’s overseas Economic and Trade Offices, including its Tokyo branch.

He added that Hong Kong was still attractive to financial talent, pointing to the boom in initial public offerings and the growing presence of family offices.

“Hong Kong is attractive to them. First, it is easy to find a job. Second, the tax is low. Third, if they want to apply for permanent residence, it is relatively easier than in Singapore,” he said.

But the Japanese consulate in Hong Kong said it had not observed an increasing trend in the number of Japanese nationals in the city following the Covid-19 pandemic, citing its own figures.

Meanwhile, the number of approved visas for British and US nationals, the two top demographics before the pandemic, recorded significant drops.

Last year, 2,472 British and 2,121 Americans were granted GEP visas to work in Hong Kong, a fall of 53.2 per cent and 47.9 per cent, respectively, from 2019.

Australians accounted for 883 applicants last year, a drop of 48.7 per cent from 2019.

Chow, the human resources consultant, said the downward trend reflected the geopolitical tensions between China and the West.

“Under this relatively hostile sentiment, the whole situation changed. Governments’ stances changed. Media coverage [on China] changed … How would I move to [China] for development?” she said.

But the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong said that the GEP figures alone failed to provide a complete picture, adding that a significant proportion of senior executives and graduates from top UK universities now entered the city under another policy, the Top Talent Pass Scheme.

The business chamber noted that the number of UK GEP approvals had increased steadily each year since 2023 and the number of UK-parented companies in Hong Kong had also grown by 20 per cent between 2023 and 2025, while the country remained the city’s largest corporate presence among European nations.

“British businesses are not just returning; they are adapting and expanding their presence to access the Greater Bay Area and wider Asia-Pacific opportunities from Hong Kong,” it said.

Government figures also showed rents for flats, as well as the number of international school applications, had increased as expatriates returned.

The private residential rental index, maintained by the Rating and Valuation Department, surged by 18.5 per cent as of June to 205.8 from the Covid-19 pandemic trough in January 2023.

Real estate services company JLL said that a primary driver of the increase was the “influx of expatriate professionals attracted by resurgent IPO activity and asset management business growth”.

The firm’s latest report, released earlier this month, showed that the overall grade A office vacancy rate fell to 12.8 per cent at the end of July, its lowest point in 31 months.

Education Bureau statistics also showed the number of places offered at international schools in Hong Kong rose by 4 per cent from 2023-24 to 2025-26, standing at 48,413.

Among those arriving in the city was Korean national Philip Jung, who was sent by his food industry company to lead the Hong Kong office in May.

The 36-year-old said he expected to spend three to five years working in the city, adding that his wife had come with him on a dependent visa.

Jung said the couple were expecting a baby next year and were considering having the child study in Hong Kong to learn English, Chinese and Korean.

“It is not easy to get in our home country,” he said.

Jung also said that while Hong Kong’s catering industry was struggling, he hoped it would gradually improve.

He added that his company expected him to help open up southern China and expand existing markets in Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam.

“Hong Kong is the platform for Asian markets, so there could be opportunities to make more business,” Jung said.

item.title: [SCMP] How the Nepal flash flood unleashed a wave of anti-China misinformation
item.description:
To scientists, the cause of this week’s deadly flash flood on the border between China and Nepal is clear: a glacier high on the Nepal side of the Himalayan range collapsed, sending catastrophic amounts of water and debris downstream.

Initial uncertainty over the cause of the event fuelled a wave of misinformation on social media, some of which pinned the blame for the event on Chinese-built infrastructure in the region.

But a war of information over China’s activities in the region continued to brew online even after Beijing and Kathmandu agreed on the scientific analysis.
item.content:encoded:
To scientists, the cause of this week’s deadly flash flood on the border between China and Nepal is clear: a glacier high on the Nepal side of the Himalayan range collapsed, sending catastrophic amounts of water and debris downstream.

Initial uncertainty over the cause of the event fuelled a wave of misinformation on social media, some of which pinned the blame for the event on Chinese-built infrastructure in the region.

But a war of information over China’s activities in the region continued to brew online even after Beijing and Kathmandu agreed on the scientific analysis.

When news of the flood broke, social media users began to speculate whether the cause of the event was natural or the result of human activity, with suggestions that the disaster had originated from the Chinese side of the border.

Some posts claimed that the flood was caused by the collapse of a Chinese dam in Tibet, while others blamed it on mega infrastructure projects in the region.

The social media account Nepal Correspondence, which claims to be a Nepal-based platform for investigative journalism, said in a post on Wednesday that the flash flood was caused by Chinese construction in the Himalayas.

“This is not only a purposeful ecological disaster but is cruel too,” the post read.

In another post on the same day, Tunku Varadarajan, an Indian-British journalist, said: “China will be the death of everyone and everything downstream of it. Literally, and metaphorically.”

In a preliminary assessment on Wednesday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said the cause was a sudden release from a Tibetan river that had been blocked by an avalanche, Nepali news portal Republica reported.

Another report by the Kathmandu Post on Thursday, citing a technical report from the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, also said a flood had entered Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River from the Tibetan side.

However, satellite analysis later pointed authorities in Nepal and China – and further abroad – to a glacier collapse in Nepal, rather than Chinese infrastructure, as the cause.

The analysis indicated that the glacier collapse occurred on the Nepalese side of the mountains, near the Langtang Lirung peak.

Daniel Shugar, an earth scientist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, told The Guardian on Thursday that initial analysis showed a large chunk of ice at 5,200 metres (17,060 feet) above sea level had collapsed vertically, falling around 1.2km (0.74 miles) into the valley floor.

“This ice and rock then flowed into a river, turning into the devastating debris flow and flash flood that we see in the CCTV footage at the border,” said Bethan Davies, the chair of glaciology at Newcastle University, told the Science Media Centre on Thursday.

That same day, China’s Ministry of Natural Resources confirmed that the deadly mudslide was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal.

Some initially believed that the ice-rock avalanche had been caused by an earthquake, as the impact of the avalanche was so strong that it registered on seismographs as a magnitude 5.2 tremor.

Brahma Chellaney, an Indian geostrategist and columnist, referred to the earthquake claims in a social media post on Wednesday, saying that a moderate seismic event could trigger a cascading disaster.

He also linked the dangers to Chinese construction.

“This will renew global attention on China’s folly in persisting with the construction of the world’s largest dam in the middle of the Himalayan seismic zone,” he said, adding that its plan to build the dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in Tibet was a “water bomb in the making”.

In another post on Thursday, Chellaney wrote: “It is now clear that the Nepal disaster was caused by a natural trigger … but amplified by Chinese hydrological modifications and infrastructure footprint along the Tibetan side of the border.

“In other words, China’s upstream actions did not cause the glacier failure but contributed to the disaster’s severity and cascading impacts downstream.”

Scientists are still not sure exactly what triggered the initial glacier collapse, but catastrophic events like this have happened elsewhere in the region, including a glacier collapse and avalanche in India’s Chamoli district in 2021.

Shugar told Associated Press on Friday that clearer satellite images indicated the bedrock underneath the glacier might have also collapsed, which could explain the glacier collapse.

But that has not prevented a blame game over early warnings.

Republica quoted NDRRMA spokeswoman Shanti Mahat as saying the authority only learned about the disaster after the flood had reportedly already swept through Gyirong Port.

She said that a lack of timely information on the Tibetan side made it impossible to issue an early warning in Nepal.

Parshuram Kaphle, a Nepali journalist, echoed the sentiment in a social media post on Wednesday, saying China had “significantly undermined us”.

“By failing to provide early warning of such a massive disaster, we suffered immense loss of human life,” Kaphle wrote.

Ouyang Chaojun, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told state broadcaster CCTV that the debris flow was moving at about 40-50 metres per second (131-164 feet per second).

“Furthermore, because the debris flow reached the Gyirong border crossing in a very short time – only about 7 minutes – there was no time for evacuation,” he added.

Hydrologist Hannah Cloke, a professor at the University of Reading, told the Science Media Centre that high up in the valley near the source of the flood, early warnings were “exceptionally difficult, no matter how advanced the technology”.

The centre quoted a number of scientists as saying that while it was not known whether climate change was behind Wednesday’s collapse, warming was exacerbating the risk of catastrophic mountain failures and flooding due to melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, and increased meltwater run-off.

“A warming environment can make these kinds of events more common or likely,” Davies said.

Ouyang said that following the mudslide, some of the other slopes in the region had become unstable, making monitoring the region essential.

Concerns have been raised over a newly formed barrier lake upstream from Gyirong county that was formed by the landslide, which CCTV said on Friday was holding the equivalent of 1,000 Olympic swimming pools of water.

item.title: [SCMP] How to be a good tourist; a guide for the modern traveller
item.description:
From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language.

Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints.

To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach.
item.content:encoded:
From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language.

Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints.

To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach.

Not far away, in seaside Portofino, the introduction of no-loitering zones has effectively put an end to selfies, unless you’re a professional narcissist and the income to be expected from sponsors or followers is greater than the potential €275 (US$317) penalty for blocking traffic.

However, much of the globally growing ill will is not about bad behaviour but merely about numbers.

Destinations that have seen many long-term rental properties turned into more profitable short-term accommodation for tourists are introducing strict regulations (British Columbia) or banning Airbnb and its ilk altogether (Barcelona).

Local satisfaction is crucial to success, but if the visited are unhappy, so are the visitors.

Tourists discover soaring head taxes, 90-minute queues and compulsory advance-purchase tickets with a timed entry, and that the quiet stroll between two pretty mountain villages they have come back to enjoy for a second time now has an entrance fee and one-way-only traffic, and yet is still a conga line.

Individual residents, municipal authorities and national tourism bureaus alike declare that they don’t dislike tourists, and don’t want to discourage them, but they do want to choose the visitors they get.

An official online Tokyo travel guide, How to stay safe and be respectful in Tokyo at night, has little to say about safety in what anyway ranks as one of the world’s least dangerous cities. Instead, it explains how not to offend locals by littering, or by drinking or smoking in public.

But if the Japanese are too polite to say straight out, “Don’t come unless you obey the rules”, José Antonio Donaire, Barcelona’s commissioner for sustainable tourism, feels no such restraint. He wants to restrict visitors to no more than the 15.7 million the city hosted in 2025, and he wants half of those to be cultural tourists – presumably people who swoon at the sight of Joan Miro’s surrealist art or Antoni Gaudi’s soaring Sagrada Família rather than their 15th Estrella Damm lager of the day.

In terms of accommodation capacity, all tourists may be equal, but some are more equal than others. These regulations, fines and fees suggest a definition of good tourists: it’s those who stay longer, spend more with local businesses, respect the needs of residents, do not congregate all in one spot and neither dive into historic fountains (€500/US$576 fine in Rome) nor indulge in drunken caterwauling at 3am (€140/US$161 in Amsterdam).

However, concentrating on attracting good tourists will still not solve the problem of volume, and some destinations are looking to spread the load.

Japan has offered some international visitors free domestic flights to destinations beyond the well-worn Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka trail that two-thirds of them take.

Spain’s new policy is to encourage visitors to avoid the summer peak, and to look beyond the supply of sun, sea, sand and potential sexual partners along its crowded Mediterranean beaches towards the equally sun-baked sleepy villages of the interior. These are all sugar-cube houses, crumbling castles and excellent walking among hills hatched with olives and vines, where good tourists eat local dishes, rather than fish and chips or pizza.

All these schemes ignore the jumbo jet in the room, though. If we don’t want a future in which the world’s major cities are to be toured by boat rather than by hop-on, hop-off bus, there must be a reduction in the emissions that make such catastrophes ever more likely.

One per cent of fliers produce 50 per cent of airline emissions, so the rest typically urge the elite to cut back first. But the good tourist understands that simply to board a plane is to be a member of an elite. Eighty per cent of the world’s population never takes to the air, so perhaps halving your own flying is not an unreasonable idea. This would reduce emissions, although the only true ecotourism is just staying at home.

In China and Europe, extensive rail systems offer less damaging ground-level travel as an easy substitute. Or there’s the option to halve the number of trips but stay for twice as long. The good tourist leaves the rentals to the locals who need the space and opts for a hotel instead.

Good tourists also avoid getting bogged down in the slough of meme-driven, artificial-intelligence-derived ignorance that is most online travel commentary. That leads to the taking of well-trodden paths between sights ranging from those of genuine cultural and historical significance to those merely of social-media-driven popularity, where the idea of being there, and being seen to be there, is more important than the actual experience.

Today, social media merely ensures that a location may go from overlooked to overwhelmed in the blink of a smartphone’s camera shutter, the image repeated in increasingly dishonest “I was here, too” postings.

The hydroelectric project next to the cliffside temple is cropped out, the sky is edited into an improbable blue and the camera angle narrowed to exclude the hordes of others taking the near-identical shot. The resulting image is of perfect beauty in tranquil solitude while the reality is anything but. And the blame cannot be laid solely at the perfectly pedicured feet of influencers. Every step you take, every post you make, people are watching you.

The good tourist travels flexibly, and keeps quiet about new discoveries. But if you follow the crowd, then it’s unsurprising that crowds are what you find.

As the late Irish travel writer Dervla Murphy told The Guardian newspaper in 2009, “Choose your country, use guidebooks to identify the areas most frequented by foreigners – and then go in the opposite direction.”

Of course, if significant numbers go in the opposite direction, there will no longer be an opposite direction, although when there are no longer “hidden gems” to be found “off the beaten track”, this will at least result in a merciful release from cliché.

There was a time when travel writing was not all how-to guides, or thinly disguised advertising, but written by a tiny number of people who ventured abroad to be a substitute for those who couldn’t.

It’s time to lead the way by sometimes going nowhere, perhaps instead sitting down with a well-informed account from the past of somewhere you might go in the future. Or might not.

Travel less, but travel better.

item.title: [SCMP] The great AI reckoning: how China is flipping the script on US’ new industrial revolution
item.description:
As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, it confronts a new world order dominated by its relationship with China. In this wide-ranging series, we examine the pressure points and possibilities in those ties, from hard tech to soft power. Here, Vincent Chow looks at how China challenges core American assumptions about innovation and technology, and the historical stakes of their competition in artificial intelligence.

In 1969, the renowned British sinologist Joseph Needham posed a series of questions about China so influential that they became known as the “Needham Question”.

At its core, Needham was trying to reconcile China’s past glories with what he saw in the China of the mid-20th century.
item.content:encoded:
As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, it confronts a new world order dominated by its relationship with China. In this wide-ranging series, we examine the pressure points and possibilities in those ties, from hard tech to soft power. Here, Vincent Chow looks at how China challenges core American assumptions about innovation and technology, and the historical stakes of their competition in artificial intelligence.

In 1969, the renowned British sinologist Joseph Needham posed a series of questions about China so influential that they became known as the “Needham Question”.

At its core, Needham was trying to reconcile China’s past glories with what he saw in the China of the mid-20th century.

Namely, why did the 18th-century Industrial Revolution happen in Europe and not China, a country that had led the world in technological innovation up until the 15th century, and what were the reasons for technology and science in China stagnating for centuries thereafter?

Like Needham, Erik Baark – professor emeritus at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology – also spent much of his decades-long career researching Chinese innovation and technology. But at a guest lecture at the Hong Kong Baptist University last month, Baark proposed a fundamentally different question – an inversion of the original.

“The central question is now this,” said Baark, author of Innovation and China’s Global Emergence. “Why is China now able to contribute to global science and innovation? More than that, why does there even seem to be an alternative dynamism in Chinese innovation?”

For decades, the West questioned China’s ability to innovate and to invent truly original technologies. China can only copy Western technology or be reliant on fat government subsidies, the critics claimed.

But this dismissive attitude has seen a clear shift in recent years as China has established itself as a global leader in a range of cutting-edge technologies, from electric vehicles to humanoid robots.

“The biggest risk to AI is China getting ahead of us,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at an event last week, underscoring the magnitude of the threat the Trump administration sees in China.

Chinese-American writer Kaiser Kuo called this “the great reckoning” in a viral essay in October. The term reflects a collective “recognition” in the West of China’s technological advances, even spawning a growing tourism industry where foreign investors and policymakers go on factory tours in China to see first-hand just how advanced the country has become.

“This reckoning touches all of humanity,” Kuo wrote. “[B]ut it falls … hardest on the United States, where assumptions about exceptionalism and hierarchy are most exposed and most fiercely denied.”

In other words, it is the US today that is trying to reconcile the past and the present – with one particular technology at the centre of its worries.

Revolving revolutions

For years now, artificial intelligence has been compared with the Industrial Revolution in its expected impact and importance.

German economist Klaus Schwab called AI the “fourth” industrial revolution in a 2015 book, while the release of ChatGPT by US company OpenAI in late 2022 has even spurred claims that AI has already ushered in the fifth such revolution.

Successive US administrations have endorsed such claims. Jake Sullivan, National Security Adviser during the Biden administration, said that “AI will define the future”.

More recently, the Trump administration compared AI’s importance with the Industrial Revolution, in that it “presents a profound economic inflection point with the potential to significantly increase the GDP of countries that embrace it”.

For the US, the civilisational stakes of its AI competition with China have become undeniable. For the first time since its founding 250 years ago, the US today is undergoing simultaneous technological, political and geopolitical revolutions, Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said.

Back then, the world was dominated by European empires such as Britain and France. To break away from the British Crown, American revolutionaries launched their independence campaign in 1765, just as the first stirrings of the Industrial Revolution were emerging in Great Britain with the rise of steam engines and other innovations that would transform the world from human-driven economies to ones powered by machines.

The US once again finds itself in the midst of overlapping revolutions, confronting technological, political and geopolitical revolutions all at the same time with the rise of AI, authoritarianism at home and abroad, and China.

“The US made the most of the Industrial Revolution, which transformed it into the world’s only superpower,” Chan said. “This time, in the age of AI, it is unclear whether the US or China will make the most of this new technological wave.”

What is innovation?

Given the high stakes, both the US and China have obsessed over their AI capabilities in relation to each other, with the strength of their respective frontier foundational models drawing the bulk of the attention.

The gap was most apparent in late 2022 upon the release of ChatGPT. The development caught China by surprise, with leading Chinese experts estimating at the time that the gap was as large as three years.

But China has caught up rapidly since then. The first breakthrough was Hangzhou start-up DeepSeek’s release of R1 in January 2025, which stunned the world due to its low reported research and development cost. Almost overnight, the gap was no longer years but months.

Another major moment occurred last month with the release of GLM-5.2 by Beijing-based Zhipu AI, known as Z.ai internationally. The model showed powerful capabilities around the same time as the Trump administration curbed the roll-out of frontier US models for national security reasons, underscoring to many the alternative path that Chinese models represent.

According to research institute Epoch AI, Chinese models were more than a year behind their US counterparts as recently as May 2024. This has narrowed to as little as four months, it said.
