Nathan Lambert, author of the AI newsletter Interconnects, puts GLM-5.2 around seven months behind the US frontier.

China’s achievements in AI models reflect the country’s rapid advances in innovative capacity more broadly, Baark said. Last year, the country broke into the top 10 most innovative economies in the world on the World Intellectual Property Organisation’s Global Innovation Index, capping off a rapid ascent from 35th in 2013.

This came on the back of an explosion in China’s R&D spending.

A March report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) found that China’s R&D investment in 2024 surpassed the US once purchasing power measures were factored in, soaring to 3.93 trillion yuan (US$551 billion) last year, according to official figures.

“China was very behind decades ago in innovation, but it has caught up very fast in the past few decades,” Dong Jielin, a former researcher at Tsinghua University’s China Institute for Science and Technology Policy and one of China’s leading experts on the history of technology and innovation, said.

For decades, Dong studied the innovation ecosystems of both the US and China through roles in academia and the private sector. But her rigorous approach meant that, while acknowledging China’s undeniable advances in innovation, she still believed China had yet to master the “zero-to-one” innovation.

In the AI community, a common term researchers use to refer to such innovations is “paradigms”, meaning a technical breakthrough that lays the groundwork for an entirely new field of inquiry and innovation.

Dong also emphasises this agenda-setting quality as central to the innovation that matters most to her.

Though Chinese models have narrowed the gap with their US counterparts, all the leading ones, including DeepSeek R1 and GLM-5.2, are still trained on advanced US semiconductor chips despite years of efforts by China to achieve self-reliance across the entire AI stack.

Both DeepSeek R1 and GLM-5.2 are also the type of AI models – large language models with strong coding ability – that were first pioneered by US start-ups OpenAI and Anthropic.

“Neither DeepSeek nor Zhipu really represent zero-to-one innovation because they improve upon US inventions through better engineering,” said Dong, the author of A Brief History of Human Technological Innovation. “Maybe China might eventually solve the problem of zero to one, but it’s not there yet.”

Different races

But not everyone agrees with this definition of innovation. For Baark, the HKUST emeritus professor, the challenge posed by China to the US is precisely its alternative approach to technological innovation.

In the realm of AI models, this is most apparent in two ways. First, while US models still lead in absolute capability, Chinese models lead in another key dimension – cost-efficiency.

Over the past year, third-party benchmark firm Artificial Analysis has consistently found that Chinese models are global leaders – beating their US counterparts – in maximising the amount of “intelligence” users can get per dollar spent. This increasingly matters as the dawn of agentic AI forces users and enterprises to seek ways to keep AI costs down.

Secondly, most frontier Chinese models are released as open-weight models, meaning that their weights – the parameters encoding their “intelligence” – are made freely available for developers and enterprises globally to use and customise for their own use cases.

These cost advantages have made Chinese models a prime target for US accusations that they are achieved through the “theft” of US models, with Anthropic and numerous US politicians all increasingly vocal in levelling the charge.

The claim is that Chinese models are entirely reliant on the “distillation” of US models, in which Chinese models are illicitly trained on US model outputs.

For Baark, the irony is that the US itself engaged in “industrial espionage” throughout much of its early years more than two centuries ago. Back then, it was the British who saw the strategic value of its new inventions and sought to make sure it would not fall into the hands of the young US, the rising power at the time.

Famously, the first US treasury secretary, Alexander Hamilton, coordinated an elaborate espionage campaign to steal and bring these technologies to the US.

“The US itself went through this catching-up process during the Industrial Revolution that China today is in,” Baark said.

“I wish they could therefore put some of their security worries aside and see the emergence of other centres of innovation as something they can actually benefit from.”

The cries of foul play also increasingly ring hollow in the Global South, where customers and firms are increasingly priced out of accessing frontier US models at premium prices.

Vince Iswara, CEO of DANA, one of Indonesia’s biggest digital wallet providers with more than 200 million users, said the company’s growing integration of Chinese open-weight models had led to a 50 per cent gain in company productivity while helping to keep R&D costs down.

Innovation under heavy cost and technological constraints is a daily reality in emerging markets. Iswara cites China’s digital payments revolution as typical of this model of innovation, where mass adoption of e-wallets was achieved through the proliferation of QR codes, in contrast to a Western payment model revolving around credit cards, which require expensive equipment such as card machines and ATMs.

Such constraints will not be unfamiliar to Chinese AI model developers. According to Epoch AI, the US has five times more AI supercomputers and three times better cutting-edge semiconductor chips than China.

Long-standing US export controls have restricted Chinese access to advanced US semiconductor chips from the likes of Nvidia, delivering a significant compute advantage for their US rivals.

But still, even with these difficulties, China has managed to remain competitive at the frontier of AI. For countries with even fewer resources, that in itself is a model of innovation.

“The China model is much more replicable for mass adoption [of new technologies] in emerging markets,” Iswara said. “There are a lot of things to learn from China.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s extreme heat exposes holes in safety net for outdoor workers
item.description:
When the day heats up, small business owner Chung Kee Wa, 68, changes how he tends his oil palm plantation in Yong Peng, in Malaysia’s southern Johor state.

Oil palms younger than three years offer little shade, so he tends them in the early mornings and evenings, spraying pesticide, applying fertiliser or weeding. “We try our best to avoid going to the plantation around noon,” Chung said.

He carries extra drinking water and, as a smallholder, decides when to slow down or change his hours.
item.content:encoded:
When the day heats up, small business owner Chung Kee Wa, 68, changes how he tends his oil palm plantation in Yong Peng, in Malaysia’s southern Johor state.

Oil palms younger than three years offer little shade, so he tends them in the early mornings and evenings, spraying pesticide, applying fertiliser or weeding. “We try our best to avoid going to the plantation around noon,” Chung said.

He carries extra drinking water and, as a smallholder, decides when to slow down or change his hours.

But not everyone shares that luxury. Many construction, agriculture and platform workers across Southeast Asia lack that flexibility because employers or output determine their schedules.

Southeast Asia is getting hotter, with the annual mean temperature rising by 0.14 degrees Celsius (0.25 degrees Fahrenheit) to 0.2 degrees per decade since the 1960s, according to an Asian Development Bank report in June.

Many Southeast Asian cities lacked adequate heat risk assessments, and regulations protecting outdoor workers from extreme heat were either weak or unenforced, the report said.

A September 2024 research brief by the International Labour Organization estimated that heat stress could erase 3.7 per cent of working hours in Southeast Asia by 2030 – equivalent to 13 million full-time jobs.

Countries like Singapore are taking note. Its Ministry of Manpower (MOM) said on August 28 that an average of six work-related heat disorder cases were reported annually from 2023 to 2025, with no fatalities.

It enhanced its Heat Stress Management Framework in September 2024, requiring measures focused on “drink, rest and shade”, alongside heat acclimatisation, wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) monitoring and emergency response plans.

Those doing heavy physical work must rest for at least 10 minutes per hour when the WBGT registers 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 degrees Fahrenheit). This rises to 15 minutes at 33 degrees.

WBGT combines temperature, humidity, wind and radiant heat, measuring environmental heat stress more comprehensively than air temperature alone.

From December 1, employers must also provide heat-stress training, cool drinking water near work areas, suitable clothing and emergency cooling provisions such as cold water, ice packs or water sprays. MOM will recommend that shaded rest areas be ventilated and insulated or cooled.

The ministry told This Week in Asia it found 56 companies with heat management lapses in the first half of 2026. These included failures to monitor WBGT, implement acclimatisation programmes or establish emergency response procedures. The companies were warned and some were fined.

Worker, not environment

But environmental readings are only part of assessing the strain on outdoor workers, according to Jason Lee, director of the Heat Resilience and Performance Centre at the National University of Singapore’s Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine.

Individual risk also depends on clothing, physical condition and the intensity and duration of the task. “We are worried about a hot worker, not just a hot environment,” he said.

In Bangkok, delivery rider Koy Phanida has reorganised her work day around the heat. “During very hot weather, I work from about 7am until 1pm, take a break until 5pm, then work again until 8pm or 9pm,” the 38-year-old said. “On days that are not hot, I work all day from 7am to 5pm.”

She rests and recharges at home because the platform provides no facilities, stretching her working day to 13 or 14 hours. “I have experienced headaches. I stop to find a cool place, take medicine, rest for a while and monitor my symptoms,” she said.

She neither sought medical care nor reported the headaches, saying she would not receive any compensation for doing so.

Koy’s unrecorded headaches illustrate Lee’s concern that reported heat illness may understate its burden.

“Heat can aggravate cardiovascular or respiratory conditions, without being recorded as the trigger,” Lee said. “Compounding this, workers who seek treatment at nearby neighbourhood clinics may not be captured in official workplace or hospital data, creating additional gaps in heat-illness surveillance.”

Malaysia’s Department of Occupational Safety and Health (DOSH) recorded only eight occupational heat stress-related cases between 2017 and 2025, director general Hazlina Yon told local media last month.

“Under-reporting on heat stress is definitely a concern,” said Wong Yan Ke, regional campaign officer for climate and forestry at the Asia-Pacific regional office of Building and Wood Workers’ International, a global union federation.

Local and migrant workers might avoid reporting symptoms for fear of being labelled “malingerers” or “disruptive”, potentially affecting future work, he said. Employers might also under-report to protect their safety records.

Drinking water is often seen as the best solution to the heat but it is just one aspect. “Resting, is the most powerful, followed by aerobic conditioning, heat acclimatisation, cooling, and then finally hydration,” Lee said. “The power of water breaks lies in the breaks.”

Lower heat strain could improve productivity, morale and worker retention while reducing accidents, Lee added.

Understanding risks

Since Singapore’s 2023 national heat advisory, several industries have sought researchers’ help to understand and address rising heat risks.

Malaysia uses DOSH guidelines rather than a stand-alone heat regime. Employers who fail to manage heat risks in the country could face fines of up to 500,000 ringgit (US$124,000), two years’ imprisonment or both under the Occupational Safety and Health Act’s general-duty provision.

Smaller firms, however, might need incentives or support to adopt such measures, Wong said.

He pointed to South Korea as a potential model. South Korean employers must provide at least 20 minutes’ rest every two hours when the apparent temperature reaches 33 degrees, while public-construction guidance allows contract extensions and says delay damages should not be imposed for heat-related overruns.

“Currently, DOSH’s guidelines are generally all right, but they are non-binding. There needs to be more teeth,” Wong said.

He called for the guidelines to be updated because they predated climate change becoming a central workplace concern and conditions had changed significantly.

Thailand sets statutory WBGT ceilings of 34 degrees for light work, 32 degrees for moderate work and 30 degrees for heavy labour. Its standard does not mention self-employed workers, according to WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand.

A study of 300 informal, seasonal sugar cane harvesters in Nakhon Sawan – conducted from January to March 2023, and published in February 2025 – found they averaged 10.1 working hours daily without formal breaks.

Researchers assessed their exposure against the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists’ recommended threshold limit value of 26.6 degrees effective WBGT for heavy work. Exposure exceeded that threshold during 90.9 per cent of working time in the hotter study month of March 2023.

Ultimately, heat protection in Southeast Asia may depend less on specified temperatures than on who controls the pace when thresholds are reached.

For Koy, the heat changes her working hours, but not her financial commitment. “Various reasons, including the financial rewards, make us want to earn more, so we work more,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why the EU is giving Arctic shipping the cold shoulder as China and Russia push ahead
item.description:
As Beijing and Moscow double down on the Arctic shipping route, Europe is hitting the brakes.

Despite being the main destination for goods along the route and accounting for most of the world’s shipping giants, Europe opposes the commercialisation of Arctic transits, wary of fragile polar ecosystems and navigational risks amid rising anxiety over Russia and China’s closer polar collaboration.

“In Europe, cooperation between China and Russia on container shipping is often viewed as another example of deepened collaboration between the two countries in the Arctic since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,” according to Patrik Andersson, an analyst at the Swedish National China Centre at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs.
item.content:encoded:
As Beijing and Moscow double down on the Arctic shipping route, Europe is hitting the brakes.

Despite being the main destination for goods along the route and accounting for most of the world’s shipping giants, Europe opposes the commercialisation of Arctic transits, wary of fragile polar ecosystems and navigational risks amid rising anxiety over Russia and China’s closer polar collaboration.

“In Europe, cooperation between China and Russia on container shipping is often viewed as another example of deepened collaboration between the two countries in the Arctic since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,” according to Patrik Andersson, an analyst at the Swedish National China Centre at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs.

Andersson said the collaboration fitted into a broader partnership, which in recent years had expanded to include joint military drills in Arctic-adjacent areas, coastguard cooperation in the Arctic Ocean and joint projects in the mining and energy sectors.

Europe’s concerns are reflected in an updated EU Arctic policy that is expected to be issued later this year.

In recommendations for the policy released late last year, the European Parliament warned that expansion of Sino-Russian ties in energy, infrastructure and polar shipping “risks consolidating a geopolitical axis of resource exploitation and restricted access”.

The recommendations proposed condemning Russia’s restrictions on freedom of navigation on the Northern Sea Route, which runs along Russia’s Arctic coast from near the Barents Sea to the Bering Strait.

The position underscores a long-standing rift between Brussels and Moscow over the route’s legal status.

Moscow has long claimed special jurisdiction over the Northern Sea Route – a major segment of the Northeast Passage – invoking Article 234 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), also known as “the Ice Clause”, to enforce strict “non-discriminatory” environmental and navigational regulations “over ice-covered areas” in its exclusive economic zone.

However, the European Union has pushed back, arguing that shrinking sea ice owing to climate change undermines Russia’s legal basis to invoke the Ice Clause for control. The EU further contends that Moscow’s transit restrictions and bans on foreign military vessels are discriminatory and clearly violate Unclos.

In its recommendations, the European Parliament called for applying international law to counter efforts that either legitimise contested shipping corridors or project geopolitical influence under the guise of scientific or economic cooperation.

Europe is concerned that commercialising the route could cement Russia’s control and development of the Arctic.

Echoing these concerns, Karen van Loon, a research fellow in the security and defence programme at the Clingendael Institute, a Dutch think tank, noted that payment for use of the route directly fed into Russian state interests.

“A service that routinely pays for Russian permits, icebreaker assistance, pilotage or other infrastructure supports a transport corridor operated by the Russian state,” van Loon said. “It also helps Moscow present the Northern Sea Route as a successful international project despite its isolation from Europe.”

She added that receiving a vessel did not imply legal recognition of Russia’s authority over the route, allowing European countries to accept port calls while still challenging Moscow’s claims under international law.

Alongside the tensions between the EU and Russia, major European shipping giants, especially top container carriers, have reaffirmed their commitment to steer clear of Arctic transit. They are driven mainly by environmental concerns, doubt over commercial viability and severe navigational hazards.

“For many Western shipping companies, the geopolitical and reputational risks so far outweigh the commercial incentives,” Andersson said.

Asked if, like its Chinese counterparts, Maersk would consider the Arctic route as other maritime chokepoints are squeezed, Vincent Clerc, CEO of the Danish shipping giant, told Bloomberg TV last month that he did not view the passage as a meaningful substitute.

Beyond environmental concerns and extreme weather unpredictability, the route “relies on sanctioned Russia to provide icebreakers and escorts throughout those waters”, Clerc said, describing the route as unlikely to play a significant role in global shipping in the coming years.

The head of MSC, the world’s largest container shipping company, had a similar view.

“Our position at MSC is clear. We do not and will not use the Northern Sea Route,” Soren Toft, CEO of the Geneva-headquartered company, said in January.

“Safe navigation cannot be assured.

“The risks for crews remain too high. And increased traffic would put additional pressure on fragile ecosystems and local communities.”

In 2019, four of the world’s five largest shipping companies – MSC, Maersk, CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd – signed a voluntary commitment launched by Ocean Conservancy, a Washington-based marine environmental NGO, pledging not to send ships through the Arctic. China’s Cosco Group did not sign the pledge.

With the Arctic warming four times faster than the rest of the world, its ecosystems were already under intense stress, Ocean Conservancy said, noting that unpredictable or even perilous conditions made each trip hazardous.

“Shipping companies comprising more than 60 per cent of global container capacity have decided that Arctic shipping is not worth the risk,” it said. “We strongly agree.”

European analysts have questioned the route’s overall commercial viability, despite the time savings and the ability to bypass geopolitical conflict zones.

Andersson said the savings in time and fuel were offset by high insurance premiums, the need for specialised ice-class vessels and elevated operational costs in harsh Arctic conditions. The economic impact of Europe staying away from the route was negligible, he said.

Meanwhile, the risks are real. According to global insurer Allianz Commercial, Arctic shipping presents a markedly higher risk profile than conventional trade routes. Operational risks dominated Arctic waters, with machinery damage and failure accounting for nearly half of all reported casualties.

Last month, a Russian tanker suffered serious damage to its hull while navigating through Arctic sea ice, resulting in an insurance payout of 53 million roubles (US$609,000), according to Russian insurer AlfaStrakhovanie.

The Russian insurer said icebreaker assistance did not eliminate the physical risks associated with Arctic navigation.

The Arctic’s remoteness and lack of infrastructure, such as port state control, tug availability and repair facilities, also made these risks particularly acute, said Captain Anastasios Leonburg, senior marine risk consultant at Allianz Commercial.

For shipping in polar waters, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) international code provides the regulatory baseline by requiring vessels to obtain a polar ship certificate based on ice conditions. But Leonburg said the framework, in force since 2017, was inadequate on its own.

Major marine insurers were applying improved due diligence requirements for Arctic transits, mandating pre-voyage surveys and specific warranties regarding vessel suitability, crew competence and operational planning, he said.

“We expect these requirements to become more widespread and more rigorous across the industry as traffic volumes increase,” Leonburg said.

Enforcing stricter compliance could help Europe regain some leverage, van Loon said, adding that Europe’s strongest influence lay not in competing with Russia for control of the route but in the ports and commercial services needed for ships using it to reach European markets.

European authorities could use sanctions screening, insurance and financial rules, as well as environmental and safety standards, to determine the conditions under which vessels using the Northern Sea Route entered European ports, she said.

European countries are already putting this strategy into practice. Last December, Denmark, joined by France, Germany and the Solomon Islands, submitted a proposal to the IMO requiring ships operating in the Arctic to switch to cleaner fuels to reduce black carbon emissions.

The move illustrates how Europe is using stricter environmental compliance to assert its influence over polar shipping.

However, Jian Junbo, director of the Centre for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University in Shanghai, said Europe should not view the Northern Sea Route solely through a geopolitical lens.

He argued that European environmental and safety standards could improve governance along the route and should not be used to obstruct its development.

“A shipping route is an international public good that should be accessible to all countries,” Jian said.

item.title: [SCMP] Could Roman concrete have clues on how Pyramid of Giza was built – and saved?
item.description:
The enduring mystery of how the ancient Egyptians built the Great Pyramid of Giza – with its 2.3 million multi-tonne stone blocks – has puzzled researchers for centuries.

Mainstream archaeology holds that the pyramids were constructed from natural limestone or granite blocks precisely cut and hauled into place.

An alternative scientific theory suggests the blocks might have been cast from an early form of concrete, but that idea has long faced a critical question: how could such an artificial material survive for more than 4,500 years, while some modern buildings could suffer wear and damage in merely a few decades?
item.content:encoded:
The enduring mystery of how the ancient Egyptians built the Great Pyramid of Giza – with its 2.3 million multi-tonne stone blocks – has puzzled researchers for centuries.

Mainstream archaeology holds that the pyramids were constructed from natural limestone or granite blocks precisely cut and hauled into place.

An alternative scientific theory suggests the blocks might have been cast from an early form of concrete, but that idea has long faced a critical question: how could such an artificial material survive for more than 4,500 years, while some modern buildings could suffer wear and damage in merely a few decades?

Now, a new study on nearly 2,000-year-old Roman concrete may provide a materials-science clue that breathes new life into the concrete hypothesis.

Published in the peer-reviewed academic journal Science Advances in July, the research reveals that ancient Roman concrete not only resists decay but actually grows stronger over centuries through a self-healing process.

A team led by Zhu Xiaohong of Beijing University of Technology, with collaborators from the University of California, Berkeley, the University of Michigan, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, analysed concrete taken from a communal latrine at Hadrian’s Villa in Tivoli, Italy.

Using high-resolution imaging, they discovered the material’s remarkable durability stems from the gradual formation of calcite crystals that fill pores and microcracks.

The healing process was driven in part by carbonation, in which calcium-rich compounds in concrete react with moisture and atmospheric carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate.

Carbonation is often considered a durability problem in modern reinforced concrete because it lowers the material’s pH, potentially allowing embedded steel to corrode.

But the researchers found that the same chemical process can contribute to mineral growth and densification in ancient unreinforced concrete.

“For unreinforced concrete, carbonation may be a good thing,” Zhu said.

This insight could extend far beyond Rome. Zhu draws a speculative connection to the Pyramid of Giza, pointing out that ancient Egypt and Rome shared a deeper technological lineage than often assumed, including the use of lime or volcanic-ash-based binders.

If Egyptian builders used a calcium-rich, concrete-like mixture, the same sort of long-term mineral growth seen in Roman concrete might have transformed initially workable material into the dense, rock-hard blocks we see today.

“The builders of the pyramids may not have deliberately poured the hard stone blocks we see today, but may instead have discovered through experience a mixture that could ‘grow’ over time,” Zhu said.

He suggests that some calcium-rich building materials could have continued to evolve after construction through carbonation, mineral deposition and pore filling, producing increasingly dense structures over long periods.

Under this hypothesis, dense calcite crystals could form around older mineral phases and inside pores and fractures, potentially reinforcing the material while reducing pathways for water to penetrate.

Such mineral growth could continue for centuries, allowing parts of the material to become progressively denser, slowing further deterioration.

He compared the proposed mechanism with natural calcite formation, in which calcium dissolved in water can move through pores and fractures before precipitating again as crystalline material.

“In other words, time is not only an eroder; it can also be a sculptor,” Zhu said.

But Zhu stressed that he had not directly studied the Pyramid of Giza and his proposal did not establish that the pyramid blocks were made from concrete or artificial stone.

“This is only a reasonable hypothesis from the perspective of materials science,” he said.

Zhu’s judgment stemmed from research in the field of cement and cooperation with field authority Ian Richardson, of the University of Leeds.

“In fact, all ordinary Portland cement, as well as natural lime-clay or volcanic ash rich in calcium sources, undergo carbonation,” he said.

Portland cement is the most common type of cement used around the world.

“It has only been around for 200 years, yet you can see it almost anywhere on Earth. It is the second-most-used material by humans after water,” Zhu said.

“I and Professor Richardson have also studied the patented cement from 1824, where modern Portland cement was patented in Leeds in Britain.

“We analysed its production technology and composition, and the related research has been incorporated into textbooks on cement chemistry by Professor Richardson.”

The ancient Rome sample contained volcanic rock fragments, lime and volcanic ash materials commonly used in Roman concrete, but the researchers found that mineral growth within the material played an important role in maintaining its long-term integrity.

Over time, the continual growth of calcite creates a self-healing effect, closing cracks and mitigating further damage caused by environmental stresses or mechanical loads

Zhu Xiaohong, Beijing University of Technology

In particular, dense layers of calcite formed around older mineral phases and within pores and fractures, reinforcing the material while reducing pathways for water to penetrate.

Rather than occurring only during construction, this mineralisation could continue over long periods, filling voids and small cracks and making parts of the concrete progressively denser.

“Over time, the continual growth of calcite creates a self-healing effect, closing cracks and mitigating further damage caused by environmental stresses or mechanical loads,” the study’s authors wrote.

Zhu said the process occurred in a wide range of calcium-rich cementitious materials.

But whether carbonation was beneficial depended strongly on how the concrete was used. In ancient unreinforced concrete, carbonation could instead contribute to densification and long-term durability.

The Roman example could eventually inform the design of modern concrete by shifting attention away from initial strength towards long-term behaviour.

For the future cement design, “experiments on a thousand-year timescale are impossible, but with a three-dimensional validation system combining accelerated testing, numerical modelling and geological analogues, we can make credible predictions”, Zhu said.

The approach could allow researchers to engineer controlled mineralisation so that concrete responded to its environment by gradually filling pores and microcracks rather than simply deteriorating.

“For ordinary buildings, ecological design that is ‘sufficient and continuously sufficient’ is far more valuable than engineering that pursues extremely high strength without durability,” Zhu said.

He said he was continuing to examine historic construction materials, including samples from Hagia Sophia in Istanbul.

“Cement and concrete have always been rather remarkable and great materials, but people may overlook them because they are so common,” Zhu said. “Although it is not exactly a hot research topic, I feel that our research is quite meaningful.”

item.title: [SCMP] Xi is in Bishkek for SCO summit. How does bloc fit China’s Eurasian strategy 25 years on?
item.description:
As Washington’s strategic focus shifts and energy and grain supply disruptions continue to unsettle the Middle East, Beijing’s expanding presence across Central Asia is expected to be in focus as Kyrgyzstan hosts the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit this week.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s presence in Bishkek is expected to put the spotlight on whether the increasingly diverse grouping can move beyond diplomatic signalling, according to analysts. The SCO’s 25th anniversary summit was also expected to offer crucial clues to Beijing’s ambitions for a more multipolar Eurasia at a time of shifting regional power dynamics, they said.

The meetings over Monday and Tuesday are themed as “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”. They are expected to focus on regional security, connectivity, energy and digital cooperation, while also addressing wider challenges including Iran, Afghanistan and food security.
item.content:encoded:
As Washington’s strategic focus shifts and energy and grain supply disruptions continue to unsettle the Middle East, Beijing’s expanding presence across Central Asia is expected to be in focus as Kyrgyzstan hosts the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit this week.

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s presence in Bishkek is expected to put the spotlight on whether the increasingly diverse grouping can move beyond diplomatic signalling, according to analysts. The SCO’s 25th anniversary summit was also expected to offer crucial clues to Beijing’s ambitions for a more multipolar Eurasia at a time of shifting regional power dynamics, they said.

The meetings over Monday and Tuesday are themed as “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”. They are expected to focus on regional security, connectivity, energy and digital cooperation, while also addressing wider challenges including Iran, Afghanistan and food security.

China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record US$106 billion last year, according to Chinese government data, making Beijing the largest trading partner of the five countries combined for the first time.

Li Lifan, an expert on Russia and Central Asia at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, said the SCO and Central Asia held special significance for Beijing.

“As global competition intensifies between the US-led West and the emerging Global South amid a fractured international order, Beijing has placed greater weight on the SCO and Central Asia as a whole,” Li said, adding that “by deepening engagement and aligning more closely with Central Asian partners, China seeks to build common ground and present a more united front”.

“Through the SCO, China can project power and influence aspects of the global order,” he said, noting that the group’s expansion showcased China’s diplomatic appeal and influence.

In China’s diplomatic hierarchy, the United Nations ranks as the highest-level platform, while the SCO follows as the most important regional body.

Founded in 2001 by China and Russia, the now 10-member Eurasian security and economic forum brings together four Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan – and also newer entrants Belarus, India, Pakistan and Iran. Turkmenistan is the only non-SCO member in Central Asia but often attends summits as a guest nation.

Zhu Yongbiao, director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at Lanzhou University, said security remained Beijing’s top priority in Central Asia, not only along its western border but across the wider region, including the protection of key connectivity projects.

“I believe China’s primary interest in Central Asia is security, that is, ensuring a peaceful and stable neighbourhood,” he said.

Regional security is expected to feature prominently on the Bishkek agenda, according to Li, with Afghanistan, intelligence sharing and counterterrorism cooperation among the main concerns.

The potential for instability spilling over from Afghanistan, combined with Kyrgyzstan’s own security priorities, gives those discussions added weight.

While the China-Central Asia trade figure reflects the rapid expansion of commercial ties, Zhu cautioned against overstating the region’s economic weight.

He said Central Asia’s limited population and economic scale, as well as “overstated claims” about its mineral and energy resources, meant the region accounted for a relatively small component of China’s overall foreign trade.

Zhu emphasised that the region’s true strategic value stemmed from its geography – sitting next to China’s western border in Xinjiang, and serving as a critical bridge between China, Russia, the Middle East, South Asia and Europe.

Infrastructure is a central focus of the SCO, highlighted by the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. Now under construction after two decades of negotiation and recent clearance from Russia, the line would create a pivotal trade artery, connecting China with Central Asia and onwards to the Middle East and Europe while plugging into an overland trade link to Afghanistan.

Li cautioned that security would remain a major challenge for the railway, as the route passes through difficult terrain and long tunnels vulnerable to terror attacks.

“Protecting this ‘steel lifeline’ is critical, as it is seen as China’s gateway to Central Asia and the Persian Gulf,” he said.

As a local saying goes: We wear Moscow’s armour, but our heart beats in Urumqi

Li Lifan, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences

The railway is part of a wider effort to develop alternative routes, such as the “Middle Corridor” linking Central Asia and the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus, Turkey and Europe. Potential routes through Iran could provide additional access to the Persian Gulf and South Asia, but remain at the planning stage because of sanctions on Iran and regional instability.

Zhu said these projects were driven by demand from Central Asian and other states, rather than by Chinese strategy alone.

“Central Asian states, South Asia and Iran all seek stronger links, making connectivity inevitable,” he said. “China’s involvement adds momentum, enhances cooperation, improves quality, and accelerates the development of related routes.”

Energy and food security are also emerging as important non-traditional security concerns for the SCO, Li added, citing fuel disruptions linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine and the impact of climate change on harvests.

Iran’s protracted conflict with the United States will also be closely watched, given the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz for both energy and grain shipments.

Meanwhile, China’s expanding economic and technological role has raised questions about its ties with Russia, which remains the region’s principal security partner.

“Central Asian economies increasingly lean on China for trade, investment, infrastructure and technology, while Russia retains military bases, security arrangements and deep political and cultural ties,” Li said.

“As a local saying goes: ‘We wear Moscow’s armour, but our heart beats in Urumqi [capital of Xinjiang].’”

Yun Sun, director of the China programme and co-director of the East Asia programme at the Stimson Centre, noted that the SCO had also served as a mechanism for managing China-Russia relations, and that its limited practical achievements reflected the geopolitical and economic differences among its members.

“Some people call it a ‘nothing burger’. But conflict prevention and management of potential animosity are also of significant value,” she said.

China’s messaging through the SCO might also evolve now that strategic pressure from Washington had eased, Sun added, saying: “This year is the first time for a decade that China does not face a dire threat on the US front.”

She noted that while Beijing previously leveraged the SCO partly to help counter US pressure, its fundamental goal – demanding global governance reform and a “more just and reasonable international order” – remained unchanged.

Li, however, cautioned that the SCO’s role in the US-China rivalry should not be overstated.

“Central Asian states tend to pursue their own interests and resist taking sides. China has framed cooperation as open and inclusive, generally refraining from pressuring Central Asian governments to ‘choose sides’,” Li said. “Their approach is best described as hedging.”

Central Asian leaders deliberately exploited great-power rivalry to preserve strategic autonomy, resisting pressure to align fully with Russia or any other power, he added.

Meanwhile, the US has been stepping up engagement with Central Asia, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio expected to visit all five former Soviet states soon after the SCO summit.

Last November, Trump hosted the leaders of the five Central Asian nations in a “C5+1” summit at the White House to sign multibillion-dollar trade and critical mineral supply chain deals.

In recent weeks, the US has pressed dozens of countries including Kazakhstan to “choose sides” in artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation. There is even talk of inviting Trump to the region, underscoring Washington’s growing interest.

Uzbekistan has approached the US about joining Pax Silica, its flagship initiative on AI supply chains, a month after it signed up for China’s own global grouping, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Kazakhstan – the first Central Asian nation to sign up to Pax Silica – joined Waico in July.

Artyom Lukin, a professor at Russia’s Far Eastern Federal University, had a more sceptical take on the SCO’s practical impact.

“I think the SCO can’t be regarded as an efficient organisation delivering tangible results,” he said. “It’s definitely a talking shop in the first place and in the second place as well. I think almost everyone understands this reality.”

However, that does not make the organisation irrelevant.

As Lukin put it: “The SCO does have a certain value as a forum for multilateral dialogue of Eurasian powers as well as a venue for diplomatic signalling.”

item.title: [SCMP] How the Philippines missed a Korean gambling racket worth US$3.8 billion
item.description:
The Philippines spent years dismantling Chinese-linked gambling compounds in dramatic, headline-grabbing raids.

But all the while, and with far less scrutiny, South Korean syndicates were building a parallel industry worth billions of US dollars – one that a spate of recent arrests suggests is still very much intact.

The most recent involved a 29-year-old Korean woman named Kim Young-sun, who authorities allege ran a network of 23 illegal online betting websites out of offices in Pasay and Quezon City that raked in an estimated 5.33 trillion won (US$3.8 billion) between November 2018 and this year.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines spent years dismantling Chinese-linked gambling compounds in dramatic, headline-grabbing raids.

But all the while, and with far less scrutiny, South Korean syndicates were building a parallel industry worth billions of US dollars – one that a spate of recent arrests suggests is still very much intact.

The most recent involved a 29-year-old Korean woman named Kim Young-sun, who authorities allege ran a network of 23 illegal online betting websites out of offices in Pasay and Quezon City that raked in an estimated 5.33 trillion won (US$3.8 billion) between November 2018 and this year.

Her arrest, announced on Monday, offered a rare glimpse into an underworld that has apparently thrived for years in the shadow of the much louder scandal surrounding Chinese-linked Philippine offshore gaming operators, or Pogos.

For almost a decade, Pogos dominated the headlines. Compounds linked to Chinese syndicates were exposed for human trafficking, torture and fraud on a scale so shocking it triggered a congressional inquiry, presidential intervention and, eventually, a permanent ban.

But while investigators trained their attention on those operations, an analogous Korean criminal economy was expanding largely unnoticed. Kim’s arrest and a related case unsealed by police in Seoul just weeks earlier suggest this economy had grown far larger than most realised.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency disclosed on August 12 that it had uncovered an illegal gambling operation using websites featuring child sexual abuse material to lure users to betting sites.

The syndicate behind it, traced to Pasay City and active from August 2019 until earlier this month, generated an estimated 47.6 billion won in revenue, while affiliated betting sites handled some 4.7 trillion won in wagers.

Two suspects, one already the subject of an Interpol Red Notice, were arrested and referred to prosecutors for alleged violations of child-protection and anti-pornography laws.

Taken together, the arrests sketch the outline of an industry hiding in plain sight: sophisticated, long-running and largely untouched by the Philippines’ anti-Pogo enforcement drive.

Hidden in plain sight

“The Chinese were sticking out like sore thumbs,” said Winston Casio, who until December served as a deputy director of Manila’s Presidential Anti-Organised Crime Commission (PAOCC).

“There were low-hanging fruits to be plucked … that worked to the Koreans’ advantage.”

Pogos – the formerly legally licensed offshore gambling firms that multiplied under former president Rodrigo Duterte – became the public face of the issue after President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr shut them down in 2024, citing links to organised crime, trafficking, fraud and money laundering. Lawmakers made the ban permanent a year later.

The accompanying raids were harrowing. PAOCC-led operations in 2023 and 2024 unearthed evidence of torture chambers and human trafficking inside Pogo compounds that fuelled investigations – including into former town mayor Alice Guo, who was sentenced to life in prison in November for her role in setting up a scam centre in Bamban, Tarlac province.

Meanwhile, Korean networks barely registered: PAOCC managed just three raids on operations linked to South Korean nationals between 2023 and last year.

Chinese and South Korean syndicates operated in similar ways, but had different specialisms, Casio said, with Korean operations tending to focus on rigged betting websites.

“They hide behind the veneer of legitimate ball games – for example, during the World Cup, Euro Cup or the NBA Finals, but the games are pre-recorded or rigged … unlike the Chinese where the scams were rooted in investment and pig-butchering scams,” he told This Week in Asia.

Korean crime networks in Southeast Asia do not operate as an extension of the region’s more deeply embedded Chinese triads, yet they are far from strangers, according to experts.

“Korean gangsters called jopok or kangpae have been running independently from triads for years, although they do work together in Southeast Asia when it’s helpful or they need to source drugs, launder money or run scams,” said Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. “Gaming and scams are no different.”

Bora Park, a research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy in Seoul, went further, suggesting that many Korean gambling rings in the Philippines had “close ties to China from the very beginning”, often forming part of multinational operations rather than being composed solely of Korean nationals.

Predating Pogos

Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said Korean-linked illicit gambling operations predated the Chinese-run Pogos that multiplied to more than 300 licensed firms at their peak.

Criminal groups began migrating to the Philippines in the 2000s alongside legitimate investors, entrepreneurs and other members of the Korean diaspora, Douglas said.

Casio added that many Korean-linked operations were remnants of once-legitimate businesses that benefited from infrastructure and networks established years earlier.

Alexander Ramos, former executive director of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Centre in the Philippines, dates the sector’s origins to the mid-2000s, when he said Korean operators ran legitimate gambling businesses within special economic zones before some splintered off into illegal operations.

Song Bong-gyu, an assistant professor at Hansei University who has tracked Korean organised crime since 2007, said the appeal of the Philippines was obvious from the start.

“Establishing operations overseas made it possible to distance themselves from Korean law enforcement while continuing to target customers in South Korea,” Song said, adding that illegal gambling operations targeting Korean nationals were already running out of the Philippines by 2014.

When the Pogo boom arrived under Duterte, it gave Korean syndicates new infrastructure to plug into. Pre-existing networks converged with Pogo-era offices, staff and payment systems, before later scattering again into smaller, harder to trace units, according to Song.

“Over time, the Philippines developed personnel, technological expertise, office and residential facilities, telecommunications infrastructure, payment channels and local intermediaries that could support offshore online gambling operations,” he said.

“Large compounds may disappear, but criminal operations can become smaller, more dispersed and less visible, while the networks connecting them remain extensive.”

The ‘balloon effect’

For her part, Park expressed scepticism that Korean organised crime was independently colonising Southeast Asia.

She argued it was far more likely that Korean operators had simply plugged into existing local or Chinese-affiliated networks that were already active in the region.

After the Philippines’ Pogo ban took hold in early 2025, Park said many Chinese-linked groups initially retreated to neighbouring countries or even to China – only for some to then move back again.

Cho Je-seong, a research fellow at the Korean Institute of Criminology and Justice, has a name for this pattern: the “balloon effect”, in which enforcement pressures squeeze criminal activity into new shapes rather than eliminating it.

“There can also be an organisational dimension to this process, in which a larger organisation becomes fragmented into several smaller groups or networks as enforcement pressure increases,” he said.

Even small cells would often run several gambling websites at the same time, Cho said, with dedicated teams for illegal bank accounts, recruitment, site maintenance and money laundering.

Last year’s passage of the law formally criminalising Pogos, building on Marcos’ executive order a year earlier, had lulled the Philippine public into a false sense of security, Casio said.

“Because of the anti-Pogo law, people think that the Pogo problem is already gone from the Philippines,” he said. Kim Young-sun’s arrest suggests otherwise.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea weighs ‘contributions’ to Hormuz as US pressure mounts
item.description:
South Korea is moving towards the possible deployment of naval assets to the Strait of Hormuz under mounting pressure from Washington, potentially making it one of the first US allies to contribute militarily to the strategically vital waterway, observers have said.

The government has reportedly drawn up plans to deploy military assets, including a naval logistics support ship and P-8A maritime patrol aircraft, to the strait.

If carried out, the deployment would mark South Korea’s first dispatch of troops overseas at the United States’ request in 22 years, since the Zaytun Division was sent to Iraq in 2004.
item.content:encoded:
South Korea is moving towards the possible deployment of naval assets to the Strait of Hormuz under mounting pressure from Washington, potentially making it one of the first US allies to contribute militarily to the strategically vital waterway, observers have said.

The government has reportedly drawn up plans to deploy military assets, including a naval logistics support ship and P-8A maritime patrol aircraft, to the strait.

If carried out, the deployment would mark South Korea’s first dispatch of troops overseas at the United States’ request in 22 years, since the Zaytun Division was sent to Iraq in 2004.

The Chosun newspaper, citing an official at the presidential office Cheongwadae, reported on Friday that Seoul was considering the deployment, which would require approval from the National Assembly.

“We are reviewing various measures related to preparedness on the Korean peninsula and we can manoeuvre within the scope that does not significantly undermine our readiness posture,” the official told journalists.

“We have repeatedly discussed ways to make substantial contributions to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, and in fact, such contributions would include military involvement.”

Cheongwadae said last month it was closely discussing “practical and military contribution measures” with Washington, while taking into account South Korea’s military readiness on the Korean peninsula and domestic legal procedures. It was the first time the government had publicly referred to the possibility of a military contribution.

Asked whether consultations were also under way with the United Kingdom, France and other countries, the official said: “We are reviewing various aspects and are in the stage of consulting necessary countries during the review process.”

Under South Korean law, the government must secure National Assembly approval before dispatching a newly formed military contingent overseas. Any proposal must specify the deployment’s purpose, force size, area of operations and duration.

The official said it was “somewhat ambiguous” whether the current situation in the Strait of Hormuz could be considered a cessation of hostilities, adding that South Korean authorities were conducting a comprehensive review of the circumstances and any mission would be limited to non-combat activities.

Yonhap news agency quoted the same Cheongwadae official as saying the government was “reviewing possible ways” to help ease tensions in the strait, but that “nothing has been decided” and consultations with the National Assembly had not yet begun.

Cheongwadae reiterated in a notice to the media on Friday that “references to combat participation, non-combat operations and search activities were merely general descriptions of various options, and nothing has been decided regarding any substantive form of contribution”.

The statement came hours after the government denied reports that it had already decided to deploy military assets to the strait.

The Chosun newspaper nevertheless reported that the government had informed Washington of its intention to dispatch a new naval logistics support ship, P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and other assets. Other reports said the contingent could also include explosive ordnance disposal personnel.

The apparently conflicting statements have fuelled questions over how far Seoul’s planning for a potential military contribution has actually progressed.

A senior military official told SBS on Thursday that discussions with relevant countries over potential ports of call and operational bases were under way. A P-8 deployment would require access to an airport in a nearby country for take-offs, landings, refuelling and maintenance, while a logistical support ship would require ports for docking and resupply.

Observers say the military appears to be reviewing options – including on missions, potential ports of call and operational bases – ahead of a political decision.

Risks and pressure

A deployment could face significant political opposition at home, particularly if it is perceived as drawing South Korea into conflict with Iran.

Boo Seung-chan, a lawmaker from the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, said any dispatch could trigger a political backlash because it would put South Korean troops in danger.

“The government appears to be in agony under unprecedented pressure from Washington, but who would want to send our young soldiers to a war which was not started by us?” he told This Week in Asia.

“Ultimately, it will depend on public opinion whether the National Assembly will give a green light to it or not.”

The Trump administration has repeatedly singled out South Korea over its reluctance to help the US in its war against Iran.

“We got very little help from other countries,” US President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News that aired on Sunday, complaining that Washington had spent billions of dollars helping other countries without receiving sufficient support in return.

“We helped them, but when it came to helping us, I didn’t put on a heavy sell, but I just said, ‘Would you like to participate?’ and they all said, ‘No, thank you’,” Trump said.

“And I said, ‘OK, thank you very much. I appreciate it.’ But I think you have to remember this stuff. I really do.”

Trump also pointed to the US military presence in South Korea.

“We have thousands and thousands – like, in South Korea, as an example, we have 40,000 soldiers over there,” he said, recalling that he had asked Seoul to “give us a little hand with Iran”.

South Korea hosts about 28,500 US troops.

Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies, highlighted the enormous pressure South Korea was under from Washington to contribute to the war effort against Iran.

Doo said US officials had focused heavily on South Korea’s possible contribution to ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz during the twice-yearly Korea Integrated Defence Dialogue held in May.

“Now South Korea is supposed to return to the table with an answer” at the next round of talks later this year, Doo said.

Seoul was also under pressure to make progress on its promised US$350 billion investment in the US, the construction of South Korea’s first nuclear-powered submarines with Washington’s consent and the restoration of wartime operational control of South Korean forces from the US military, he said.

President Lee Jae Myung is expected to visit the US later this month to attend the United Nations General Assembly.

“Talks over all these key issues appear stalled and the Hormuz deployment would serve as the only possible way out of this quagmire,” Doo said.

Shin Beom-chul, a senior research fellow at the Sejong Institute, said the government’s apparent shift towards considering a Hormuz deployment could be linked to US moves to resume dialogue with North Korea.

“At a time when the US could engage North Korea and potentially bypass South Korea, the government may be seeking to repair and strengthen its relationship with Washington through the deployment,” he said.

Kim Yeol-soo, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for Military Affairs, predicted that South Korea and the US could reach an agreement on a deployment within weeks, with about 150 South Korean servicemen potentially being sent.

“To avoid getting caught in the crossfire, South Korea should send a clear signal to Tehran that its mission is not to antagonise Iran but to secure freedom of navigation and peace,” Kim said.

However, Professor Yang Moo-jin at the University of North Korean Studies was adamant that South Korea should not deploy forces while the legality of the Iran war remained in dispute.

“Using the lives of young people – the very people who represent our future hope – as a tool of diplomatic negotiation runs counter to the spirit of national sovereignty that places young people at the centre of our society,” Yang said.

“With tensions already running high, expanding the scope of South Korean military activities could increase the risk of becoming directly entangled in an armed conflict.”

item.title: [SCMP] Another Chinese national dies in US immigration custody, raising profiling fears
item.description:
The Chinese-American community expressed anger and concern on Thursday over the death in custody of a Chinese national by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement [ICE] on US territory.

Wei Lianyong, 51, reportedly died in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) on August 23, although the scandal-plagued agency did not disclose the death until this week.

“Asian-Americans, Chinese-Americans, should be very concerned about this and very energised to stop what is essentially an attack on the existence of the community,” said Gabriel Chin, professor at the University of California, Davis School of Law.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese-American community expressed anger and concern on Thursday over the death in custody of a Chinese national by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement [ICE] on US territory.

Wei Lianyong, 51, reportedly died in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) on August 23, although the scandal-plagued agency did not disclose the death until this week.

“Asian-Americans, Chinese-Americans, should be very concerned about this and very energised to stop what is essentially an attack on the existence of the community,” said Gabriel Chin, professor at the University of California, Davis School of Law.

“We should not accept the idea that Chinese immigration is a bad thing because it’s Chinese because that’s inevitably going to affect the position of US citizens of Chinese ancestry.”

Wei was arrested on August 21 by the Northern Mariana Islands Department of Public Safety on criminal charges following an alleged assault on a family of five at their home, according to ICE.

The next day, he was taken into ICE custody in advance of deportation proceedings in Saipan, the archipelago’s capital. On the morning of August 23, ICE said he was found “unresponsive” in his prison cell and taken to a local accident and emergency hospital where “life-sustaining interventions were initiated” before he “passed away” at 7.30am. The cause of death remains under investigation, it added.

Wei reportedly fifth Chinese national to die in custody of ICE or US Border Patrol

Wei is at least the fifth Chinese national who has died in the custody of ICE or the US Border Patrol since March 2025, according to Associated Press tracking.

Chinese-American advocates said ICE has been recruiting so rapidly under US President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration and deportation policy that standards are not always great.

“You see it in terms of the ICE agents who are field agents who have no idea what they’re doing and are constantly doing things like accidentally shooting somebody who’s completely innocent,” said Justin Sadowsky, legal director with the Chinese-American Legal Defence Alliance, an advocacy group.

A related outcome is the rise of deaths in custody due to heat, lack of food, insufficient medical care or mental stress tied to incarceration. “It’s not surprising that eventually this would happen to a Chinese person in the Northern Mariana Islands. It was just a matter of time,” Sadowsky said.

Analysts added that the Trump administration’s immigration policies are part of a broader pattern seen in recent years that has scapegoated immigrants and Asian-Americans for Covid-19, eroding US competitiveness and the more cutthroat economy.

“What we are seeing in Saipan is the tragic, inevitable result of an aggressive use of government power,” said Chris Kwok, a New York-based Asian-American Community Organiser. “You cannot separate this lack of transparency and basic duty of care from the broader, hostile climate being engineered right now.

“When an administration is simultaneously trying to dismantle birthright citizenship and ramping up opaque ICE detentions, it sends a terrifying message to Asian-American and immigrant communities: your existence is viewed as illegitimate, and your rights are expendable,” he added. “We will deport you to random third countries. We don’t care if you die in our custody.”

ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said it notified the Chinese consulate and his next of kin “or other designated contact”. It was not immediately clear what part of China Wei came from.

The Chinese Consulate General in Los Angeles confirmed it was notified of Wei’s death.

“We have expressed serious concerns to the relevant US authorities over this incident and required a timely and thorough investigation into the cause of Mr Wei’s death, notification of the findings, measures to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents, and assistance to the family of the deceased in handling the aftermath,” the consulate said in a statement.

Beijing has also repeatedly raised concerns with Washington about detainee treatment, medical intake delays and overall conditions inside federal detention centres.

DHS, which described Wei as a “criminal illegal alien from China”, said he was charged with assault with a dangerous weapon, disturbing the peace, assault and battery, and aggravated assault and battery.

It did not say whether charges were dropped after his death, why the death was not revealed for nine days and whether a medical exam was performed as required.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments,” the agency said. “All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility.”

CNMI is a US territory in the North Pacific Ocean located roughly three-quarters of the way from Hawaii to the Philippines. The 14-island archipelago currently has a population of around 42,000, of which around 3,300 are of Chinese descent.

US government ignores international protests over deaths in ICE detention: analysts

Analysts said the Trump administration has largely brushed aside protests from foreign governments over deaths and treatment of their citizens in ICE detention, although Beijing has a louder voice than most others.

“Given the upcoming summit meeting and President Trump’s responsiveness to individual appeals and contacts with international leaders, if this gets brought up at the summit, Trump is likely to respond,” said Chin.

Often, added Sadowsky, any such people-to-people issue at summits becomes part of a broader negotiation involving tariffs and related issues.

“My guess is the United States government isn’t going to publicly admit wrongdoing or apologise. That just doesn’t seem to be what the United States government is doing with ICE these days,” he said. “Maybe this could be used to attract concessions from China, but I don’t expect it to resolve the issue.”

The Chinese community is hardly the only community facing such treatment, but the number of people facing discrimination and ill-treatment is on the rise, Sadowsky said.

“There’s definitely been an increase in stops, including stops of US citizens, and ICE harassing Chinese people, because they’re casting wide nets and using racial profiling.”

“I don’t expect anything other than it’s going to get worse,” he added.

Unlike most of the rest of the US, the local government controlled the territory’s labour and immigration policy between 1978 and 2009, creating a loophole that attracted large numbers of Chinese.

Under these carve-outs, clothes made on Saipan could be legally labelled as “Made in the USA” and shipped to the mainland United States duty-free and quota-free, while avoiding US federal minimum wage standards or many immigration restrictions.

That led dozens of Chinese-owned textile factories to employ tens of thousands of mainland Chinese contract workers, mostly young women, resulting, by the late 1990s, in foreign contract workers vastly outnumbering the local population.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s blueprint for economic success: plan, but be prepared to adapt
item.description:
In the discussion on Hong Kong’s first ever five-year plan, much ink has been spilled on the merits of a planned economy. The most recent example of this was Anthony Rowley’s commentary that cited Singapore as an example of a highly successful planned economy.

Unfortunately, he misrepresents what planning in Singapore is about. There are lessons that Hong Kong can draw from how the Singapore government navigated a changing environment – but not the ones Rowley highlights.

It is quite understandable why an observer would view Singapore as a planned economy. After all, signs of order are all around. Nearly 80 per cent of Singaporeans live in public housing; the city is well-designed, green, and manicured. Clearly, this is a city that has been meticulously planned and engineered for decades.
item.content:encoded:
In the discussion on Hong Kong’s first ever five-year plan, much ink has been spilled on the merits of a planned economy. The most recent example of this was Anthony Rowley’s commentary that cited Singapore as an example of a highly successful planned economy.

Unfortunately, he misrepresents what planning in Singapore is about. There are lessons that Hong Kong can draw from how the Singapore government navigated a changing environment – but not the ones Rowley highlights.

It is quite understandable why an observer would view Singapore as a planned economy. After all, signs of order are all around. Nearly 80 per cent of Singaporeans live in public housing; the city is well-designed, green, and manicured. Clearly, this is a city that has been meticulously planned and engineered for decades.

Above all, Singapore’s politics is carefully managed by a ruling party that has been in power since 1959, and political dissent is often constrained by a paternalistic state.

But the idea of the Singapore economy as a top-down, dirigiste and planned one is a caricature at best. While various government agencies in Singapore engage in planning (loosely defined), the city state has never had five or 10-year plans, nor set production targets the way the Eastern bloc countries and China did.

Policies, not plans

Singapore’s first finance minister and deputy prime minister Goh Keng Swee was openly disdainful of socialist planning, saying that “planning as we know it has a limited value. Economic policy is more important”.

In economic policy, perhaps the most important difference between the Singapore economy and Hong Kong’s is the role of the state in industrial development.

Since the establishment of the Economic Development Board (EDB) in 1961, the Singapore state has promoted manufacturing as one of the key engines of the economy. Even today, manufacturing output comprises an astonishing 19 per cent of Singapore’s GDP, compared with less than 1 per cent in Hong Kong.

The EDB – or any other economic agency – has never produced five-year plans, so that cannot be the reason for Singapore’s success in industrialisation and industrial upgrading. But thanks to industrial policy, Singapore is a key node in global value chains in various high value-added industries such as electronics, petrochemicals, precision engineering, and pharmaceuticals and biotech to name a few.

The lesson from Singapore here is that five-year plans are much less important than specific policies that drive industrial diversification and upgrading.

A plan is simply a declaration of intent; whether that intent becomes reality depends on the right policies being formulated and how they are implemented. It is also quite common for governments to come up with bold visions and ambitious intents; what is much rarer is the capacity to execute change effectively.

With industrial policy, this means ensuring sound macroeconomic fundamentals and having the right microeconomic tools – such as tax incentives, foreign labour allowances, vocational training and worker upgrading programmes – to develop the desired industries.

But none of this was static or unchanging: external shocks and changing domestic conditions often necessitated changes to Singapore’s economic policies in ways that no five-year plan can foresee.

Quick to adapt

A second common error is to mistake the precision of the plan for its validity or quality. Even in a free-market economy like Hong Kong’s, there is a fascination bordering on obsession with setting precise targets or key performance indicators (KPIs) for government. The logic is that since much of what government does not lend itself easily to market metrics, targets or KPIs impose the necessary discipline on government.

This obsession is not always healthy. A target may be very precise, but it could also measure the wrong thing. This is not to diminish the value of planning, but to emphasise the importance of adapting quickly to changing conditions.

Being large bureaucracies, governments are often creatures of habit; their behaviours do not change quickly or easily even when circumstances require them to do so.

You just start it and hope for the best

Goh Keng Swee, Singapore’s first finance minister

When asked in 1992 if he had started out with a master plan in mind, Goh replied: “I had no initial vision. You just start it and hope for the best.” In many respects, Singapore’s economic success was the result of constant adaptation and improvisation.

For example, Singapore’s original economic plan was import-substitution industrialisation. This was one of the motivations for Singapore to join the newly established Malaysian federation in 1963 – to create a common market.

When Singapore separated from Malaysia in 1965, the plan was clearly no longer workable. Singapore adapted quickly and embraced export-oriented industrialisation, laying the foundations for the highly globalised economy it became a decade or so later.

Another example of adaptation was the practice of adjusting Central Provident Fund (CPF) contribution rates as a macroeconomic stabilisation tool. Singapore has, on various occasions, adjusted employer contribution rates in response to changes in macroeconomic conditions – lowering them to maintain cost competitiveness when faced with negative demand shocks, and raising them to deal with wage and inflation pressures.

Pay attention to process

Finally, the real value of a plan lies in the process rather than the plan itself.

A five-year plan is limited in at least two ways. First, the relatively short time horizon means that it is almost inevitable that the plan would be a collection of (achievable) goals that the various parts of the government have already set for themselves. It is unlikely to contain much that departs from existing priorities.

Second, because the emphasis of a five-year plan is to come up with specific deliverables, it is unlikely to catalyse a creative (re-)imagination of the future. Five-year plans are usually linear extrapolations of present trends, with targets adjusted marginally upwards to reflect the government’s enthusiasm in new areas – such as artificial intelligence.

Governments often overestimate their ability to change things in the short term but underestimate it over the long term. This bias informs Singapore’s approach to planning. Because much of what a government does on a routine basis is short term, the two main forms of planning that the Singapore government undertakes adopt a much longer time horizon. The emphasis is also on long-term strategy rather than near-term deliverables.

In city planning, for instance, the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s concept plan is reviewed once every decade and covers a time horizon of 50 years. Meanwhile, its master plan guides the city’s physical development over the next 10 to 15 years.

Since the turn of the century, the city state has also embraced scenario planning as a way of thinking (creatively) about the future.

Unlike five-year plans, the main goal of scenario planning is not to come up with a single plan for government with specific goals, targets or KPIs. Neither is scenario planning meant to produce predictions or forecasts. Instead, it is to generate distinct, plausible stories about the future (even if they seem improbable), question long-held assumptions, and surface the challenges and opportunities in the various scenarios.

Unlike five-year plans that are based on a particular view of the future, scenario planning is a much more divergent process that aims to anticipate various possible futures.

More recently, the Singapore government has expanded its capabilities in what it calls “futures thinking”.

It set up a Centre for Strategic Futures about a decade ago to “build a strategically agile public service ready to manage a complex and fast-changing environment”. The centre’s logo, with a black swan embedded, reflects its ambition to develop the government’s foresight and its ability to adapt.

This idea of planning as thinking creatively about the future is about as far as one can get from the world of five-year plans.

item.title: [SCMP] Word on the StrEAT: 6 Hong Kong chefs share pre-service rituals that fuel their kitchens
item.description:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path
item.content:encoded:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path

“We have a fairly small team of four – including [a] dishwasher! We [start the night] by greeting everyone and checking on each other. Show a bit of love to everyone.

“The playlist changes from Cantopop to more casual lofi pop songs like Keshi. Andy Hui is one of Sean’s (our Texan GM’s) favourites. Our team ritual is to sing together. It opens up our voice more before the night starts. ⁠After service begins, we are definitely more locked in to serve our guests.

“We also always stash gummies inside our kitchen to sweeten our service – a bit of a sugar rush also helps!”

Chef Sean Yuen, Jija by Vicky Lau

“Five minutes before service is the ‘calm before the storm’. Everyone is running their final checks, and the air is noticeably tense. I review tonight’s cover count, find out when the peak hour hits, and check for any VIPs or special dietary requirements. Once I have those numbers in mind, the rhythm of the night becomes completely clear.

“Downing a shot of espresso right before service not only wakes me up, but also acts as a mental trigger to switch into battle mode. [We] turn on all the heat lamps at the pass and the moment those lights go on, it means all the prep work is done.

“One hour into service, everyone is fully in the zone – hyper-focused, with the entire kitchen running at a fast yet meticulously organised pace. During peak rush hours, taking a two-second break to grab a sip of water gives me a quick moment to pause, clear my mind, and jump straight back into position.”
